en: *Collected Explanations of the Four Teachings of Tiantai*, Volume One (with Preface).
In the winter of the fourth year of the Zhi-ping era, I was staying at Miaoguo Monastery to the west of the prefecture to give lectures.

In the summer of the following year, several students of the new school requested that I provide a written commentary to resolve the points in the *Tiantai Si Jiao* recorded by Master Gwan of Goryeo. At that time—

Zhiquan, based on the categories of the *Zhechuan* (Huzhou) school, delineated the beginnings and endings of the textual sections and compiled the essential principles for interpreting the doctrinal statements scattered throughout various parts of the canon.
In less than twenty days, he completed three fascicles, titled the *Sijiao jishi* (Collected Explanations of the Four Teachings).
Although the initial draft was just finished and had not yet been refined, it was already being transcribed and circulated by scholars; thus, it became widely known among the people of the world.
One raises objections against He Yan’s *Ji jie* yet never considers Du Yu’s *Ji jie* as an impediment;
since the *ji jie* of Confucian scholars already exists in two versions, why should one be surprised by the current titles? Alas, such is the delusion of those with the narrow vision of a tube!
Now, in the ninth year of Xining, while at Danyun West Monastery, during the intervals between lecturing and instructing—
Thereupon, I examined the commentaries on the *Xiachuan* (Wujing zaji), finding them not entirely satisfactory. Consequently, I composed my own set of topical outlines (*kewen*) in a single fascicle;
furthermore, upon reviewing previous collective exegeses (*jijie*), I found them to be somewhat negligent and incomplete. Thus, I have revised and embellished this work in three fascicles.

However, I am troubled by the fact that my own insight is barren and my phrasing and reasoning are crude and obscure, such that I have been unable to fully illuminate the profound mysteries of the sages and worthies.
This has been prepared merely for the sake of beginners, serving simply to demarcate the punctuation;
those in distant or nearby regions who encounter this newly revised text need no longer retain the uncorrected versions.
*Annotated Commentary on the Outline of the Fourfold Teaching System of Tiantai*, Volume One (Compiled by Hui Yongjia based on Master Guan’s original text).
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Congyi of Yongjia.
*Collected Explanations of the Fourfold Teaching System of Tiantai*, Volume One.
The commentary on the *Tiantai sijiao yi* (An Explanation of the Fourfold Teaching System of Tiantai) divides this text into two parts: first, the title; second, the main body.

Regarding the title, the four characters "Tian" (Heaven), etc., are specific, while the character "yi" (system/instrument) is general. Within the specific title, "Four Teachings" refers to the Dharma, while "Tiantai" refers to the person [who established it].
A person is named according to their place of origin; it is recorded that Mount Tiantai is the very site where the Great Master Zhizhe resided.
Because the star Tai on the celestial sphere corresponds to this mountain, it is called Mount Tiantai.
It is also called Mount Tiandi (Ladder to Heaven), for this mountain is so high and precipitous that it is like a ladder by which one may ascend to heaven; hence its name.
The name "Tiāntíshān" (Heavenly Ladder Mountain) was later erroneously transformed into "Tiāntái" (Heavenly Terrace). "Tiān" (Heaven) means "dǐān" (summit) or "xiǎn" (manifest);
it is situated at the pinnacle of all things and is clearly visible. In spring it is called Cāngtiān (Azure Heaven); in summer, Hàotiān (Vast Heaven); in autumn, Míntiān (Compassionate Heaven);
and in winter, Shàngtiān (Supreme Heaven). Before the primal qi had differentiated, they were blended into one; once the Two Polarities were distinguished, the pure ascended as...
That "the heavens turbidly sink to become the earth" is merely a worldly (secular) teaching; therefore, it is cited here.

If one follows the Buddhist teachings, "heaven" (*ten*) refers to that which is most supreme and luminous—the heavens of the three realms: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. "Terrace" (*tai*) refers to the Three Terraces:

the Upper Terrace is the Star of Vacuous Essence (*Kūshō*), the Middle Terrace is the Star of Sixfold Purity (*Rokujun*), and the Lower Terrace is the Star of Curved Birth (*Kyōshō*); they are also called the Three [Terraces].

Each terrace has two stars, totaling six stars, which are called the "Six Talismans of the Great Terrace. A "talisman" (fu) refers to the manifestation of the stars. The upper terrace represents the Son of Heaven;
the middle terrace represents the feudal lords, dukes, high ministers, and great officers; and the lower terrace represents the seven classes of commoners.
Regarding the "Four Teachings," some say they refer to the transformative laws of the four teachings; according to these transformative laws, there is both substance and...

Master Guan [Zhi] based himself on the *Daben lu* (Record of the Great Canon) to extract that passage, as it concerns only the "teachings of transformation" (*huàfǎ*). Some say it refers to the "four teachings of the transformative ritual" (*huàyí sìjiào*).

To provide scriptural proof, he cites a passage stating: "The four teachings of the transformative ritual are complete in both text and meaning; they spontaneously encompass the four categories such as the Tripitaka (*sān zàng*) and so forth.

Others say that while the "four teachings" refer to the "teachings of transformation," the character "ritual" (*yí*) refers to the "transformative ritual. Still others say it applies universally to all.

Some say there are eight teachings (and so forth). Now, I maintain that all such explanations are merely products of human sentiment and do not fundamentally grasp the reason for the title’s establishment.
To examine the title itself, it speaks only of the "four teachings"—some call them the "teachings of transformation" (*huàfǎ*) and others the "modes of transformation" (*huàyí*).
To cling exclusively to one perspective is not entirely appropriate. I maintain that this title possesses both a general and a specific meaning; generally speaking, [it refers to...]
Generally speaking, this pertains to the Dharma of transformation (*dharmatā-vinaya*), whereas specifically it corresponds to the Dharma of transformation itself. Why is this?

It is because the title merely mentions the "four teachings" (*catur-dharma*) without yet distinguishing between the Dharma of transformation and the ritual of transformation; therefore, they are explained through the lens of both the general and the specific.

For instance, since the title of the "Life Span" chapter (*Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) in the *Lotus Sūtra* does not explicitly state "Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-bodies," the text [proceeds accordingly].
The phrases [of this preface] employ both general and specific explanations of the title of that treatise; if one applies that logic to this, how could it not be so?

"Goryeo" (the character 麗 is pronounced *lǜ* with the *zhī* tone)—a name for a country among the Eastern Barbarians—was recorded by the Goryeo śramaṇa Dìguān. Regarding the two individuals whose names are recorded, "Goryeo" refers to the name of a state among the Eastern Yi peoples. As the *Lunyu* says, the Master...
"Regarding the desire to dwell among the nine tribes of the Eastern Yi, the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning) states: 'There are nine kinds of Eastern Yi; the third is the state of Gao-li.
It is sometimes written with the character 驪 (*li*), yet people all pronounce it as *li* or *lì*. The term 'Śramaṇa' is a Sanskrit word meaning 'diligent in cessation.
This refers to those who have left the household life, for they diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas and cease all unwholesome practices; thus it is named."
Regarding the two characters "Dìguān" (Contemplation of the Truths), which are the name of the Dharma Master, the śramaṇas, Śākya, and others have analyzed them according to their usual methods;
some interpret them as the Three Truths and Three Contemplations—how could this necessarily be so?

The compiler, following the fundamental texts of the Tiantai teachings, has recorded here the essentials of the Five Periods and Eight Teachings to show later students the general outline, so that they may understand it. If...
If one understands this, one will not be confused regarding the various sections.

The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai divides the two texts into three parts: first, a detailed exposition of the dharma and its meaning; second, from "Now" onwards, a brief recording of the essential outline; third, [the conclusion].

I respectfully conclude with this exhortation; these three sections may also be compared to the three divisions [of the *Lotus Sūtra*]. First, the exposition of the Dharma’s meaning in detail, which has two parts:

first, the formal exposition, which has two parts. First, the general demonstration. Regarding the phrase "Tiantai" already mentioned in the section on the subject of the established teaching, the fact that it is stated again here is consistent with the literary structure of the text.
Alternatively, it may be used to distinguish [Zhiyi] from the earlier generation of Zhizhe (the Master Zhi). Thus it is said.
Regarding "Tiantai Zhizhe": the *Real Record of Master Fu Dashi* of a previous generation states, "At that time there was the Great Master Zhizhe;
his secular surname was Lou, his name was Lingcan, and his courtesy name was Desu. He was a native of Zhushan Li in Wushang County.
If this is the case, the inclusion of "Tiantai" serves to distinguish him from those of previous generations, such as [Master] Guangzhai and others.
He also established four teachings; since these are the Four Teachings of Tiantai, this serves to distinguish them [from other systems].

My ancestor, the Venerable Zhiyi, was given the childhood name Guangdao (Light of the Way) and also named Wangdao (King of the Way). These names were established based on his birth and the dream of his mother.
His Dharma name is Zhizhe; "zhi" (止) means stillness. This title was bestowed by his teacher after he had left the household life, derived from his virtue.

For the sake of his name, and because he employed the meaning of tranquility, this wise one personally received [the teaching] at Vulture Peak and attained profound awakening through Great Enlightenment (*Mahāsū*).
He propagated both Samādhi and Prajñā while simultaneously excelling in the Vinaya. Consequently, for the Prince of Jin, he conferred the Bodhisattva Precepts and established his dharma-name, saying:

"Your Majesty has respectfully followed the holy prohibitions; you shall be named King Total Retention (*Saṃdhāraṇa-rāja*). The Prince said: "The Master transmits the Lamp of the Buddha; it is fitting that you be called 'Wisdom' (*Jñāna*)."
Before he was conferred the precepts by the King, he was sometimes called the Tiantai Ācārya;
however, as this account follows his later status, he is referred to as Zhizhe. His complete manifestation in the *Biézhuàn* cannot be fully exhausted here.
As for the "Great Master," he was a model for kings, dukes, and great officials, and one whose great virtuous conduct served as a teacher for the multitude.
By means of the Five Periods and Eight Teachings, the interpretation and classification of the entirety of the sacred teachings transmitted to the East is exhausted without exception.
Second, regarding the "by means of" (yi) used in the following [classification], "yi" signifies "to employ. The Five Periods are enumerated below;
the reason Tiantai clarifies the Five Periods is to reveal that there is a sequential order in the years of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
The establishment of the five flavors is intended to manifest how the Tathāgata transforms and benefits the various capacities of sentient beings.

The citation of the four teachings of the transformative ritual is for the purpose of distinguishing the Tathāgata’s ceremonial procedures for appearing in the world. As for the term "transformative dharma," it serves to demonstrate the Tathāgata’s method for transforming sentient beings.
Thus, the purport of the five periods and eight teachings is as such; I shall first indicate them here, and will address them in detail below.
Regarding the "easy-to-understand" classification and interpretation: "classification" (pan) refers to dissecting and distinguishing; "interpretation" (shi) refers to explaining and resolving.

For example, classifying the *Avataṃsaka* as "Sudden" (*dun*) based on the ritual of transformation (*huayi*), and then interpreting the *Avataṃsaka* through the distinct and perfect teachings of the transformative dharma (*huafa*), is the case here.

Since all other [scriptures] are explained according to this same principle, Jingxi stated: "The 'Sudden' and so forth constitute the great outline of the classification of teachings (*panjiao*). This is the "Treasury" (*zang*).

This is the outline for explaining the meaning, which consists of the questions, judgments, and explanations. Regarding the determination of the four periods (*catur-yuga*), it is also applicable to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The answer is that this must be distinguished: if one judges according to the four teachings of the transformational ritual (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*), then they are judged as belonging to the four periods;

since the judgment is thus, the explanation follows the same principle. As for the present text stating, "Judging and explaining by means of the five periods and eight teachings," and so forth, this is the case.
Thus, the judgment and interpretation are also applicable to the *Lotus Sūtra*. Why? Because the *Lotus Sūtra* is judged to be the fifth period;

it is not a matter of the formal schema of sudden or gradual teaching. Since it is explained as a teaching of pure and perfect [teachings], it is not a mixture of "combined" or "intermingled" teachings.
If one follows this intention, it differs slightly from the explanation of Jingxi [Zhiyi]. Question: If that is so...
Is there nothing that does not contradict Jingxi? Answer: Each has its own reason; how could they possibly be in contradiction?
Furthermore, because Jingxi was commenting on the *Nianjing* (Thus Have I Heard) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he judged and explained it as being prior to the *Lotus Sūtra* itself.

Since the *Lotus Sūtra* transcends the eight teachings and stands outside the four periods [of the Buddha’s teaching], he stated: "If it were not the 'Thus' that transcends the eight, how could it be... [and so forth].

Regarding the "judgments and explanations" (pan-śih) found within this text concerning what has been heard in this sutra: these are the comprehensive classifications of the five periods and eight teachings used to explain the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime of teaching;
thus, they apply universally to both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. As for the "flowing eastward":
the Buddha was born and preached the Dharma in Western India, but since the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, Indian monks have brought the Dharma toward this Eastern land.

Just as flowing water is said to "flow eastward" because it is unobstructed, so too is a "generation" (*kalpa*) defined. If one generation were taken as thirty years, its meaning would remain limited;

however, in the present context, we simply adopt the explanation of "successive generations. Thus, this refers to the single generation of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, and not to those of Vipaśyin and the others.
Question: Regarding the statement that the eight teachings were judged and explained as "flowing eastward," how is this understood?

Since the Secret Teachings (Guhyaka) were not among those transmitted, there was no formal compilation; how then can one generally speak of the "classification and explanation of the eight teachings"?
To answer this, we shall briefly address the general course of the matter: the classification of the Tathāgata’s preaching includes both the Exoteric and the Esoteric.

Therefore, one speaks generally of the "classification and explanation of the eight teachings. For this reason, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, and other texts all refer to them as such.

The "Secret Meaning" mentioned previously does not refer to the yellow scrolls and red axes found within the Tripitaka as being secret sutras; rather, it refers to the use of the Secret Teaching to analyze and explain [the scriptures]. Question: Since you have already analyzed and explained the various sutras using the Eight Teachings, why do you not classify the *Tiewei jing* (Sutra of Trapusa and Bhallika) among these eight categories, such as the Sudden Teaching? Answer: The Eight Teachings mentioned here are all phenomena that transcend the world (*lokottara-dharma*). The *Tiewei jing*, however, is a worldly scripture (*laukika-sūtra*) and therefore cannot be classified among them. Furthermore, this sutra was preached for the sake of laypeople; since the Eight Teachings are exclusively for the ordained community, it is not included therein. Moreover, the Eight Teachings are established based on the principle of the Three Vehicles, whereas this sutra belongs to the One Vehicle. For these reasons, it is not categorized among the Eight Teachings. Furthermore, the Eight Teachings are established based on the principle of the Two Truths, whereas this sutra is based on the principle of the Middle Way. For these reasons as well, it is not categorized among the Eight Teachings. Finally, the Eight Teachings are established based on the principle of the Four Noble Truths, whereas this sutra is based on the principle of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. For these reasons, it is not categorized among the Eight Teachings. It is for these various reasons that the *Tiewei jing* is not classified among the Eight Teachings. However, because it is a teaching of the Buddha, it is nonetheless subsumed within the Eight Teachings. This is because the Eight Teachings encompass all the teachings of the Buddha. Therefore, although it is not explicitly categorized among the Eight Teachings, it is implicitly contained within them. This is the meaning of the statement: "It is not that there is no classification, but rather that it is not explicitly classified. Regarding the *Tiewei jing* (Sūtra of the Householder), which discusses the destruction of delusions and the realization of truth: when the Buddha first appeared in the world, he preached the five precepts and ten wholesome paths for this householder;
these merely benefit humans and devas and do not constitute the fundamental teaching for the sages who appear in the world.

Therefore, it is not classified as a "sudden" (*dun*) teaching and so forth. However, if one discusses its doctrinal affiliation, it may be subsumed within the Tripiṭaka of the Deer Park. Thus, [the text] asks: "The Householder?"
It is said in the sutras that three hundred people attained the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*) and the Four Heavenly Kings attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*);
this refers to the Mahāyāna teaching. Why, then, do you say they are included within the Tripiṭaka?

If one considers them according to the explicit and indeterminate teachings (*nītārtha-avyākṛta-deśanā*), then there is no contradiction in having three hundred people attain the patience of faith and so forth. If [the classification] follows the explicit...
If explained according to the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), the *Tiewei jing* belongs to the teachings for humans and devas;

since humans and devas are collectively included within the Tripiṭaka of the Deer Park, it is said that the "five vehicles" exist only at the Deer Park. *Qìng* (罄) also means "exhausted" or "complete."
Regarding the "five periods":
[the text] first provides a general overview and then lists them individually. First, the five periods; second, the initial section which cites the preceding and establishes the names:

1. the Avataṃsaka period; 2. the Deer Park period (wherein the four Āgamas were taught); 3. the Vaipulya period (wherein the Vimalakīrti, Saṃthānāṅgāra, Laṅkāvatāra, Śūraṅgama-samādhi, and Suvarṇaprabhāsa were taught).

1. The period of the *Prabhāsa*, *Śrīmālā*, and other sūtras; 2. The period of the four Prajñās (the teaching of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Prajñāpāramitā-ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, *Vajracchedikā*, *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā*, and other various Prajñā sūtras); 3. The period of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Second, the following illustrates the first period by citing the metaphor from its specific title. The full title is *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka*.
"Mahāvaipulya" refers to the Dharma; "Buddha" refers to the person; and "Avataṃsaka" (Flower Ornament) is the metaphor.
This means that the causal flowers are able to adorn the resultant virtues. Among the seven types of titles, this is the first.
First, regarding "The Fully Endowed" (*Saṃpuṭa*): this is because when establishing the title for the *Avataṃsaka* period, it is not based on location.
Since there are seven locations throughout the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, how could one establish it as "the time of the seven locations"?
Therefore, the period is established solely by means of the sūtra’s title; this not only encompasses all seven locations, but its name is also elegant and sublime. Second, the Deer Park.

Regarding the designation "at the Deer Park": this name was established based on the very first location. Since the Buddha first delivered the teaching to the five bhikṣus at this place, why not establish the time based on the title of the sutra?
Answer: The titles of the four Āgamas are numerous and their locations are not uniform;
how could one establish the time by calling it "the Four Āgamas"? Therefore, for the time being, we refer to the first location and call it "the Deer Park."
In the *Xiuyuan* (苑), the Dharma is elucidated through its setting; these words are indeed excellent. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Formerly, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta was hunting in the forest when he saw two herds of deer, each consisting of five hundred.
There was one leader of the herd whose body was the color of the seven treasures; this was the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni. There was another leader, who was the Bodhisattva Devadatta."
When Śarabha saw that the king’s retinue was slaughtering his herd, he gave rise to great compassion and went directly before the king.
As the men shot at him, their arrows fell like rain; yet the king saw that this deer felt no fear or dread, so he commanded them not to shoot.
Once the Deer King had arrived, he addressed the king, saying: "For the sake of a mere trifle of pleasure and sport, [you have caused] the herd of deer..."
"At one time, all shall equally undergo death; if you wish to provide offerings, you should take turns sending them every day.
The Deer King approved of these words. Thereupon, the two leaders each took turns sending deer.
Among the herd of Devadatta’s deer, there was a doe who said to her leader: "It is my turn to die; however, I am pregnant, and my offspring is not yet due."
"I beg you to grant me your consideration so that the deceased may attain rebirth and the living may not suffer unjustly. The King was incensed and said, "Who does not cherish their own life?
You have come here only to trouble me; go! That mother deer thinks my King is unkind and lacks discernment, yet she gives rise to such reckless anger—it is not worth speaking with her.
Thereupon, [the doe] went directly to where the Bodhisattva King was and related the situation in full.
She addressed the King, asking her doe-mother, "What did your master say? The doe-mother replied, "My master was unkind;
he failed to provide for me and instead gave rise to anger. Great King, because your benevolence extends to all beings, I have come to seek refuge in you.
As I am now, heaven and earth are vast and far away, leaving me with no one to whom I can appeal. O Bodhisattva, please consider this and have pity on me."
"If I disregard this and allow my son to be killed unjustly, and if another deer is appointed in his place before his turn has come, how can such a thing be permitted?
There is only I who must take his place. Having resolved this, he went of his own accord to the king's presence.
The king asked him, "Are the herd of deer exhausted? Why have you come here? The Deer King replied:
"O Great King, you are so compassionate that no one offends you; all things flourish and never come to an end, like those herds of deer.
Since someone has informed me of this, I feel pity for them. If I do not intervene when such an injustice occurs, it would be no different from being as insentient as wood or stone.
This body will not last long and cannot escape impermanence; therefore, I must compassionately rescue them from their suffering and distress."
Upon hearing these words, King Anantaguṇa spoke this verse: "I am indeed a beast, known by the name 'Deer-headed Man.
Though you are a beast, you are called 'Man-headed Deer. Speaking according to principle, it is not by physical form that one is human.
If one possesses compassion and kindness, though a beast, one is truly human. From this day forward..."
"I do not eat any meat; I bestow fearlessness upon you, so you may set your minds at ease.
Because the deer found peace and the King attained benevolence and faith, and because it was the dwelling place of the herd of deer, it is called the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*).

It is also named the Pomegranate Garden (*Āmrapālīvana*) after the trees, and the Sage’s Garden (*Ṛṣivaṇa*) after the sages who resided there. It was here that the Buddha first turned the Wheel of Dharma. (Note)
The four Āgamas are: first, the Dīrgha-āgama; second, the Madhyama-āgama; third, the Saṃyukta-āgama;
and fourth, the Ekottarika-āgama. "Āgama" is translated here as "Incomparable Dharma. The Ekottarika-āgama elucidates the causes and effects for humans and devas;

the Madhyama-āgama elucidates the profound meaning of true tranquility; the Saṃyukta-āgama elucidates various meditative concentrations (dhyāna); and the Dīrgha-āgama... [elucidates... the long discourses.
This clarifies the refutation of the non-Buddhists. Regarding the "Vaipulya" (fangděng) period: "fang" (方) means vast; "děng" (等) means equality.
If it is "great vaipulya" (dà fāngguǎng), its rational nature is expansive, hence it is termed "Great Principle" (dà lǐ); it is "correct" (fāng), and its inclusion of abundance is "vast" (guǎng).
The "vaipulya" of the present [teaching] refers to the Vaipulya of phenomena, wherein all four teachings are expounded together and the three truths are discussed simultaneously.

Regarding the principle of Vaipulya (fangděng): among the five periods, with the exception of the Deer Park [period], it exists in all others, because all Mahāyāna teachings discourse upon the three truths;
thus, it is said that the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras [apply to these]. Regarding the phenomenon of Vaipulya, it properly belongs only to the third period.
This is truly because the *Avataṃsaka* only discourses on the Perfect (yuán) and the Separate (bié), whereas the Deer Park...
In the *Yuanyang*, at the beginning, only the *prajñā* of the Tripiṭaka is clarified; at the end of the gradual [teaching], it extends to the Shared, Distinct, and Complete [teachings].
These Dharma-gates taught during these three periods are not yet universally extensive or detailed in their explanation of the Four Teachings.

It is only during the third period that all four teachings are fully expounded, which is precisely why the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/Prativedha) is uniquely distinguished. Question: If that is so, since the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* already contains the four teachings, why [is it not classified as such]?

Question: Is it not established as the period of the Vaipulya (fangděng)? Answer: Within the *Nirvāṇa*, these four are merely retrospective explanations; therefore, they are not designated as the period of the Vaipulya.
Furthermore, the establishment of periods follows their respective meanings; how could one apply the term "Vaipulya" to all cases by a single rule?
Question: This period of the Vaipulya is established based on the Dharma; why then is it not [established] by means of the titles of the sūtras and their locations?
If one asks whether this refers to the time of his establishment [as a Buddha], the answer is that within the Vaipulya (fangděng) scriptures, the titles of the sutras are not of only one kind;
how could their locations all be identical? Therefore, if one simply subsumes them under the category of Vaipulya, there is nothing that is not included.

The commentary states: "Vimalakīrti" is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Pure Name" (Jìngmíng). Because the three delusions have already been purified, he is the True Body (dharmakāya), and this is his name.
Pervasive omnipresence is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). Since this sutra was spoken by the lay practitioner Vimalakīrti, it is titled the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
"Sikṣānanda" is the name of a deva; its full title is the *Sikṣāsamuccaya-brahmāparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
The sutra states that to the east, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Pure and Clean, and the Buddha’s title is...
The sun and moon illuminate that land, where there is a bodhisattva mahābrahmā named Suvikrāntavikrāmin who has come from there (and so forth).
Laṅkā is the name of a city; here it is called "Inaccessible," for only those with supernatural powers can reach it.
Thus, that sūtra says: "The Buddha dwelt on the summit of Mount Malaya by the shore of the great ocean, within the city of Laṅkā."
(As stated above) Regarding *Śūraṅgama*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says that *Śūraṅgama* in the language of Qin means "valiant appearance" (*jiànxiàng*).
It distinguishes the various aspects of the practices of the samādhis according to their quantity and depth, just as a great general knows the strength and numbers of his troops.
When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot destroy him, just as the military commander of a Wheel-Turning King [cannot be overcome].
"Where the Jewel reaches, none dare to destroy it"; it is also translated as "the ultimate fulfillment of the task.
*Samādhi* is the Qin (Chinese) term for "the sphere of right mental activity," also called "straightening and stabilizing concentration.

Since sentient beings have had their minds constantly crooked since beginningless time, when one cultivates *samādhi*, the mind becomes upright and straight. This is the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva.
This differs from the ten-fascicle version translated by Paramiti during the Tang dynasty. As for the title *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, it is established through metaphor.
Since the sutra text states, "This *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*," the *Profound Meaning of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa* explains that the Dharma itself is used as a metaphor;
one should understand that the two characters "this" (*shi*) and "it" (*ci*) in the sutra serve as a metaphor to represent the Dharma.
This refers specifically to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*. Xuán [Zhiyǐ] says: "The 'Dharma' refers to what is called the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
He further explains that the "analogy" (*dṛṣṭānta*) refers to how those of sharp faculties understand the Dharma by taking it as an analogy;
that is, the Dharma of the three virtues—the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*—is precisely this very Dharma that constitutes the three aspects of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.

"Characters are metaphors. Those of dull faculties understand these three characters of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* as metaphors intended to represent the immeasurable, profoundly deep Dharma-nature and the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of the Dharma.
Although those of sharp faculties are intimate [with the meaning] while those of dull faculties remain distant, despite this intimacy or distance, neither may be discarded.
While both are preserved, they are merely a single metaphor; the ancient masters knew only to employ them as such.
To attempt to equate the Dharma with the analogy when one’s faculties are not yet sharp is precisely what was refuted by Tiantai.

How much more so for those who follow the ancient masters, whose own analogies for the Dharma are already incomplete; how then could they understand the principle of "equating the Dharma with the analogy"?
This meaning is crystal clear—why need there be any doubt? I am concerned that recent commentaries and records, in their exegesis of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, [fail to grasp this].
Regarding the title and the textual passages, both titles are erroneous; therefore, for the sake of this discussion, I shall briefly indicate the general outline.
For a detailed clarification, there is a separate treatise (*yi zhang*) [which says...]. As for "Śrīmālā," she is Queen Śrīmālā.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "King Prasenajit and Queen Mṛgāramātṛ addressed one another, saying, 'Queen Śrīmālā is...'"
"My daughter is wise and of sharp faculties; she has mastered the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-paripṛcchā Vaipulya Sūtra*.
Regarding the "time of the four Prajñās": *Prajñā* is called *banruo* (般若) in Sanskrit, which translates as "wisdom" (*prajñā*).
Because "wisdom" (*hui*) is a light and shallow term, the Sanskrit sound is retained. This establishes the period based on the title of the sutra; the commentary notes it as the *Mahāprajñā*.
"Mahā" (摩訶) here translates as "Great. Regarding the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (光讚經), it says:
"Thereupon, the World-Honored One, from the root of his tongue, completely covered the Buddha-field and emitted hundreds of thousands of countless rays of light that illuminated the trichiliocosm.
Within those rays of light, golden-leafed lotus flowers naturally sprang forth; upon each of these lotus flowers, various Buddhas were preaching the Dharma."
Because this sutra is preached, it is known that "light" (*ābhā*) refers to radiance and "praise" (*praśaṃsā*) refers to exposition and so forth.

"Vajra" is used as a metaphor; this vajra is used as a metaphor for the dharma of *prajñā*. Regarding the "essence of gold," its substance does not diminish even after being refined a hundred times, and it is bright, pure, and capable of shattering all things; therefore, it is used as a metaphor for the dharma of *prajñā*. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*).
It is said that by striking the *vajra* with a goat horn upon the tortoise shell, it will shatter (and so forth).
Regarding the ancient classification of the Prajñāpāramitā, there are five periods: first, the *Mahā*; second, the *Vajra*; third, the *Devarāja*; fourth, the *Prasphuta*;
and fifth, the *Rājan*. Our present school refutes this, asserting that the *Prasphuta* is merely the upper fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which was placed later.
Because it is a translation of the word "ear" (śrotra), it cannot be taken as having the meaning of "a different time.

Nevertheless, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* must have existed prior to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, as is fully detailed in the *Shiqian*. The *Dapin* (Large Version) is simply the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*; it is merely listed again here in this text.

Furthermore, because there are the *Xiaopin* (Small Version) and the *Fangguang* (Luminous Emission), it says "and so forth" regarding the various *Prajñāpāramitās*. Regarding the fifth point, the time of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Nirvāṇa*, it is because...
Since these two sūtras are identical to the *amṛta* (the finest essence), they are combined as being taught at one time.
This [time] is also established by means of the titles of the sūtras. Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma Lotus" (*Puṇḍarīka*);

because its meaning—comprising the phases of bestowing, unfolding, and setting aside—is difficult to comprehend, it is illustrated through the three aspects of the lotus. As for *Nirvāṇa*, the full expression is *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Now, this is translated as "Great Parinirvāṇa. "Great" refers to the Dharmakāya; "Extinction" (Nirvana) refers to liberation; and "Passing" (Parini) refers to Prajñā.
These are unified yet distinct, fused and subtle, non-dual.
This constitutes the five periods, also known as the five flavors.
Third, regarding the "lower summary" which is also called the "five flavors": the *Avataṃsaka* is the flavor of milk; the Deer Park [teachings] are the flavor of curd;

the Vaipulya [teachings] are the flavor of fresh butter; the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the flavor of matured butter; and the two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, are the flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

The textual passage concerning these five flavors appears in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, as will be cited below. As for the textual passage on the "five periods," it is based upon various sections [of the canon]. Which ones? The *Avataṃsaka*... [text fragment ends].
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the Bodhimanda where he first attained perfect enlightenment is clearly indicated as the beginning.
Although the various schools of the Hīnayāna claim it was his first attainment, this is merely from the perspective of those with limited faculties who perceive it as the beginning.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that he immediately cast off his jeweled necklace and put on coarse, tattered garments; thus, we know that the Deer Park is clearly indicated as the second stage. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states that the Tathāgata...
Since it has been exactly sixteen years since his attainment of the Way, we know that the Vaipulya (fangděng) is clearly the third. The *Renyang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states:
"Twenty-nine years after the Tathāgata attained the Way, he already preached the Mahāprajñāpāramitā for my sake. Thus, we know that the Prajñā is clearly the fourth.
The *Fahua jing* (Lotus Sūtra) states: "More than forty years have passed since his attainment of the Way," and so on, as recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

It is said that at the time of his parinirvāṇa, it is therefore known that the fifth [period] of the two sutras is clarified. Question: When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he attained enlightenment at thirty;

during twelve years he preached the *Āgamas* and so forth, for eight years the Vaipulya (*Vaipulya-sūtras*), and for twenty-two years the various *Prajñāpāramitās*. For eight years he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and on the full moon day of the second month, he preached the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

Now, regarding the *Avataṃsaka*: *Note: This passage outlines the traditional Chinese Buddhist chronology of the Buddha’s preaching career, correlating specific periods with the delivery of major scriptural collections.*

Question: Over how many years was it preached? Answer: Some say that the *Avataṃsaka* and the Deer Park [teachings] occurred simultaneously, and thus were combined within the twelve years at the Deer Park.
Now, I say this is not so. Furthermore, the ancient masters said that the period of the *Avataṃsaka* is long;
Master Jingxi said, "One should know that the *Avataṃsaka* extends to the end of the future. How could one definitively state it lasted only twelve years?
One must know that for the Tathāgata, there was but a single instance of leaving home and attaining enlightenment;

from the beginning to the end, his great capacity (mahāmūla) was nothing other than the *Avataṃsaka*, while his small capacity (hīnamūla) perceived it as evolving gradually until its awakening at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Thus, it is truly credible that the *Avataṃsaka* spanned fifty years. Therefore, it is said: "The great vision [sees] the beginning and end without change; the small vision [sees] only the three weeks."
If one were to insist that the sequence and classification of the five periods of time are not the intended meaning here, how could you arbitrarily cite them to raise an objection?
As for what are called the "eight teachings":
Second, the eight teachings below the eight [vehicles] are explained in two parts; first, the formal exposition in three sections. First, citing the preceding and stating the names:
Sudden, Gradual, Esoteric, Indeterminate, Tripitaka (Āgama), Shared, Distinct, and Perfect.
Second, under "Sudden," the specific indications: the Sudden is first because its vehicle, time, and flavor all occupy the beginning. Why is this so?

When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he first taught the Avataṃsaka section at the very beginning. Just as the sun first illuminates the mountains, or as milk first emerges from the cow, its flavor is at its most primal.
Question: How do the "Sudden Teaching" (Dun-jiao) and the "Sudden Section" (Dun-bu) differ? Answer: Their names differ, but their meaning is the same.

Since the teaching is established according to its section, the Dharma itself is identical. Why is this so? Because that which the Tathāgata taught at the outset is named the Sudden Teaching; it is comprehensive.
This sudden teaching differs from others and is thus called the "Sudden School" (*Tonbu*); since "school" (*bu*) refers to the teaching itself, how could there be any difference?

"Gradual" (*zen*) means gradual succession; it refers to the three stages of gradual progression. This is because the two vehicles realized the Truth at Vārāṇasī, were reprimanded during the Vaipulya period, and were refined through the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Thus, we know that the gradual sequence primarily concerns the two vehicles and the partial bodhisattvas.
If all Great Beings have already entered into reality, they cannot be categorized by gradual stages.

Regarding "secret," this refers to the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power of hidden and cryptic teaching, which causes sentient beings not to know one another's [levels], thereby allowing them to obtain both gradual and sudden benefits;
thus it is called "secret. In these various texts, the manifest and indeterminate are explained first, followed by the secret.
Regarding the present text on the secret [teachings], for the sake of following the conventional mode of discourse, I have first clarified the secret [teachings].
The system of exoteric and esoteric teachings established by our own school is precisely a continuation of the Great Master Nāgārjuna. Why is this?
For in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, various devaputras dwelling in the void offered praise, saying: "I see that in Jambudvīpa, there is a second dharma."

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da zhidu lun) explains this passage as follows: "When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, eighty thousand devas attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Cunda the Bhikṣu had previously attained the first fruit [of the path]. Now, when the Wheel of Dharma is turned again, immeasurable devas attain the patience of non-arising.
Question: The first turning involved few, while this current turning involves many; how is this so?
Question: Is it similar when the great is used as a metaphor for the small? Answer: The Dharma wheels of all Buddhas are of two kinds: first, the manifest; second, the secret.

When the wheel was first turned, eighty thousand śrāvakas and one person saw it, while the bodhisattvas saw immeasurable asaṃkhyeya persons attaining the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and so forth; therefore, it is called the secret teaching. If, at the first turning, eighty thousand and one...

The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) is an explicit teaching of the indeterminate category. Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, after the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa has posed thirty-six questions, the Tathāgata praises him, saying:
"When I first attained perfect enlightenment, there were likewise bodhisattvas who came to inquire about these same meanings.
One should know that this, too, is a secret teaching. According to the *Xuanshan*, this is termed "secret" (*bi*).
According to the *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, this is called the "distant original," as is analyzed in the *Supplementary Notes* to the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] (and so forth).

However, one must understand that "secret and indeterminate" refers merely to differences discussed in terms of those who hear differently despite listening together—namely, whether they know each other or do not know each other.
Question: Regarding the Secret Teaching, even those below the Buddha [in rank] are still not [able to... the Arhat... [text fragment].
Regarding the question of how it is possible for [the teachings] to have been received, some offer this explanation:
"Ānanda was at the stage of a Śrāvaka, and therefore he did not transmit [them]; Nāgārjuna was at the stage of a Mahāsattva, and thus he knew them. Now, I say this is not so.

For instance, since Ānanda had already mastered the four *yānas*, why must he necessarily be considered a Śrāvaka? There were many Bodhisattvas; how could it be that only Nāgārjuna was able to know the secret [teachings]?
Because it is esoteric, one must understand that the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* contains secret meanings through the praises offered by the devaputras;
it is for this reason that Nāgārjuna was able to compose treatises clarifying both the exoteric and esoteric wheels of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).

Otherwise, why would the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* specifically single out this passage to clarify the esoteric meaning of the Deer Park [teachings]? Furthermore, the treatises composed by the various Bodhisattvas are exceedingly numerous.

Why was it not explained? Therefore, we know that if it were not for the secret intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) addressed to those at the Deer Park within the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, Nāgārjuna would have had no basis to clarify the Esoteric Teachings; thus, their credibility can be affirmed. Question:

Does this single teaching of secrecy pertain only to the four periods (*catur-yuga*), or does it pervade all five flavors (*pañca-rasa*)? Answer: If one discusses the general meaning of "secrecy," then it applies to all five flavors.
All of these are contained therein. As for the secret teachings within the transformative rites (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*), they are restricted to four periods;
thus, the subsequent text states: "As in the previous four periods," and all other passages are likewise explained in this way.

If it were the fifth period, it would be an explicit teaching (*vyañjana-dharma*) rather than a secret one, and it would be a definitive teaching (*niyata-śāsana*) rather than an indeterminate one. This applies if it refers to the fifth flavor (*pañcama-rasa*).
Furthermore, regarding the discussion of the "esoteric" (mystery), there are two meanings. First, as in the three stages [of the parable], those who were previously informed are employed;

thus, in the "Exposition of the Dharma," the "Parable of the Great Vehicle" is fully heard, and by means of the account of past lives, one should know that this esoteric element actually constitutes a revealed teaching.
This is because all are equally perfect and wondrous, sharing a single flavor, and are therefore not like what preceded it, where they were mutually unaware of one another. Second, the dharma...

Regarding the statement that the Lotus Seat has a hidden meaning in contrast to other directions: what is this? Since it was not yet appropriate for other directions to reveal [the truth], they did not know this;

now, those among the humans and devas who have only recently begun their practice upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* have also not yet fully understood whether the worlds of the ten directions are open or not, and thus they do not know that. Nevertheless, the sutra is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Although it is not directly perceived after the opening of the *Mūla-bhūmi*, one may still infer that there is room for a single session throughout the ten directions;

this is what is meant by saying "it certainly does not exist [in other times]. Question: In the *Shiqian* (Exegesis on the Profound Meaning), it is stated that the secret teaching is bestowed horizontally and is never non-pervasive.
Why, then, was it just said that it is restricted to the four periods? Answer: How can one take the statement that it is "never non-pervasive" and thereby [misconstrue] the secret...
Does the Esoteric [Teaching] pervade the *Lotus Sūtra*? Now, it is said that there is no time when it is not pervasive; it simply manifests throughout the four periods.

If one were to say otherwise, how could one reconcile the fact that the *Lotus Sūtra* is manifest (*vivṛta*) and not esoteric (*guhya*)? One must establish the meaning through its principles rather than being constrained by the literal words.

Question: Since the Esoteric within the Ritual of Transformation (*saṃdarśana-vidhi*) already pervades the four periods, why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* specifically address only the Deer Park?
Wen answers: This is because in the sutras, the various devaputras state that this second turning of the Dharma wheel was at the Deer Park;

thus, it is considered the first turning. For this reason, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* follows the scriptural text and designates the Deer Park alone as the site. However, if one seeks the truth according to the underlying meaning, it actually pervades all four "flavors" (the four periods of the Buddha's teaching).

Therefore, it can be said that there is no time when [the teaching] is not universal, and it is not fixed to one place. As stated in the *Miaoxuan*: [The text continues with the citation from the Miaoxuan.]
The manifest and the indeterminate, and the secret and the indeterminate—now this text abbreviates;

it does not mention the "indeterminate" within the "secret," but mentions only the "indeterminate" within the "manifest. Question: It is clear from the *Miaoxuan* that both the secret and the manifest possess the indeterminate.
If both the secret and the manifest were discussed solely in terms of the determinate, how could this be proven? Answer: The wise value clarity.

Those whose understanding of this principle is obscure cling to its literal text; yet since it is said that the manifest and the secret are "not fixed," how could there not be a fixed [distinction] between them?
Therefore, Jingxi said: "The manifest and the secret, as well as the fixed and the unfixed, are discussed in contrast to one another. Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The *Lotus Sūtra* is fixed.
Is it not the case, then, that the manifest has both fixed and unfixed aspects? One should know that the sudden and the gradual are likewise manifest.
Since the explicit teachings are thus revealed, so too are the secret ones; how could one not believe that the meaning of the text is such?

The "indefinite" (aniyata) nature of the explicit teachings means that although the Tathāgata expounds with but a single voice, it causes all sentient beings to mutually perceive and realize it, such that the benefits they receive differ;
therefore, it is called "indefinite. As stated in the *Miaoxuan*: "Although the five [disciples] attained realization..."
Although the teaching on the Great [Vehicle] was delivered all at once on the High Mountain (Vulture Peak), it did not hinder the wandering and transformation [of the Buddha] at the Deer Park.

According to the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), regarding the "manifest and indeterminate" [teaching] for the eighty thousand [beings] and the five hundred people, some may harbor doubts:

"When the eighty thousand realized the Great [Vehicle], did those of the Two Vehicles know it or not? If one says they did not know, how does this differ from the 'secret' [teaching]? If one says they did know..."

As for those of limited capacity at the Deer Park, how could they possibly know the Great? The answer is: when eighty thousand and five people heard together of arising and ceasing, it was called "revealed";
yet while the five saw the Small, the eighty thousand realized the Great—this is what is meant by attaining the sudden within the gradual.
Thus, the sudden teaching on the High Mountain does not preclude the Deer Park; this is precisely what is meant by attaining the sudden within the sudden.

Gradually, as others failed to understand, various divergent opinions arose; yet they arbitrarily distinguished between the Exoteric and Esoteric within the indeterminate, completely abandoning the teaching on the simultaneous arising and ceasing of hearing.
[Question: The meaning of the "Exoteric Indeterminate" is clear; whether one knows it or not, it remains still not fully understood.
[Answer: Since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that at the first turning of the wheel, the śrāvakas saw eighty thousand [dharmas] and [the Buddha] alone, therefore...

It is known that although within the Deer Park eighty thousand individuals mutually recognized and awakened one another, in reality, from the perspective of the śrāvakas' own eye of wisdom, they truly did not yet know the teaching of awakening to the Great [Vehicle];
they only knew that eighty thousand had attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharmanetra-viśuddhi*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that only upon attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is one named as having awakened to the Great; thus, we know the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* relies upon the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
