His sixteen-foot form is the "coarse" aspect. "Donning" them signifies the manifestation of skillful means (*upāya*). It is quiescence.
The "patience of cessation" (*nirodha-kṣānti*) refers to subtlety and gentleness; "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) refers to the concealment of reality.

It demonstrates the descent from Tuṣita, the entrustment to Māyā’s womb, the dwelling in the womb, the birth, the taking of a consort, the begetting of a son, the renunciation, the six years of asceticism, and thereafter, beneath the Bodhi tree, sitting upon a seat of grass, he manifested the initial stage of the *hīna-nirmāṇakāya* (inferior response body).
In the Deer Park, he first taught the five persons the doctrines of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and so forth.

Second, it is shown that he subsequently applied the "Small Vehicle" transformation from below; herein, the initial mention of "showing from [below]" and so on merely refers to the pedagogical sequence of first employing the Great and later the Small.
If one discusses the Tathāgata’s reality, there is only the single initial attainment, for how could there be a distinction between Great and Small?
That sixteen-foot [image] is not otherwise; for how could the Tathāgata have undergone the process of entering the womb and attaining enlightenment twice?
"Tuṣita" is translated here as "Contentment," because in that heaven one knows contentment regarding the objects of the five desires;
it is the fourth heaven of the Desire Realm. Thus, the *Śūramgama-sūtra* (Ruiying jing) states: "The Bodhisattva was born in Tuṣita Heaven."

Having served as the teacher of the various devas, his merit perfected and his will fulfilled, the time for his destiny arrived; he was to descend and become a Buddha, taking birth in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in India.

As the *Mahā-śāstra* states, because the Buddha constantly dwells therein, Tuṣita Heaven is situated in the middle among the six heavens of the desire realm and the three heavens above and three below of the Brahma realm. Being centered in this heaven, he descended to be born in the central continent.
In the middle of the night, he descended his spirit into the Central Land and proceeded along the Middle Way; at midnight, he entered into parinirvāṇa.
Māyā—translated here as "Queen of Heaven"—was the mother. When the Bodhisattva first descended to manifest his transformation, he rode a white elephant through the essence of the sun;

while his mother was sleeping during the day, he appeared in her dream. He entered through her right side, and when the lady awoke from her dream, she knew of herself that her body had become heavy, for the Bodhisattva was within.

The purity of the womb is free from defilement; it is also called "right wisdom" (*samyak-prajñā*) because when entering the mother's womb, one knows one is entering, and when leaving, one knows one is leaving.
While in the womb, one does not give rise to desire for the mother nor anger toward the father—this is what is meant by "right wisdom.
Before descending from Tuṣita Heaven, the Bodhisattva first contemplates the human realm through four kinds of observations, the first of which is...
At times there are eight conditions: first, when the human lifespan ranges from eighty thousand years down to one hundred years;

second, when observing the land, it must be the Middle Kingdom; third, when observing the caste, if he prizes majestic power he is born into the Kṣatriya class, and if he prizes wisdom he is born into the Brāhmaṇa class—the other two castes are lowly and cannot produce a Buddha.
Regarding the four ways of birth, the fourth—birth from the womb—is such that only Queen Māyā, the consort of King Śuddhodana, was able to conceive the Bodhisattva;
these [three] belong to the Hīnayāna. As for the Mahāyāna, it is as stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "Riding upon a sandalwood pavilion, he entrusted himself to the mother’s womb.
As for dwelling in the womb, there is no dwelling in the womb in the Hīnayāna, simply because the Hīnayāna lacks the teaching of permanence.
Because [the previous account] involves arising and ceasing, the current text briefly lists those who dwell in the womb as being merely an additional detail.

In the Mahāyāna, however, there is indeed dwelling in the womb, precisely because the Mahāyāna is eternal and unchanging. Regarding those who emerge from the womb, the *Ruiying jing* (Sūtra of Auspicious Responses) states:
"On the eighth day of the fourth month, at night when the morning star appeared, he manifested birth from the right side; upon touching the ground, he immediately walked."
After taking seven steps, he raised his right hand, stood still, and declared:

"In the heavens above and upon the earth below, I alone am the honored one," and so forth, until the descent of the thirty-two auspicious omens. Regarding the taking of a consort: a consort is a mate, a virtuous partner.
Prince Siddhārtha had three wives: first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; and third, Mṛgajā. Yaśodharā means "Famous Name."
It is heard that Gopī—here translated as "Bright Maiden"—was the Crown Princess; at the age of seventeen, the King took her as his consort.

As for the son born to her, when a Buddha appears in a land of shared purity, there are still the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*); thus, during his time as a Bodhisattva, he manifested the birth of a son. This son was Rāhula.
When the Crown Prince sought to leave the household life, his father the King would not permit it; yet, because he did not cease his earnest entreaty, the King...
If you say, "If you have a son, I will allow you to leave the household life," the Crown Prince points to the Queen’s womb and says,
"Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son. How can this be reconciled with the *Adbhutadharmaparyāya-sūtra* and the *Prātihārya-sūtra*,
both of which state that Rāhula is the son of Gopī, while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* both state that he is the son of Yaśodharā?
One should know that Yaśodharā is the mother who gave birth [to the Buddha], while Gopī is his maternal aunt.
The *Śāstra* clarifies that Gopīdhā was a precious woman who was barren; she is indeed Gopī. If one considers her in a former life, Gopī was Yaśodharā in the present day.
As for Sunakṣatra, he was the half-brother of Rāhula; it is also said that he was the Buddha’s half-brother.

The term "child" (兒) is also referred to as "son" (子). Taking a consort and fathering a son are not among the eight aspects [of a Buddha's life], but are merely presented to illustrate those events in sequence.
His renunciation and ascetic practices are analyzed in the following text. Herein, one should demonstrate the two bodies—the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
Regarding the two bodies of the birth and dharma in the Hīnayāna: from the time after emerging from the womb, through the seven steps, up until the six years of asceticism.

The birth of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) occurs when, after completing the practice, one is born again; this is the instantaneous severing of the afflictions of views and thoughts through thirty-four moments of mind to achieve Buddhahood.

The birth of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the attainment of the wisdom corresponding to wondrous enlightenment at the site of the terrace of tranquility. Regarding the birth of the Mahāyāna physical body, it refers to the time of emerging from the womb, when one takes seven steps in each of the ten directions.
Regarding the birth of the Dharma-body, it refers to the attainment of the wisdom corresponding to wondrous enlightenment at the terrace of the path of quiescence.

Regarding the phrase "after six years," the *Wenju ji* (Record of Textual Explanations) states: "If the Prince left the city at nineteen and attained enlightenment at twenty-four, then he would have left home at twenty-five;

if he attained enlightenment at thirty, then he would have left home at twenty-one. Since these accounts reflect different perspectives on the capacities of the audience, there is no need to reconcile them.
Alternatively, it is said that he left home at nineteen and attained enlightenment at thirty, having studied under the immortals for six years."

This human claim lacks any authoritative basis. Furthermore, there are various differing accounts in the major and minor texts, as fully analyzed in the *Supplementary Notes* (*Buzhu*) to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the *bodhi* tree, it is also called the Buddha-tree, the Original Auspicious Tree, or the Path-tree.
"Bodhi" means the Path and Awakening; "Buddha" means Awakening. Because he attained the Path beneath this wooden tree, it is so named.
Regarding your point that he used grass as a seat, the *Sutra on Cause and Effect* (*Hetuphala-sūtra*) states:

"Śakra Devānām-indra transformed himself into an ordinary man named Śrī (Auspiciousness) and, holding clean, soft grass, offered it to the Bodhisattva to serve as his seat. The wooden tree and grass seat symbolize birth and cessation;
thus, the "inferior response body" (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*) corresponds to the śrāvakas, while the "superior response body" (*praṇīta-nirmāṇakāya*) corresponds to the bodhisattvas.

If one were speaking according to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it would not be appropriate to call it "inferior"; however, judging by the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it is indeed called the "Inferior Response" (Hīna-nirmāṇa).
As for why he first acted for the five men: it is because those five were the first among humans to perceive the Truths (satyadarśana); because the fourfold assembly is fully present among humans;
and because the devas attain the Path within the human realm—therefore, he first acted for the five men. When the Prince first entered the mountains, his age was... [text ends]

Nineteenth: His father the King, out of longing for him, dispatched five men to attend upon him—namely, Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Daśabalakāśyapa, and Gopaka Māṇava. Of these, two were sons of his mother and three were sons of his father.
Two held sensual desire to be purity; three held asceticism to be purity. The Prince applied himself diligently to practice.
The two practitioners of asceticism abandoned him and departed; three remained to attend upon the Prince.
He abandoned his ascetic practices and returned to accepting food, ghee, and oil. Those three also abandoned him and departed.
The Prince first went to the hermit Ārāḍa Kālāma and asked, "Is it possible, according to your Dharma, to practice the holy life? He replied, "It is not impossible."
Regarding this Dharma, how did he know and realize it for himself? The Sage said: "I have transcended the sphere of consciousness and attained the sphere of nothingness.
Having gone to a secluded place and practiced its realization, he led the assembly of princes and reflected that this Dharma does not lead to Nirvana;
therefore, he went further to Udraka Rāmaputra and said, "I wish to [practice] in your Dharma."
Having studied under him, he replied that there was nothing he could not ask. [The teacher] asked, "Do you know this for yourself through direct realization?

He replied, "I have attained the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) by passing beyond the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); having long since realized it, I have cultivated its attainment.

Thereupon, together with his retinue, the prince further reflected that this dharma would not lead to *nirvāṇa*. He then went to Mount Elephant Head (*Gajaśīrṣa*), to the village of the Brahmin Vaira.
At the banks of the Nairañjanā River, he vowed not to rise from this seat; thereupon, he attained perfect enlightenment. He reflected on who was worthy to be delivered first.
Having reflected, he thought it would be well to deliver the two seers first. Then, a voice in the air said: "The two seers have already died;
I know this as well. He reflected again, saying: "In the past, five men attended me through great hardship; they must be delivered first."
This refers to [the Buddha] going to the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to preach the teaching of the Four Noble Truths for these five men;
furthermore, he taught the matter of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, the Six Perfections, and so forth, thereby transforming the Pratyekabuddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Thus, the provisional bestowal of the Lesser Vehicle is complete with the three vehicles fully present, while incidentally serving as a Bodhisattva. As for what is called "leaving home," it refers to the inferior response of transcending the分段 (pudgala-bheda) realm.
The *Gṛha-viśeṣa-sūtra*, the *Dvaya-maraṇa-gṛha-niḥsaraṇa-sūtra*, and the *Prātihārya-sūtra* explain in detail the characteristics of the ascetic practices of one who has gone forth;
students should investigate these, as the conditions for truth and the means of deliverance will be analyzed below in the subsequent text.
If considered in terms of time, it refers to the sun illuminating the deep valley (the second period).
Second, regarding the "deep valley" in terms of location, it refers to the secluded depths of mountains and rivers; furthermore, a valley is a stream where water flows through a ravine.
This metaphor illustrates the Teacher of the Tripiṭaka transforming beings according to the three vehicles.

If considered in terms of flavor (*rasa*), just as curd is produced from milk, so too are the ninefold *sūtras* produced from the twelvefold scriptures (the second [of the three] abbreviated flavors).
Third, if considered in terms of transformation— just as churning milk produces curd— the ninefold [teachings] are in fact the realization of transforming the ordinary person into a sage.
That which is said to have emerged from the Buddha as the twelve divisions of the scriptures is merely a conceptual designation arising from their characteristics.

The *Śraddhābhūmi-parivarta* (Chapter on Faith and Understanding) states: "By means of skillful means, he secretly dispatched two men—śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—who were of haggard appearance and lacked majesty, saying:
'You may go to that place and speak gently to the impoverished son, saying, "We will hire you to clear away the dung. "
Regarding the fourth section, "The Lower Part on Resolute Belief," the cited scriptural passage is divided into three parts. First, the citation of the sutra: "By means of" refers to its function.

"Expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to the skillful artifice that is provisional. "Secretly dispatching" means to conceal the ultimate reality as "secret" and to point toward the partial truth as "dispatching.
In terms of the teachings, the "full letters" are "secret" and the "half letters" are "dispatched. In terms of persons, it means to secretly maintain the conduct of a bodhisattva within.

Regarding the manifestation of the Secret [Vajrayāna] externally as Śrāvakas to dispatch two persons: the four great disciples merely attained realization up to their own level and did not dare to enter the Bodhisattva path;
thus they are called "two persons. Since Pratyekabuddhas belong to the Middle Vehicle and are subsumed within the category of Śrāvakas, Kāśyapa and the others are included in the Middle Vehicle.
Now that they have attained realization, this refers to those who have reached their respective limits.

Regarding the two persons: if categorized by dharma, they are the two of *satya* (truth) and *pratyaya* (condition); if categorized by principle, they are the two of the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*);

if categorized by person, they are the two of the *śrāvaka* and the *pratyekabuddha*. The "superior" [category] eliminates the peripheral persons to signify the one true truth, the one Great Vehicle teaching, and the one Bodhisattva person.
Thus, we know that eliminating the peripheral persons and secretly eliminating the two persons are merely the Great [Vehicle].

The minor differences in reality and authority differ; since the Master of the Teaching has already cast off his precious robes for tattered rags, the disciples likewise conceal their inner [attainments] while manifesting outwardly, so that the provisional practice may lead to the ultimate reality and skillful means be revealed. The commentary states: "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" refers here specifically to persons, as previously demonstrated.
As for those with "haggard appearance and form," this refers to those who do not cultivate [the path] within the teachings of the Two Vehicles.
The marks and signs (lakṣaṇānuvyañjana) merely speak of suffering, impermanence, and impurity; this is precisely what is meant by the "withering of physical form.

Internally fearing impermanence constitutes "withering" (jiao), while externally encountering the eight sufferings constitutes "emaciation" (cuì). "Withering and emaciation" refers to sorrow and anxiety.

In terms of persons, it means that the various Bodhisattvas conceal their original essence and manifest through provisional forms; this is not a definitive teaching (nītārtha), for they lack the ten powers (daśabala) and the four [fearlessnesses].
Those who lack fearlessness are called "those without majestic power. Because the Small Teaching is adapted to those of small capacity, you may go to them.
The Great Teaching clarifies principles that are direct and real; therefore, it says, "run quickly to seize him. The Small Teaching clarifies principles that are circuitous and obscure;

therefore, it says, "speak slowly. "Hired" means to take on labor for wages. The defilements of the views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-saṃyojana) within the Truths of Suffering and Accumulation are like excrement.
The analogy that the Two Vehicles rely on the teachings to practice, thereby removing the filth of views and afflictions and taking the price of the Dharma of cessation and extinction,
is perfectly clear. What meaning does this summarize?
The second point addresses the question raised below.
The answer following it explains that after the sudden teaching, the Tripitaka Teaching was expounded for twenty years, during which time [the Buddha] constantly had [Śāriputra] remove filth;
this signifies the meaning of destroying the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāvanā-kleśa).
Regarding the third answer, which follows the "sudden" [teaching]: after the *Avataṃsaka*, he traveled to the Deer Park to manifest the provisional based upon the ultimate.

As for the "twenty years," in terms of principle, this refers to the true and the conventional; in terms of persons, it refers to the two vehicles; and in terms of afflictions, it refers to the delusions of views and thought.

Therefore, it is said that there is one liberation through the realization of the truths (*dṛṣṭi-satya*) and nine liberations through the unimpeded contemplation of thought (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). There are nine unimpeded [knowledges] and nine liberations.
Furthermore, the twenty years spent severing the fetters through the two paths of insight and cultivation;
the twenty years spent severing the five lower and five upper fetters; the twenty years spent severing the afflictions of delusion (*kleśa*) within the Two Vehicles;
and the twenty years spent severing the remaining fetters by relying on the two types of practitioners—these constitute the twenty years from the emergence of the Two Vehicles.
Because he came to respond to the Buddha through this opportune occasion, it is said that "he himself saw his son return after twenty years.

Because he had resided in the stage of the Two Vehicles and was now turning the Mahāyāna teaching, it is said that "for twenty years he has managed the affairs of the household. Each of these two phrases has its own underlying reason.

Question: The two meanings [of the first phrase] may be so; however, how is it that there are ten [years] in the latter case? Answer: The Two Vehicles each have their own [distinctive characteristics].

This is because of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*). Therefore, "twenty years" and so forth is the application of the metaphor; "breaking through the afflictions of views and thought" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) is the application to the actual teaching (*dharmopasaṃhāra*).
There are two meanings for the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*): first, from the perspective of liberation, meaning that by perceiving the principle (*tattva*), one is able to sever these delusions;

second, from the perspective of their own nature, meaning that "view" itself is provisional (*prajñapti*), and this "provisionality" refers to the three types of provisionality and the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*).

"Reflection" (si) refers to contemplation; having already attained the first fruit of the path, one further contemplates the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) capable of severing the afflictions of greed, hatred, and so forth within the three realms.

"Obscurity" (fan) refers to delusion, and "disturbance" (nǎo) refers to agitation; these constitute the obscurity and disturbance of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*).
Next, the Vaipulya section, including scriptures such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, is explained.

This section is divided into four parts. First, regarding the classification within the section itself, there are three sub-sections. First is the heading of the section and the citation of the scriptures;
the phrase "such scriptures as" refers to those briefly listed in the preceding commentary. Question: Many scriptures were taught during this Vaipulya period.

For what reason is only the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and others specifically designated? The answer is: as for the period of the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras, it was precisely during this time that the various sutras were subjected to censure and rebuke;

however, the instances of such censure were very few and did not equal those found in the *Vimalakīrti*, which rebukes partiality and refutes the Hinayana. Therefore, its initial designation is indeed purposeful.
"Refuting the partial, rejecting the small, sighing over the great, and praising the perfect.

Regarding "discerning the intent" (*bianyi*) in the second phrase "refuting the partial": it is because the intent of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings lies in refutation and censure that it is called "discerning the intent.

Here, eight characters are listed for the sake of literary convenience; however, according to the logical sequence of meaning, one should say: "refute the partial, praise the perfect, reject the small, and sigh over the great."
"Small sighs and great lutes" refers to the art of archery; "partial" means biased, and "broken" means crushed.
"Sighing" refers to praising, and "extolling" refers to lauding. "Small" refers to the Śrāvaka vehicle, while "great" refers to the Mahāyāna gate.
Thus, because one must critique the biases of the three teachings, it is necessary to extol the perfect and real Dharma and to crush the Lesser Vehicle; only then can one praise the Mahāyāna gate.
"These eight characters encompass the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* and exhaustively reach the depths of the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings.
Thus, the "Chapter on the Disciples" in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* refutes the Hinayana; the "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas" rebukes the partiality [of the two vehicles];
the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" praises the Great [Vehicle]; and the eulogies of Mañjuśrī and the Layman [Vimalakīrti] extol the Perfect [Teaching]. Furthermore, the disciples...

Since the chapter already speaks of "refuting the small," how could it not involve "praising the great Bodhisattvas"? Furthermore, since one chapter already uses "rebuking the partial," how could it not involve "extolling the beautiful"?
Moreover, the "Disciples Chapter" employs different methods of refutation: sometimes using the three teachings, as in the rebuke of Maudgalyāyana;

and sometimes using the Perfect Teaching, as in the rebuke of Śāriputra. This is merely a brief indication; the details are as analyzed in the Commentary (*Śū*), following the positions established by the ancients.

Is it truly the case that the Śrāvakas were rebuked and the Bodhisattvas were extolled? [Question: Does this rebuke begin during the Vaipulya period, or was it already employed during the Deer Park [period]?
[Answer: One who has already attained the fruit of realization is fit to be rebuked for taking the price of their attainment;
it is simply that this is explicitly stated during the Vaipulya period. Therefore, the Tathāgata commanded his disciples to question Vimalakīrti.
They all declined, saying: "In the past, at such-and-such a place, I was rebuked by him;

therefore, I am unable to go to inquire after his illness. Even when we arrive among the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings, we will likewise be rebuked, just as Śāriputra was rebuked by the Brahma King and the heavenly maiden.
When asked about the assembly of śrāvakas, they replied that upon reaching the Vaipulya, they would come to know the Great [Vehicle].
Because they already know and understand the vehicle, Kāśyapa said: "We are like parched seeds regarding this Mahāyāna.
When asked why they do not feel alarm or fear, he replied: "Because we have already received the price and realized the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*);

therefore, we can endure the reproaches of Vimalakīrti and the insults of Aṅgulimāla. However, if one were in the *Avataṃsaka*, since the price has not yet been received, one would merely [be afraid]."

Generally, when those in the mundane flow are transformed by means of the Great [Vehicle], they must be struck with awe; otherwise, they cannot escape being burned by the fire-houses of the three realms.

By what means, then, can they understand the Buddha’s wisdom and the Great Dharma? It is through the Tathāgata’s skillful means, which penetrate deeply into the nature of sentient beings and guide them step-by-step.
This is why the "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" employs the parable of the elder and the impoverished son to illustrate this meaning.
However, this is clear:

the four teachings all speak of the *pitaka* as the "half-character" teaching, while the *Tong*, *Bie*, and *Yuan* [teachings] constitute the "full-character" teaching; because the full is taught in contrast to the half, it is called the "contrasting teaching."
The three and four teachings are all explained together here below to demonstrate that within the gradual teaching, the transformative methods of the four teachings are fully present.

Generally speaking, the various Vaipulya (fangdeng) sutras do not transcend these four teachings; however, some may clarify only the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), such as the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, while others contain all four teachings, such as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*. One can understand this by reflecting upon whichever sutra one is considering. Therefore:

This refers to the teaching that all four *yānas* are expounded together. Regarding the "half-letters" (*ardha-akṣara*) and "full letters" (*pūrṇa-akṣara*), the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:

"For example, a householder has an only son whom he constantly loves and cherishes. He intends to take him to a wise teacher, yet fearing he may not achieve success quickly, he brings him back immediately.
Out of his deep affection, he diligently instructs him day and night, but teaches him only the half-letters and does not teach [the full letters]."
The reason for teaching the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra was that his son’s capacity was not yet sufficient;
"Vyākaraṇa" refers to the *maṃzì* (full letters). This translation, "Root of Letters," is the very foundation of worldly characters.
Although it is a non-Buddhist treatise, it contains no heterodox teachings—is this perhaps the work of one exercising great skillful means? If one applies this analogy to the Dharma:
The "half-syllables" (*ardha-akṣara*) refer to the ninefold canon of the Hīnayāna, while the "full syllables" (*pūrṇa-akṣara*) refer to the twelvefold canon of the Mahāyāna;

this can be understood through comparison based on both persons and principles. Because the "full" teachings of the *xūng-bié-yuán* (Shared, Distinct, and Perfect) are spoken in contrast to the "half" teachings of the Tripiṭaka at the Deer Park, it is said that "the full is spoken in contrast to the half.
As for the "half" of the Tripiṭaka within the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras), this refers to those who have just begun their practice.

Now, the statement that the Deer Park [teaching] is for the purpose of refuting [other views] is merely provisional; the name "fulfillment" (pūrṇa) in the Shared Teaching must be understood in terms of the subsequent Separate and Perfect Teachings.
If categorized by time, it corresponds to the mealtime (the third period).
Second, if we consider this in terms of time, it corresponds to the moment in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* when the sun shines upon level ground.

Regarding what is called "mealtimes," the *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* states that there are four mealtimes: early morning is the mealtime for the devas; midday is the mealtime for the Buddhas of the three periods;
afternoon is the mealtime for animals; and dusk is the mealtime for ghosts and spirits. What is referred to here as "mealtimes" refers specifically to the early morning.
When it says "at the time of the various devas eating," if one were to say "midday," it would again overlap with the *youzhong* (禺中) period and so forth;

therefore, we know that the meaning of the "level ground" analogy applies universally to the time of eating, the *youzhong* period, and midday. Here, we take the time of eating to represent the Vaipulya (fangdeng), which is precisely the time of the "level ground" in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
If we consider it in terms of flavor, just as fresh butter (*navanīta*) is produced from curd,
so too does the Vaipulya emerge from the ninefold canon (*navāṅga*). (Third, regarding the transformation of the *pitaka* [teaching] into the universal [vehicle],
just as curd becomes fresh butter— curd being processed by churning, which is merely the instrument for extracting the butter from the curd— the ninefold canon...)
The characteristics of their mutual arising can be understood accordingly.

The *Śraddhābhūmi* chapter states: "After this period has passed, the mental characteristics manifest mutual trust; they enter and exit [the state] without difficulty, yet that which they abide in still remains in its original place."
