One must understand that this refers to the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā*, which states: "The Sudarśana [Mountain] has four terraces; The distance between them is ten thousand [yojanas] each.
Extending outward, they measure sixteen, eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas]. The Yakṣas Sthira-śiras, Mālā-dhara, Sadāmada, and Mahārāja Dwell respectively on the four tiers.
They also reside on the other seven mountains. The second is the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; 'Trāyastriṃśa' means here..."
Thus, there are thirty-three [deities]. On the summit of Mount Sumeru there are four peaks; on each peak there are eight heavens, and four times eight makes thirty-two.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, dwells in the center, making thirty-three. The *Kuśaloka-śāstra* verse says:
"At the summit of the Wondrous High Mountain, eighty thousand [yojanas] high, dwell the thirty-three devas. At the four corners are four peaks where Vajrapāṇi resides."

The palace is named Sudarśana (Good Appearance), measuring ten thousand *yojanas* in circumference and five thousand in height. It is made of gold, and within this city is the Palace of Victory (*Vaijayanta*), which measures one thousand *yojanas* in circumference.
As for the statement that there are "thirty-three" [gods] who dwell therein, this refers to those who naturally inhabit the summit of this mountain;
it does not mean that there are thirty-three distinct groups of beings excluding Śakra. Regarding those who practice the ten wholesome paths of action alone, if at night...
Having already practiced [the preliminary stages], one further cultivates the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Since there is no meditative concentration in this realm and one is born there by practicing only the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), it is called "practicing alone. Third is the Yāma Heaven;
*Yāma* means "time" or "good time," because in this heaven, at every moment and for the most part, they proclaim happiness. Fourth is the Tuṣita Heaven; *Tuṣita*...

This [heaven] is called "Joyful Contentment" (Tuṣita) and also "Sublime Contentment" (Sudhāvatī), because within this heaven, one gives rise to joy and contentment regarding the objects of the five desires.
The fifth is the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), because there, one creates emanations of objects and finds pleasure therein.

The sixth is the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), because there, one is able to freely transform both one's own and others' objects. The four heavens mentioned above all dwell in the void.
This is truly because one cultivates the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), whereby the retributive fruit abides in emptiness.

One who has not yet reached this concentration is said to be "not yet arrived" (*aprāpta*) or "not yet entered" (*anupraviṣṭa*). Because one is able to abandon desire even before the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) has manifested, it is called "not yet arrived" or "not yet reached.
Thus, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "If one sits upright, restraining the body and harmonizing the breath, [merging...]"
However, when the body is serene and still like a shadow in the clouds—vast, open, and pure—even though it is thus pure, one still perceives the marks of body and mind;
this is called the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
From this point onward, suddenly the body, head, clothing, bedding, and all such things within the concentration of the desire realm are no longer seen, being as bright and clear as empty space.
The stability of the body is an obstacle to the matter; this obstacle to the matter obstructs the future and causes the body to become empty, whereby the future [attainment] is set forth.

This is called the sign of the stage of "not yet reached" (*anāgamya-bhūmi*). If an ignorant person were suddenly to obtain this and claim it is the nature of the "patience of non-arising" (*anutpāda-kṣānti*), their innate obstacles would still remain.
Since they have not yet entered the first dhyāna, how could they erroneously calculate that they have attained the patience of non-arising? This is what is meant by "innate obstacles."
These are the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Next, regarding the eighteen heavens within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), these indeed consist of pure forms, unlike the defiled colors of the desire realm.
Within the three heavens of the first dhyāna, the "Assembly of Brahmās" (*brahmapārṣadya*) refers to the Brahmā King himself.
Regarding the "people," there are two [categories]: first, the Brahmapurohitas (Ministers of Brahmā). "Brahmapurohita" means they are the ministers of the Brahma King;

"purohita" means to assist or to aid. Second, the Mahābrahmās (Great Brahmās). They are called "Great" because they are the lords of the world. Regarding the three heavens of the second dhyāna: first, the Parīttābhas (Limited Light).
They reside at the beginning of the second dhyāna, and as their light is still slight, they are named Limited Light. Second, the Apramāṇābhas (Immeasurable Light). Their light...
Because its brilliance surpasses all that precede it and is without limit, it is called "Immeasurable Light" (Amitābha).

As for the Heaven of Light-Sound (Ābhāsvara), when the beings of this heaven speak, pure light issues from their mouths; since "sound" (*śabda*) refers to speech, and furthermore, because those beings lack discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), as well as vocal sounds, they communicate solely by means of light—hence it is called the "Heaven of Light-Sound. Furthermore, the flames of the fire calamity reach...
When those newly born gods in this celestial realm first appear, all the established gods are filled with fear. To reassure them, they say, "Do not fear! Do not fear!

Because they maintain mindfulness of the radiance of fire, this realm is called Ābhāsvara (Light-Sound); in the new translations, it is termed *Abhāsvarā* (Utmost Radiance). Regarding the three heavens of the third dhyāna:
the first is Parīttaśubha (Limited Purity), so named because at the beginning of the third dhyāna, purity is only slightly refined. This...

Because its purity is superior to the former and is without limit, it is called "Immeasurable Purity" (Apramāṇa-śubha). Because that purity pervades everywhere, it is called "Universal Purity" (Śubha-kṛtsna).
Regarding the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna, "Cloudless" (Anabhraka) is a name established based on its support;
although those below the third dhyāna are said to be empty, their supports still possess clouds, whereas from the fourth dhyāna upward, all clouds have been removed.
This heaven dwells in space without clouds; it is the foremost of the four dhyānas and the beginning of the Cloudless realm (Anabhraka).
For this reason, it is named "Cloudless" from the outset. Because its inhabitants possess the power of merit, they are born in this heaven;

as the result of the aforementioned cause, it is called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava). Because the fruit experienced therein is vast and extensive, it is called the Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala).

The meaning of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) has already been clarified above. As for the Heaven Free from Affliction (*avṛha*), "affliction" (*vṛha*) refers to the confusion and entanglement that arises;

because there is no such confusion in this heaven, it is called the Heaven Free from Affliction. As for the Heaven Free from Heat (*atapa*), because there is no heat or distress in those born in this heaven, it is called the Heaven Free from Heat.
As for the Heaven of Excellent Vision (*sudṛśa*), their physical bodies possess such superior and auspicious marks that they are clearly visible.

Therefore, they are called the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*). As for the Heaven of Good Manifestation (*Sudarśana*), because their physical forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) are increasingly superior and can manifest with great excellence, they are called the Heaven of Good Manifestation.
As for the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*), among all the heavens of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), this heaven is the highest and ultimate, beyond which there is nothing superior;
thus it is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form. Regarding "freedom from the coarse distractions of desire," this refers to the coarseness of the forms within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The mind was previously distracted, but now it is free from that; one attains the subtle forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the mind becomes concentrated.
One who has not yet emerged from the "cage of form" remains within the form realm, enveloped by form; this is called the "cage of form.
To sit and attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and to obtain the names of the concentrations refers to the four fundamental dhyānas. This...
Regarding the four dhyānas, they are also called the four samādhis. In various texts, the four dhyānas and eight samādhis are mentioned;

although the four are included within the eight, they are listed separately because when the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) are contrasted, those of the form realm are termed "dhyāna" (meditative absorption) and those of the formless realm are termed "samādhi" (concentration).

Thus, one speaks of the four dhyānas and the four formless concentrations (catvāry ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ). Furthermore, when the form and formless realms are contrasted with the distracted state of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the former are collectively referred to as "the upper [realms]."

Because both realms (the form and formless realms) equally receive the designation "dhyāna," it is said that the four dhyānas are also called the eight concentrations (*samādhi*) or the eight dhyānas.

Furthermore, since the upper two realms are collectively termed "dhyāna-concentration" (*dhyāna-samādhi*)—in contrast to the "disturbance-dhyāna" (*kṣobha-dhyāna*) of the desire realm—and because they are also called "tranquility" (*śānti*), various sacred teachings employ these terms inconsistently according to their specific usage.
Regarding the four heavens of the three formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), they are called "formless" (*arūpa*) to distinguish them from the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).

Regarding the claim that there is no form (*rūpa*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the tenets of various schools differ. The Mahāsāṃghika school asserts that while subtle form exists, coarse form is absent;
therefore, it is called "formless. Thus, the gods of the formless realm can manifest billions of bodies, all of which occupy a space no larger than the tip of a hair.
As the *Āgama* sūtras state, when the tears of the gods in the formless realm fall, they are like a fine drizzle in the springtime.
Those standing at the Buddha’s side are all transformation bodies, manifesting according to the occasion in various sizes; they are not bodies produced by karmic fruition.

The *Renwang jing* lists the assemblies of the Formless Heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the form within the Formless Realm is not something known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
Thus, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teach that there is form [there]. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma* states that there is form within the Formless Realm.
The precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) are non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).

Because they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object and are pervasive, these material precepts follow along with the untainted states even up to the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun) states that matter is non-informative and does not reach the Formless Realm;
thus, there is a disagreement between the schools regarding whether matter exists in the Formless Realm. If one wishes to know the position of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* on matter:
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) does not reach the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). One should consult the *Tiantai Dabubu Zhu* (Supplementary Notes on the Great Works of Tiantai).
Furthermore, the *Antarābhava Sūtra* states that when the Tathāgata reached the formless realm, the various gods of the formless heavens prostrated before the World-Honored One.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says that the olfactory faculty of a Bodhisattva perceives the fragrance of the palaces in the formless realm. Whether there is form or no form, one must examine this for oneself with care.

Regarding the "sphere of empty space" (*ākāśāyatana*): when a practitioner becomes weary of the cage of form (*rūpa*), which is like a prison or a jail, and desires to escape from it, they cultivate insight-wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to eliminate the three kinds of form.
Having attained birth in this heaven, which is empty and non-existent, it is called the "heaven of the sphere of empty space.
Regarding the "sphere of consciousness" (*vijñānāyatana*): when a practitioner becomes weary of the boundlessness of empty space, they then cultivate insight and relinquish that [space].
Taking the sphere of infinite space as a further object of cognition is called the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Regarding the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*):
when a practitioner becomes weary of the boundlessness of the sphere of infinite consciousness, they abandon it and enter into nothingness; this is called the Heaven of Nothingness.

Regarding the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*): those who abandon the perceptions of both extremes and enter meditative absorption are called practitioners of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

Becoming weary of the sphere of nothingness as being like a state of delusion, and regarding the sphere of perception as being like an abscess or a sore, they seek a higher concentration called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Thereupon, they abandon both extremes and seek birth in this heaven.
It is also said that when ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists attain this concentration, they claim it is the realization of *nirvāṇa*, because they have severed all perceptions.
It is called "neither-perception" because the community of Buddha’s disciples knows, as it truly is, that there exists the affliction of subtle perception;
it is called "not non-perception" because [perception] is not entirely absent. Because these two—gain and loss—are discussed together, it is named "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the four *skandhas* (aggregates). They are called *skandhas* because they conceal the true reality; *skandha* means "accumulation. Regarding the term "four," the word for form (*rūpa*) is used [to designate the first aggregate].
The term *skandha* appears interchangeably in various texts; it was translated as "aggregates" (*yin*) in the old versions and as "heaps" (*yun*) in the new translations.

Although what has been explained above, from the hells up to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, differs in its experiences of suffering and joy, none escape being born again after dying and dying again after being born; therefore, it is called "birth-and-death" (*saṃsāra*).

Second, regarding the explanation of "birth and death" from top to bottom: since the preceding section combined the specific categories into a general whole by stating that "the birth and death of the six realms," and having already finished explaining the six realms according to the previous six sections, we now explain the term "birth and death.
It is said thus because many people do not understand its underlying reason.
This is the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) as it truly exists according to the Hīnayāna teachings.

Third, this concludes the establishment of the truth of suffering by means of the three [categories], because the dharmas understood by those of the Tripiṭaka are truly existent, whereas the dharmas understood by those of the Mahāyāna are all like illusions; how could the sevenfold two truths not be so?

Contemplate this. Regarding the two truths of origination (*samudaya-satya*): the two truths of origination are divided into three parts. First, the enumeration and categorization; second, the explanation of the names. Regarding the two truths of origination: [the first part] is the initial heading and listing of the categories. Second, the explanation of the names. Regarding the two truths of origination: [this is the heading].
This is the designation of the name. What is called "origination" (*samudaya*) has the meaning of "gathering together.

This refers to the mind and various karmas corresponding and aggregating to summon the fruits of birth and death. Thus, there are three kinds of karma: first, wholesome karma, which consists of the ten wholesome paths;
second, unwholesome karma, which consists of the ten unwholesome paths; and third, immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*).

The four dhyānas and eight samādhis are the movement of the four minds; when views and afflictions combine with prior karma, these concentrations can summon and accumulate the bitter fruits of birth and death within the three realms.

This refers to the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*). The second point—that "the afflictions of views and thought" constitute the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)—is as follows:

the afflictions of views and thought refer to the four abodes within the realm (*dhātu*), while from the perspective of the supramundane realm, they comprise the five abodes. The definition and meaning of the terms "views and thought" have already been clarified in the preceding text.

Furthermore, they are called the afflictions of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-kleśa*); the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*); defiled ignorance (*kliṣṭājñāna*); delusions of grasping at signs (*nimittagraha-kleśa*);
the ignorance of the secondary branches (*śākhā-pratyaṅga-avidyā*); pervasive delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*); and delusions within the realms (*dhātu-gata-kleśa*).
Third, it further states that the following list of alternative names refers to the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), which possesses various designations;

therefore, they are listed here. Regarding the terms "seeing" (*darśana*) and "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*): "seeing" refers to the afflictions abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which are the delusions of seeing (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);

"cultivation" refers to the afflictions abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), which are the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*). Regarding the term "four abodes" (*catur-vāsika*): if the delusions of seeing are severed, [the remaining afflictions] no longer exist.
Because the preceding and following [sections] are thus unified, they constitute a single dwelling (*vihāra*).
As for the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), they are divided according to the sequence of the three realms; therefore, they are separated into three dwellings. "Dwelling" means attachment;

because one possesses the afflictions of views and thought, one dwells within the three realms and cannot escape the burning house. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "defiled ignorance," the text reads "polluted" (*dūṣita*).
This is an error in terminology. The two delusions of *darśana* (viewing) and *bhāvanā* (cultivation) are capable of producing birth and death, and are thus termed "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*).
Not awakening to objects is termed "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). However, within the Hīnayāna, two types of ignorance are established:

defiled ignorance has *avidyā* as its essence, while non-defiled ignorance has inferior wisdom (*hīna-prajñā*) as its essence; this refers to [the failure to discern] taste, potency, maturation, virtue, time, and quantity.

In the *Great Commentary on the Ear-Section*, having already cited this note, it further states that "grasping at signs" refers to the six coarse delusions (*ṣaḍ-audārika*) of the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*. These are what are called:

the sign of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), the sign of calculating names (*nāma-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*), the sign of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*), the sign of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*), the sign of initiating karma (*karma-samutthāna-lakṣaṇa*), and the sign of suffering bound by karma (*karma-bandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, it is said that grasping the signs of birth and death through the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*) is termed "grasping at signs. Furthermore...

Regarding the statement that "the branches and their extremities are ignorance," the term "branches and their extremities" is designated in contrast to the "root"; all such designations are metaphorical.
Therefore, within the obstructions of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, ignorance is the root; the ignorance that obstructs the truth is the branch and its extremity.
Not understanding the Dharma-realm is called ignorance, for there is nothing therein to be enlightened. Why? Because the Middle Way within the Dharma-realm is the metaphor.
Just as the great earth is called "non-comprehension" because it obscures the Middle Way— this being ignorance (*avidyā*)—

and just as the root of a tree arises depending upon the earth and is thus called the "root," so too does fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) give rise here to further delusion and the grasping at false appearances,
like branches and twigs growing from a root; this is the most subtle [obscuration] among all obscurations.

Ignorance gives rise to the hindrances that obstruct true vision, namely the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*). It is further stated that "universal hindrances" (*sāmānya-āvaraṇa*) are so named in contrast to "particular hindrances" (*viśeṣa-āvaraṇa*);
universal hindrances refer to the derivative ignorance (*mūla-vijñāna-anu-bandhin avidyā*), while particular hindrances refer to the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

As for the "afflictions as numerous as motes of dust," these are also subsumed under the category of particular hindrances. The *Wenju ji* (Notes on the Text) states: "The two hindrances are nothing other than the afflictions."

Regarding these two obstacles to the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), if discussed separately, the ignorance prior to each respective stage consists solely of the "dust-like" [obstructions] regarding external objects beyond one's realm.
However, if considered comprehensively across all stages above and below, this ignorance encompasses both internal and external ignorance as well as fundamental nescience (*avidyā*).

Thus, it should be understood that these are merely different ways of classifying—either by opening out or condensing—the categories. Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* explains the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and that which resembles the obstacle to knowledge (*jñeyābhāsāvaraṇa*).

Our own school, however, relies on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to open up [the delusions] into three categories. Therefore, the "obstructions to wisdom" (jñeyāvaraṇa) encompass both the obstructions regarding phenomena and principle;
the obstruction regarding phenomena refers to the delusion of *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like delusions), while the obstruction regarding principle refers to the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).

If one classifies pervasive delusions according to the four teachings, and specific delusions according to the Separate and Complete Teachings—for instance, as in the case of the *rajas-reṇu* delusions—[the distinctions are as follows].

Since these are distinct delusions that pervade both within and outside the realms, as well as the four teachings, how can it be said that they exist exclusively in the Separate and Perfect [teachings]?

One must know that pervasive delusions apply to all three vehicles; in both the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the four teachings, one must subdue and sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Therefore, distinct delusions belong specifically to what is severed by Bodhisattvas; in the four teachings, all Bodhisattvas [must sever them].
The severing of "dust-like" delusions pertains only to the first two teachings, which do not sever the distinct delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the stages of severance for both the general and specific delusions, as well as their respective habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), as elucidated in the various doctrinal sections of our school, the explanations differ. Why is this? The *Zhi guan* states:

"In the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*), one destroys the delusions of views; from the second to the seventh stage of faith, one destroys the delusions of thought; and from the eighth to the tenth stage of faith..."

Regarding the statement that "faith severs the habit-energies," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "At the moment of first arousing the mind, both the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted;

though not yet exhausted in the realm beyond [the three realms], they are exhausted within the realm. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains: "From the eighth stage of faith up to the tenth stage of faith, the habit-energies are exhausted. Here, "habit-energies" refers generally to the dust-like and ignorance-afflictions (*moha*) beyond the three realms.
As for the citation from the *Avataṃsaka*, it is because one who has newly realized the first *bhūmi* (stage) is looking back toward the ten stages of faith; therefore, it is so stated.

This refers to the exhaustion of both active afflictions (*kleśa*) and residual habits (*vāsanā*) within the realm of the senses. The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states: "The Two Vehicles sever the common [afflictions], while Bodhisattvas sever the distinct ones;
whether common or distinct, their ultimate exhaustion occurs only in the Buddha. Quoting the *Dichijing* (Bodhisattva-bhūmi Sūtra), it says:

"If one enters the ninth stage of pure meditative concentration, the common and distinct afflictions and their residual habits are all exhausted. Someone has explained this as follows: "The 'common afflictions' refer to the fundamental propensities (*anuśaya*) of the Perfect [Teaching] up to the seventh stage."
It is said that through faith one exhausts the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), reaching a point where the common and distinct habits are exhausted at the stage of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, it is stated that at the Buddha-ground, not only are the distinct [habits] exhausted, but the common ones are also brought to their ultimate limit, because the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) pervade the ten directions. Another person has said: "The common [habits] have been exhausted for a long time;

this is merely a general statement made in reference to the preceding stages, saying they are 'all exhausted. I maintain that this explanation accords with the interpretation in the *Fuxingji* (Supplementary Notes) regarding the first *bhūmi*.
This refers to the sequential intention of exhausting the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) through the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Furthermore, some say that both pervasive and specific delusions (*paryavasthāna*) are exhausted upon reaching Buddhahood; this is based on the pervasive and specific delusions of one's own level within the realm beyond [the triple world].

Others say that the primary and habitual aspects of pervasive delusions are exhausted prior to the stage of the Perfect Abiding (*yuan-zhu-qian*), while the primary and habitual aspects of specific delusions are exhausted from the first abiding (*prathama-vihāra*) upward until Buddhahood; this is explained according to the vertical progression of stages.
The statement that "the pervasive and specific afflictions are exhausted at the stage of Buddhahood" is spoken in terms of a horizontal progression.

Now, I say that what is clarified in the *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation)—namely, the exhaustion of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) within the realm of the ten stages of faith—is merely following the sequential order of the Path of Teaching.

If one relies on the perfect and subtle [teaching], then one must clarify the principle of the "six identities. Why? Because the five grades of practice are precisely the stage of contemplative action (*darśana-mārga-prayoga*), and the six sense faculties are...

These are the three contemplations of similarity; from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) upward, one partially realizes the three contemplations, and wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*) is the ultimate three contemplations.

Thus, the general and specific aspects do not transcend the three delusions. Since the contemplation of the truths regarding these three delusions is wondrous at every stage, how could there be any falling away—whether horizontally or vertically—between prior and subsequent stages?

The general presentation of names and numbers: first, the explanation of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) constitutes the presentation of the names; "there are eighty-eight" constitutes the presentation of the numbers. These are: (1) the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), (2) the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), (3) the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), (4) the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and (5) false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—the above are the sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*); (6) ... [text continues] ... the dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya*). The above are the five views. Next, there are twenty-eight doubts (*vicikitsā*). Next, there are thirty-two attachments to desire (*rāga*). Next, there are sixteen ignorances (*avidyā*). Altogether, these constitute the eighty-eight afflictions of the delusions of view. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "eighty-eight": the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that these are the eighty-eight delusions of view. This is because the delusions of view are sharp and easily severed, whereas the other afflictions are dull and difficult to sever. Therefore, they are designated as the eighty-eight delusions of view. Regarding the term "delusions of view": it refers to the various types of views that arise from the delusion of incorrect discernment. They are called "delusions of view" because they are views that are themselves delusions. Alternatively, they are called "delusions of view" because they are views that cause one to fall into error. As for the term "eighty-eight": this indicates the total number of these afflictions. Specifically, within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten delusions of view; within the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are nine each. Thus, there are forty-six in total across the three realms. Furthermore, there are four doubts, twenty-eight attachments to desire, and sixteen ignorances. Summing these together results in the eighty-eight. Regarding the ten delusions of view in the realm of desire: these are the five views of the self-identity, the view of extremes, the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and observances, and false views. Among these, the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes are each divided into two types: those associated with pleasure (*sukha-samprayukta*) and those associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-samprayukta*). The remaining three views are each associated with both pleasure and equanimity. Thus, there are ten delusions of view in the realm of desire. Regarding the nine delusions of view in each of the realms of form and formlessness: excluding the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes, the remaining eight views are each associated with equanimity. Thus, there are nine in each realm. Regarding the four doubts: these are the doubts concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the path (*mārga*). Regarding the twenty-eight attachments to desire: these consist of the nine grades of attachment in the realm of desire, multiplied by the three types of objects—desire, form, and formlessness—resulting in twenty-seven, plus the attachment to the realm of form itself, totaling twenty-eight. Regarding the sixteen ignorances: these consist of the eight ignorances associated with the realm of desire and the eight ignorances associated with the two higher realms, totaling sixteen. Summing these categories together results in the eighty-eight delusions of view. This is because the delusions of view are the most prominent and serve as the primary basis for the other afflictions. Second, regarding the specific explanation of their numbers, the text is divided into two parts: first, listing the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) as the basis; second, the individual explanations. First, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*):

From the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one further calculates either annihilation or permanence; to calculate either annihilation or non-annihilation, or permanence or non-permanence, by adhering to one extreme is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Third, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) refers to generating attachment toward what is not *nirvāṇa* and grasping it as supreme; this is called the grasping at views.
Fourth, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) refers to erroneously maintaining and clinging to that which is not the true dharma of precepts and observances, as follows:

1. The non-Buddhists who observe precepts such as those of the chicken or the dog are said to possess "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). 2. The five types of wrong views consist of using a distorted mind to grasp at principles while denying cause and effect;

this is called "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). 3. The sixth, greed (*rāga*), refers to the act of drawing things toward oneself without satiety. 4. The seventh, anger (*pratigha*), is defined as persistent fury that does not cease. 5.
The eighth, delusion (*moha*), arises fundamentally from ignorance (*avidyā*) and a lack of understanding. 6. The ninth, pride (*māna*), is essentially based on self-reliance and arrogance.

Since the five dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*)—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the [four] "whetted" [afflictions] such as greed—are already established as such, the [remaining] views such as the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) and false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) may be understood by analogy through reflection. Question: Since the five dull afflictions such as greed are already considered afflictions of thought (*cetanā-kleśa*), why are they included within the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*)? Answer: [They are so included because] they arise simultaneously with the afflictions of view. Just as when one sees a snake, fear arises, so too when one holds a view, these [dull afflictions] arise concurrently. Furthermore, because they obstruct the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they are subsumed under the category of the afflictions of view. Moreover, since they are abandoned through the path of seeing, they are designated as such. This is like the case where, although the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are cultivated in all stages, they are specifically named after the stage in which they are first cultivated. Thus, although these [five dull afflictions] are indeed afflictions of thought, they are also categorized among the afflictions of view. Therefore, it is said that the five dull afflictions are both afflictions of thought and afflictions of view. This concludes the section on the afflictions of view. The remaining [afflictions], such as greed and anger, are exclusively afflictions of thought. This concludes the explanation of the ten afflictions. Now, in discussing the delusions of volition (*vitarka*), there are three types. First, innate volition (*sahaja-vitarka*), which arises simultaneously with the physical form;

for example, when a female is in the mother’s womb, she conceives love for the father and aversion toward the mother, while a male in the mother’s womb conceives love for the mother and aversion toward the father.
This is so by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) and does not arise through deliberation; thus it is called "innate. Second...
When one gives rise to discursive thought (*vitarka*) based on speculative views, these constitute the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) among the delusions of view;

although they are delusions of thought (*vicikitsā-kleśa*), because they arise from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), they are nonetheless subsumed under the category of delusions of view.

The "thought-afflictions bound to the three realms" refers to the nine grades of thought-afflictions of the three realms, which are abandoned during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). As for innate thought-afflictions and those arising from discursive investigation...

"Having severed the delusions of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*), one also simultaneously eliminates the four [types of] volitional thoughts. Furthermore, since the *Zhi guan* clarifies that the five [faculties] are "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*), how could it be that these consist solely of delusions of views?

How could anger and desire ever be absent? Therefore, within the category of the sharp, there are also the dull; those who sever the delusions of views are merely designated as having "severed the sharp."

The dullness within the sharp [faculties] is called the "back-ward driving" (pṛṣṭha-prahāṇa) affliction; when the sharp [faculties] are eliminated at the time of seeing the truths (satyadarśana), the back-ward driving afflictions are likewise eliminated.
Furthermore, it is asked: why must these five dull [afflictions] necessarily be greed and hatred? Consider wriggling insects:

they truly do not engage in reasoning, yet they raise their claws, spread their fins, and glare with eyes of pride. How could such base ordinary beings ever maintain views while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down?

Because the mind constantly arises while lying down, we know that the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) are not without their sharp counterparts (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). Although the sharp afflictions arise, these sharp ones belong to the category of the dull;
they arise upon the back of the dull afflictions. Once the primary dull afflictions have departed, the secondary afflictions on their back are also eliminated.

Therefore, both the afflictions of insight (*darśana-heya*) and those of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) encompass both the sharp and the dull. This is especially so when considering all ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*) that exist prior to the arising of dhyāna.
All these are termed "dull" (mṛdu) because they arise from concentration and manifest as views; all ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are collectively termed "sharp" (tīkṣṇa).

According to the *Fuxing liaojian* (Examination of the Auxiliary Commentary), prior to attaining dhyāna, even if one gives rise to afflictions through past habitual tendencies or develops the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) based on the present aggregates (skandha), these still belong to the category of dull underlying tendencies.
They are abandoned by the first fruit (srotāpanna) and are common to ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana), lying latent within the body as obstructions.
Because true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava*) eliminates these afflictions spontaneously upon seeing the principle of the Truths (*satyadarśana*), it differs from what arises subsequent to dhyāna;

nor does it differ from what existed prior to the arising of dhyāna, for even if non-Buddhists and others have attained dhyāna concentration through not yet seeing the Truths and have severed the dull underlying tendencies (*mṛdu-anuśaya*),
they have never severed even a hair’s breadth of the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), as such view-afflictions continue to manifest.

Because the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and those that lie latent are [of this nature], one should know that the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of view are not to be taken as the sole standard.
Since the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are both innate (*sahaja*), the delusions of view are likewise so. For instance, ordinary people constantly give rise to the notion of "I";

since this is the natural law (*dharmatā*), is this not something that arises simultaneously with the physical form? Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states regarding the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādānaskandha*):...
The view that clings to the aggregates as a mind and superimposes the notions of "I" and "mine" is called the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
This is further divided into two types: the innate (*sahaja*) and the conceptual (*vikalpita*). Regarding the innate, it is manifested by all ordinary beings, even down to birds and beasts.
Regarding the conceptual, it arises from the speculative calculations of non-Buddhists; how much more so for those bound to the realms of existence?
Volition is also called "delusion regarding objects"; thus, volition that deludes regarding objects differs from volition arising from speculative views.
These ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya), when distributed across the three realms and four truths with their respective increases and decreases, constitute eighty-eight.

2. Regarding these ten *anuśayas*, the following section on the enumeration according to the realms (*dhātu*) is divided into three parts. First, the general indication concerning the increase and decrease as they traverse the Four Truths across the three realms: Question:

Since the preceding heading specifies that the essence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) consists solely of the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*), why is it now said that they "traverse the Four Truths"?
Answer: While the objects of delusion must be traversed through the Four Truths, the essence of the afflictions that arise is limited to the Truth of Origination alone.
Tishou asked: "If it is possible for delusion (*moha*) to exist regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), what can be said regarding the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*)?

He replied: "Because one is deluded by suffering and its origin, one is likewise obscured regarding the path and cessation. Therefore, all four truths equally belong to that which is deluded. Since they are all objects of delusion, delusion arises toward them all;

thus, one cannot use the fact that suffering and its origin are states of delusion while the path and cessation are states of awakening to create an obstacle [to their being objects of delusion]. Furthermore, one must..."
One knows that the accumulation of afflictions and karma constitutes the deluder, while the fruit of suffering—birth and death—is that which is deluded;
since both subject and object are deluded, and both the Path and Cessation are likewise obscured, the delusions of view must be traversed through the Four Truths.

That is to say, in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) for the truth of suffering; seven each for the truths of origin and cessation (excluding the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and attachment to precepts and observances);
and eight for the truth of the path (excluding the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes). When these are combined across the four truths, they total thirty-two.

The second [section] clarifies the specific distinctions within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). It further divides into two parts. First, regarding the statement that the ten latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) are fully present within the suffering of the Desire Realm:

this is because suffering is the fruit of outflows (*āsrava*). Sentient beings, failing to understand the nature of this retributive physical form, falsely establish a "self" through the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Consequently, they further falsely calculate the fruits of the aggregates (*skandha*) as being either existent or non-existent, eternal or annihilated, thereby adhering to one-sided extremes.

Therefore, there is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, because one clings to what is inferior as being superior and reckons it to be *nirvāṇa*, there is the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Moreover, because one maintains non-vows with this very body, there is the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Again, because one practices false dharmas with this body and denies cause and effect, there is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). And because one clings to the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth while remaining in hesitation and indecision, [there is doubt].

Because there is the delusion of doubt and the darkness of ignorance, there is the confusion of delusion (*moha*). Thus, these seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) all arise upon the basis of the fruit of suffering;
because their characteristics are closely associated with it, they are called "closely associated delusions" (*sāmantaka-kleśa*).

As for the three types of delusion—greed, hatred, and pride—they exist only because of the preceding seven [tendencies] acting in opposition to or in conformity with others; therefore, these three [exist] in relation to suffering.
The objects of the truths (*satya*) have characteristics that are distant; thus they are called "distant delusions" (*viprakṛṣṭa-moha*). Question:

Since the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) belongs to the cause [of suffering] while the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is the effect, why is it included among the "proximate delusions" (*āsanna-moha*) under the Truth of Suffering? Answer: Because one calculates various ascetic practices and clings to what are not actually precepts as being the true cause, it is therefore subsumed under the proximate delusions within the Truth of Suffering. [In the Truths of] Origination (*samudaya*) and Cessation (*nirodha*), there are seven each, excluding [the clinging to precepts and observances].

The reason for abandoning the three fetters associated with the body is that origination (*samudaya*) is the cause of the conditioned and the tainted (*sāsrava*), while cessation (*nirodha*) is the fruit of the unconditioned and the untainted (*anāsrava*);
neither of these arises from the objective realm of bodily suffering. Therefore, through the cessation of origination, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is eliminated.

Once the view of a self-identity is absent, the views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) likewise do not exist. Why? Because of the [view of] extremes...

Because the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) conceives of the body—the fruit of suffering—as being subject to annihilation or permanence, the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is that which is maintained by the body rather than the precepts themselves.
Therefore, these two [clinging to views and clinging to rules] exist in dependence upon the body. Since the view of self-identity is already absent, how could these two exist?
Thus, among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) within the Truth of Origination, the afflictions of clinging to views, false views, and doubt are both direct and indirect [afflictions].
Delusion arises in conjunction with these four types of afflictions; because their characteristics are so closely associated, they are termed "intimate. Why is this?

Because the cause of the accumulation of outflows (*āsrava*) is fundamentally an inferior dharma, yet one clings to this inferior dharma as being *nirvāṇa*—this constitutes the view of holding to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, by reckoning these outflows to be false and erroneous causes and thereby repudiating the true cause and effect, one gives rise to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) herein.
Because of hesitation, there is doubt; because of the delusion and darkness of ignorance, there is delusion. Therefore, these four types are called the "intimate afflictions.
As for the three—greed, anger, and pride—they are called the "distant" [afflictions]; they are explained by analogy with the above and carry no further special meaning.
Among the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) mentioned below, four are distant and three are intimate. The three that are intimate are false view, doubt, and delusion.

Why are these delusions called "proximate"? Because the mind grasps at principles and denies the reality of cause and effect, there are the two delusions of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*);

ignorance (*moha*) is also included by analogy with the preceding cases. Therefore, these three are called proximate delusions. As for the three types—attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*)—they are called "remote," as previously explained.

Now, regarding why the delusion of clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is called remote: [it is because it does not directly deny the truth of cessation].
This is because the essence of the *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) consists in grasping that which is inferior as being superior;

furthermore, this *nirodhasatya* (truth of cessation) is itself an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), truly superior fruit, and not a conditioned, false, and inferior phenomenon. Therefore, the *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* is remote from the *nirodhasatya*.

If the *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* directed toward suffering and its origin were direct, it would be because one clings to the very nature of suffering and its origin—which are themselves inferior phenomena—as being [superior].

Because it is considered superior, it is called "clinging" (*parāmarśa*). Regarding the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are excluded, with the exception of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Since the Path is the cause for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), and furthermore is not based on the body, there is no view of a self-identity; and since the view of a self-identity is absent, the view of extremes is likewise absent.

Now, if the views of a self-identity and extremes are absent, there should also be no clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Why, then, does this [clinging] exist under the category of the Truth of the Path? Answer:

Regarding the lower [afflictions] associated with the precept-and-vow attachment (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): that which arises based on the body is called "intimately associated with the Path" (*mārga-samprayukta*).

Lower precept-and-vow attachment arises solely from false views; this is termed "distant delusion. Why? Because among the eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding the Truth of the Path, three are intimate and five are distant.

The five that are distant consist of the three distant [tendencies] from the preceding [Truths of] Suffering and Origin, plus four distant [tendencies] from Cessation, to which precept-and-vow attachment is further added; thus, there are five.
What is meant by "distant"? Because the Truth of the Path is fundamentally the true cause, it is not a cause that is not a cause like the observance of mere rules and rituals;

therefore, the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not established as a direct affliction. These five types of afflictions, including the clinging to rules and rituals, arise only from the three direct afflictions of false view, doubt, and delusion, and are thus all considered distant afflictions.

Furthermore, the four [factors] including the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are "distant," as previously indicated.
