Second, regarding the explanation of the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), there are eighty-one categories.

The explanation of these afflictions of thought is divided into three parts; first, the general indication of their names and numbers. Therefore, as for the aforementioned afflictions of view (*darśana-heya-kleśa*)...
When the faculty of mind (*manas*) gives rise to delusions of volition (*cetanā*) through mental objects (*dharmas*), these arise in relation to the five faculties and five objects;

furthermore, when one does not conceive of a self (*ātman*) regarding the six objects, these are all delusions of volition (*sahaja-kleśa*). Where there is the conception of a self, this is termed a delusion of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
This means that the three realms are divided into nine stages (*bhūmi*).
Second, regarding the detailed explanation of the three realms, it is further divided into two parts. First, a general indication of the nine stages: as for the "nine stages," they are:

(1) the stage of the desire realm where the five destinies dwell together; (2) the stage of the first dhyāna, the joy and bliss born of seclusion; (3) the second dhyāna, the stage of concentration... [and so forth].
1. The Stage of Joy and Bliss (the fourth dhyāna); 2. The Stage of Sublime Bliss Free from Joy (the fifth dhyāna); 3. The Stage of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness (the sixth dhyāna);
4. The Stage of Infinite Space; 5. The Stage of Infinite Consciousness; 6. The Stage of Nothingness; 7. The Stage of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception. Question:
Since all realms from Yāma upwards already dwell in space, why are they called "stages" (*bhūmi*)? Answer: [Because they serve as the foundation for the cultivation of meditative concentration.]
The term "ground" (*bhūmi*) is applied by virtue of what is supported upon it; it does not refer to ground consisting of sand, mud, earth, or stone.

When the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is combined as one ground and the four dhyānas and four concentrations (*samādhi*) are taken as eight, they together constitute the nine grounds. Within this single ground of the desire realm, there are nine grades of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.

Regarding these nine grades: they are the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*), the middle-of-the-high (*madhya-adhimātra*), the lowest-of-the-high (*mṛdu-adhimātra*), the highest-of-the-middle (*adhimātra-madhya*), and so forth.
Middle-middle, middle, middle-low, low-low, high-low, middle-low, low-low.
Second, regarding the number [of afflictions] in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) categorized by stage (*bhūmi*), the text is further divided into two parts.

First, concerning the statement that there are nine grades of greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*) in the Desire Realm: it should be understood that these four each have nine grades; for now, they are collectively stated as being nine.

Regarding the "uppermost of the upper" category of the three grades of defilements: one must first understand that there are three grades of delusion—namely, upper, middle, and lower—and that within the upper grade there are further three sub-grades;
thus it is called "uppermost of the upper. As it is with the upper grade, so it is with the middle and lower grades as well.
In each of the eight upper stages, there are nine grades [of afflictions], excluding the latent tendency of anger (*pratigha-anuśaya*).

Regarding "the two upper [realms]" and "the eight lower [stages] of the form and formless realms," one must understand that "excluding anger" refers to the exclusion of the nine grades of delusion associated with anger.

As for why these are called "delusions of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*) and not "delusions of seeing" (*darśana-heya*), it is because they have already been severed by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); logically, there can be no doubt regarding them, as they are [already eliminated] through the Path of Seeing. Thus, they are delusions of cultivation.
Since one has already traversed the three realms and contemplated the four truths, why does one not traverse all four [truths] here?
If we follow the analogy that the forty *li* of water represent the delusions of vision (*darśana-heya*), then this single truth-condition should correspond to ten *li*.

Because it does not arise transversely, it is called "one drop," yet its cumulative weight is extremely great—it may even amount to ten or forty *li*. Since these waters are what are severed by the contemplation of the four truths...
The delusions severed by the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) contemplate only the single Truth of Cessation, or alternatively, contemplate any one of the Four Truths as they wish;

this is like ten *li* of water. Thus, the Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "That which is severed by the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) is like forty *li* of water; that which remains is like a single drop from the tip of a hair.
Regarding the eighty-eight [delusions] of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the eighty-one [delusions] of the path of cultivation, are these fixed according to the gates of the teachings?

In responding to capacities, the teaching may be extensive or concise; how could it be fixed? As it is said, regarding the three fetters, the five higher-tier fetters, the five lower-tier fetters, and so forth—the number of views and afflictions is immeasurable and boundless.
Thus, they total eighty-one.
The concluding text for these three cases can be seen [in the source].

All that has preceded regarding the differences between *darśana-heya* (afflictions abandoned through vision) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation) constitutes, in total, the truly existent *samudaya-satya* (truth of origination) according to the *Hīnayāna* (Zàngjiào) teachings.
Third, the preceding section concludes with the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*):

the Truth of Cessation is divided into three parts. First is the designation of its name; that which is called "cessation" has the meaning of unconditioned cessation (*asaṃskṛta-nirodha*), as the bonds of karma have already been severed.

When [defilements] are exhausted, there is no longer birth and death nor any afflictions or burdens; therefore, it is called "extinction" (*nirodha*). Furthermore, because one gives rise to untainted vision and severs [afflictions], it is termed "extinction.

The extinction of karmic afflictions is called "extinction with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirodha*); because the causes are extinguished, the fruits are extinguished, which is called "extinction without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirodha*).
The cessation of the previously mentioned suffering and its origin reveals the partial truth (*tathyasaṃvṛti*).

Second, the cessation of the aforementioned [suffering and origin] below indicates the essence of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*); because the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation are manifested, the term "partial truth" used previously refers to that which does not include the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
The extinction of causes leads to the realization of true extinction, yet this is not itself the True Truth (*tattva-satya*).

This section below, "Extinction of Causes," distinguishes that while it is through the extinction of causes that one realizes the principle of truth, this extinction itself is not called the True Truth. Why?

Because the principle of truth is like the moon, while suffering and its accumulation are like clouds; the Path is like the clearing away [of the clouds], and extinction is like [the moon being revealed].

Since the four truths have already been discussed, one should know that the Truth (satya) is established separately from them. Suffering (duḥkha) and its Accumulation (samudaya) are merely capable of obscuring and cannot themselves afflict or defile;
the Path (mārga) and Cessation (nirodha) are capable of revealing [the truth], yet the principle is fundamentally pure. Therefore, the Truth of Reality is neither contrary nor conformable;
however, in terms of practice, it can be both conformable and revealing. Thus, through Cessation, one realizes the True Emptiness, while Suffering and Accumulation serve as...
The conventional path and cessation are termed "true" based on their relation to the inverse and the conforming. Because suffering and its origin are contrary to truth, they are called conventional;
because the path and cessation accord with principle, they are called true. This does not mean that the path and cessation are themselves the ultimate truth.
Regarding the Four Truths of the Path:
the Four Truths of the Path are divided into two parts. First, the designation of their names: "Path" (*mārga*) means that which enables passage.

Both the Right Path (*samyag-mārga*) and the Aids to the Path (*mārga-saṃbhāra*) assist one another to enable passage to *nirvāṇa*; therefore, they are called the "Path. The thirty-seven factors (*triṃśat-saptaka-dharma*) take principle as their object.
The practice of wisdom is called the right path; various remedies and meditative concentrations are called the aids to the path.
Furthermore, patience, knowledge, non-obstruction, and liberation are called the right path, while the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called the aids to the path as skillful remedies.
Briefly stated, these are morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*); extensively stated, they are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
Regarding the two brief formulations, the subsequent commentary is divided into two parts. First, the presentation of the brief and the extensive:

although the extensive treatise contains thirty-seven factors, when abbreviated, they do not go beyond the three—morality, concentration, and wisdom. Why is this? For instance, among the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is itself "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*); how could it be otherwise?
Is it not wisdom? Among the five faculties and five powers, the fourth is named concentration; within the Eightfold Path, right livelihood avoids what is improper—is this not indeed morality?
These names reveal themselves, yet when corresponding to their respective applications, they clarify the three trainings in detail according to their specific meanings.
These thirty-seven [factors] are combined into seven categories (*kośa*).
Second, regarding the detailed explanation of these thirty-seven, the section on the broad text is divided into three parts: first, the enumeration of the categories;
"thirty-seven" refers to the four, the three, the two, the five, the single seven, and the single eight. "Categories" (*pin*) means classes, groups, or dharmas; thus, there are thirty-seven dharmas.
Because the various categories differ from one another, they are called "chapters" (*pāda*). Now, in discussing the chapters on the Path (*mārga-pāda*), there are four kinds:

first, the sequential order of mutual generation, wherein the generations do not become confused. For example, when one contemplates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*) arises;

because of right effort, concentration and wisdom arise in equal measure; from these arise the bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*); and further, the five faculties (*indriya*) arise, which are incapable of being shaken or destroyed.

The arising of the five powers (*pañca-balāni*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅgāni*), and the vision of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga*) constitutes their sequential generation.

Second, regarding their correspondence to the stages (*avasthā*): the four foundations of mindfulness correspond to the stage of the foundations of mindfulness; the right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) correspond to the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*); the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhi-pāda*) correspond to the stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*);

the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) correspond to the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*); the five powers correspond to the stage of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*); the seven factors of enlightenment correspond to the stage of the two fruits; and the eightfold path corresponds to the stage of the fruit of Arhatship.

Regarding the third point, concerning the correspondence with the stages of the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*): these thirty-seven factors (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) should be understood as being categorized according to their respective divisions.
Each of these categories is practiced by the practitioner individually; how could it be that a practitioner must traverse all thirty-seven factors in their entirety before attaining realization?
Regarding the fourth point, concerning mutual inclusion: for example, since there is no dharma other than the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this is so.
The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are able to encompass all dharmas; since this is so for the foundations of mindfulness, it is likewise for the other categories.
Thus, the thirty-seven factors are "arising in sequence" (*anuloma*) when practiced by a single person. When practiced by many people, they are "according to their respective divisions.

If the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) precede the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), they are called "arising in sequence"; if the seven factors of enlightenment follow the eightfold noble path, they are called "corresponding to the stages" (*pratipakṣa-sthāna*).
Furthermore, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) pertain both to the direct path and the auxiliary path;
they also pertain to the contaminated (sāsrava), the uncontaminated (anāsrava), and that which is both contaminated and uncontaminated, as is explained in detail in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

I. The Four Foundations of Mindfulness: 1. Contemplating the body as impure (the aggregate of form). 2. Contemplating feelings as suffering (the aggregate of feeling). 3. Contemplating the mind as impermanent (the aggregate of consciousness). 4.
Contemplating phenomena as non-self (the aggregates of perception and mental formations). II. The Four Right Efforts: 1. To prevent unarisen evil states from arising. 2.

To eliminate evil states that have already arisen. 3. To bring about the arising of unarisen wholesome states. 4. To increase wholesome states that have already arisen. III. [The Three Bases of Power]... (as above)
The four bases of psychic power (desire, intention, energy, and wisdom); the five faculties (faith, energy, concentration, wisdom, and mindfulness); the five powers (the same names as the faculties);

the seven factors of enlightenment (mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity); and the eightfold noble path (right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right effort, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right livelihood).
214. Below, the enumeration of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is listed. First, regarding the four applications of mindfulness:
the objects of contemplation—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—are each observed through the four aspects of impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self; thus they are called "the four.

Since "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is the observation and "application" (*upasthāna*) is the object, it is termed "applications of mindfulness. Question: Since the four applications of mindfulness are wisdom (*prajñā*), why are they named after "mindfulness"? Answer: [See below].
For the use of those who are beginners, mindfulness is employed as the dominant factor; because it does not falsely grasp at other objects of attention, it is designated by the name "mindfulness.
First, regarding the contemplation of the impurity of the body: because sentient beings are deluded and inverted, they cling to their own bodies and claim them to be pure.
To transform these beings, the Noble Ones employ the method of impurity to destroy that inversion of purity and cause them to realize the truth.
Because it is the principle of emptiness, it is said that one contemplates the impurity of the body. One must know that this is the correct path and a truly authentic contemplation.
Why is it called "correct and real"? Because the present body possesses five kinds of impurity. What are these five? First, impurity of the seed:
because the two drops of red and white from the union of the parents form this body. Second, impurity of the dwelling place.
First, it is impure by its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇāśubhatā*) because within the mother’s womb, between the stomach and the intestines, it is surrounded by various kinds of filth.
Second, it is impure by its own characteristic because after emerging from the urinary tract, one must lie upon excrement and filth, and the nine orifices constantly flow with them.

Third, it is impure by its own nature (*svabhāvāśubhatā*) because therein exists only a mass of feces and urine, wrapped in the large and small intestines, the belly, and sinews, and smeared with blood.
Fifth, because ultimate impurity consists of being cast away among the graves after old age, sickness, and death, like a withered and decayed log.

Second, regarding the contemplation that sensation is suffering: it is because sentient beings reckon the sensations of the six sense organs as pleasure, failing to realize that this so-called pleasure is actually the cause of suffering;
therefore, they are led to contemplate truthfully that the sensations of the six sense organs upon contact with the six sense objects are all [suffering].

All these are suffering; how should one observe them? Furthermore, sensation is not comprised of anything other than three types: first, painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*); second, pleasant sensation (*sukhā-vedanā*);

and third, neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukhā-vedanā*). Painful sensation arises from painful conditions; because it is perceived as pain by the mind, one sees painful sensation as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Pleasant sensation accords with the mind, yet its destruction is necessarily painful; [the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation... is not... [painful].

The mind that delights in equanimity is itself the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Therefore, when the six sense faculties encounter the phenomena of the six sense objects, there are always three types of sensation (*vedanā*);
these three sensations are all suffering. Regarding the contemplation of the mind as impermanent: sentient beings do not realize this and instead claim it exists eternally;
therefore, one is led to contemplate the mind as being merely a name, never abiding for even a moment, but shifting and flowing out in every successive thought-moment.
If one cannot even preserve one’s breath, how could one possibly recognize the mind as being constantly present upon inhaling?

Regarding the fourth contemplation on the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*): "Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the normative principles, namely wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, and neutral phenomena.
Sentient beings all cling to these phenomena, imagining them to be a self, saying, "I am able to perform wholesome deeds, unwholesome deeds, and neutral deeds. For this reason...
One must roughly examine each and every phenomenon within this Dharma: "Wherein is there a self? In what does the self abide?
Are wholesome phenomena the self? Are unwholesome phenomena the self? Are indeterminate phenomena the self? If all phenomena were the self, then the self would be infinite;
if they are not the self, why do you cling to them and thus delude yourself? One should investigate in this manner.
I have thus paired the five aggregates (*skandhas*) such that the two aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are designated as "dharmas.

Because of perception, one performs formations—performing either wholesome or unwholesome actions; this is why it is said so. Question: If we discuss the five aggregates, mental consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) is the most subtle;

in the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), why does the mind occupy the third position? Answer: This is merely for the sake of convenience in verbal expression; there is no other underlying meaning.
Regarding the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*): "abandoning the perverse" is called "right," and being without indolence is called "effort. First, as for "preventing unarisen evil from arising":
although various afflictions and delusions have not yet arisen, they will inevitably arise later; therefore, one must diligently cultivate [the means] to prevent them.
1. Not producing [unwholesome states]; 2. Causing those already arisen unwholesome states to cease:
since afflictions, karma, and so forth have already arisen, one applies diligent right practice to cause them to cease; 3. Causing unarisen wholesome states to arise:

since the wholesome factors of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path have not yet arisen, one cultivates right effort to cause them to arise; 4. Causing arisen wholesome states to increase.
Once the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment have arisen, one should apply right effort to protect them, causing them to increase further so that they are not lost.
Regarding the "four bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*): *pāda* means mind or intention; because they bring the mind and intention to fulfillment, they are so named.

Regarding the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): when mindfulness, right effort, wisdom, and concentration are increased such that wisdom is predominant while the power of concentration is still slight, one now attains the fourfold power of concentration consisting of desire, mindfulness, energy, and wisdom. Because the mind and its objects are thus integrated through concentration, all that is wished for is accomplished;
therefore, they are called the bases of psychic power. Alternatively, as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Just as one who has feet is able to go and return."
Furthermore, "the bases of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda) correspond to what is desired by the mind; that is, they accord with one's intention. First, "desire" refers to the aspiration for joy;

because one aspires to attain concentration, one causes practice to be perfected. Second, "mindfulness" refers to the mental application of attaining concentration; because one maintains mindfulness, one causes practice to be perfected.

Third, "effort" refers to striving for that concentration without interruption or distraction. Fourth, "wisdom" refers to the sequential order of the dharma-realm, as well as both tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā). All...

It says: "Contemplating" means that by contemplating the objects observed within the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the mind does not wander, and thus the power of concentration (*samādhi*) is accomplished.
Here, it mentions "wisdom" (*prajñā*); since the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are concentrations characterized by wisdom, it cites wisdom to manifest concentration.
Alternatively, one might suspect that the character for "wisdom" (*hui*) should be "contemplation" (*si*), which refers to "contemplating."

The four or five faculties (*indriya*) are able to give rise to what is called "roots" because they are difficult to move; thus, these five dharmas are like objects that have roots, for they are difficult to move when [the mind is] in error or inversion.
Therefore, having faith in the correct aids is called "faith" (*śraddhā*); striving to seek the correct aids is called "diligence" (*vīrya*);
being mindful while seeking the correct aids is called "mindfulness" (*smṛti*); and seeking the dharmas of the correct aids without distraction is called "concentration" (*samādhi*).
Therefore, it is called "concentration" (samādhi) because it serves as the primary support for wisdom; skillfully cultivating that wisdom is what is meant by "wisdom" (prajñā).
Regarding the five powers (pañca-balāni), "power" has the sense of functional efficacy. These five dharmas possess the power to sever evil and expel obstacles;

thus, while the general meaning of the faculties (indriya) and the powers does not differ, they are distinguished based on the difference between being able to generate [wholesome states] and being able to expel obstacles. Therefore, they are divided.
There are two [aspects].

Regarding the six or seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) means awakening or clear comprehension; "factors" (*aṅga*) refers to constituent parts. First, regarding "one-pointedness" (*ekāgratā*):

it means that through concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one brings about equanimity, such that within a single moment of thought, no fluctuation between sinking and agitation is perceived. Second, regarding "discernment" (*vīmaṃsā*): it means being able to skillfully...
Discerning truth from falsehood is the method [of the third stage]. Third, "exertion" (*vīrya*) refers to practicing with diligence and remaining free from deviant conduct.
Fourth, "joy" (*prīti*) refers to the mind attaining wholesome dharmas and giving rise to gladness. Fifth, "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*) refers to being light, sharp, and at ease.
The *Dharmadhātu-krama* and the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* both state that when the mind is observed to be floating or agitated, one should immediately remove it.
Because it removes mental agitation, one attains the flavor of the Dharma; because it removes the coarseness of body and speech, there is lightness, agility, and composure.

Furthermore, this is merely a difference between new and old translations. The *Śata-dharmaprakāśamukha-śāstra* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas) states: "Because one is far removed from heaviness and coarseness (*dauṣṭhulya*), and the body and mind are harmonized and relaxed, it is called 'light ease' (*praśrabdhi*).
Is not "being far removed" (*viyoga*) precisely the meaning of "removing"? Regarding the six types of concentration, these refer to meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Seventh, "abandonment" (*upekṣā*) means to abandon all delusions and errors in order to seek the truth. Seventh, the "eightfold noble path" (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*):
that which is not deviant is called "right," and that which can lead [to liberation] is called a "path. Regarding "right view" (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), it refers to clearly seeing the Four Noble Truths.
Regarding "right thought" (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), it refers to contemplating and deliberating with untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*). Regarding "right speech" (*samyagvāc*)...
"Right speech" means that one's mouth does not utter deviant words. "Right action" means cultivating all pure deeds. "Right effort" means abandoning deviant ascetic practices.
"Right concentration" means seeking untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative absorption. "Right mindfulness" means being mindful of the factors that assist the Path.
"Right livelihood" means avoiding the five kinds of wrong livelihood. Regarding the five wrong livelihoods, the first is:
1. Out of desire for gain and offerings, falsely manifesting wonders and marvels; 2. Out of desire for gain and offerings, personally proclaiming one's own merits; 3.

Out of desire for gain and offerings, divining good and bad fortune through physiognomy and omens while preaching the Dharma to others; 4. Out of desire for gain and offerings, raising one’s voice and displaying an air of authority to cause others to feel awe;
5. Out of desire for gain and offerings, speaking of the offerings one has received in order to stir the emotions of others.

However, as for the names and numbers of the Four Truths listed above, they apply generally to the three lower teachings;

it is only that they differ according to the breadth or narrowness, superiority or inferiority, and whether they involve birth-and-death, non-arising, the immeasurable, or the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskāra) of those respective teachings. Therefore, their names and numbers will not be listed again below.

Second, as previously stated, the following demonstrates that the names of the Four Truths apply to the Mahāyāna. Regarding "names and numbers": the names—suffering (*duḥkha*), accumulation (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*)—are themselves the numbers.
Regarding "broad and narrow": the objects of the Four Truths in the *Zàng* (Āgama) and *Tōng* (Shared) teachings consist only of the six dharma-realms, which is termed "narrow.

The objects of the Truths in the *Bié* (Distinct) and *Yuán* (Perfect) teachings encompass all ten realms, which is termed "broad. Regarding "superior and inferior": [the text continues as follows:]... [The text provided ends here; the translation reflects the available portion.]
Because the *zang* (treasury) is distinctively clumsy, it is termed "inferior" (*lie*); because it is pervasive, perfect, and skillful, it is termed "superior" (*sheng*).

Furthermore, when the four teachings are compared with one another, only the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) is uniquely superior. Regarding the term "non-arising" (*wusheng*): because delusion regarding the Truth is slight, it receives its name from principle (*li*).

What is meant by "from principle"? It refers to non-arising. This is what is called the absence of the characteristic of oppression in Suffering (*duḥkha*), and the absence of accumulation in Origination (*samudaya*).

The mark of non-conjunction is the cessation of the mark of arising; the path is the mark of non-duality precisely because the matters of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path are themselves the true principle (*tattva*).

Therefore, from the absence of oppression in suffering up to the non-duality of the path—since these are the true principle—how could there be anything contrary or compliant within the true principle?
For this reason, the matters of suffering, its origin, and so forth are designated as [the Four Noble Truths].
"Arising and arising is non-arising. Because non-arising is the principle (*li*), it is said that "non-arising" receives its name from the principle.

As for "immeasurable," because it is heavy within delusion, it receives its name from phenomena (*shi*). That which is called suffering has immeasurable aspects, as the fruits of the ten realms are not the same;
the accumulation [of suffering] has immeasurable aspects, as the causes of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsa*) differ.

The cessation of existence possesses immeasurable marks, for the various *pāramitās* are not one; the Path possesses immeasurable marks, for there are distinct *dharmamukhas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To speak of "non-action" (*akṛtya*) is because it is a minor matter within delusion; thus it receives its name from the perspective of ultimate principle.

That which is called the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all suchness (*tathatā*); there is no suffering (*duḥkha*) to be abandoned. Worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) are fundamentally pure; there is no origin (*samudaya*) to be eliminated. Extremes and heterodoxy—[are likewise empty].
Within this, there is no Middle Way to be cultivated and no birth-and-death to be transcended; nirvana is such that there is no extinction to be realized.

Therefore, regarding the matters of suffering and its origin, if one acts with purposeful effort, then within those very phenomena, one abides in the Middle—free from thought, free from recollection, and free from contrived activity.

Because one abides in the Middle, there is no suffering to be abandoned, nor is there anything such as original purity to be attained; thus it is called "non-action" (*anabhisamskāra*). Question: [What is] the wondrous?
The *Xuanyun* states: "Because one is deluded regarding *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*, there are *duḥkha* (suffering) and *samudaya* (origination);

because one understands *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*, these are called *mārga* (path) and *nirodha* (cessation). Is this the same as or different from the "unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) Four Noble Truths" of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*?

Answer: Although it speaks of "delusion" and "understanding," delusion and understanding are themselves the Middle Way; therefore, they are termed "unconditioned. Thus, the *Miaoxuan* says: "It is precisely within phenomena..."
Yet within this, there is no one who creates or acts. Delusion is practicing in opposition to the Way, while awakening is practicing in accordance with it.
These two modes of practice—opposition and accord—are themselves the phenomena; the name "non-action" is applied specifically to their underlying principle.

How could the phenomena, which are the principle itself, be hindered by the distinctions between the opposition and accord of delusion and awakening? It is precisely the principle within these phenomena that is called "without thought" and "without creative action. Nevertheless...
The principle-inclusion is precisely the phenomena of the principle; delusion and awakening are non-dual because they are identical to the principle.

Thus, the Profound [Mystery] and *Zhi-guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) are the same and not different. Since people’s ways of maintaining their doctrines vary in many ways, those with discernment should rely upon the ancestral teachings.
Nevertheless, within the Four Noble Truths, the first two truths are categorized as worldly cause and effect (the fruit of suffering and the cause of accumulation),
while the latter two truths are categorized as supramundane cause and effect (the fruit of cessation and the cause of the path).
Third, regarding the four truths, the section explaining their causes and effects is divided into two parts; first, the actual presentation.
Question: Why are the worldly and supramundane [truths] presented with the effect first and the cause second?
The second section, "Distinguishing the Two," is divided into two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. [The question:
"Why is it so? [The answer: "Because the faculties of the śrāvakas are dull; they know suffering and sever the origin, aspiring for the fruit and practicing the cause.

Regarding the second part, the answer: "Because the faculties of the śrāvakas are dull, they know suffering, etc. This contrasts with the sharp faculties of the pratyekabuddhas, for whom the cause comes first and the fruit follows.
Those of keen faculties first sever the cause, whereby the fruit of suffering is naturally extinguished; those of dull faculties only recognize suffering and then begin to sever its cause.
Why is this? Because Śrāvakas must first fully comprehend the fruit of suffering within the twenty-five realms of existence before they sever the cause of accumulation (saṃudaya).
Furthermore, aspiring to the fruit of unconditioned cessation (nirodha-satya), they then cultivate the cause of untainted cultivation (mārga-satya).

However, this discussion of the sequence of cause and effect is based on the Śrāvaka vehicle; it cannot be used to determine the sequence for the three types of Four Noble Truths—Shared, Distinct, and Perfect.

As stated in the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), in the case of the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-satya*), the fruit comes first and the cause follows;

furthermore, because cessation (*nirodha*) occurs before the Path (*mārga*), cessation is placed later. In contrast, both the Unarisen (*anutpāda*) and the Immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) truths state that suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) come first.

The Path, Cessation, Non-action, and the Four Truths of Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Path; furthermore, as in the "Chapter on the Four Truths" of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, they are likewise listed only as suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path.
The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) further explains their sequence by stating that the fruit is coarse and thus placed first, while the cause is subtle and thus placed later.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* says: "For those of dull faculties in the Hīnayāna, one cultivates the cause in view of the fruit; [the order is] cessation first, then the path."

Regarding the path of those of sharp faculties in the Middle Vehicle: before the cessation of the former [stage], the latter does not yet exist. This is explained in the context of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
It is said that a *śrāvaka* practices the cause while carrying the fruit, whereas a *pratyekabuddha* practices the cause while looking toward the fruit.

While for a *śrāvaka*, one practices the cause of the second fruit while carrying the first fruit—and likewise for the second and third fruits—for a *pratyekabuddha*, the practice of cultivation is not established as having partial fruits.
Therefore, one should practice the causes with the hope of attaining the fruit; the application of the text must not be restricted.

third, the contemplation of counting the breath for sentient beings with excessive distraction; fourth, the contemplation of dependent origination for sentient beings with excessive ignorance; fifth, the contemplation of the Buddha’s mindfulness for sentient beings with many obstacles.

Second, the first five [stages] and the subsequent explanation of the stages are divided into two parts. First, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is divided into two. First, the explanation is further divided into two.
First, the external ordinary person (*bāhya-pṛthagjana*) is divided into three. First, the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-vasthāna-citta-sthāpana*):

what is explained in the Tripiṭaka Teaching as the settling of the mind—the seven worthies (*saptakalyāṇa*) and the seven sages (*saptārya*)—is taught based on the "existence gate" (*bhāva-mukha*) of the *Abhidharma-śāstra*. These categories listed in the *Wu tingxin miaoxuan* and the *Zhijiao miaomiao* do not differ from those presented now, except that they take *ānāpāna-smṛti* (counting the breaths) as the initial stage. If, within the *Wei miaozhong* [section]:

It merely mentions the five *sthāpanā* (cessations) without listing them in full; the *Śīzhǎn* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) points to their location in the section on "Counteracting" (*pratipakṣa*) in the seventh fascicle of the *Zhìguān* (Meditation and Insight).

Therefore, my current commentary relies largely upon the *Zhìguān*’s main text. Within the Four Teachings (*sijiao*), it simply mentions the "expedient means of the realms" (*dhātu-upāya*) and does not establish a separate "Buddha-recollection" (*buddhānusmṛti*) gate.

Question: Why is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) not established as the first? Answer: If one follows the followers of the numerical school (*saṃkhyā-vādin*), [the sequence is as follows...]
If one takes the contemplation of impurity as the beginning because it distinguishes the sequence according to the gate of dhyāna, then counting the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is placed first.

However, since these methods follow the specific ailments of individuals, how could their order be fixed? The five *sthāpanās* listed in the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* are largely identical to those in the *Miaoxuan*;
however, the "expedient means regarding the realms" (*dhātu-upāya*) for treating the affliction of selfhood is placed fourth.

One must not overlook the similarities and differences among various texts. *Miaoxuan* states: "Because there is concentration (*samādhi*), it is called 'stopping' (*ting*); because there is wisdom (*prajñā*), it is called 'contemplation' (*guan*.

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it says they are called "stopping" because they involve abiding in purity. *Weimingxuan* states: "Stopping means to cease [distractions].
This refers precisely to cultivating the five dharmas and abiding in the cessation of the five faults. One must understand that this is a conceptual visualization (*parikalpita-saṃjñā*).

The "Aids to the Path" (bodhipakṣya-dharma) and the contemplation of the body as impure within the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*) differ from the correct contemplation of reality.
For sentient beings with excessive greed, the practitioner of impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) conceives of a woman’s beauty as a worm-infested pus-filled corpse;
if lust does not cease, he conceives of her as having a snake’s mouth; if he craves edible food, he conceives of it as worms; and if he craves delicious soup, he conceives of it as filth.
One should conceive of liquids as milk and curd; one should conceive of the marrow and brain as being the garments one is attached to, and conceive of those garments as skin.
Furthermore, there are four types of objects of attachment: first, visible color; second, shape; third, exquisite touch; and fourth, service.

One should apply the contemplation of impurity to each of these. When the contemplation of impurity is perfected, the perversion of regarding the impure as pure is extinguished. Moreover, there are the four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding the gate of contemplating impurity (*aśubha*), there are the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), among others.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that none of those who practice the contemplation of impurity can conceive of the Buddha’s body as impure, because the Buddha’s body is free from defilement;
only the Buddha himself is able to perform the contemplation of impurity regarding his own body.
Regarding the object of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) for sentient beings who are prone to anger, there are three types of objects: enemies, friends, and neutral persons.
Since each of these—enemies and friends—is further divided into three categories (superior, middling, and inferior), and there are also neutral persons, there are seven types of objects.
To each of these seven objects, one bestows three kinds of happiness (superior, middling, and inferior). Thus, the *Abhidharma* states that loving-kindness arises from [the category of] friends.
This means that from the moment one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one establishes all sentient beings into three categories: enemies, friends, and neutral parties.
Furthermore, one distinguishes these into superior, middling, and inferior grades. First, one directs genuine aspiration toward superior friends—namely, one's parents and other respected elders.
Because they have long practiced evil, one must cultivate a mind of benefit and eventually bring about a mind of gathering them in.

The perception of benefit is thus; it continues in this manner until even toward one's greatest enemy, one attains right and correct abiding, which is called the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*).
Compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are likewise. Equanimity, moreover, arises from neutral persons. In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), it says:

"What is meant is that when first practicing, one causes one's superior relatives to attain lower happiness; next, one practices so as to cause superior relatives to attain middle happiness and neutral relatives to attain lower happiness."
One practices joy in succession so that those who are superior kinsmen obtain superior joy, those who are middling kinsmen obtain middling joy, and those who are inferior kinsmen obtain inferior joy.
Next, one practices so that middling kinsmen obtain superior joy, inferior kinsmen obtain middling joy, and neutral persons obtain inferior joy.
Next, one practices so that inferior kinsmen obtain superior joy, neutral persons obtain middling joy, and inferior enemies obtain inferior joy. Next, one practices [further].
First, one practices so that neutral persons obtain superior happiness, those with inferior enmity obtain middling happiness, and those with middling enmity obtain inferior happiness.
Next, one practices so that those with inferior enmity obtain superior happiness, those with middling enmity obtain middling happiness, and those with superior enmity obtain inferior happiness.

Next, one practices so that those with middling enmity obtain superior happiness and those with superior enmity obtain middling happiness. Finally, one practices so that even those with superior enmity obtain superior happiness; this is the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Since this is so for compassion and joy, it is likewise for equanimity (*upekṣā*). When cultivating the mind of equanimity, one begins with neutral persons.

If one were to first abandon attachment toward kin, there is the fear that craving might arise; if one were to first abandon resentment toward enemies, there is the fear that anger might arise. Therefore, one cultivates equanimity starting from neutral persons.
Among enemies and kin, enemies are easier to abandon [with regard to equanimity], and thus one next abandons the enemy. Among enemies, one first abandons those who have caused the greatest harm.
Next, regarding the intermediate [level], it is next to abandon those who were previously close; next, the middle; and finally, the superior. In the *Vibhāṣā*, it is asked:
"To what place of happiness does one grant sentient beings? The answer is: some say it is the happiness of the third dhyāna, because it is the most excellent among forms of happiness.

Others say it is the happiness of the four requisites, because one has already experienced them. Still others say it is the happiness belonging to places where one has previously practiced, up until...

Regarding the contemplation practiced while dwelling in one's station to attain the Mahāyāna, some say: "Among the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, and others, who are the 'superior,' 'middling,' and 'inferior' objects of affection?
To the question of what persons are indicated by the terms "enemy," "relative," and "neutral person," the answer is:

the "superior relative" refers to one's parents; the "superior enemy" refers to those who have harmed one's parents. The "middling relative" refers to one's brothers; the "middling enemy" refers to those who have harmed one's brothers.
"Lower" refers to one's own kinsmen; "lower hostile kinsmen" refers to those who cause harm. "Middle persons" refers to ordinary friends—those who are neither hostile nor kin.

Regarding the "counting of breaths" (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) for the many scattered sentient beings: this is the oral instruction on the entrance to dhyāna. In the *Dhyānapāramitā*, it clarifies that there is [breath].
The four are: first, wind (*vāyu*); second, qi; third, panting (*chuan*); and fourth, breathing (*xi*). That which has sound is called wind; that which is congealed and obstructed is called qi;
that where inhalation and exhalation are incomplete is called panting; that which is neither sounding nor obstructed, where inhalation and exhalation are both complete, is called breathing.

It is like a continuous thread that seems to exist. To guard panting leads to exhaustion; to guard qi leads to obstruction; to guard wind leads to dispersion; to guard breathing leads to stabilization. A Master said: "First..."
Counting the exhalations prevents the breath from becoming strained and the body from feeling distended; it makes the body and mind light and agile, facilitating entry into *samādhi*.

Some masters say that one should first count the inhalations, for by following the breath inward, one easily enters meditative concentration, cuts off external objects, and the physical strength becomes light.
Other masters say that there is no fixed rule regarding inhalation or exhalation, as one should follow what is most convenient. This concludes the preceding discussion.

In both cases, neither is permitted; since counting both [the inhalation and exhalation] together gives rise to affliction, one should cease this. The mind that performs the counting is the "counter," while the breath is the object to be counted.
Controlling the mind by counting from one to ten so that it does not become distracted is called "counting the breath" (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

If one counts fewer than ten, or reaches eleven, these are all instances where the counting of the breath has increased or decreased, resulting in a failure of skillful means in the practice of counting the breath.

Because the mind is not distracted, it easily enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*); thus, the contemplation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-vipaśyanā*) for deluded sentient beings, as well as the cessation of delusion and the purification of the mind, are fully present in various texts, which need not be recorded here in detail.
Deluded sentient beings, regarding the contemplation of causes and conditions, are confused and inverted; failing to understand causes and conditions, they deny their existence.

When the fruit of delusion arises and one wishes to remedy this deluded mind, one must observe the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the three periods, two periods, or a single thought-moment, as explained in detail in the various expositions of the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequence of the Dharma Realm). Furthermore, the contemplations for remedying delusion are not uniform;
for instance, the *Abhidharma* states that practitioners who adhere to views employ the "expedient means of the realms" (*dhātu-upāya*).
As an antidote to the delusion of fools— who, failing to understand that the five aggregates (*skandha*) are an accumulation of afflictions resulting from past karma,

and being thus bewildered, conceive of a self within conditions— there are times when they practice by drawing near to spiritual friends, hearing the true Dharma, and giving rise to correct reflection.
They are then able to analyze and break down their own bodies through the method of the elements (*dhātu*), namely the six kinds of elements such as earth and so forth.
Furthermore, the earth element is moistened by the water element so that they do not separate; the water element is supported by the earth element so that it does not flow away;
the fire element matures [it] so that it does not become stagnant or decay; the wind element moves [it] so that it may increase;
the space element is empty so that food may enter and exit; and because of the presence of the consciousness element, one is then able to perform [actions].

Because all things arise from a multitude of conditions, they are entirely devoid of self. According to the Mahā-sūtra, those who are strongly attached to the notion of self should analytically discern the eighteen *dhātus*.

This distinguishes between the general and specific categories of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*). In the Abhidharma-śāstra, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute half of the ten material *dhātus*;
the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) constitutes half of the seven mental *dhātus*; and an additional single element, the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*), is added.
The sutra is slightly different; however, if one follows the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, it refutes the self by means of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Causes and conditions refute the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; because the three times are a continuous succession, there is no annihilation. Because the three times pass away in alternation, there is no eternity.
Furthermore, the past refutes eternity, the future refutes annihilation, and the present simultaneously refutes both annihilation and eternity regarding cause and effect.

Regarding the analysis of the two worlds: how is it that the twelve links of dependent origination are complete within the present and future worlds? One conceives attachment toward the father and aversion toward the mother;

this is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). When the father’s body is left behind, one claims it as one's own; this is termed "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). [The remaining links] up to old age and death should be understood through reflection.
Of these, the first ten belong to the present, and the final two belong to the future; one should examine them therein.
How can there be a self? By means of a single moment of causal conditions, one shatters the attachment to its nature; thus, within a single moment of mind, the twelve [links] are complete.
Because one sees forms with the eyes and gives rise to craving, this is ignorance; the creation of karma is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so on until old age and death.
Therefore, when one understands causal conditions, the attachment to nature perishes. This is the abandonment of clinging to a self, as well as the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Regarding the nature of these three types [of delusion], which one is actually "ignorance"? The teaching gates differ according to the specific remedies applied to various capacities;
however, according to the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, it is specifically through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that ignorance is treated. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks:
"The twelve links of dependent origination are profound and difficult to see; if ignorant people cannot even comprehend shallow and proximate teachings, how much less can they understand this?"
Again, it is said: "Observe dependent origination. In response, it is said: A "deluded person" does not refer to one who is as ignorant as cattle or sheep;
rather, this refers to a person who, while seeking the path of the Buddha, gives rise to various false views due to their initial observations.
Such a deluded person should observe dependent origination. This observation of dependent origination is the same as the observation of dependent origination practiced by a Pratyekabuddha.
The meaning of these differs: here, it is merely the contemplation that serves as an auxiliary to the Path, whereas the Pratyekabuddha possesses the correct contemplation of dependent origination.

Furthermore, this [contemplation] briefly observes the causes and conditions of the three periods of time to remedy ignorance, while the Pratyekabuddha, possessing sharp wisdom, contemplates the causes and conditions of hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, both in direct and reverse order.

Regarding sentient beings with many hindrances who practice the contemplation of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*): if within the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is called the "hindrance of sleep";

if in the context of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, it is called the "hindrance of oppressive circumstances. As for the "hindrance of sleep," when this hindrance arises, one must contemplate the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Sambhogakāya Buddha;
once the object of focus becomes clear, one can immediately break through the hindrance. As for the "hindrance of oppressive circumstances," [it refers to] practicing...

When in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if the body suddenly experiences pain, or if one perceives oneself as being headless or limbless, or if external objects such as earth, water, fire, and so forth appear as oppressive phenomena, one should reflect:
"The Dharma-Buddha is signless (*animitta*) and formless (*arūpa*); how could there be any objective realm (*viṣaya*) to cause oppression?

In the *Cidi Chanmen* (Successive Stages of Meditation), it is said that there are three primary obstacles: first, dullness and mental obstruction (*styāna-middha*). Regarding the obstacle of dullness: [text continues].
The Buddha of Response (Nirmāṇakāya) cures the two evil thoughts; the Buddha of Contemplation (Sambhogakāya) cures the three afflictions of being oppressed by sensory objects;

and the Dharma-Buddha (Dharmakāya) cures those [afflictions]. Furthermore, the text establishes greed, anger, and delusion, along with distraction, as the objects to be cured, each having three corresponding remedies.

I have not cited them all here. The mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) explained in the *Xuánzàng* and the *Zhǐguān* is identical to the present text. This is also the case regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
Question: Why does the *Yunjie fangbian* (Cloud-Realm Expedient Means) omit the treatment of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*)? Answer:

Because it establishes the gateway of the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*), it does not establish the gateway of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The six perfections require the application of causal conditions and antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

Mindfulness of the Buddha serves as an antidote for the oppression of objective realms. What has been shown above is based on [the principle of] antidotes; if one were to apply a transformative antidote, [the six perfections would be required].
As clarified in the *Mahāyāna-śāstra*, for those with excessive greed, one teaches the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); for those with excessive anger, impurity (*aśubha*);

and for those with excessive delusion, contemplation on the finite and the infinite (*antānantya*). If these are not applied as remedies but rather the opposite, the result can be understood accordingly.

If the afflictions are treated simultaneously—whether two or three—the medicines must likewise be two or three. For example, if one possesses both desire and anger, one must employ [the appropriate antidotes].

Purifying the compassionate mind treats them; as for treating them through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is through the correct contemplation of the dharma-nature that all illnesses are treated.
This principle is explained in detail in the *Chanmen* and the *Zhi guan*; students should seek it therein.
2. The Foundation of Mindfulness of Specific Characteristics (as in the four foundations of mindfulness mentioned previously).
2. The foundation of mindfulness of specific characteristics has already been explained in the preceding section on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
3. The Foundation of Mindfulness of General Characteristics: contemplating the body as impure, and that sensation, mind, and phenomena are all impure, up to the contemplation of phenomena.

There is no self in the body, sensation, or mind, and likewise no self in between; this should be understood by analogy. (The three preceding sections are called the stage of the outer ordinary person, also known as the stage of equipment. Third, the mindfulness of general characteristics:

the present text clarifies only the generality of the object while briefly omitting the analysis of the particularity of the object and the generality of the contemplation. Why is this? For one practicing the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it is necessary to clarify four propositions: first, the generality of the object; second, the particularity of the contemplation; third, both [generality and particularity]; and fourth, neither. Herein, the object and the contemplation are both general. What is meant by this? In cultivating the foundations of mindfulness, one must clearly understand these four categories: first, the generality of the object; second, the particularity of the contemplation; third, both; and fourth, neither. In this case, the object and the contemplation are both general.
1. "Distinct" refers to mindfulness of distinct characteristics; 2. "Total observation of both objects" is as in the present passage; 3. "Distinct observation of both objects" is as when it says:
one contemplates the body as impure, contemplates the body as suffering, contemplates the body as impermanent, and contemplates the body as non-self;
as it is with the body, so it is for all [objects] up to contemplating phenomena as non-self; 4. "Total observation of both objects through contemplation."
This means that just as one observes a single object, one simultaneously sees four objects; just as one employs a single contemplation, one is fully equipped with four contemplations.
Thus, when object and contemplation are each distinct, they are already shallow and coarse; the latter three phrases are even more profound and subtle.
Therefore, it is said that "object and contemplation reach four. Regarding the terms "general" and "particular": taking one as the particular and four as the general—if [it concerns] the object...
If one observes that there is no disagreement [regarding this], the term "three categories" (*skandha*) refers to sections or divisions, much like chapters or segments.
It has not yet seen the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena); because its mental activities do not transcend the principles of ordinary existence, it is called an "external ordinary person.

As for the term "provisions" (*sambhāra*), it is established by way of analogy: just as a person traveling a long distance must necessarily prepare provisions for their life and sustenance, so too does the practitioner [require these].
It is likewise: those who wish to transcend the three realms must cultivate the five *smṛtyupasthānas* as provisions to nourish the life-force of the fivefold *dharmakāya*.

Second, regarding the clarification of the inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are four stages, namely: *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*. (These four stages constitute the inner ordinary beings and are also termed the stage of application [*prayogamārga*]. Furthermore...)
This is called the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).

Second, regarding the "inner ordinary person" (*adhyātma-prthagjana*): because their minds gradually perceive the *dharmatā* and roam within the principle, they are termed "inner. "Ordinary" (*prthagjana*) here means "constant.

Thus, these inner ordinary persons naturally comprise four stages; those at the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) will certainly reach *nirvāṇa*, and those at the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) never again sever the roots of goodness.

Patience (*kṣānti*) prevents falling into the evil realms; the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) brings about liberation from birth. Regarding the stages of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*): there is one [level] called "Lower";

for "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), there are two, namely "Lower" and "Middle"; for "Patience," there are three, namely "Lower," "Middle," and "Upper. For the "Supreme Worldly Dharma," there is one, namely "Upper. These are fully explained as in the *Miaoxuan* and other treatises.
As for the single stage of "Heat," it is established by way of analogy; it is like using [a fire-drill] to produce fire.
Because the fire has not yet manifested despite the practice being uninterrupted, there is first the sign of warmth (*ūṣmagata*). Thus, the Abhidharma says:
"Wisdom regarding the objects of knowledge is like the friction of two fire-drills; it is able to exhaustively investigate all existence until the fire of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises.
For this reason, it is called 'warmth. Furthermore, just as gathering flowers in the summer produces a warm vapor, so too is it for the practitioner."

By applying oneself to the aforementioned foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) without ceasing, although the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*) has not yet been personally realized, a sign like the heat of a fire appears first;
therefore, it is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). One should know that this stage of Heat possesses two meanings: first, it is a stage where one departs from the realms and planes (*dhātu-bhūmi*);
second, it is a stage where one may still fall back. However, at this stage, the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are not severed. Second is the stage of the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), which occupies...

Because it is superior to the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat), it is called *mūrdhan* (Summit). Thus, the Abhidharma states that these immovable roots of goodness (*akopya-kuśalamūla*) abide at this summit;
because they are free from all faults, one is able to enter into *kṣānti* (Patience). If it were otherwise, one would regress and remain at the stage of *uṣmagata*.
It is like a person climbing a mountain: if they do not reach the summit, they fall to the four sides. Therefore, there are those who regress from the stage of the Summit, for [it is] due to...
When practitioners come to dwell in the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*), many afflictions arise and they may regress.

Those who do not regress are practitioners who, externally, draw near to virtuous friends, and internally, increase their practice of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) while seeking higher stages; therefore, they do not fall back.
Regarding the three stages of patience (*kṣānti*), the *Abhidharma* asks: "What is the meaning of 'patience'? It answers: "It is that [the practitioner] regarding the Four Truths..."
Because it constantly increases the practice of equanimity and the desire for joy, it is called patience (*kṣānti*).

Furthermore, one should know that the endurance of the desire for the Dharma of the Four Truths is termed patience. Moreover, patience is so named because of its acceptance, subduing, and forbearance.
Once the wisdom of contemplation is profound, all karmas and afflictions are accepted and subdued so that they do not arise; this is patience.

Within this stage, it is further divided into three: first, "Lower Patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), which takes the four truths across the upper and lower realms of the triple world as its object and the thirty-two aspects (*ākāra*) as its cognitive faculty;

each of these is clearly and perfectly understood without error—namely, that the truth of suffering in the desire realm is suffering, empty, impermanent, and selfless, and the same applies to the form and formless realms.
The arising of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) in the desire realm through causes and conditions occurs likewise in the higher realms;

the cessation of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) through the sublime detachment from all exhaustion occurs likewise in the higher realms; the path of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) as the correct track and vehicle occurs likewise in the higher realms.

To perform this universal contemplation of the eight truths and thirty-two aspects within the three realms is called "Lower Patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). One then contemplates the dependent origination of the aggregates (*skandha*).

That which is called impermanence, being oppressed by impermanence, is called suffering (*duḥkha*). The disappearance of the characteristics of identity and difference is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The cessation of "self" and "what belongs to self" is called non-self (*anātman*). Because it can bring about the fruit of suffering, it is called accumulation (*samudaya*).

Because one contemplates the six causes, it is called cause (*hetu*). Because one illuminates the four conditions, it is called condition (*pratyaya*). Because it brings about the suffering of future existence, it is called origination.
It is called "Arising" because it gives rise to all things; it is called "Cessation" because it exhausts all suffering; it is called "Extinction" because it extinguishes all afflictions;
it is called "Nirvāṇa" because it is the supreme state; it is called "Sublime" because it transcends birth and death; it is called "Departure" because it can reach Nirvāṇa;
it is called the "Path" because it is a non-perverted dharma; and it is called "Right" because it is the sphere of activity for the noble ones.
Because it functions as a trace-vehicle leading to the three liberations, it is called a "vehicle" (yāna). The old interpretation states: "Emptiness, exhaustion, and the correct trace-vehicle.

The new interpretation states: "Impurity, tranquility, suchness, practice, and emergence. There is further detailed discrimination, which is roughly as explained in the second fascicle of the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary).

Regarding the "two kinds of patience" (*kṣānti*): this must be discussed in terms of the reduction of objects (*ālambana*) and the reduction of practices (*caryā*). "Reduction" means contraction. "Objects" refers to the objective spheres of focus, namely the three [realms].

Regarding the "eight truths" as the objects of the practitioner's contemplation: the practices that take these as their cognitive objects are the [contemplations] of suffering, emptiness, and so forth, under each of the eight truths.

Since the four truths of the desire realm are discussed individually, while those of the form and formless realms are discussed collectively, there are eight truths that serve as the objective domain.
Under each truth, there are four modes of contemplation; thus, with four for each of the eight, there are thirty-two modes of contemplation in total.
It is held that if the objects of the cognitive modes (*ākāra*) are reduced, all others are likewise reduced;
however, only the *duḥkha-satya* (suffering) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is absolutely impossible to reduce, as it must be retained to serve as the objective support (*ālambana*).

If the cognitive modes are reduced, among the thirty-two modes there are eight whose names are identical to those of the objects, and these are also reduced along with the objects. Therefore, [only]...
It is said that there are twenty-four lines under each of the Four Truths; the remaining [truths] are likewise reduced [by four], leaving only four lines under the Suffering of the Desire Realm.
Why is this? It is because among practitioners, there are those who cling to views and those who cling to craving.
Among those with sharp faculties who cling to views, there are further two types: first, those who cling to a self and remain in ignorance (*avidyā*).
When one practices the three [remaining] modes of conduct as an antidote, the other three must be diminished.
Second, regarding attachment to "mine": one remains with the practice of emptiness as the antidote, while the other three are also diminished.
Regarding attachment to craving, which has dull roots, there are further two types: first, attachment to pride, for which one remains with the practice of impermanence as the antidote.

The remaining three practices are also diminished. Second, regarding the attachment to indolence and the retention of ascetic practices as a remedy, the remaining three practices are likewise diminished.
This is called the seven cycles of diminishing conditions and the twenty-three cycles of diminishing practices.
What are their characteristics? One should know that they begin from the Truth of Suffering of the Desire Realm, and proceed next to the Form and Formless Realms.
First, the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the realms; second, the truths of origin (*samudaya-satya*) of the desire realm; third, the truths of origin of the form and formless realms;

fourth, the truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) of the desire realm; fifth, the truths of cessation of the form and formless realms; sixth, the truths of the path (*mārga-satya*) of the desire realm;
and seventh, the truths of the path of the form and formless realms. From this point, for the four [truths] below the path, one reduces the practice by one vehicle (*yāna*) at a time.
Furthermore, by observing the Truth of Suffering in the Desire Realm, one eliminates the seven conditions across the upper and lower realms until only one mode of practice remains;
observing the suffering of the Desire Realm with two moments of mind is called the stage of Middle Patience (madhyā-kṣānti).

Third, as for Superior Patience (adhimātrā-kṣānti), one further cultivates the observation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) until there is only one mode of practice and one moment of mind observing the suffering of the Desire Realm.
It is called the stage of Supreme Patience (*adhimātrākṣānti*) because it is the foremost among the four stages of the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Thus, the *Abhidharma* states:
"It is the foremost in the world, hence it is called the Worldly Supreme. This [stage] also takes a single object (*ālambana*), a single mode of activity (*ākāra*), and a single momentary mind;
because it further increases and excels within the stage of Supreme Patience, it is the Worldly Supreme. This Worldly Supreme is distinguished with respect to a single individual.

Thus, there are no three grades when considering them in relation to many individuals; rather, they are divided into three grades: Śāriputra is superior, Maudgalyāyana is middling, and all others are inferior.

Following the World-First Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), one gives rise to the Receptivity to the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). This Receptivity to the Dharma of Suffering consists of sixteen moments.

Starting from the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there is one receptivity and one knowledge at each stage, following their respective order, until the time of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), where it first arises.

The arising of one patience (*kṣānti*) is called the fifteenth moment of mind; the subsequent arising of one knowledge (*jñāna*) is called the sixteenth moment of mind, which is the first fruit (*phala*).

Regarding these sixteen moments of mind: under each of the [four] truths, there is one dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) and one dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), as well as one subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and one subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Thus, under the eight truths, there are eight patiences and eight knowledges; these are termed the ten untainted (*anāsrava*) moments.

When the six minds have exhausted the afflictions of the views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) pertaining to the four truths, this constitutes the first fruit (*srota-āpanna*). The "patience" (*kṣānti*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) regarding the form and formless realms are termed "inference" (*anumāna*).

As for the term "preparatory practice" (*prayoga*), it means that since one has already cultivated the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) among the external ordinary persons (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), at this stage of the internal ordinary persons (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*), one merely increases the power and practice of those foundations of mindfulness. Regarding the term "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*), it refers to the cultivation of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*)...
These are the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

The aforementioned stages of the inner ordinary beings (*adhyātma-prthagjana*) and the outer ordinary beings (*bahirdhā-prthagjana*) are collectively termed the "ordinary stage" (*prthagjana-bhūmi*), and are also called the "stage of the seven preparatory practices" (*saptavidha-upāya-bhūmi*).

Second, the preceding summary states that they are called "preparatory practices" (*upāya*) because they are so named from the perspective of progressing toward [the goal]. These are the seven [stages] above.

This stage is the expedient means for entering the first fruit (srotāpanna); it is also called the "Seven Worthies" (*sapta-kalyāṇa*). "Worthy" (*kalyāṇa*) means "virtuous," referring to those who are adjacent to the sages.

Next, the stages of the sages are explained, which are also divided into three: first, the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*, the first fruit); second, the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*, the second and third fruits); and third, the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).
(4) The Four Fruits.

Second, the division of the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*) is twofold: first, regarding the "Path of Seeing" (*darśanamārga*), this refers to the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) that perceives the principle of the True Truths;

second, regarding the "Path of Cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*), this refers to the repeated cultivation of the untainted path; third, regarding the "Path of No-More-Learning" (*aśaikṣamārga*), this refers to the analytical discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
To investigate the ultimate reality is called "learning" (*śaikṣa*); when delusions are exhausted and the ultimate truth is fully realized, it is called "beyond learning" (*aśaikṣa*).

The *Abhidharmasamaya-śāstra* clarifies that the path of seeing consists of sixteen moments of mind, which constitutes the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). The second fruit is merely the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Since all the *Abhidharma* treatises clarify that the path of seeing occurs within fifteen moments of mind and the path of cultivation begins at the sixteenth moment, it is said that the path consists of sixteen moments of mind.

The *srotāpanna* who realizes through the application of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)—the term *srotāpanna* here being translated as "cultivating the untainted" (*anāsrava*)—is now examined in detail:
if it is said that the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) consists of fifteen moments of mind, this is stated with reference to the beginning;

if it is said that the path of seeing consists of sixteen moments of mind, this is discussed according to the conclusion. The same applies to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). As the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "The three stages abandon the views."

Regarding the first four stages (*bhūmi*), one speaks of the abandonment of views; regarding the latter, one uses the example of the sixteen moments of mind to speak of the paths of seeing and cultivation, etc.

In the present text, the path of seeing is taken as the first fruit, following the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā*. One should know that there are seven stages within the noble state (*ārya-avasthā*): first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*);
second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—these are the dull and sharp-witted persons who enter the path of seeing during the fifteen moments; third, the one of faith...
Having understood the four views and attained the five bodies of realization, one enters the path of cultivation through the stages of faith and dharma-practice.

This includes the Arhat liberated at six times and the Arhat liberated not dependent on time; these correspond to entering the path of no-more-learning through the stages of faith and dharma-practice.

In the *Miaoxuan*, the seven sages are explained as follows: "Sage" (*ārya*) means correctness. When the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) clearly arises, one abandons the state of an ordinary person and enters the state of a sage, perceiving the truth.

Regarding this principle, Jingxi said: "Those who abandon the mundane and enter the sacred, having reached the stage of 'patience with suffering' (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*), will necessarily enter the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*) through an immediate succession.

Now, speaking from the perspective of the latter [the general definition], it is said that 'the sacred' (*ārya*) applies generally; thus, the first two stages among the seven types of noble ones (*saptāryapudgala*)—both consisting of fifteen moments of mind—are designated as 'sacred' when one reaches the sixteenth moment of the first fruit. If one were to speak directly [of the specific case]..."
Regarding the fifteen moments of mind, one is not yet called a noble one (ārya) and remains within the causal stage;
