therefore, although all sixteen moments of mind are untainted (anāsrava), they are designated as "approaching" (pratipannaka) only up to the fifteenth moment.
First, the *srotāpanna* (translated here as "Stream-enterer"): at this stage, one has severed the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the three realms that are abandoned through insight;
because one perceives the True Truths, it is called the Path of Insight (*darśana-mārga*), and it is also termed the Stage of the Noble Ones (*ārya-bhūmi*).

The second section, the "Explanation of the Categories," is divided into three parts. First, regarding the statement on the Path of Seeing: "The Stream-enterer" refers to one who has first entered the stream of the Dharma of the Noble Path toward Nirvana.

The commentary explains that the name "stream" (*srotas*) for the first fruit has both a reverse and a forward sense. The stream of birth and death is the "reverse" stream, which the *Srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) opposes;

the "forward" stream is the stream of the Path, which the *Srotāpanna* follows. Thus, there are two types of streams. Regarding the first, the stream of birth and death, the *Srotāpanna* goes against it. Regarding the second, the stream of the Path, the *Srotāpanna* flows with it.
Because one enters this stream, the meaning of "Stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) must be explained accordingly. Some say "entering the stream," while others say "ditch-flow";
these are merely differences in the translators' intentions. At this stage of the first fruit, views have ceased and principle is revealed;
one will no longer be reborn in the four evil destinies.

Second is the Sakṛdāgāmin, here translated as "Once-returner. In this stage, among the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through cultivation, one has completely severed the first six grades while the final three grades still remain; therefore, one returns once more.

Second, regarding the factors of the path of cultivation: first, concerning the two initial fruits, because the nine grades of desire-realm afflictions have already been severed as to six grades while the lower three grades remain, one returns once more to be born in the desire realm to sever them.

It should be understood that there are three types of persons regarding the severance of the nine grades of desire-realm delusions: first, those who sever them spontaneously, which refers to those who sever them spontaneously by passing through seven births.

Regarding the exhaustion of the nine grades: first, sequential abandonment, wherein one necessarily abandons two after two and five after three; second, gradual abandonment, which follows a fixed order;
third, skipping abandonment, which is not fixed and may involve abandoning five or six grades, eight or nine grades, and so forth.

In the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it is taught that sequentially abandoning five grades is called the candidate for the stage of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and abandoning six grades is called the fruit of Once-returner; [abandoning seven or eight grades is called] the candidate for the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

The "grades" (pinda) refer to the stage of the candidate for the fruit of *anāgāmin* (*anāgāmipratipannaka*). The nine grades are named the fruit of *anāgāmin*. By transcending and severing five grades, one is called a "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*).
Upon reaching the sixth grade, one is called a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*). Upon reaching the eighth grade, one is called a "one-seed" (*ekabījika*).
In the *Upadeśa* (Auxiliary Treatise), the nine grades are first correlated with seven births: namely, the "superior-superior" (*adhimātrādhimātra*) can moisten two [births].

The superior, middle, and inferior [levels] of the superior [stage], and the middle and superior [levels] of the middle [stage], each moisten one birth; the middle-middle and inferior [levels] of the middle [stage] together moisten one birth;

and the three inferior levels of the inferior [stage] together moisten one birth. According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says: "Having abandoned the third or fourth category of the desire realm, one is a 'family-to-family' (*kulaṃkula*);
having abandoned five categories, one is a 'once-returner' (*sakṛdāgāmin*); having abandoned six, one is a 'non-returner' (*anāgāmin*). Yet he himself asks: why is this so?

Question: Why are those who abandon one, two, or five categories of defilements not called "those who go from family to family" (*kulaṃkula*)? Answer: Because when two are abandoned, three must necessarily be abandoned; and when five are abandoned, six must necessarily be abandoned.
This is because a noble one (*ārya*) initiates the preparatory application (*prayoga*). Thus, the meaning of this sequential abandonment is the same as that of the present text.

That is to say, when two are abandoned, one necessarily reaches the third; when five are abandoned, one necessarily reaches the sixth. This sequence of abandonment corresponds to the *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) of the present text.

Next, regarding the meaning of "gradual abandonment" (*krama-prahāṇa*), it is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*. Since three or four categories [of afflictions] are exhausted, they are designated as "one who goes from family to family" (*kulaṃkula*).
Therefore, the objection is raised: why are those who abandon one, two, or five categories not also called "one who goes from family to family"?

One must understand that this objection uses the meaning of gradual abandonment to challenge the case of "leaping abandonment" (*vyutkrāntaka-prahāṇa*). Thus, when we reach the answer, the response follows the question by presenting the case of gradual abandonment.

It is said that this meaning of "successive abandonment" (*anupūrva-prahāṇa*) is the same as that in the present text; thus, the first, second, and fifth stages are not termed *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).

This is because, according to the principle of successive abandonment, one must necessarily reach the third stage. Therefore, it is evident that abandoning the third and fourth stages is termed *kulaṃkula*, which constitutes a "leap-over" abandonment (*vyutkrāntaka*).
This leap-over abandonment is precisely what is referred to in the subsequent sections on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* as "small leap-over" (*mṛdu-vyutkrāntaka*).

When an ordinary person on the level of mundane existence has not yet attained the dhyāna of the form realm, or while practicing the dhyāna of the desire realm has not yet abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm,

this person— upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind— transcendently abandons five categories [of afflictions] and is called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family). Since these five categories are the same as the four categories [previously mentioned],

is it not the case that the *kulaṃkula* who transcendently abandons [afflictions] through calm abiding and insight is identical to the one described in the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* as being born into two or three families by abandoning three or four categories?

Is their meaning the same? Is it not the case that in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the "candidate for the fruit of Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*) who has abandoned five [fetters] and the "Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*) who has abandoned six [fetters] correspond to what is called the "candidate for and fruit of the sixth and fifth [stages]" in the context of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā?

Thus, this is merely taking the case of one who transcends the stages—where the candidate for and fruit of the *Kulaṃkula*—and naming it as "possessing superior virtues," which is spoken of with intentional emphasis and deprecation. If...
Now, by examining the degrees of skipping (vyutkrāntaka) and the amount of life-reduction (*upapadya-parihāṇi*), one can determine the relative height of the resulting fruits.
Thus, both skipping and sequential progress apply to those who go from family to family (*kulaṃkula*) as well as to those approaching the fruit. Therefore, it is said:

"Whether by skipping or sequentially, one advances to abandon three or four [fetters] and is subsequently reborn in two or three places among the gods. Some say that abandoning three is sequential, while abandoning four is skipping; however, this is not so.

Regarding the "transcending by stages" and "simultaneous transcendence," human understanding differs, leading to many variations in interpretation; however, as I have sought the meaning of the text, I have explained it as above.

Since the general outline has been clarified, the specific details can now be understood. Regarding the four types of transcending the ordinary stage (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:

first is "transcending by severing the root. Being originally in the stage of an ordinary person, one gradually eliminates the afflictions of the three realms (*tridhātu-kleśa*) through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and worldly wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*).

Wisdom cuts off [defilements] to a greater or lesser extent up to sixteen moments of mind; according to the number of categories of defilements originally cut off, one receives the name of the fruit of *anāgāmin* and so forth.

Second, the "minor leap" (*svalpātikrānta*) is as cited above. Third, the "great leap" (*mahātikrānta*) refers to hearing the Dharma once and, upon being addressed with "Welcome," immediately becoming one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Fourth, the "great great leap" (*mahāmahātikrānta*) refers to the sudden exhaustion of both active afflictions (*kleśa*) and residual habits (*vāsanā*).
This refers to the Tathāgata.

Regarding the three types of Anāgāmin, "Anāgāmin" means "one who does not return. In this stage, one has severed the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of desire; progressing further, one severs the latent tendencies of the [remaining] eight stages above.

Regarding the third fruit (Anāgāmin): the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm have now been completely severed, and because they will no longer return to take birth in the desire realm, they are called "Non-returners" (Anāgāmin).
As for those who descend from the Brahma realm to the three lower realms, according to the *Ratnakoṭa Sūtra*, this refers solely to not returning to take birth in the desire realm;
it does not mean that they are unable to descend briefly. Therefore, descending briefly and [receiving] birth...

The meaning of "arising" (*upapatti*) is thus distinguished by its categories. When it is said that one advances to sever the afflictions of the eight stages above, this refers specifically to the seventy-two grades of the realms of form and formlessness.
Therefore, it is necessary here to clarify the meaning of *anāgāmin* (non-returner), which consists of five types:

first, the *antarāparinirvāyin*; second, the *upapadyaparinirvāyin*; third, the *sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*; fourth, the *anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*; and fifth, the *ūrdhvasrotas*. These are the five kinds of *anāgāmins*.

Regarding the three types of *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who go upstream) and the three types of *parinirvāyin* (those who attain parinirvāṇa), these are combined with those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), and those who attain parinirvāṇa without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) as one general category; within this, the *ūrdhvasrotas* and the others each retain their original distinctions, resulting in nine types of parinirvāyins.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, each of these three categories of "going toward" [parinirvāṇa] is further divided into three—namely, the swift, the non-swift, and the long-drawn-out—based on the analogy of sparks flying from a fire. This is the intended meaning.
It should be understood that these five, three, and nine types of *parinirvāṇa* all refer to *rūpa-parinirvāṇa*.

Regarding the six types of *parinirvāṇa*, they consist of the five mentioned above plus *dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāṇa*. Regarding the seven types of *parinirvāṇa*, they consist of the six mentioned above plus *ārūpya-parinirvāṇa*.

Regarding the eight types of *parinirvāṇa*, they consist of the seven mentioned above plus *aniyata-parinirvāṇa*. The *Abhidharmakośa* does not establish *dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāṇa* [as a separate category].

One should know that the *sābhisamaya-parinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa upon arising) is included in the desire realm; the three, five, and nine types [of *antarā-parinirvāyin*] are included in the form realm;
and the *anabhisamaya-parinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa without having arisen) is included in the formless realm.

As for the *aniyata-parinirvāyin* (one of indefinite time), because it applies to all types of parinirvāṇa, the Abhidharma first lists five types, then subdivides the *antarā-parinirvāyin* into three types, making seven in total with the original five, and further adds the *sābhisamaya-parinirvāyin*.
Regarding the *ārūpya-parinirvāyin* and the *aniyata-parinirvāyin*, they have been explained in detail as analyzed in the *Fuxing shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Shu-chi*).

Although various texts of our own school cite the names of the *aniyata-parinirvāyin*, they do not explain their meaning; thus, scholars have not failed to offer various interpretations based on their own sentiments.
Upon reading the newly translated *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, I first encountered its true meaning. Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Not... [and so forth].

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa through meditative concentration (*niyata-abhisamaya*), they may attain parinirvāṇa in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm. If they are in the desire realm, they are subsumed under "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*);

if in the form realm, they are subsumed under the five types [of *antarāparinirvāyin*, etc.]; and if in the formless realm, they are subsumed under "attaining parinirvāṇa in the formless realm" (*ārūpya-parinirvāyin*). This is consistent with other explanations;

those who do not attain parinirvāṇa through fixed timing (*aniyata-abhisamaya*) apply to all forms of wisdom (*prajñā*), fitting together like the two halves of a tally. Those who are dull-witted [fail to grasp this].
Those who do not understand this find their ears confounded and their hearts startled.

The four types of Arhats—here translated as "Those Beyond Training" (aśaikṣa), "Those Without Rebirth" (anutpāda), "Slayers of the Foe" (arhat), and "Worthy of Offerings" (dakṣiṇīya)—have exhausted both the delusions of views and the delusions of thought;
they have severed the bonds of the disciple, yet the bonds of the fruit still remain. This stage is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, or Nirvana with Remainder.

If the extinguishing of the physical body and the cessation of wisdom is called *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana without remainder) or "solitary liberation," these correspond to the three meanings of the three fruits of the path beyond training (*aśaikṣa-mārga*):
the fruit of no-arising, the fruit of slaying the thief, and the fruit of being worthy of offerings. Furthermore, there are three meanings pertaining to the causal stage:

destroying evil, terrifying Māra, and being a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). Specifically, "destroying evil" pertains to the causal stage, while "no-arising" pertains to the resultant stage; "terrifying Māra" pertains to the causal stage.
In the fruit [of the path], he is a slayer of thieves; in the cause, he is a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). In the fruit, he is one worthy of offerings (*arhat*);

in terms of destroying evil, he maintains pure precepts and destroys the evils of the seven branches [of bodily and vocal action]. In terms of being "unborn," he does not undergo birth within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
In terms of "terrifying Māra," when he first left the household life, he terrified the celestial Māras; because his Way was perfected, he transformed the people under his influence.

"Slayer of Thieves" (*Arhat*) is a name established according to its meaning; it refers to one who harms living beings as "thieves. The *Erya* states: "Insects that eat the joints of seedlings are called thieves.
Because the defilements (*kleśa*) within the three realms are like insects that consume the seeds of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the Arhat is translated as "Slayer of Thieves.

Regarding the term "Beggar for Alms" (*Bhikṣu*): having left the household life in purity, one sustains oneself by begging, thereby remaining free from wrong livelihoods (*mithyājīva*). Regarding the term "Worthy One" (*Arhat*)...
The "offerer" should attend the offerings of humans and devas. As for the "bondage of the child," the afflictions of view and thought are the children of the house of the five aggregates;
because they bind and dwell within the three realms, it is called the "bondage of the child.
As for the "bondage of the fruit," the fruits of the aggregates are the fruits of the house of the child; it refers to the body being constrained by its physical form.
Because they have not yet perished, they are called "fruition-bonds" (*phala-bandhana*). If an Arhat remains with a physical body, they have only severed the "seed-bonds" (*bīja-bandhana*);

since the fruition-bonds—consisting of the body and the extinction of wisdom—are no longer present, the afflictions of delusion are extinguished through the severing of view-delusions and thought-delusions. Because a body still remains, this is termed "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
When this body perishes, it is termed "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). *Nirvāṇa* is translated here as "extinction and transcendence" (*mie-du*). Question: [Regarding] existence...
Question: Are the nirvāṇas with remainder and without remainder the same as or different from conditioned and unconditioned liberation?
Answer: They differ greatly and agree only slightly. Conditioned liberation is that which is associated with untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Unconditioned liberation is the total exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus, the conditioned and unconditioned [liberations] pertain only to nirvāṇa with remainder.

"Collecting the ears" means to gather [the senses]. "Ashes" refers to death, to extinction; "extinguishing the body" refers to the aggregate of morality (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*), and the two types of liberation (*vimukti*).
"Extinguishing wisdom" refers to gnosis (*jñāna*) and insight (*darśana*). What is called the "aggregate of morality" is the precepts concomitant with the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
The "aggregate of concentration" is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). "Gnosis" is the gnosis of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). "Liberation" is that which remains.

"Liberation" (*vimukti*) and "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*) refer to the illuminating wisdom-eye of liberation; that is to say, it is the self-knowledge of having attained the first, second, third, or fourth fruit of the path.
When Śāriputra entered parinirvāṇa, the Buddha asked Cūḍapanthaka, and Cūḍapanthaka replied to the Buddha regarding the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*):
that which does not perish is so called because, being devoid of karmic activity, it continues into future ages and is thus termed "non-perishing. Why is this?

In this state, although the physical form and the unmanifest (avijñapti) precept-body have perished, the karma of the unmanifest precept continues to be attained and does not cease, because it follows the path of karma into the future.
Therefore, such a person attains liberation alone and is called a "solitary" (gūdha) Śrāvaka. As for self-discipline:

by means of the precepts one purifies oneself, by means of concentration one disciplines oneself, and by means of wisdom one delivers oneself. Furthermore, as for "self-disciplining": [it refers to]...
The name is established based on the cause, whereas "Self-Deliverer" (Svayambhū) is a title established based on the fruit.
This concludes the brief explanation of the stages of the Śrāvaka.
Third, the brief conclusion below summarizes [the preceding].
Next, the Pratyekabuddha is explained; he is also called the Solitary Realizer (*Pratyekabuddha*).

This section on the two types of Buddha-sons is divided into three parts. First, regarding the dual designation "the one who awakens through conditions" (*pratyayabuddha*) is also called the "Solitary Realizer":

one should state that in Sanskrit this is *Pratyekabuddha*, which is translated as "one who awakens through conditions" and is also called a "Solitary Realizer. It does not mean that the one who awakens through conditions is...

These are the Pratyekabuddhas. It is precisely because Pratyekabuddhas appear during the time of a Buddha, whereas Solitary Realizers (Pratyekabuddhas who do not encounter a Buddha) do not meet with the appearance of a Buddha in the world that the Pratyekabuddhas of the *vargacārin* class—those who teach and transform their disciples—also exist during times when no Buddha has appeared in the world.

If they were not to preach the Dharma, they would not be of the *vargacārin* type. Master Ci'en Ji, citing the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (*Renwang jing*), further enumerates the assembly of Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore...
Regarding the statement that five hundred *pratyekabuddhas* came from the mountains to the Buddha’s presence when Śākyamuni appeared in the world:
how should this be interpreted? The *Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states: "Both *pratyekabuddhas* and *arhats* [are of] two kinds, great and small.

The 'small' are those born among humans when no Buddha-Dharma exists; they personally realize the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and, if their seven births are completed, do not receive [further rebirth]."
One who attains enlightenment through self-awakening after eight births is neither called a Buddha nor an Arhat. Regarding their spiritual power, they are inferior to those such as Śāriputra;
yet, having practiced for two hundred kalpas, their three "multitudes" (triskandha) are thrice more exalted, and their wisdom is even stronger.
They may attain thirty-two marks or thirty-one marks and so forth—these belong to the causal stage.
If one hears of the causes and conditions for practicing the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), one becomes a Lesser Pratyekabuddha;

if one practices the shared foundations of mindfulness until the principles and phenomena are fully matured, and is endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge (vidyā) and the eight liberations (vimokṣa), one becomes a Greater Pratyekabuddha.

Regarding the "three many" [factors], the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that they are achieved through three: first, associating with virtuous friends; second, hearing the sound of the Dharma; and third, the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā).

The *Prajñāpāramitā* states that there are three "many" factors: making many offerings to the Buddhas, attending extensively to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and inquiring about the essential points of the Dharma at the abodes of many Buddhas.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also speaks of three things that bring much merit: making offerings to the Buddhas, seeking the Dharma, and so forth. Some take these to be the field of merit, the time, and the seed;
thus, the "three many" factors exist in both their small and great forms. Now, regarding the interpretation of the meaning of these three "many" factors:
Is it not evident that what I have now demonstrated is necessarily so?
Encountering the Buddha’s appearance in the world, one receives the teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Second, encountering the Buddha’s subsequent detailed explanation, which is divided into two parts; first, the Pratyekabuddhas, which is further divided into two; first, the heading indicating the twelve [links] received.

Regarding "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): these twelve factors are called "causes" because they mutually induce results through their interaction, and "conditions" because they depend upon one another.

Specifically: (1) Ignorance (*avidyā*) [the afflictive hindrance, the path of afflictions]; (2) Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) [the karmic hindrance, the path of karma—these two links belong to the past];

(3) Consciousness (*vijñāna*) [the initial moment of taking rebirth in the womb]; (4) Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) [name being the mind, form being the physical substance]; (5) The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) [the formation of the six faculties within the womb]; (6) Contact (*sparśa*) [after emerging from the womb]; (7) Feeling (*vedanā*) [the experiencing of the qualities of objects as pleasant or unpleasant].

1–5. From *vijñāna* (consciousness) to *vedanā* (feeling), these are called the five present fruits. 6. *Tṛṣṇā* (craving): craving for forms, men, women, gold, silver, money, goods, and so forth. 7. *Upādāna* (clinging): whenever one perceives any object, a mind of grasping arises;

these two [factors] are future causes belonging to the category of afflictions (*kleśa*), just as ignorance (*avidyā*) belongs to the past. 8. *Bhava* (becoming): when karma has already been accomplished, this is a future cause belonging to the path of action (*karmapatha*), just as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) belong to the past.
9. *Jāti* (birth): the taking of birth in the future. 10. *Jarāmaraṇa* (old age and death): these are the objects to be extinguished.
Second, the section on detailed explanation has two parts. First, a general enumeration of the objects to be eliminated:

"Ignorance" (*avidyā*) refers to the absence of wisdom and lack of clarity in past lives. Regarding the phrase "obstructing the path": that which hinders and blocks the light of wisdom is called an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*);
that which enables one to traverse the states of suffering is called the "path" (*mārga*). Second, "conduct" (*caryā*) refers to what is practiced and what is performed. One.
Because it accumulates all karmas, it is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*). As for what is termed "limbs" (*aṅga*), "limb" carries the meaning of branches and offshoots.
It is also called the twelve-layered city, the twelve thorny gardens, the twelve entanglements, and so forth, as detailed in the *Xuanzan* (Profound Commentary) and various treatises.
Regarding the "three consciousnesses": since there are afflictions and karma, the deluded consciousness of a single thought-moment takes recourse in the mother's womb.

Regarding "vital breath" (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*): at the time of entering the womb, there are three factors—first, life-force (*jīvitendriya*); second, consciousness (*vijñāna*); and third, warmth (*uṣman*).

Following the mother’s breath as it moves up and down and enters and exits is called "life-span," which is precisely the wind of respiration. That which is neither putrid nor decaying is called "warmth.
That which is the mental faculty within this [body] is called "consciousness. Regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): because the mind consists merely of designations, it is termed "name" (*nāma*).
As for "form" (*rūpa*), it is called "form" because its nature is that of resistance and obstruction. Regarding the "five or six bases" (*āyatana*):

while in the mother’s womb, the eyes, ears, and so forth are produced, serving as the points of entry for consciousness and the mind; they are also called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they are capable of producing consciousness, hence they are called "faculties.
Regarding the "six contacts" (*sparśa*): this refers to the six faculties, once born, coming into contact with the six objective spheres (*viṣaya*). Seven...

1. Feeling (*vedanā*): Because the sense faculties and their objects have already made contact, there is that which experiences [the sensation]. 2. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*): Because one experiences through causes, defiled craving arises.

3. Grasping (*upādāna*): Because of defiled craving, one seeks out and grasps. 4. Becoming (*bhava*): Once the causal karma has been completed, it is capable of producing a fruit. 5. Birth (*jāti*): Since the cause already possesses the fruit, one undergoes birth. 6. Aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) [implied by the sequence]:

Because the cause already possesses the fruit, one undergoes birth. (Note: The provided text lists "birth" twice; the standard twelvefold chain implies "aging and death" as the final link following "birth.")
Regarding "old age and death": once the physical form has been born, it must inevitably undergo old age and death.
Therefore, these twelve bases are analyzed by tracing them both in reverse and in forward order; thus, they are collectively listed as the objects to be extinguished.
This is merely a difference in how [the factors] are expanded or condensed relative to the previous Four Noble Truths.
Second, regarding the expansion and condensation as distinguished below, there are two parts: first, the actual analysis; second, the presentation of the headings.

Regarding the first, the presentation of the headings: "What is meant by expansion and condensation? It refers to the condensation of these five branches—ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—into the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); the remainder..."
The seven branches constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Second, regarding the inquiry "How so? and below, the reason why the five branches are combined to form the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is that the essence of these five branches consists of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*);

since karma and afflictions are the cause, and the cause is precisely origination, these five are the Truth of Origination. As for the remaining seven branches being combined to form the Truth of Suffering:
The seven branches are precisely the fruits of the present and the future; since these fruits are the suffering of birth and death, [they are so designated]. Question:

The twelve links of dependent origination are distinguished as two—suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*)—in terms of their opening and closing. How, then, should one discuss the opening and closing of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*)? Answer:

If one cultivates the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) to extinguish and eliminate suffering and its origin, this constitutes the discussion of the opening and closing of the path and cessation. Why is this so? Furthermore:
Since the "origination" (samudaya) and "suffering" (duḥkha) to be abandoned are both comprised within the twelve [links], how could the path that serves as their antidote not be likewise?
Since the names differ while the meaning remains the same, for what reason are they stated repeatedly?
Second, regarding the section explaining the name and resolving doubts, there are two parts. First, as for the doubt:

since it is said that the twelve links of dependent origination and the four noble truths differ in their names through various modes of expansion and contraction, yet are identical in meaning regarding cause and effect, one might ask: "Since the four noble truths have already been explained, why are the twelve links of dependent origination taught again?"

First, because their capacities (*indriya*) and dispositions (*yogyatā*) differ; second, as an explanation for those of lesser capacity, which is divided into two parts. First, explaining that it is specifically for the two types of persons—*śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*—because their capacities and dispositions differ, they can be inspired;

"capacity" (*ki*) refers to the potential, and "disposition" (*i*) refers to what is appropriate. Since the faculties of *śrāvakas* are dull, they can [attain realization] by contemplating the Four Noble Truths as a whole.

Regarding the arousal [of the path], since the faculties of those who aspire to the state of a Pratyekabuddha differ—some being sharp while others require sequential contemplation of the twelve links—it is all the more necessary to arouse [the path] according to their respective capacities;

for as causes and effects differ in their temporal sequence, the dispositions of sentient beings vary accordingly. Therefore, whether [the teachings] are expanded or condensed does not constitute redundancy.
Therefore, the person of the pratyekabuddha first contemplates the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Second, the actual demonstration of the object and the contemplation is divided into two parts; first, the heading:
namely, "ignorance conditions formations, formations condition consciousness, and so on, up to birth conditions aging and death"—this is the process of arising.
The second part, the "Explanatory Section," is divided into three sections. First, the sequential deduction of the objects:
if one contemplates cessation, with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; and so on, until with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease.

Second, regarding the contemplation of dependent origination through downward progression from cessation (*nirodha*), various texts describe differences in how the *pratyekabuddha* contemplates the twelve links in both forward (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) order.

What are these? According to the *Āgama-sūtras*, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) and ending with old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is called "forward contemplation," while beginning from old age and death and ending with ignorance is called "reverse contemplation. Jingxi says: "If..."

Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas who initiate contemplation on their own: how should they contemplate the arising and ceasing of sentient beings through the forward and reverse orders of the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* meditative states?
Since the *aṅga* (limb/factor) exists at the beginning, this refers to the *saṃskāra-aṅga* (volitional formations) within the sitting meditation, because good and evil exist [therein].

Thus, the *Śuǎnqǐ* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhìyǐ*) first initiates contemplation with the *vedanā-aṅga* (feeling), which follows the sequence of the Four Noble Truths; this is explained in the *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the *Fǔxíng*).
The judgment states that there are two ways to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*): First, inferring the cause from the effect.

For example, as previously discussed, one traces back from sensation (*vedanā*) to ignorance (*avidyā*). Once it is known that ignorance gives rise to sensation and the other links, one then refrains from generating the mind of sensation and so forth.
Second, inferring the effect from the cause. For example, by tracing back to the link of existence (*bhava*), one knows that it will inevitably summon future results.

Furthermore, although there is a sequence of cause preceding and effect following, because those who follow the path of the pratyekabuddha generally first infer the cause in order to know the effect, the *Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that when a pratyekabuddha contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), there are two meanings: first, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and second, views (*dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the initial contemplation of craving, there are again two meanings: first, analytical investigation (*anvaya-paryeṣaṇā*), and second, contemplative refutation (*vipaśyanā-bhedana*). First is analytical investigation.
This person, having heard the Dharma of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, understands with faith and clarity that all things belong to craving and affliction;
therefore, by contemplating this, they enter emptiness to seek spontaneous wisdom and reach the fundamental source.
Cultivating the five methods of cessation, they attain the various dhyānas and, recognizing craving and affliction, investigate why this craving arises.
Upon arising, one immediately knows that this craving arises from sensation; sensation arises because of contact; contact arises because of the six sense bases;
the six sense bases arise because of name-and-form; name-and-form arises because of volitional formations; volitional formations arise because of ignorance;

and ignorance, in turn, is caused by past afflictions. This is the method of retrogressive analysis. As for the progressive analysis, one traces how this craving is able to produce [subsequent states].
Regarding grasping (*upādāna*), it can produce becoming (*bhava*); becoming produces birth (*jāti*); birth produces old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Thus, by investigating in both forward and reverse order across two lifetimes, three lifetimes, ten lifetimes, and hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of lifetimes, one clearly and distinctly understands the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

This is called the object of observation and the object to be extinguished. As for the two types of contemplation that destroy [these links], the contemplation of this link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is as follows:

Contemplating the defiled five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the contemplation of the resultant, indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) five aggregates.
Contemplating ignorance (*avidyā*) is the removal of the defiled five aggregates. Furthermore, contemplating grasping (*upādāna*) is the contemplation of defiled afflictions (*kleśa*);
contemplating becoming (*bhava*) is the contemplation of the wholesome and unwholesome five aggregates, up to birth, old age, and death in the future. This...

This is called "the contemplation of the progressive and regressive investigation that shatters all inversions. Because inversions are extinguished, ignorance and everything up to future birth-and-death are all extinguished without remainder;
this is the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination through the progressive and regressive investigation that shatters craving.
Second, the shattering of views also has two meanings: first, investigation; second, contemplation-shattering. Regarding the first, investigation: if one holds a view...

The worldly deities and the world—whether eternal, non-eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, or neither eternal nor non-eternal—these constitute the four views regarding the self and the world (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
These views are themselves the four graspings (*upādāna*). Tracing back from these four graspings, their cause is the four cravings (*tṛṣṇā*).

The cause of the four cravings is the four feelings (*vedanā*). The cause of the four feelings is the four contacts (*sparśa*), and so on, down to the four volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), whose cause is the four [ignorances] (*avidyā*).

If one proceeds by way of forward analysis, one analyzes how the four *upādāna* (grasping) factors give rise to the four *bhava* (existence) factors, and so on, up to the future factors of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
As for the two contemplations that refute [the extremes], one contemplates these four graspings— the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the four views (*dṛṣṭi*)—

in this sequence until reaching ignorance (*avidyā*), thereby refuting the past views of "having gone" (*gatam*), "not having gone" (*agatam*), "both having and not having gone" (*gatāgatam*), and "neither having nor not having gone" (*naivagatam-nāgatam*).
Just as the views of "the self goes" and "the self does not go" defile the five aggregates, one likewise contemplates the four graspings to reach future birth,
aging, and death, thereby destroying the views of finitude, infinitude, both finitude and infinitude, and neither finitude nor infinitude;
these views of the self and the body defile the five aggregates— thus one investigates through both direct and reverse order.
Contemplating and breaking [delusions] is called "breaking through views," which refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Because one awakens to the principle of the True Dharma (*satyārtha*) by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one is called a *pratyekabuddha* (Solitary Realizer).

Third, as for the contemplation of the lower [stages], this concludes the names of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). Question: Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas, their faculties were sharp in past lives, so they were able to awaken on their own.

Question: Why must the Way be taught by the Buddha? Answer: Because upon hearing it taught, one quickly attains realization; if it were not taught, one would not yet awaken. Question: Why is the fruit not established for Pratyekabuddhas? Answer:
Because the faculties of Śrāvakas are dull, the fruit is established for them; because the faculties of Pratyekabuddhas are sharp, the fruit is not established for them.

Furthermore, because the faculties of Śrāvakas are dull, they first contemplate suffering (*duḥkha*); because the faculties of Pratyekabuddhas are sharp, they first contemplate origination (*samudaya*). Question: Why does the Pratyekabuddha not...?

Question: Since Pratyekabuddhas establish the path of skillful means and possess sharp wisdom, having already awakened to the Way before encountering a Buddha, why must they enter the Way through the preliminary skillful means?

Answer: As for whether a Pratyekabuddha who has attained self-awakening still receives the precepts: if they have already generated the unconditioned [non-informative] karma (*avijñapti*), they certainly do not receive them again;
however, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* clarify that even those on the stage of "approaching" (*pratipannaka*) Pratyekabuddhahood still possess the "approaching" state toward Pratyekabuddhahood.
The analogy is likewise presented in the *Mahāyāna-saṃbhāra-samāna-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which clarifies that the ten stages of the śrāvaka correspond to the ten stages of the Buddha:

first, the stage of receiving the three refuges; second, the stage of faith; third, the stage of faith in the Dharma; fourth, the stage of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); fifth, the stage of training in the Buddha’s precepts;
sixth, the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*); seventh, the stage of the srotāpanna; and so on, up to the tenth, the stage of the arhat. These constitute the ten stages of the Buddha.
1. The Stage of Fulfilling Practice; 2. The Stage of the Causes and Conditions for Self-Awakening; 3. The Stage of Awakening to the Four Noble Truths;
4. The Stage of Profound Wisdom; 5. The Stage of the Eightfold Noble Path; 6. The Stage of Awakening to the Dharma-Dhātu and the Space-Dhātu; 7. The Stage of Realizing Quiescence; 8.
The Stage of the Six Supernatural Powers; 9. The Secret Stage; 10. The Stage of the Gradual Thinning of Habit-Energies. These are the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva.

In accordance with various sūtras, the Buddha has ten stages (*bhūmi*): first, the Stage of Profound, Difficult-to-Comprehend, Vastly Luminous Wisdom and Virtue, up to the tenth, the Stage of the Treasury of the Ocean of Wisdom.

Question: How are the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the Śrāvaka and the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Pratyekabuddha to be distinguished from the general and specific characteristics of the aforementioned foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)? Answer: The general characteristics of the Śrāvaka and the specific characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha are each...
Regarding the characteristics of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in their general and specific aspects, these two types—general and specific—have already been clarified above;
therefore, the general and specific cannot be standardized as one.

As for the *pratyekabuddha*, they appear in an age when no Buddha exists; dwelling alone on a solitary peak, they contemplate the transformation of phenomena and personally realize non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Therefore, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
Second, to clarify the Pratyekabuddha: it is not necessarily the case that such a person has never encountered a Buddha and must always dwell alone on a solitary peak;
rather, one who attains awakening by themselves is termed a Pratyekabuddha. Thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states: "There was once a king who went out to a park..."
In the early morning, while sporting in a grove where flowers and fruits were lush and exceedingly delightful, the king, having finished his meal, lay down to rest.
The king’s daughters all gathered flowers, thereby damaging the grove.
When the king awoke and saw this, he reflected upon it and realized that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, attaining a mind free from outflows (*anāsrava-citta*).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speaks of the Pratyekabuddha fruit arising: when a Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita and emits light that illuminates him, he awakens and immediately abandons his body;
yet he does not perceive where he has been transferred. To what place is he transferred? To a place where there is no Buddha.

Even if it were within this world-system, it would be a place where the Buddha’s teaching does not reach. Although he who attains supernatural powers (abhijñā) may know this, he does so only to protect the spiritual capacities of sentient beings.

By this, one should know that there are not two Buddhas in the world; because they wish to see the Buddha, they neither abandon their bodies nor are they moved elsewhere, as is explained in various texts.
Although their names differ, there is no distinction between their stages of practice.
Regarding the third pair of names, the section on distinguishing similarities and differences is divided into two parts. First, the similarity in terms of different positions:

because the two persons differ in name but are identical in their arising and ceasing, and because there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority in their state of practice, they are not differentiated.
This person’s severance of the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms is the same as that of the *śrāvakas*.

Second, regarding this person’s lower [level], there is a distinction between them and the *śrāvakas*, which is divided into two parts: first, they are the same because they sever the manifest outflows (*paryavasthāna*).
Furthermore, because they further subdue the residual traces (*vāsanā*) of their former abodes, they surpass the Śrāvakas.

Second, because they further subdue the residual traces of the lower [stages], they differ from the "habitual" (*abhyāsa-vāsanā*). That is to say, "residual traces" (*vāsanā*) refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);

these are the "portions of the outflows" (*paryavasthāna-aṃśa*), such as the case of a person whose feet have been bound for a long time: even if suddenly released, although there is no longer [actual] binding, when they walk, [the gait] still lags.
There are residual habits (*vāsanā*), just as when fragrance remains in a vessel, even after the scent has been removed, a lingering trace still persists.
As a great sutra says: "My robe, my bowl, I go, I come"—because one still speaks of "I," the residual habit of the delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi-moha*) remains.
Śāriputra’s anger toward Piṅgala and his pride are the residual habits of the delusions of thought (*saṃjñā-moha*); because anger and pride still exist, the śrāvakas remain bound by these.

Because Pratyekabuddhas eliminate only a small portion of it, it is said that "Pratyekabuddhas penetrate the residual habit-energies. Those who practice in groups (*vargacārin*) and transform others must necessarily sever the *reṇu-saṃkhyeya* (dust-like) afflictions;
how could they not penetrate the habit-energies? Let the student examine this carefully. I fear that a detailed explanation of habit-energies would be too cumbersome, so I shall stop here for now.
Next, to clarify the stages of the Bodhisattva:
the three Bodhisattva stages are divided into two parts. First, the Sanskrit term is *mahābodhisattva*, also called *bodhisattvamahāsattva*;
it is translated in the old style as "beings with the mind of the Great Way. Above.
This is because they seek the Great Way in order to transform sentient beings through downward manifestation; the new translations refer to them as "Awakened Beings" (*bodhisattva*).
From the initial generation of the mind, they take the Four Noble Truths as their objective field, give rise to the Four Great Vows, and cultivate the practices of the Six Perfections.

Second, the section on the explanation following the initial [introduction] is divided into two parts. First, regarding the causes of practice, there are further two sub-sections. First, the general outline:
Now, within the systems of other schools, the Two Vehicles are not distinguished as either Small or Great, nor are Bodhisattvas distinguished according to the four teachings (*catur-yāna*).

How, then, can one interpret the texts of the sūtras and śāstras? According to the Tripiṭaka-bodhisattva, their initial generation of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*) takes conditioned arising and cessation (*utpāda-nirodha*) as its object.

Based on the objects of the Four Truths, one establishes the Four Great Vows and cultivates the practices of the Six Perfections. If there were no objects of the Truths, upon what would the vows and practices rely?
If the aspiration for enlightenment is deviant or excessive, the myriad practices are applied in vain. If there were no Great Vows, how would this differ from the Two Vehicles?

If there were no such practices, the mind would be empty of its resolve. When the objects and vows are complete, the Six Perfections arise; these conditions of universal pervasiveness are called [the Bodhisattva path].

Extensively restraining one’s own mind is called "vow" (*praṇidhāna*); seeking fulfillment is called "aspiration" (*praṇidhi*). From generosity, precept-keeping, and so forth up to wisdom—this is the sixth [perfection].
It is by means of these that one crosses from this shore of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), over the middle current of afflictions (*kleśa*), and reaches the other shore of nirvāṇa;

thus they are called "crossings. Because the fruit is explained within the context of the cause, it is said as such. This is the meaning of this Bodhisattva subduing delusions while practicing the causes.
Although they are the same as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are not entirely like ordinary beings who sink into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

This is because the primary transformation through the Three Piṭakas (*tripiṭaka*) is for the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) to sever delusions and exit the realms; whereas the secondary transformation is for Bodhisattvas to merely suppress their delusions.

If one says that the severing of delusions must entail exiting the realms, [this is not so], for Bodhisattvas, out of compassion, remain within the three realms (*tridhātu*) to teach and transform others.
Sentient beings, including those of the two vehicles, will certainly think: "If even a bodhisattva who has severed delusions still remains within the triple world, why should we not be the same?
This would obstruct the realization of those of the two vehicles that they have "accomplished what was to be done" and will no longer undergo future existence.
Therefore, it is said only that the bodhisattva subdues delusions; this is the primary teaching for the Mahāyāna regarding the bodhisattva.

Because they are *bodhisattvas*, those who take birth through the severing of fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), those who take birth through the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the distinct teaching on the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), and those who take birth as a manifestation of the *dharmakāya* according to the teachings of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*)—the *Wenming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) states:

"The *bodhisattvas* of the Tripiṭaka [teaching] take birth while still possessing fetters by means of their vows, or they manifest bodies within the five destinies (*gati*) through supernormal powers to teach and transform sentient beings. The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "[This occurs] during the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*..."
Within the cycle of birth and death, by the power of their vows, they take birth within the evil realms.

First, they cause those who have not yet crossed over to cross over—this corresponds to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) through the vow: "I vow to deliver all sentient beings, who are infinite.

Second, they cause those who have not yet attained liberation to attain liberation—this corresponds to the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) through the vow: "I vow to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), which are inexhaustible. Third, [those who have not yet...]
To bring peace to those who are not at peace is a Dharma-gate; one vows to learn this immeasurably—this takes the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) as its object.
To cause those who have not yet attained Nirvāṇa to attain Nirvāṇa is the Unsurpassed Vow to Accomplish the Buddha-way; this takes the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya) as its object.
2.1. The Section on Individual Explanations (unfolding below) has two parts. First, regarding the explanation of the Truths as the object and the Great Vows:

one must understand that Bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭakas, by means of the four gates, remedy their six defects, clearly comprehend the Four Noble Truths, give rise to the Four Great Vows, subdue the afflictions, and transform others.
Why is this? Regarding the six defects, the first is stinginess (*mātsarya*); the essence of the defect of stinginess is affliction (*kleśa*).
The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that the truth of suffering—the cycle of birth and death—is summoned by the truth of the origin, which is affliction;

furthermore, having observed his own past delusions and seeing that sentient beings today remain unaware, he gives rise to the resolve for enlightenment. He inwardly contemplates impermanence and practices giving exclusively to destroy all forms of stinginess.
By causing both others and himself to escape from the truths of suffering and its origin, he practices giving. This is called [the perfection of giving].

The cessation of the stinginess and affliction regarding the Truth of the Path is called the cessation of the stinginess and affliction regarding the Truth of Cessation. This being so, it is likewise for the others.

From the perspective of existence (*bhava-mukha*), the self (*ātman*) and the person (*pudgala*) cannot be found; there are only real dharmas (*dharmāḥ*). One is deluded regarding these real dharmas and erroneously gives rise to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*).

Real dharmas do not abide, arising and ceasing moment by moment. From the perspective of emptiness (*śūnyatā-mukha*), the self and the person have never existed from the beginning, even though real dharmas exist.

The Dharma floats in emptiness and possesses nothing further than what was explained above regarding the gate of both existence and non-existence. The provisional "self" and "person" are no different from what preceded them;
it is simply that real dharmas themselves are both existent and non-existent. The gate of neither emptiness nor existence merely transcends existence and non-existence.
All other points are as previously stated; therefore, the Bodhisattva subdues delusions by refuting emptiness and studies all four gates extensively.
Because of the arousal of the aspiration for practice, one reaches the state of Buddhahood, termed "Perfectly All-Knowing" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*).

Having reached the ultimate realization of both the conventional and the ultimate truths, the afflictions of view and thought, as well as the habitual tendencies of the *dharmas* of the sands of the Ganges, are all exhausted. Question: Previously, the four truths were listed as suffering, origin, cessation, and path;

why does this text now say "suffering, origin, path, and cessation"? Answer: The former refers to the Śrāvakas, while the present passage concerns the Bodhisattvas. As Jingxi said: "Furthermore, regarding the four..."

Regarding the sequence of the Truths—Suffering, Origin, Cessation, and Path—wherein Suffering and Origin are placed first and Cessation and Path second, and where Path and Cessation are placed first and Suffering and Origin second:

although these four modes of presentation, such as arising and cessation, differ in their skillfulness or subtlety, there is none that does not first involve knowing suffering and abandoning its origin, followed by practicing the Dharma of the Path and subsequently attaining Nirvana.

Therefore, this differs slightly from the order commonly listed. Furthermore, the sequence of priority and posteriority is established according to the capacities of sentient beings (*yathā-pratyaya*).

In the passage cited above, it was asked why the Four Noble Truths are observed by both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas. The answer is that, for the time being, they are distinguished according to their respective vehicles;
however, when one investigates their ultimate meaning, they actually apply to all three vehicles. It was further asked whether the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination apply to all three vehicles.
The answer is as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "There are four kinds of wisdom for observing dependent origination: first, inferior wisdom..."

Through contemplation, one attains the wisdom of the śrāvaka; through contemplation, one attains the superior wisdom of the pratyekabuddha; through contemplation, one attains the supreme wisdom of the bodhisattva; through contemplation, one attains the Bodhi of the Buddha. Question: May the six pāramitās also be practiced by those of the three vehicles? Answer: No. How could there be those of the two vehicles who possess stinginess, greed, broken precepts, or even ignorance? Question: [The second part of the answer: There are two types of people. First, those who have not yet severed their afflictions; second, those who have already severed their afflictions. Among those who have not yet severed their afflictions, there are some who practice the six pāramitās while still harboring stinginess, greed, broken precepts, and ignorance. Because they do not abandon these faults, they are unable to attain the fruit of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. However, because they practice the six pāramitās, they will eventually attain the fruit of Buddhahood. As for those who have already severed their afflictions, they do not practice the six pāramitās. Why? Because they have already attained the fruit of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha. Therefore, it is said that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they encompass all dharmas. Why? Because the six pāramitās include all the teachings of the Buddhas. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the mother of all Buddhas. Also, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the root of all dharmas. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the antidotes to the four māras. Why? Because the six pāramitās can sever the four māras. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās can destroy the four māras. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the cause of the three bodies. Why? Because the six pāramitās give rise to the three bodies. For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the cause of the three bodies. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the treasury of all merits. Why? Because the six pāramitās contain all merits. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the treasury of all merits. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the gate to liberation. Why? Because the six pāramitās open the gate of liberation. For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the gate to liberation. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the vehicle of the Buddhas. Why? Because the six pāramitās carry the Buddhas. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the vehicle of the Buddhas. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the armor of the bodhisattvas. Why? Because the six pāramitās are the armor of the bodhisattvas. For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the armor of the bodhisattvas. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the weapons of the bodhisattvas. Why? Because the six pāramitās are the weapons of the bodhisattvas. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the weapons of the bodhisattvas. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the provisions for the journey. Why? Because the six pāramitās are the provisions for the journey. For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the provisions for the journey. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the light of the world. Why? Because the six pāramitās illuminate the world. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the light of the world. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the medicine for sentient beings. Why? Because the six pāramitās cure sentient beings. For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the medicine for sentient beings. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the field of merit. Why? Because the six pāramitās are the field of merit. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the field of merit. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the source of all virtues. Why? Because the six pāramitās are the source of all virtues. For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the source of all virtues. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the foundation of the Dharma. Why? Because the six pāramitās are the foundation of the Dharma. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the foundation of the Dharma. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the ladder to the heavens. Why? Because the six pāramitās lead to the heavens. For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "The six pāramitās are the ladder to the heavens. Therefore, we know that the six pāramitās are exclusively the path of the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the six pāramitās are the path of the Mahāyāna because they are the bridge to nirvāṇa. Why? Because the six pāramitās cross over to nirvāṇa. For example, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "The six pāramitās are the bridge to nirvāṇa. Therefore, we

Because the practice of the six perfections for one's own cultivation as a Bodhisattva and the practice of the six perfections for transforming others differ in terms of what is taken up and what is relinquished,
the truths, objects, and perfections may be either general or specific.
Having already resolved to attain enlightenment, one must practice the deeds to fulfill that vow.
Second, "Having already... and so forth, explains the section on the practice of the six perfections, which is divided into two parts. First, it concludes the preceding and introduces the subsequent;

it concludes the preceding by resolving the mind and introduces the subsequent by generating the practice of deeds. [The text states: "If one merely resolves the mind, that is very easy; however, its actual practice is what is difficult."
"Filled" (*tian*) means to block, to add, and to fill.

During three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one cultivates the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), and during one hundred kalpas, one plants the seeds for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Second, within the section explaining the three lower [stages], there are two parts; first, the heading.
Regarding the expression "three asaṃkhyeya kalpas," this refers, for the time being, to the limits of time as discussed in relation to Śākyamuni’s cultivation of the bodhisattva path.

The second section, "Explanation of the Three Asaṃkhyeya Kalpas," is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the three *asaṃkhyeyas*, the six *pāramitās*, and further subdivisions. This is further divided into three:

first, the individual citation and explanation of the *Abhidharmakośa* and other treatises; second, that twenty cycles of increase and decrease constitute one intermediate *kalpa* (*antarakalpa*), and eighty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute one great *kalpa* (*mahākalpa*);
third, the passage from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* stating that a Brahmā’s robe weighs three *zhu* and requires three years to brush once, covering forty *li*.
When a stone of eighty *li* is completely worn away, it constitutes a minor eon (*antarakalpa*); when one of one hundred and twenty *li* is completely worn away, it constitutes a middle eon;

and when [a stone of] one hundred and twenty *li* is completely worn away, it constitutes a great eon (*mahākalpa*). One who does not practice and study within these eons is not a bodhisattva. Furthermore, the *Yingluo jing* states:
"A stone of one *li* or ten *li* in breadth and width, wearing down by the weight of three *zhu* of celestial clothing over the span of years counted by human days and months—this takes three years."
One brushing away this stone until it is completely gone is called a *kṣudra-kalpa* (minor eon); reaching forty *li* is also called a *kṣudra-kalpa*;
reaching eighty *li*, within the Brahma-heaven, there is a pearl of radiant light made of a hundred jewels used to calculate days, months, and years;

brushing away this stone once every three years is called a *madhyama-kalpa* (intermediate eon); reaching eight hundred *li*, the robes of the Śuddhāvāsa deities weigh three *zhu*. By means of these...

If a *śuddhāvāsa* deity were to wipe away this stone with a cloth made of the light of a thousand jewels for three years—counted by the cycles of suns, moons, and years—the time required to exhaust it is called one *mahā-asamkhyeya-kalpa*. There are two kinds of *kalpas*:
as stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, the first is that which is called an *asamkhyeya* because its days, nights, seasons, and years are immeasurable; the second is the *mahā-kalpa*.
Because it is immeasurable, it is called *asaṃkhyeya*. The great eons (*mahākalpa*) traversed by Bodhisattvas are termed three *asaṃkhyeyas*.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, eighty intermediate eons (*antarakalpa*) constitute one great eon. Three such great eons are called the "three *asaṃkhyeyas*.
This refers to the fifty-second number within the sequence of sixty numbers, which is named *asaṃkhyeya*; when these great eons are accumulated, they form the three *asaṃkhyeyas*. Since...
If they have accumulated immeasurable [aeons], why speak of "three"? It is not that they are immeasurable; rather, the term is used to indicate that they cannot be counted.
Thus, we know that in reality, they can indeed be counted. In the *Catuḥśataka-vimokṣa-sūtra*, there are sixty numerical categories, whereas the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* cites only fifty-two.
Regarding the remaining eight numbers, the *Kośa* states that they were lost. These fifty-two numbers are fully contained within the *Abhidharmakośa*. As for what was said...
Furthermore, regarding the mention of Śākyamuni and others: because the Buddhas of the Three Piṭakas manifest themselves as Bodhisattvas, Śākyamuni is now specifically cited to clarify this point.

This is truly because Śākyamuni has already attained the fruit of Buddhahood; wishing to cause sentient beings to know that the fruit arises from causes, whenever the various teachings speak of practicing the causes, they generally refer to Śākyamuni, whereas when discussing the fruit of Buddhahood, they mostly rely on Maitreya.
To cause sentient beings to know that causes elicit corresponding fruits, the Four Great Teachings state:

"From the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind until the non-interruption of the fetters (saṃyojana), while sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), both the active afflictions (kleśa) and their latent tendencies (vāsanā) are exhausted.

Because this is the teaching of the Buddha, Nāgārjuna stated: "The Bodhisattva does not sever the fetters; this is the Buddha’s skillful means (upāya). During the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, one does not yet know that one will become a Buddha."
Regarding the two *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they were known [to the Buddha] but not spoken; regarding the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they were both known and spoken.
This is not the word of the Buddha, but rather what was taught in the *Vibhāṣā* by the Arhats. Nāgārjuna, wishing to clarify the Mahāyāna gateway, refuted this doctrine point by point.
Even if one were to explain the meaning according to the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna, although it is not the word of the Buddha...
Regarding the statement that [the teaching] can also be used, the *Fahua Wenju* (Textual Exegesis of the Lotus Sutra) quotes the *Āgama*, saying: "The Bodhisattva does not sever [the roots of good].

Jingxi [Zhiyi] says: "Since it is also clarified in the *Āgama* that they do not sever them, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s refutation of the provisional does not mean it entirely denies their existence.

Regarding the statement that Kātyāyanīputra composed [the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna*], this is said from the perspective of the treatise he produced and his own philosophical tenets. As for the term "limitation" (*fenxian*), it refers to the divisions [of the stages].
This is a fixed limit.
From the time of Śākyamuni until the Buddha Śikhin, he encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas; this is called the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.
During this period, he was constantly free from female form and the four evil destinies, and he constantly practiced the six perfections; yet, he himself did not know that he would become a Buddha.
If one looks toward the stage of the Śrāvaka, there are the five *sthāpanā-citta* and the general and specific *smṛtyupasthāna* (the outer ordinary person).
Second, the "From Antiquity" section, which is the formal explanation, is divided into three parts. First, regarding the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*:
in the past, this Śākyamuni was a potter who encountered the former Śākyamuni entering the city for alms; finding his appearance extraordinary, he gave rise to a virtuous mind and made offerings.
Having made offerings to that Buddha, he made this vow, saying: "May it be that when I attain Buddhahood in the future, it shall be no different from now.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In a previous life, Śākyamuni was once a potter named Mahāprabha.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni, whose disciples were also named Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; [he served] both the Buddha and his disciples."
He went to the potter’s house, whereupon the potter offered three things as an act of charity: a grass seat, a lamp, and honey syrup.
He then made this vow: "In a future age of the five corruptions, may I become a Buddha no different from the present Śākyamuni;
his clan name is Śākya, which in Chinese means 'Capable Benevolence' (Néngrén), and he also delivered [beings] at Wójiao [Wòjiāo]; Śikhi, fully called Jì."
That Śikhin is also called Śikhi; according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is translated as "Jewel Topknot" (*Ratna-śikhin*), and is also called "Jewel Summit" (*Ratna-mūrdhan*) or "Held Topknot.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is rendered here as "Fire. Regarding the phrase "always free from female form and the four evil states," the text is very concise;
however, the *Fuxingji* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) states that he is free from five things: first, he is free from the state of the evil realms.
1. Retreating from it; 2. being free from poverty; 3. being free from female form; 4. being free from physical deformity—these constitute non-retrogression in practice.

5. Being free from forgetfulness and attaining five merits: first, being born into a noble family; second, being born among humans or devas; third, obtaining a male body; fourth, having all faculties complete;
fifth, recollecting past lives—these constitute non-retrogression in thought. One attains these [merits] crosswise during the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.
Because all three meanings are attained when one is free from the five obstacles during the third stage, the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* extends up to the hundred great kalpas;

thus, it encompasses the three types of non-retrogression. Therefore, reaching this point is called "superior patience" (*adhimātra-ksānti*). According to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*, the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* constitute the three non-retrogressions.
However, according to the *Śāstra* (Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya), the lower, middle, and superior levels of patience (*kṣānti*) are taken as the three non-retrogressions.

In the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the stages of the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) and "summit" (*mūrdhan*) are identified as the practice (*caryā*), while "patience" (*kṣānti*) is identified as mindfulness (*smṛti*). Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Although a bodhisattva possesses the five supreme and wondrous sensual desires, they do not give rise to craving or attachment because they possess the contemplation of impermanence.

Nevertheless, such a bodhisattva does not yet know for themselves that they shall become a Buddha; this is because their stage is still that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) outside [the noble path].

There are those who possess the principle and whose minds are moistened by the water [of faith], yet though they practice the six perfections, they do not yet know how to attain Buddhahood. This is referred to as "looking toward" (wang).
It is because the seven stages of worthiness belong to the level of the śrāvaka; here, we clarify the sequence and depth of the bodhisattva’s cultivation of practice.

Therefore, it relies upon the categories of the outer ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) and the inner ordinary person (adhyātmapṛthagjana) to elucidate this meaning; hence, it is called "looking toward. This refers to the bodhisattva.

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "For a Bodhisattva, one does not discuss stages or levels, nor does one sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), but merely cultivates the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
If one were to discuss sequential stages, they could only be measured in depth or shallowness by comparison with the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

From the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one gives rise to compassion and vows, observes the Four Noble Truths, and takes the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) as the primary gateway, specializing in the cultivation of the six perfections; through the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), one destroys the realm of hungry ghosts."

With *śīla* (precepts) he rescued those in the hells; with *kṣānti* (patience) he ferried across those who were animals; with *vīrya* (diligence) he pulled out those in the asura realm; with *dhyāna* (meditation) he brought tranquility to humans; and with *prajñā* (wisdom) he illuminated the hosts of devas.
From the time of Kāśyapa Buddha until Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he encountered seventy-six thousand Buddhas; this is called the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
At that very time, by using seven stalks of lotus flowers as an offering and covering the mud with his hair, he received the prediction (vyākaraṇa) and was named Śākyamuni.

At that moment, he knew within himself that he would become a Buddha, though his mouth could not yet express it; if one looks at this from the perspective of the stage of a śrāvaka, it corresponds to the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata).

Secondly, regarding the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* and the Buddha Dīpaṃkara who appeared therein: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when the Prince was born, a light like a lamp emanated from his entire body;
therefore, he is called Dīpaṃkara (The Lamp-Maker). Upon attaining Buddhahood, he is likewise named Dīpaṃkara, or alternatively, Dīptāloka (Light of Radiance).
The term "dīpta" refers to that which has a stand, while "dīpa" refers to that which is without a stand. This is the meaning of the character for "dīpta."

Some claim that the fixed characters [of the text] are incorrect; however, regarding the auspicious response of covering the mud with his hair while offering seven stalks of lotus flowers to receive the prediction of enlightenment, the *Ruiying jing* states:
"In the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I was a bodhisattva wearing a deer-skin garment.
I saw a royal maiden named Gopī holding seven blue lotus flowers. The Bodhisattva pursued her and called out, 'Sister, please wait!'"
Śreṇika immediately purchased five stalks of lotus flowers with five hundred silver coins;
the princess kept two for herself and said, "I am currently too weak to go forward myself, so please offer these two flowers to the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas on my behalf.
He consented. A short while later, the Buddha arrived, and the king, his ministers, and the common people each scattered famous flowers, all of which...
When the Bodhisattva fell to the ground, he saw the Buddha and immediately scattered five stalks of lotus flowers, which remained suspended in mid-air without falling.
He then scattered two more flowers, which stayed fixed upon both shoulders of the Buddha.
