The Buddha, knowing his intention, prophesied for him, saying: "In the ninety-first kalpa hence, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."
At that moment, Śakra rose into the air, seven *ren* above the ground, and descended from above to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
Seeing the ground was soaked and muddy, he took off his deerskin garment, but it was insufficient to cover the mud.

He then loosened his hair, spread it upon the ground, and requested the Buddha to tread upon it. [The character for "to respond" (*ying*) should be read as "to divide" (*fen*); "fen" means a tally or a portion.]
Śākyamuni is also called Śākyamunī; these are merely different transcriptions of the Sanskrit sounds, for "Munī" means "silent.

That he knew within himself he would become a Buddha, yet was unable to speak of it with his own mouth, was truly because the Bodhisattva’s stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) possesses the gradual principle of the "water of dharma," whereby he attained internal self-knowledge of his future Buddhahood. However, regarding this...
Because the Four Noble Truths had not yet become clear, he was unable to speak of them.
Subsequently, from the time he encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha until Vipaśyin Buddha, he met seventy-seven thousand Buddhas;

this marked the fulfillment of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa. At that time, he knew for himself and also spoke to others that he would certainly become a Buddha, free from any doubt regarding himself or others.
Aspiring for the stage of a Śrāvaka corresponds to the *mūrdhan* (Summit) stage.
Thirdly, from the perspective of the lower [stages], this clarifies the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

Regarding Vipaśyin—here translated as "Victorious Observation" (*shèngguān*), also "Pure Observation" (*jìngguān*), "Victorious Vision" (*shèngjiàn*), or "Universal Vision" (*biànjiàn*)—it is truly one who, when speaking to others, declares that they will certainly become a Buddha.
Because the Bodhisattva’s stage is within the "Dharma of the Summit" (*mūrdha-dharma*), one realizes the water of principle internally and clearly understands the Four Truths externally;
thus, one attains self-knowledge and can also explain it to others. According to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, it says: "I first generated the aspiration for enlightenment under Śākyamuni;
I completed the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa under Ratnottama Buddha; I completed the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa under Dīpaṃkara Buddha; [and] under Kāśyapa..."

According to the *Śākyamuni-buddha-sūtra*, [Śākyamuni] completed three asaṃkhyeya kalpas; as for the differences between this and the various texts of the *Abhidharmakośa*, one should know that "completing" refers to the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, while "having completed" refers to the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Furthermore, these may simply be differences arising from the Buddha’s adaptation to the capacities of his audience.
Having completed the cultivation of the six perfections for such a duration as described in the three sūtras,
this concludes the exposition on the meaning of the bodhisattva herein; these points all originate from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and the *Vibhāṣā*.
Furthermore, dwelling for a hundred kalpas, one plants the causes for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), cultivating one hundred merits to produce a single mark.
Second, further dwelling in the lower clarity, there are two parts to planting the marks and signs: first, the actual explanation of planting, which is cultivation;
that is, the cultivation of the karma of the marks during the hundred kalpas. Question: What mark is planted first? Answer: Some say the first is planted as the level soles of the feet.
Regarding the initial establishment [of the stages], some say that one first plants the seeds for the eyes because one first observes sentient beings with great compassion;
although this interpretation exists, it does not necessarily accord with the timing, for how could one plant them simultaneously? What then is the sequence?
The meaning of "merit" (*puṇya*) has many paths and is difficult to define definitively. Some say that curing a single blind person in a great trichiliocosm constitutes one unit of merit.

Regarding the second point, the meaning of merit, [the text] asks: "How much is defined as one unit of merit? The answer is: some say that a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) possessing sovereign power over the four continents constitutes one unit of merit;
others say that Śakra possessing sovereignty over the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*) constitutes one unit of merit.
Regarding what constitutes a single unit of merit (*puṇya*), some say it is when all people—except for those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ci-ap-chu*)—perform a single act;
others say it is when the sentient beings of a great trichiliocosm together obtain one unit of merit;
others say it is when the blindness of everyone in a great trichiliocosm is cured; and others say it is when one saves the lives of a thousand people from death.

It is also said that there is nothing with which it can be compared; this is because when a Bodhisattva enters the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, they contemplate the causal conditions for the seeds and characteristics of great practices, and their merit is immeasurable, known only by a Buddha—how much more so for a Bodhisattva cultivating the ten wholesome paths, each of which involves five mental states:
namely, the lower, the middle, the upper, the upper-upper, and the upper-middle. These constitute the first five mental states of initial aspiration.
Up to the point of being fully endowed with five mental states, these hundred mental states are called the "hundred merits" that constitute one mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

The meaning of "merit" has many paths; it is because [these various merits] are equalized into one that they are so designated. However, there is a difference between the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the Bodhisattva.
Why? The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Prior to the tree of enlightenment (*bodhivṛkṣa*), the four perfections (*pāramitā*) are fulfilled."
Regarding the fulfillment of the two *pāramitās* at the stage of Buddhahood:
because he surpassed nine *kalpas* by praising Buddha Tiṣya, the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* *pāramitās* were fulfilled ninety-one *kalpas* after Buddha Viśvabhū.
However, if the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the six *pāramitās* are fulfilled during the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, how are these discrepancies to be reconciled? One must...
To know that the fulfillment of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) over the three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas of the *Mahā-śāstra* refers only to the fulfillment of mundane (sāmānya) dhyāna and mundane wisdom;
even upon reaching the foot of the tree, one must still rely on supramundane (nirvikalpa) dhyāna and wisdom based on principle (*tattva*).

This is because, although the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the eight stages have already been severed during the causal period according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) remain unsevered; therefore, [at that stage] only contaminated (*sāsrava*) means are employed.

Therefore, although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) mentions the term "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*), it states later, beneath the section on the King of Trees (*bodhi-vṛkṣa*), that one severs the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) by means of thirty-four moments of mind.
However, in the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is held that when one practices dhyāna, the afflictions have already been severed and are not severed again.

This is because the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* follows other schools (*nikāya*), according to which even though the out-flows are severed, they are not yet designated as "severed" [until a specific stage]. Thus, it reaches [this point].
Since even under a tree one merely severs non-perception (*asaṃjñā*) and all eight stages are termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*),
we know that the differences between the two treatises result from their differing schools.
In the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), each has its own time of fulfillment.

Third, the section on the practice of the lower [stages] clarifying the characteristics of the fulfillment of the six perfections; this text is divided into two parts, the first of which is the heading:
"As King Śibi fulfilled dāna by substituting himself for a pigeon; King Samantaprabha fulfilled śīla by renouncing his kingdom;

the Rishi Kṣāntivādin fulfilled kṣānti by remaining free from resentment while being dismembered by King Kaliṅga; and Prince Mahādāna fulfilled vīrya by draining the ocean and standing on one foot for seven days."

Praising Puṣya Buddha, he advanced to the stage of Śrāmaṇera; while meditating atop a crow’s nest, he reached the stage of *pūrṇa*; as the minister Māgandika divided Jambudvīpa into seven parts, he pacified their disputes;
through the perfection of wisdom, he looked toward the initial stage of the śrāvaka, which is the level of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).

Second, as in the Śibi-jātaka: when the Bodhisattva Śākya was formerly a king named Śibi who had obtained the *Namo-rakṣaṇī-dhāraṇī* and regarded all sentient beings as his only son, Śakra, Lord of Devas, knowing that his life was about to end, sought out the Buddha to ask about his doubts;
yet though he searched everywhere, he could not find him. At that time, Viśvakarman, the celestial master of craftsmanship—
Māra said to Śakra, Lord of Devas: "There is a Great Bodhisattva who has fulfilled the six perfections and will before long attain Buddhahood.
Śakra then replied, "I must go and test him. Śakra transformed himself into a hawk, while Viśvakarman changed into a dove.
The hawk pursued the dove until it reached the king’s armpit. The hawk spoke to the king, saying, "Give me back my dove! The king replied, "I am not in your presence."
"However, I have previously made a vow to deliver all sentient beings; how could I give this pigeon back to you?
The hawk said, "Am I not also a sentient being? Why do you deprive me of my food? The King asked, "What do you eat?
The hawk replied, "I eat flesh and blood. The King then reflected: "This body of mine is constantly subject to old age and death; it will not last long."

When the flesh had rotted away, the king took up a knife to cut more meat to give to the hawk. The hawk spoke again, saying, "You must follow the principle of equality so that the weights are balanced;
do not deceive me. The king then weighed the pigeon against his own flesh; as the pigeon’s body grew heavier, the king’s flesh gradually became lighter.
Thereupon, the king used his hands to pull at the scale until he was exactly equal to the pigeon. At that time, the various devas sighed in praise, saying, "O Bodhisattva..."

When Śākyamuni thus rescued this small pigeon, at that moment heaven and earth shook violently, the waters of the ocean surged with waves, flowers bloomed upon withered trees, and the heavens rained fragrant water. The hawk said to the pigeon, "Truly you are a Bodhisattva;
a Bodhisattva possesses no heart of sorrow or distress. Thereupon, his body and flesh were restored to their former state, according to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions).
*Śibika* means "to give" (*yǔ*) in this [language]; the character *jiā* (迦) was omitted in older translations. *Dāna* means "giving" (*bōshī*).

Regarding King Puming’s renunciation of his kingdom when it was filled with corpses: according to what is taught in the *Renwang jing*, if one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he was actually King Sudhāma;
these are merely differences between the Chinese and Indic names. This king constantly relied upon the observance of the precepts.
Keeping his word, he did not speak falsely. Desiring to go out for a stroll, he had just reached the city gate when a man of pure conduct came to beg, saying, "The King is a person of merit;
have compassion on my poverty and suffering. The King said, "Wait for me until I return to the kingdom.
Thereupon, he entered the park to wander and play. At that time, there was a king of birds named Mṛgapāda (Deer-foot) who had made a vow with a mountain deity to seize [the King].
When nine hundred and ninety-nine kings had come through the air and seized the king to take him away, Sutasoma shed tears like rain.
Mṛgāra said to him, "O great Kṣatriya, why do you weep? Sutasoma replied, "I do not fear death;
I only regret that since my birth I have never spoken a falsehood, and when leaving the city, I promised [to remain pure]."
While practicing generosity, he now lost his reputation and felt self-reproach in his heart. When Mṛgāra heard this, he released Sudaṃsa back to his own country.
After seven days had passed and the king had finished his practice of giving, he went to Mṛgāra’s place. Seeing him arrive, Mṛgāra was glad at heart and praised him, saying:
"You are truly a man of truth who does not lose his integrity. At that time, Sudaṃsa extensively praised truthful speech and censured the nobility of falsehood.
It is said that Mṛgāra, through this pure faith, subsequently released all the kings and sent them back to their respective kingdoms.
This account differs slightly from that in the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra*. *Śīla* is translated here as "excellent goodness," because it consists of maintaining the precepts and practicing virtue.
As for the seer Kṣānti being cut to pieces by King Kali without resentment and thus fulfilling his perfection of patience: this seer was dwelling in a forest.
While he was practicing patience in the middle [period], King Kali took his women and entered a garden for recreation.
After they had finished eating and drinking, the king lay down to rest. At that time, the women gathered flowers and entered the forest to make offerings to a rishi.
The rishi then preached the Dharma to the women; as they listened to the teaching for a long time, they forgot to return. When the king rose from his rest, he did not see them.
The women, carrying swords, searched for him and eventually found him before the rishi. The king asked the rishi, "What are you doing?

The rishi replied to the king, "I am practicing loving-kindness and patience. At that time, the king used his sword to sever the rishi's hands, feet, ears, and nose, and said to the rishi, "If you do not feel anger, this is what is called patience. The rishi replied:
He said, "I am free from anger. The king asked, "Who would believe this? The seer replied, "If I truly practice patience, let my blood turn into milk.
When it happened exactly as he had said, the king became terrified and took his daughter back to the palace. *Kṣānti* means "patience" or "endurance.
*Kali* means "an evil age without the Way," or alternatively, "strife and contention. *Ṛṣi* means "seer" or "sage"; *yāti* means "to depart" or "to pass away"; and *vṛddha* means "old."
Because he did not die but instead entered the mountains, his name is composed of the radicals for "person" (人) and "mountain" (山).
Prince Mahātyāga (大施太子) crossed the sea and stood on one foot for seven days to praise Buddha Puṣya.

When his vow was fulfilled, Prince Mahātyāga entered the sea for the sake of the people of his kingdom to gather treasures and obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel ocean; however, at the moment he was lying down, the ocean deity seized it.
When the pearl was lost at sea, Mahātyāga (Great Generosity) made a vow to drain the ocean to seek the pearl for the sake of saving sentient beings.

When the devas questioned him, he replied to them, "I shall continue this life after life without ceasing. Because the devas perceived his practice to be so diligent and energetic, they assisted him with their supernatural powers to drain the waters of the great ocean.
When the water had receded by half, the nāgas saw the reduction of the water and sent the pearl back to him; thereupon, he practiced *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

The character *zhù* (杼) is the same as in the current text; however, in the *Fuxing* (輔行) and various other texts, it is written as *shū* (抒). Both *zhù* and *shū* are pronounced with the *shén yǔ* (神與) rhyme.
The correct usage is the character *shū*. It means "to remove" (*chú*) or "to draw out" (*zhuó qǔ*). *Zhù* (杼) also means "an oak chest" (*xiàng*) and is pronounced with the *zhí lǚ* (直呂) rhyme;

neither of these meanings accords with the present context. *Shū* (抒) is also pronounced with the *xú lǚ* (徐呂) rhyme, meaning "to drain water. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "At that time, there was a Buddha named..."
Triśaṅgu had two disciples: the first was named Śākyamuni, whose karmic conditions for practicing the path for the benefit of others had ripened earlier;
the second was named Maitreya, whose karmic conditions for practicing the path for his own benefit had ripened later. That Buddha thought:
"It is difficult to turn many people toward one person, but it is very easy to lead one person toward many. I wish to cause Śākyamuni to attain enlightenment first."
Therefore, the Buddha abandoned his two disciples and entered the mountains; Śākyamuni likewise entered the mountains to seek his teacher.
While he was practicing correct conduct, he suddenly saw the Buddha within a cave, having entered the fire-element samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), his majestic radiance blazing brilliantly.
As he walked past, he forgot to set down one foot for seven days. Then, he spoke a verse in praise of his original teacher: [Verse omitted per instructions]

In heaven and earth, within this realm, in the Hall of Much Learning (Mahāśrava), in the palace of the departed, and throughout the ten directions, there is no man, no bull-king, and no Great Śramaṇa equal to him.
Because of this diligence, he transcended nine *kalpas* and attained Buddhahood before Maitreya. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"In praise of Puṣya Buddha, it is said that in the heavens above and the world below, there is none [equal to him]."
Just as there is no one like the Buddha in the worlds of the ten directions, I have seen all that exists in those worlds, yet none is equal to the Buddha.
*Qiao* means to lift up. *Tiṣya* and *Puṣya* differ in their Sanskrit pronunciations; they are also rendered as *Fusha* or *Digā*.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states that *Puṣya* is one of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), specifically the constellation *Aśleṣā* (the Ghost).
This is the name of a constellation; it is because the Bodhisattva’s birth was in correspondence with this [constellation]. Master Qingliangguan said:
"Puṣya is also called Boshā, which means 'increasingly flourishing,' as it signifies the excellence of clear understanding and the ultimate truth.
Tiṣya is also called Tishē, which means 'speaking deliverance,' referring to preaching the Dharma to deliver others. Alternatively, it is said to mean 'speaking with unimpeded eloquence.'"
Regarding "surpassing nine kalpas": it means surpassing nine out of the hundred kalpas; therefore, there are only ninety-one kalpas.

According to the old *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, both "nine kalpas" and "ninety-one kalpas" refer to great kalpas (*mahākalpa*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that twelve kalpas were surpassed;
this is because the conditions [for the teaching] differed, and the Buddha merely spoke of an increase or decrease in number. This is pointed out in the *Fahua wenju*.

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that he "transcended nine kalpas," but this is likely a textual error. Regarding Śramaṇa Śakra, who attained the perfection of dhyāna with a magpie's nest atop his head:
this refers to the ṛṣi Śrīgupta (Śramaṇa Śakra). There are those who depict him in the form of a monk, but this is incorrect;
this ṛṣi had attained the fourth dhyāna, wherein inhalation and exhalation cease, and he sat beneath a tree, motionless as a pillar.

The Immovable Bird saw the Immovable One and, thinking him to be a tree, laid an egg upon his head. When the Rishi emerged from his meditative concentration, he became aware of the bird and the egg on his head.
He then reflected: "If I were to move away, the mother bird would not return, and the egg will surely be destroyed.
He entered concentration once more; only after the fledgling had flown away did he rise and proceed on his journey. [Thus spoke] the minister Gubhin.
Regarding the division of Jambudvīpa into seven parts to pacify strife, the Bodhisattva Kṣemadatta (劬嬪), whose wisdom was perfected,
contemplated and analyzed with a great mind how the Brahmin minister Kṣemadatta had divided the great earth of Jambudvīpa into seven portions,
such that all the large and small cities, towns, villages, and hamlets were likewise divided into seven parts.
Regarding *Ghūpin-tuo* (劬嬪陀), I have not yet heard a translation for this term. Dhyāna and Prajñā merely suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*);

as for severing the afflictions, it must be through dhyāna and prajñā that take principle (*li*) as their object. Question: Since these [practices corresponding to] the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) have not yet severed the afflictions, can they be called "perfections" (*pāramitā*)?
Answer: Although the afflictions have not yet been severed, why could they not be called "perfections" when speaking of the fruit within the causal stage?

Regarding the term "pāramitā": previously it was stated that the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) were completed after three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas; yet now it is further stated that there is a specific time when each of the six perfections reaches fulfillment.

One should understand that this explanation of the time of fulfillment for the six perfections is identical to what was previously called the "completion" (*niṣṭhā*) of the six perfections—completion itself is fulfillment.
This is said in contrast to the śrāvakas, who possess only inferior patience (*kṣānti*); this is from the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-vyākhyā*.
It is said that planting the karma for the thirty-two marks after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* corresponds, by comparison, to the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).

However, what is clarified here— namely, the time when the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are fulfilled— is actually intended to be shown following the previous section on the completion of the cultivation of the six perfections.

Next, entering the stage of the candidate for Buddhahood (abhiṣekabhūmi), he is born in Tuṣita, enters the womb, emerges from the womb, leaves the household life, subdues Māra, and sits unmoving in perfect enlightenment;

this constitutes the stage of medium patience (*madhyākṣānti*). In one momentary instant, he enters the stage of superior patience (*adhimātrākṣānti*), and in another momentary instant, he enters the stage of the world’s foremost position (*laukikāgradharma*).
The second section, concerning the descent and the approximate completion of the stages of Buddhahood, is divided into four parts. First, it clarifies the first five signs.
Since the previous Buddha has already entered extinction, this Bodhisattva immediately succeeds him; therefore, he is called a "Successor" (Upapadya). These are: 1. Descent from Tuṣita; 2.

Entrustment to the womb; 3. Birth from the womb; 4. Renunciation of the household life; and 5. Subduing the Māras. Regarding these, the first four signs have already been briefly explained in the preceding text.
The five marks of subduing Māra possessed by the Fully Enlightened One pertain to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
If one refers to the Mahāyāna, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, it does not mention subduing Māra; rather, it adds "dwelling in the womb" to constitute the eight marks.
This is because, in the essence of the Mahāyāna, Māra is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). As for the statement in the *Wenju ji* that Buddhas of all four teachings subdue Māra, this refers to—

The ritual of transformation cannot be discarded; for the Lesser Vehicle’s subduing of Māra is fully documented in various sūtras and śāstras. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "At midnight he left the household life;
after six years of ascetic practice, beneath the Bodhi tree, he shattered eighteen trillion demonic armies and hosts of ghosts, thereby attaining the Unsurpassed Way.
Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara-sūtra* (or *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā*) says: "The celestial Māra and the Buddha engaged in mutual debate and refutation; the Buddha..."
The Man says: "I shall surely die in battle; I will never live out my days as one subdued by others. The Bhikṣu says: "What do you seek?
I sit beneath the tree, finding joy amidst the thickets and forests where venomous beasts dwell. The Man says: "Arisen clouds are fearsome and the darkness is profound;
surrounded by the celestial Māras, how can you not be startled? The Buddha says: "In antiquity there was the True Way, which the Buddha has attained—a state of tranquil serenity."
This is the most supreme Dharma for utterly eliminating ignorance; it is the treasury of fullness. While I sat here, I joyfully [overcame] the great treatises of Māra.
Furthermore, the *Śuddhāvāsakāyika* devas stood on three sides, watching as the Buddha and Māra engaged in a contest of difficult questions and debate.
When the celestial Māras retreated and fled, they did not stop even at the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*). The Buddha said to Māra: "Throughout my three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*..."

"Only after practicing austerities for kalpas does one attain bodhi; you have merely established a single unobstructed assembly to be rewarded as the Lord of Devas—how can you engage me in such conflict?
The Māra asked, "Who can bear witness to this matter? The Buddha pointed to the earth and said, "She knows me.
Thereupon, the Earth Goddess emerged to testify, and the Sky Goddess transmitted the testimony up to the Brahma world.
The celestial Māra was subsequently subdued, whereby he attained the Samādhi of Immovability and accomplished the Unsurpassed Way.

Because the middle stage of patience (*madhyakṣānti*) contracts the contemplation by taking the suffering of the desire realm as its object, it extends from the descent from Tuṣita and entering the womb up to the subduing of Māra.

"Kṣaṇa" here means a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-ksana*); thus, immediately after subduing Māra, within a single thought-moment, he attains the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātrakṣānti*) and enters the World-Highest Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Having given rise to the thirty-four moments of true, untainted mind, he suddenly severed the habitual tendencies of both *darśana-heya* (viewing) and *bhāvanā-heya* (cultivation) afflictions;
sitting beneath the Bodhi tree made of wood, with blades of grass serving as his seat, he manifested the body of an inferior response-body Buddha, sixteen feet in height.

Second, "Arising of Truth" and below clarifies the thirty-four moments of mind of the sixth stage: the eight patiences (*kṣānti*), the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), the nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*), and the nine liberations (*vimukti-jñāna*).
According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, because [the afflictions] have not yet been severed at the time of the cause, one severs them all collectively beneath the King of Trees;
thus it says "thirty-four. If one follows the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa* and *Vibhāṣā*, it is said that the afflictions of the first eight stages [are severed].

When practicing dhyāna, one has already completely severed the nine grades of the non-percipient realm; the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are fully present, and their cessation occurs through the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The remainder is as previously cited and is fully contained in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary).
In response to the invitation of Brahmā, he turned the Wheel of Dharma three times to deliver those of the three root-natures.
The third section, "Receiving the Invitation from Brahmā," clarifies the seventh characteristic, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, which states:
"In the past, there was a king whose first queen gave birth to a thousand sons. Desiring to test the order in which they would attain Buddhahood in the future, Krakucchanda drew [the lots]."
The first tally was for Śākyamuni, and the fourth tally reached Vairocana, who obtained the thousandth tally.

The second lady gave birth to two sons; the elder vowed to become a Brahmā King and invite his thousand elder brothers, the Buddhas, to turn the Wheel of Dharma, while the younger vowed to become Guhyapada-vajrapāṇi to protect the teachings of his thousand elder brothers.
Thus it is said in the *Ruiying Jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) regarding the Buddha.

He emitted light from his brow that reached the seventh heaven, where the Great Brahmā, knowing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, felt compassion for the three realms, seeing them all in decay and suffering because they had not yet attained the Dharma for transcending the world.

Having seen a Buddha for the first time in a vast period of time, the various devas rejoiced, desiring to hear the Dharma; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "At that time, the various Brahma-kings and..."
The various heavenly lords, Śakra, and the Four World-Protecting Kings requested me to turn the wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the "three turnings of the wheel of Dharma," the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "I turn the wheel of Dharma throughout the great trichiliocosm; that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure.

The first is called the "turning of demonstration" (*darśana-vartana*), which indicates its characteristics. That is to say: "This is suffering; this is the cessation [of suffering]; this is the path. The second is... [text fragment ends]
"Exhortation to turn" (*pravartana*) means to exhort others to practice, saying: "This is suffering; you should know it. This is the origin; you should abandon it. This is cessation;
you should realize it. This is the path; you should cultivate it. The three types of "turning through realization" (*abhisamaya-pravartana*) refer to citing one's own realization to lead others:
"This is suffering; I have already known it and shall not need to know it again," and so on, up to: "This is the path; I have already cultivated it and shall not need to cultivate it again."

"Further cultivation" refers to *tuan* (transferring), which means to deliver or transport; "wheel" (*lun*) refers to crushing and grinding. By means of this Dharma, one delivers others into the [path], crushing their delusions and burdens;
thus, each successive turning gives rise to the eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening—the twelve practices.
This is fully detailed in the text and commentary of the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "Delivering the three faculties" refers to the three [vehicles].
He is the vehicle.
Having dwelt in the world for eighty years, manifesting the appearance of an aged bhikṣu, his fuel exhausted and his fire extinguished, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
this is the fruit of Buddhahood according to the Tripiṭaka.
The fourth section, "Abiding in the World," clarifies the eighth point to be known: the Tathāgata’s manifestation of an eighty-year lifespan.

Although this is based on the teachings of the *Hīnayāna*, there is no contradiction from the perspective of the *Mahāyāna*. Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that he left home at the age of seven and attained enlightenment at thirty;
likewise, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* also state that his physical body born of parents was young.
Regarding "afflictions such as illness" and the "exalted marks of the *saṃbhogakāya*": since it says "eighty," this refers to the aged bhikṣu; "bhikṣu" means "one who begs for alms.
As for "the fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted": the Buddha-body is called "fuel" and wisdom is called "fire.

When the support of wisdom—the *saṃbhogakāya*—ceases, wisdom perishes. This interpretation accords with the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and is identical to the present text. If [discussed] according to the Great [Vehicle],...

The "vehicle" (yāna) takes the faculties of beings as its fuel and the timely response [of the Buddha] as its fire; when the faculties of sentient beings are exhausted, the Buddha’s response likewise ceases.

This is established entirely by means of metaphor. One must understand that while the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) definitely involves arising and ceasing, the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna is truly without arising or ceasing.
It manifests arising and ceasing, yet it does not cease while ceasing, and it ceases while not ceasing, as is fully detailed in various [scriptures].
This passage is not explained at length here.

Although the practices and the realization of the fruits of the three types of people discussed above differ, they are alike in severing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), alike in escaping the triple world, and alike in realizing the limited truth; they have merely traveled three hundred yojanas to enter the illusory city.

Third, the above and below provide a general conclusion. To speak of the fruit within the cause means that because the Bodhisattva has severed [the afflictions] and so forth, he has completed the severance and subsequently attains Buddhahood.
However, because the principle of True Truth (*tattvārtha*) does not fully possess all phenomena, it is called "partial" (*ekāntika*);
it is also called "merely empty" (*śūnyatāmātra*). A *yojana* is also called a *yojanana*; this is translated as "limit" (*pramāṇa*), and is also called...
"Combined" means "corresponding," perhaps forty *li* or sixteen *li*, similar to the distance between postal stations (*yì*).

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that [the Buddha] transformed [the distance] of more than three hundred *yojana* into a single city. Regarding this, the *Zhǐguān* states there are three meanings:
first, in terms of the place of birth and death, meaning the retributions of the three realms amount to three hundred; second, in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*), meaning...

The delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) consist of one hundred and five; the five higher fetters (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya*) consist of one hundred and five, while the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) consist of one hundred, totaling three hundred.
The five higher fetters are restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment to the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).

The five lower fetters are the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), greed (*lobha*), and hatred (*dveṣa*). Thirdly, regarding the wisdom of contemplation, through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one knows these three hundred [delusions]. Thus it is said.

The Sūtra says: "Knowing that within all births and deaths, afflictions, and evil realms there is a single guide who well understands the obstructions and openings, the ascending and descending, and the five divisions," as recorded in the *Wenju ji* (Record of Textual Phrases) and its supplementary notes.
The brief explanation of the scriptural teachings of the Tripitaka is concluded.
Third, the brief explanation below serves as the conclusion.
