Next, to clarify the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna):

this teaching is divided into three parts. First, it establishes this teaching; second, it correctly explains the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising (anutpāda) to transform persons of the Three Vehicles, so that they may together realize the True Principle.
It is called the "Shared Teaching" (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*) because it shares with the preceding *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teachings and shares with the subsequent Distinct and Perfect Teachings;

thus it is named the Shared Teaching. Second, "shared with the preceding lower [teachings]"—the explanation of the text is divided into four parts. First, the brief explanation of the name and meaning is divided into two sections. First, regarding the shared aspect with the preceding [teachings]:

those of dull faculties realize the fruit in a manner largely identical to the *Āgama* teachings; therefore, it is "shared with the preceding. Those of sharp faculties, upon seeing the Middle Way, do not... [text continues].
Because they differ from the Separate (Bibiao) and Perfect (Yuan) [teachings], it is said that they "pervade" (*tong*) the latter four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

There are three meanings of "pervading": first, pervasion of both cause and fruit, which refers to the teachings of the present stage; this also pervades the preceding stages. Second, pervasion of the cause but not the fruit, which refers to those who receive the transmission.
Third, pervasion of the Separate and the Perfect, which refers to those who rely on the transmission for guidance; these two cases pertain to the pervasion of the subsequent stages.

Furthermore, it is from the perspective of the specific teaching that the name is derived: because these three types of persons equally enter into emptiness through the path of non-verbalization regarding the substance of form (*rūpa*), it is called the "Shared Teaching" (*tongjiao*).
Second, regarding the explanation of "shared" (*tong*) by proceeding from the lower [teachings] to the specific teaching itself: it refers to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
The three types of persons [of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva vehicles] alike, by means of the path of non-discursive speech, realize that the substance of form enters into emptiness;
while verbal discourse pertains to phenomena, non-discursiveness is the principle. This path is the wisdom of contemplation that penetrates phenomena as principle; it is the path of the unborn.

By means of this path-substance, one understands that the dharmas of the six classes of ordinary beings—form and mind—are like illusions and transformations; they are the conventional reality of illusory existence.
There are only names; these names do not exist internally, externally, or in between, but are eternally self-existent and so forth—therefore they are empty.

That which is illusorily existent is itself emptiness, which is the True Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, the common meaning shared by these three persons is due to the identity of what they have realized;

as the preceding text states, this "penetrates" the previous *pitaka*. However, because there are differences in terms of the teaching (*dharma-paryāya*), we now further address it from the perspective of the ineffable.

It is said that the substance of the Way is the emptiness of form. Furthermore, one must know that these eight—teaching, principle, wisdom, severance, practice, stage, cause, and fruit—all pervade those of the three vehicles.
Why? Because they equally receive the teaching of non-arising, they are "pervasive in teaching";

because they equally take as their object that form is itself emptiness, they are "pervasive in principle"; because all dharmas do not arise and Prajñā does not arise, they are "pervasive in wisdom. [The stage of] Srotāpanna...
Whether it be wisdom or abandonment, this is the penetration of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). All are the penetration of the practice of the Mahāyāna.
They share the same penetration of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). They share the same penetration of the cause of Prajñā. They share the same penetration of reaching the fruit of Sarvajñā.
Based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the ten stages such as "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) constitute the sequence of stages for this teaching.

Second, based on the extensive explanation of the sequence of stages in the latter part of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the text is divided into two parts. First, the extensive explanation of the stages of the specific teaching itself, which has four sections.
First, a general indication of the indefinite categories of the specific teaching established by our own school; these are merely the Vaipulya and Prajñā [sūtras].

Among these, there are three stages studied together which are categorized as the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). Because the meaning of the "Dry Wisdom" (*ganhui*) and the "Ten Stages" (*shidi*) in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is clearly manifest, they are specifically highlighted here.

First is the Stage of Dry Wisdom; because it lacks the water of principle, it receives this name. It corresponds to the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāiwǎn*) and is equivalent to the five [stages] of the Treasury Teaching (*zàngjiào*).
The three stages—stopping the mind (*cittasthāpana*), general observation (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and specific observation (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*)—are equal.
Second, the detailed explanation of the text is divided into ten sections. First, regarding the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*):

although its wisdom is crude, it is similar to the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), as it possesses wisdom that operates externally to the principles of the mind and conduct through the three types of observation—the five stopping methods (*pañca-sthāpanā*), general observation, and specific observation—as well as the Tripitaka.

Second, the stage of the nature of the ground (*gotrabhūmi*) is similar to attaining the water of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), whereby one subdues the afflictions of views and thoughts; this corresponds to the stage of the inner ordinary person (*antarapudgala*) and is equal to the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the Tripitaka Teaching.

Regarding the "dharma" of the nature of the ground: it refers to the nature of illusory existence, which is the very emptiness of mind; as one wanders within the principle, the water of the nature moistens and nourishes [the practitioner].
Nevertheless, although this is so, when compared to the stage of the Sages, it is like comparing brass to gold; thus it is called "similar.

Because the afflictions of view and thought are not yet eliminated, it is called "subduing the delusions. Although the teachings differ, the fact that those within the stage of the Inner Ordinary Beings subdue their delusions is invariably the same;
therefore, it is equal to the four roots of merit in the Tripiṭaka.
The "thirty-six stages of the person" (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi):

regarding the term "eight persons," these refer to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*). Because they possess the eight patiences but lack even a single fraction of full wisdom, they are described in this way.
For the four truths of the desire realm, there are four patiences and four knowledges; the same applies to the form and formless realms.

In this way, the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) of the desire realm are termed "dharma" (*dharmajñāna-kṣānti* and *dharmajñāna*), while those of the form and formless realms are termed "subsequent" (*anvaya*).
The eight patiences and eight knowledges arise from the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); one patience and one knowledge arise in succession until the time of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
At that point, the first patience that arises is called the fifteenth moment of mind, and the subsequent knowledge is called the sixteenth moment of mind. Now, regarding the eight patiences:
These are the fifteen moments of mind.

In these two stages—the stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*) and the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*)—one enters the samādhi of non-interruption (*ānantarya-samādhi*) to sever the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the three realms.

Having exhausted all views through insight, one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and realizes the principle of the True Truth; this is equal to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) of the Tripitaka Teaching.

The fourth, the stage of seeing (darśana-bhūmi), is the vision of the truth. Because the wisdom of the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*) is uninterrupted, it is called "uninterrupted" (*anantara*).

Regarding these two stages being said to enter the "uninterrupted," the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation), and the *Da si jiao yi* (Great Outline of the Four Teachings) all state that one enters the uninterrupted at the third stage.

As for the statement that this is equal to the first fruit of the *Hīnayāna* (Zangjiao), this is based on the explanation in the *Miaofa lianhua jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) concerning the seven [stages].

The "Noble Stage" refers to the noble ones who are correct; through the manifestation of the clear understanding of the Patience regarding Suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), they abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and enter the nature of a noble one (*ārya*).

The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) explains: "Regarding 'abandoning the ordinary and entering the noble,' once the stage of Patience regarding Suffering is reached, one enters the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) immediately and without interval.

This is now explained from the perspective of the subsequent [attainment], referring to them generally as "noble persons. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states: "Patience is the cause. Please observe this passage.
To know the third stage is called being a noble one (*ārya*); this is stated from the perspective of a general discussion based on what follows.
However, if explained from the beginning—that is, discussing it specifically—one is still at the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) stage and is still termed a "cause.

Because one is about to abandon the nature of an ordinary person and turn toward the nature of a noble one, yet has not yet fully attained the state of a noble one, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says: "Just as at the fifteenth moment of mind, although the seven knowledges already exist..."
Because the eight *kṣāntis* (patiences) have not yet entered the stage of fruition, the *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* (path-patience following the analogy) is still termed a cause.
According to the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, there are three levels of the Shared Path (*sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*): first, the ten stages common to the Three Vehicles, as listed in the present four teachings;

second, the shared level of the Three Vehicles of the Shared Teaching, which borrows the names of the distinct [Bodhisattva] stages; and third, the shared level of the Shared Teaching, which borrows the specific names of the distinct stages.
Regarding the stages for teaching Bodhisattvas, these two meanings are as cited below. In the *Miaoxuan*, it is stated that one borrows specific names to refer to the common stages;
thus, while the specific names are distinct, their meaning is universal. Furthermore, by borrowing the specific name "Bodhisattva" alone, one refers to the Bodhisattvas of the common three vehicles.
Although the designations differ—specifically in the establishment of the term "patience" (*kṣānti*)—the underlying sense remains the same.

The general purport is the same; taking the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* as a standard, the stage of "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) is the name for the Bodhisattva’s "Patience of Subduing" (*vinaya-kṣānti*).

Although the name borrows from a specific [Abhidharma] context, its meaning must necessarily rely on the universal [Bodhisattva] system. Thus, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "If the third stage eliminates views, then the fourth stage should eliminate thought;
if the fourth stage eliminates views, then the third stage should not yet have eliminated them. Therefore, the elimination of views across these two stages serves as the point of entry and exit."

Contemplating that there is neither exiting nor entering contemplation—if there is no exiting or entering, then there are not two stages; if there is exiting and entering, one is not at the stage of those with the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
The Master [Vasubandhu] defends this by saying: "The Sūtra speaks thus because it uses the specific to reveal the general.
The meaning of the specific [stages] is extensive, while the meaning of the general [stages] is brief. If one says there is neither exiting nor entering contemplation regarding the three stages...

Regarding the abandonment of views, if one speaks of the first stage, it refers to the four stages; if one speaks of the abandonment after the views have been severed, this is a case of borrowing a specific term to name a general category.
Recent scholars have extensively asserted that the third and fourth stages are called "opening" (kai), while the ten stages of the bodhisattva are called "closing" (gō).

They claim that the third and fourth stages are not differentiated from the preceding ones, thus naming them "closing," whereas the distinction between Buddhas and bodhisattvas is called "opening. This has not yet [been fully resolved].
One should know that this opening and closing is found in which texts.

Regarding the five *tanūbhūmi*s (stages of attenuation), the abandonment of the first six of the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm is equal to the two fruits of the *piṭaka* teaching (*āgama*).
These five *tanūbhūmi*s are called "attenuated" because the afflictions of the desire realm have become somewhat light.

The sixth stage, the Stage of Separation from Desire (*vairāgyabhūmi*), involves the exhaustion of the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm through the path of cultivation; this is equivalent to the third fruit in the Tripitaka Teaching.
It is called "separation" because the afflictions of the desire realm are entirely eliminated.

The seventh stage, the Ground of the Accomplished (kṛtāvibhūmi), exhausts all afflictions of both views and cultivation within the three realms; however, it only severs the manifest outflows (āsrava) and cannot yet eradicate their residual habits (vāsanā).
This is like wood that has been burned into charcoal. It is equal in rank to the four fruits of the Śrāvaka vehicle according to the Tripitaka Teaching.
The seventh stage is called the "Stage of the Accomplished" (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*) because the work of abandoning through wisdom has been completed; thus it is termed "accomplished.

Since the two delusions of views and afflictions have been eliminated, they are not called "secondary" but "primary" (*sākṣāt*). Because the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) that have long been practiced remain entirely intact, it is said that [the delusions] cannot invade.
Contemplative wisdom is like fire, the primary afflictions are like wood, and the latent tendencies are like charcoal.
The eighth stage of the Pratyekabuddha further erodes the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), like burning charcoal until it becomes ash.

Although the eighth stage of the Pratyekabuddha can erode the habit-energies—described as "burning the charcoal" yet not entirely exhausted because some ash remains—it is ranked higher or lower than the common stages.
The treatise states that these three types of persons are identical in severing the active afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because they enter *nirvāṇa*, they are called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*); this is like wood that has been burned, which still possesses charcoal and ash, and thus is said to have "high and low" [parts].

Regarding this, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the two vehicles prior to the seventh stage share [the path] with Bodhisattvas; hence they are called 'common' to Śrāvakas.
If this is so, why are those from the eighth stage upward—who have transcended the stages of the two vehicles—also called "common" to Bodhisattvas?

Answer: The initial names are established according to their origins, whereas the subsequent ones differ because the stages of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles] diverge from beginning to end. Question:
Since the contemplation of the seventh stage is exhausted, why is the sixth stage called "shared with śrāvakas," while the eighth is called "pratyekabuddha"?

Why is the seventh stage called "shared with pratyekabuddhas"? Answer: The general meaning is comprehensive and leisurely, as detailed in the subsequent analysis; one should read the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) to understand it.

Exegesis: In the ninth Bodhisattva stage, although the fundamental afflictions (*āsrava*) are completely severed—being thus identical to those of the Two Vehicles—the Bodhisattvas still sustain residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) to moisten rebirth.
Thus, they practice both the path of cultivation and the path of insight (*vipaśyanā*), sporting with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and purifying Buddha-fields.

In the ninth Bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*), when the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) have already perished, it is called the "exhaustion of the active outflows" (*āsrava-kṣaya*).

This is because, from the perspective of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), this is identical to that of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). However, if one wishes to benefit others, one must sustain the residual habits (*vāsanā*). "Sustain" means to support; "habits" refers to the remaining traces of the afflictions of views and thought.

"Moistening" means to moisten and give rise to life, which refers to the arising of the physical form within the realm of segmented birth (*paricchinna-janma*). This is what is meant by "sustaining the [residual] views."

Because the energy of contemplation (*cintā*) is divided and moistened with benefit, rebirth is thereby received. This is truly because the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyayāna*) does not clarify the Middle Way;

lacking a basis in the fundamental, how could it act in accordance with the capacities of beings? Therefore, although the Bodhisattva has severed the active outflows (*paryavasthāna*), he does not exclusively realize emptiness.

Out of compassion and pity for all beings, he desires to rescue sentient life; yet, as the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have already been severed beforehand, there is nothing further [to be removed].
Because one undergoes rebirth due to afflictions and karma, that which sustains the residual forces (*vāsanā*) serves as the basis for benefiting sentient beings;

yet this must first be maintained by retaining these remaining habits. Furthermore, by augmenting this with a mind imbued with emptiness and the Four Great Vows, one moistens birth within the triple world to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings. At such a time, one should contemplate deeply.

Through the two truths, one progressively severs the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Since both matter and mind are devoid of cognition, and even the inferior wisdom regarding the "dust-like" [phenomena] is severed, the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) thereby become manifest.
One should know that habitual tendencies cannot moisten rebirth; here, they are merely retained for this purpose.

Furthermore, the support of these tendencies exists only in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*); as for those who speak of the contemplation of the Path, "Path" refers to transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
The contemplation that leads directly to emptiness and the contemplation that emerges from emptiness into the conventional—because these two proceed together, they are called "the dual emergence.

Emerging into the conventional to transform sentient beings and roam through all worlds is like a child’s play; therefore, it is called "playful sport" (*vikrīḍita*). In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is asked:
What is meant by the "playful sport" of the supernormal powers? The answer is: Just as a magician manifests various transformations, so too does the Bodhisattva.
For this reason, it is called "play" (*krīḍā*). Furthermore, among the three samādhis, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is supreme, while all other dharmas of practice are termed "inferior.
It is like the play of a child. Question: Since a bodhisattva should simply give rise to samādhi, why is there a need for "play"? Answer:
Because the bodhisattva’s mind has already given rise to samādhi and delights in entering and emerging from it, this is also called "play"; it is the name for spiritual power (*ṛddhi*).
The "Heavenly Mind" is generally termed the "nature of wisdom"; this innate wisdom penetrates and illuminates all things without obstruction, and is therefore called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*).

To speak of the fruit within the cause, it is named the "purification of Buddha-lands. If sentient beings have a mind of intense passion, heavy with stinginess and greed, the Bodhisattva transforms them, causing them to give rise to right view and become free from parsimony; he vows that when he attains Buddhahood, his land shall be pure.
Purifying all right views so that one can abandon sentient beings and come to that land is called "purifying the fruit-buddha-field within the cause.
Since this is the case, the same applies to those obscured by breaking the precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, and delusion;
this is also explained accordingly. The *Jingming ji* states: "Within the Tripiṭaka Teaching, there is no teaching of a pure land, because of afflictions..."
Because one is born through the moistening power of karma, there is no error in attaining Buddhahood within a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-lokadhātu*).

There are the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), yet there is no teaching of a pure land (*śuddha-kṣetra*). If the teaching lacks the practice, one will ultimately never attain Buddhahood;

if there is no cause for a pure land, a Buddha without practice exists, and if there is teaching but no person [to hear it], the practice of the six perfections has a cause but no fruit. Since the practice lacks its fruit, it conversely becomes a non-practice; this is the general principle.
People also say that if one practices the path of the Pure Land according to its respective teachings, although the texts exist, they are intended for those who are capable of being received;

thus, Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) possess knowledge of the Pure Land. [However,] knowing the principle of the Buddhas of the ten directions, the followers of the Two Vehicles (Ersheng) feel it is not appropriate for them to know this.
Out of self-disparagement, they never seek it, and thus do not bring it forth. Therefore, although Bodhisattvas know [of the Buddhas], they still...
Since "eternal extinction" (nirvāṇa) fundamentally contradicts the meaning of "taking up earth," we know that this Buddha has no human [teacher] and his teaching is provisional.
Because the teaching is provisionally bestowed and does not accord with causal practice, there is no need to laboriously scrutinize these provisional teachings.

Based on the insight of a Pratyekabuddha, who perceives a hundred buddha-worlds, one should likewise understand that there are buddhas in the ten directions; it is only feared that at the point of perception, they do not realize their existence.

Furthermore, since it is known that even within a single world-system there is but one Buddha performing transformations, this poses no contradiction; thus, even among the twenty schools, there are those who allow for the knowledge of Buddhas in the ten directions.
This is also appropriate as a gradual progression toward the Great Teaching. Consequently, followers of the Two Vehicles both know and do not know [the Buddhas].
For Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching who cultivate the causes for a Pure Land, if they rely on "leaping over stages," then it is pure.
Since the meaning of "lands" (bhūmi) permeates all teachings, there are four lands that encompass sentient beings both horizontally and vertically;
because there are five distinctions in the timing of their reception [of the teaching], these are known as the realms of humans and devas, as well as those of the four teachings.
When the karmic conditions for the ten Buddha-grounds have ripened, one suddenly severs residual habit-energies through the wisdom of a single thought-moment of correspondence;
sitting beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems upon a seat of celestial robes, one manifests as a Buddha in an inferior-superior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The tenth section, the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), is divided into three parts. First, regarding the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood: according to the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery), the Bodhisattvas of the same stage are distinguished by specific names for their stages of patience (*kṣānti*).

In the tenth stage, the Buddha-ground, the characteristics of attaining Buddhahood are as follows: relying upon his original vows and residual habits (*vāsanā*), he is born in Jambudvīpa and manifests the eight phases of enlightenment (*aṣṭābhinirhāra*).

The first five of these phases are identical to those in the Tripiṭaka teachings; however, regarding the phase of attaining Buddhahood, it is described that beneath the Bodhi tree, he attains [enlightenment].
The wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*) corresponds with the principle of the truth of non-arising (*anutpāda-satya*);

by severing the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), one is called a Buddha. Therefore, this wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment should not be said to consist of thirty-four moments of mind;

it should be understood as being merely the mindfulness of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*). As for the severing of residual habits, these were completely severed during the stage of a Bodhisattva, leaving only the remaining traces.

Because it is a residual portion (*avaśeṣa-bhāga*), the "portion" refers merely to the severed remnants of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). To attain Buddhahood, these remnants are precisely what must be transformed; they are the residual breaths of that which remains.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, crystal, red pearl, and agate are called the seven treasures (*sapta-ratna*).
Wooden trees are inferior treasures, while these are superior; they represent the superior teaching of the universal Dharma, surpassing the Tripiṭaka, and are like celestial garments.
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests that all dharmas are like illusions; thus, it is the same as what is realized by the Buddhas of the Tripiṭaka.

However, the manifested body of the Buddha of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇayāna*) differs from the three feet and one cubit, or one *li*, of the Tripiṭaka Buddhas; its physical dimensions span ten *li* or ten billion *li*, and its radiance is majestic and sublime.
Therefore, it is called the "superior response-body" (*viśiṣṭanairmāṇikakāya*). Alternatively, it is said that merely [realizing] emptiness is termed "carrying" (*dai*).
The inferior Middle Way within emptiness is called "superior" because the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) contains the principle of the combined body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

thus, the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s account of attaining enlightenment belongs exclusively to the Distinct and Complete Teachings (*bieyuan*). The enlightenment at the Deer Park clarifies only the three baskets (*piṭaka*) and the six-foot body;

it does not mention the attainment of Buddhahood by the Shared Buddha. Since the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñā* sūtras discuss the eight phases of manifestation, we know that the Sage’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
If one says that the two secret places are not absent,
[it is because] for those of the three vehicles' faculties and natures, the wheel of the Four Truths of Non-arising is turned;
this is the second, the downward-turning wheel of Dharma.

When conditions are exhausted and one enters extinction, both the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are eliminated together, like charcoal and ash being consumed entirely.

Regarding the third stage, when conditions are exhausted and one descends into *nirvāṇa*, the *Miaoxuan* also states that he entered *parinirvāṇa* between the twin *śāla* trees, leaving behind relics as a field of merit for devas and humans.
The "Buddha-ground" (*buddhabhūmi*) refers simply to the severance of residual habits and the attainment of the Way; viewed from the perspective of causes, it is the culmination of all.
When both the manifest afflictions and their habitual tendencies are removed, the residual traces (vāsanā) remain entirely like charcoal; when they are slightly diminished, it is like ash.
In the stage of Buddhahood, both charcoal and ash are entirely absent because, during the stage of a Bodhisattva, the wood has already been burned away.
The Sūtra speaks of "three animals crossing a river," referring to the elephant, the horse, and the rabbit, which serves as an analogy for the differing ways in which delusions are severed.
Furthermore, the Sūtra states that while all three vehicles realize the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they are not yet called Buddhas; this is precisely what is taught here.

The three sutras cited below as scriptural evidence refer to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The elephant symbolizes the Bodhisattva, the horse represents the Pratyekabuddha, and the rabbit corresponds to the Śrāvaka.
The river water is a metaphor for the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Although the three animals cross the same river, the elephant’s strength is greatest, the horse’s is next, and the rabbit’s is weakest; yet the river water remains one and the same. Thus, by means of the elephant and the horse...
The rabbit’s feet have long and short [hairs], and thus there are differences in the depth of the river they cross.

For this reason, although the three vehicles are identical in their realization of emptiness, the śrāvaka eliminates only the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), while the pratyekabuddha attenuates the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). The bodhisattva, however, cuts off the active afflictions while sustaining the habitual tendencies to moisten rebirth.
One should know that there are indeed distinctions of superiority and inferiority in entering emptiness; one must understand that these three vehicles are established according to the Dharma.

Cause and effect are identical when distinguished from the perspective of the person; thus, while the causes and effects of the three vehicles differ, that which is conventionally termed "illusory existence" is the principle known as "the emptiness of all phenomena," which is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Since both illusory existence and its emptiness are attained by all three vehicles, the meaning is clear:
those of the two vehicles are not yet Buddhas. This is because a Bodhisattva remains at the stage of the cause and therefore is not yet designated a Buddha.
When the treatise reaches the point of naming the fruit "Buddha," how can there be any doubt? However, for now, it is explained in terms of the causal stage; thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"The true nature of all phenomena is attained by three types of persons. Miaoxuan (Miao Xuan) judged this to be the "partial truth" (*pradeśasatya*).

The statement that the words are from the *sūtra* within the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* may perhaps be an error. Nevertheless, when a treatise cites the Buddha’s teaching, is that not indeed what is meant by "the *sūtra* says"?
However, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that while both the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) also attain the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), they are not called Buddhas.

Yet, it merely says that within the category of the two vehicles there is no "Shared Teaching" (*paryāya-śikṣā*); this must be further verified through such sūtras as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*.

This teaching [concerns] the three vehicles: their causes are the same while their fruits differ. Although the realization of the fruit differs, they are identical in severing *dṛṣṭi-heya* (afflictions eliminated by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions eliminated by cultivation), identical in transcending the *paricchinna-bhava* (limited existence), and identical in realizing the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*).

Fourth, this section concludes by demonstrating the similarities and differences: the three causes are largely the same, while the three fruits are slightly different; because they are largely the same...

Because the *prajñā* practiced by the various vehicles differs slightly, their cultivation of the exhaustion of outflows (*kṣayajñāna*) is not equal; yet, though they differ, they are the same in that they equally sever [afflictions] and equally realize [the fruit].

As cited previously, the eight meanings are entirely identical. If one considers the Three Vehicles according to the *Tripiṭaka* teaching, the Truths (*satya*), Conditions (*pratyaya*), and Faculties (*pāramitā*) differ, the three causes are vastly different, and while the three vehicles have subtle distinctions, the three fruits are slightly the same; yet, though they are the same, they differ, as illustrated by the eight points cited in the middle fascicle.
Regarding the term "segmented," it refers to the segmented births within the three realms and six destinies, consisting of distinct physical parts and segments.
However, among bodhisattvas, there are two types: those of sharp faculties and those of dull faculties.

Second, regarding the extensive explanation below that applies [the teaching] across both preceding and succeeding stages, the text is divided into two parts. First, both [the sharp and dull faculties] are indicated together because it is intended to clarify their relationship before and after;

therefore, it says, "Thus. Although the cessation of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) by the Two Vehicles is set aside and not further discussed, the reason for mentioning only the Bodhisattvas here is to distinguish between the two types—sharp and dull—within their own ranks.
However, this [distinction] generally applies to the Two Vehicles prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
If one attains the benefit of both flavors, one may also advance; this is the "Manifest" (Kengyo) teaching, which is not restricted to the "Secret" (Mikkyo) and is universally pervasive.
If one is dull-witted, one sees only partial emptiness and does not see non-emptiness; thus, they merely accomplish the practice for the fruit-stage Buddha according to this specific teaching.
Although the causes differ, the fruit is equal to that of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zōgyō); therefore, it is said to be "pervasive" (tsūzen) with respect to what precedes it.
Second, regarding the two types of dull [faculties], there is a dual explanation of the lower [stage]. This is divided into two parts:

first, explaining how this universally accords with what was previously stated—that by seeing only partial emptiness, one becomes a Buddha of the present teaching, which corresponds to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*) within the aforementioned common position.

Because the cause of flourishing flowers results in the attainment of the actual fruit, and the stage of the fruit resides above this, it is called "the head. All of these are established as names based on metaphors; although the causal practices differ, in terms of...
Regarding the teaching, the fruits and the *pitakas* are explained in their entirety; regarding the realization, cause and effect are distinguished.
Furthermore, citing one teaching and one realization serves to clarify the meaning that precedes them; the interpretation lies herein. If it were not so, why would it be?
Therefore, how could the subsequent text be pointed out as a comprehensive explanation? Thus, I now divide the sections, daring to say they are in perfect accord.
If a bodhisattva of sharp faculties not only perceives emptiness but also perceives non-emptiness—non-emptiness being the Middle Way—this is divided into two types:
if they perceive the "mere middle," they are received by the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao); if they perceive the "not-mere middle," they are received by the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao).
Therefore, it is said that this applies to both subsequent [teachings].
Second, the explanation of the latter two [faculties] through the sharp and dull: first, the direct explanation. It is not merely that those with sharp faculties see emptiness;

they first temporarily agree with the dull, while also seeing non-emptiness, which subsequently reveals their superiority. Because one person’s sequence of practice differs from the other, it is said "not merely.

Since it mentions "non-empty," this precisely refers to the Middle Way. The Middle Way is what is expounded by the Distinct (Bie) and Complete (Yuan) teachings; here, it specifically refers to the Distinct teaching.

However, the Middle Way does not fully possess all dharmas, like the moon outside the clouds or a lotus flower emerging from the water; thus, the perfect expression (*paryāya*) not only possesses both extremes.
Furthermore, within this single school, the clarification of the Middle Way is twofold: first, that which is free from annihilationism and eternalism belongs to the two preceding teachings;

second, that which is based on Buddha-nature belongs to the latter two teachings. Because these teachings are provisional, they are merely called "Middle" in name according to their principle; this is the distinct [teaching].
Within the teaching on Buddha-nature, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is called "true stillness yet constant illumination," wherein all things are none other than the *Vairocana* Middle Way.

Although there are both "limited" and "unlimited" [teachings], they are all termed "sharp faculties" (*liken*), as they all lead to the subsequent [stages] of the Distinct and Perfect teachings; such is their meaning. Question:

Since the explanation of the meanings of the Four Teachings is already exhaustive and leaves nothing out, why is it necessary to further clarify the doctrine of "reception and transition" (*shoujie*)? Answer: Have you not heard...?

Is "receiving and being received" (*shoujie*) not the same as the four teachings? Therefore, one must know that the beginning and the end are identical; thus it is said that the four teachings are the same from start to finish.

Conversely, because they differ in their beginnings and ends, it is said that there are three types of "receiving and being received. Although these three types of reception are distinguished, the Mahāyāna encompasses them all;

why, then, should one find it difficult to further clarify the process of reception? Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that one hears the Middle Way in the eighth stage and cultivates the Middle Way in the ninth stage. Such is the teaching.
This [teaching] is neither universal nor particular; it does not observe the eternal [nature] from the beginning to the end of the Universal Teaching (*pāryāyika*).

Since those of the Particular [Vehicle] have already realized the Middle Way at the first stage (*bhūmi*), how could they only hear of the Middle Way at the eighth stage? Therefore, one must explain this passage by means of "reception" (*saṃdhāna*).

According to the scripture, it speaks of the lower faculties as being in the eighth or ninth stages; however, based on the underlying principle, there should also be those of medium and superior faculties. Thus, it indeed exists.

The three faculties (*indriya*) that receive the "reception" (*pratigraha*) are further divided into three types: the Perfect Reception of the Perfect, the Perfect Reception of the Separate, and the Separate Reception of the Perfect.
What is called "reception" refers to the Middle Way receiving True Suchness (*tathatā*), like gold receiving brass; two substances join together, and for this reason it is so termed.
Those who follow the lower faculty do so because one wishes to demonstrate the Middle within the True; therefore, they must wait until emptiness is realized before [the Middle] becomes manifest.

Pointing out [the teaching] so that one may deeply contemplate emptiness, one sees non-emptiness; having already seen the truth through the two superior faculties (the middle and superior roots), one then points out the emptiness within the middle.
Because the true emptiness of the middle and superior [faculties] is shallow, it is said that the teachings mostly accommodate those of inferior faculties.
Is this meaning prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, or does it also apply to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Answer: It exists in all five periods; what is there that is not?

It must be determined thus: one must know that the "reception" (*jiejie*) prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is called the "reception of the assembly," while the reception within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* at the Deer Park is the "reception of the Dharma.
The secret discussions regarding the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* are subsequently explained as such. Therefore, the reception exists throughout all five periods. Question:
Does this reception apply only to Bodhisattvas, or does it also extend to the Two Vehicles? Answer: The reception prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* applies only to Bodhisattvas.
In the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the Two Vehicles’ teachings, as well as within the *Lotus Sūtra*, those who are "received" (*pratigraha*) include not only the Two Vehicles but also Bodhisattvas;

thus, all those in the *Lotus Sūtra* who are received across the Three Vehicles do so by way of the "exoteric" *Lotus Sūtra* and prior teachings, and the reception of Bodhisattvas is likewise the same.
Question: What is the distinction between "receiving" (*pratigraha*) and "being received" (*pratigṛhīta*)? Answer: To distinguish them provisionally, "receiving" refers to—
Question: When considering the capacity that is received [by the Buddha], one should investigate it thoroughly; how could there be any separation?

If the question concerns receiving [the teaching] by a single capacity, then the same applies to the response. Answer: The mutual resonance of the response and the stimulus cannot be partial. Question:

Does "receiving" refer to those already established in the tenth stage (bhūmi) of the Shared Teaching, or does it reside in the first stage or first dwelling of the Separate and Perfect Teachings? Answer: Following the ancient tradition and the fundamental principle, it refers to the tenth stage.

Regarding the stages of practice through teaching and realization within the *bhūmis* and *vihāras*, they are summarized as previously explained; for details, one should consult the various texts. Question:
At what stage does one receive the "reception" (*parigraha*), and into what stage does one enter?

This section of analytical selection is divided into two parts. First, the question concerning the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*): at what stage does one receive the reception, and furthermore, into what stage does one advance?

At what stage do those entering the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] receive the transition? Answer: Regarding the differences among the three faculties of those receiving the transition, those of superior faculty are received at the third or fourth stage;
those of middling faculty are received at the fifth or sixth stage; and those of inferior faculty are received at the seventh or eighth stage.
The second part, the answer, is divided into two sections. First, regarding the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the three capacities are established;
this answers the previous question concerning at which stage one receives the "reception" (*pratigraha*). Regarding the superior capacity, the "three stages or four stages":

although the third stage is within the *anantarya-samādhi*, it remains a cause rather than a fruit and is not yet entirely saintly, being merely on the verge of becoming so. Thus, at the third stage, one is not yet fit to receive the reception.
Therefore, Jingxi said: "From the beginning of the fourth stage up to the ninth stage, all receive the name 'receiving and being received.

The fourth stage is considered superior, the sixth and seventh stages are middling, and the eighth and ninth stages are inferior. Thus we know that it is only from the fourth stage onward that one discusses receiving and being received.

If one is to be received into the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), it must necessarily be at the level of a sage (*ārya*). However, Jingxi also stated: "The wisdom of the Dry Intellect Stage (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) and the Nature Ground (*prakṛti-bhūmi*) is still inferior."

Therefore, it is also not received under the name of "reception" (jiejie). Thus we know that the stages of the three grounds follow one another without interval and must necessarily reach the fourth ground.

This is stated from the perspective of the subsequent [stages] and is generally referred to as the "sage. Consequently, it is provisionally called the "upper root" of the three grounds; yet, speaking with definitive certainty, one must reach the fourth ground.

The phrasing and meaning are relaxed and comprehensive, so one should exercise proper discernment. Nevertheless, the stage of reception applies to both the *Tong* (Shared) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings.
Regarding the separate treatment here, the reason we now categorize them by way of the three faculties in general is that this current text specifically clarifies the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

Furthermore, the division of the middle and lower faculties against the stages of attainment also differs from the text cited previously from Jingxi; however, one may infer the meaning for the upper faculty by analogy with what has been explained above.

The teachings received differ according to whether they are "semblance" or "true": if one is received at the semblance stage, it is distinct from the ten *pariṇāmanā* (dedications) and the ten *śraddhā* (faiths);
if one is received at the true stage, it is distinct from the first *bhūmi* and the first *vihāra*.
The second point, concerning the "receiving" (so-jie), distinguishes between the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] as being "True" and "Simulated";
this is the answer to the previous question regarding at what stage one enters the Separate and Perfect Vehicles. The *Jingming ji* states:

"If, from the perspective of the receiving, that which is received is common to both [vehicles], yet the Separate and Perfect are the 'receivers,' then by taking the principle of what can be received as the object, it causes the subject to possess the capacity for the function of receiving; this is the meaning of the principle."
In the case of "penetration" (*tong*), it inherently contains both the capacity [the faculty] and the object [the teaching].

If one does not explain it through the sense of "receiving" (*jie*), how can one clarify that within penetration, for those of sharp faculties, the arising of the faculty depends upon receiving [the teaching], and that the reception awaits the maturation of the capacity? This is because, from the perspective of the response [the teaching] looking toward the capacity [the faculty], penetration is the object received.
Conversely, if one looks from the perspective of the capacity toward the response, then the Distinct and Complete [teachings] become the objects received. Now, it is said: "The object..."
That the teachings received differ between the real and the semblance is precisely because the capacity of the recipient corresponds to the response of the Buddha.

This may also be described as follows: the "teachings received" refers generally to both the real and the semblance, while the distinction between them pertains to the specific levels of the Perfect and the Partial.

Thus, "real" refers to the true path and true realization; "semblance" refers to the provisional and similar reception; and "reception" (shou) refers to the capacity of the recipient to accommodate and sustain the teaching.
Regarding the term "receiving" (*bei*): when the capacity for receiving is appropriate and the recipient is ready, it is called "receiving," which means being covered or encompassed.
Within the teachings of the Distinct and Perfect [Vehicles], the Middle Way is "covered" and "encompassed" so as to provide a connection; therefore, it is called "being covered.

Alternatively, it may be said that those of sharp faculties in the Shared Teaching are "covered" by the arrival of the Distinct and Perfect Vehicles. Thus, both the capacity (*ji*) and the response (*ying*) possess the meaning of being "covered. Therefore, it is true... [text ends].

"Connecting the stages" (*wei-jie*) is also called "superior advancement" (*sheng-jin*). "Resembling the stage" (*si-wei*) is also called "connecting according to the stage" (*an-wei-jie*). This refers to those of inferior capacity;

for those of inferior capacity, superior advancement mostly reaches the true stage of abiding (*zhu-zhen-wei*). As for those of middling or superior capacity who enter, this is not fixed; one must examine their specific position.
If they connect [to the Bodhisattva stages], they enter before the seventh stage of the distinct [teaching]; if they enter the distinct [teaching], it is at the tenth *zhù* or the eighth *bǔ*.
As for entering the distinct [stages] of the ten practices and the ten dedications, since the entry into the distinct is thus, the entry into the Perfect [Teaching] should be understood accordingly.

If the Perfect connects with the distinct stages, it connects with the stage of the Worthies (*bhadra*). Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "This means that by employing the former teaching, there is a beginning but no end;

having already employed the seventh and eighth stages, one does not reach the ninth and tenth. By employing the latter teaching, there is an end but no beginning; one uses only the stages of dedication."

There is no need for dwelling or practice; this is also the inferior faculty (*mṛdu-indriya*). The progression and regression of the eighth and ninth stages should be understood by analogy with the third and fourth [stages]; consider this deeply.

The *Miaoxuan* (Mysterious Profundity) distinguishes three "receptions" (*sambandha*) based on the provisional teachings (*yāna*), whereas *Zhi Guan* (Cessation and Contemplation), which accords with ultimate principle, speaks only of one reception.

Although the distinction between the opening and closing of the three receptions and the one reception is such that their meanings mutually encompass one another, when distinguishing them according to the provisional teachings and ultimate principle, the three and the one must be differentiated. Thus, the Perfect Reception encompasses the Separate [Vehicle].

Question: Regarding the superior faculties in the Ten Abidings, the middling faculties in the Ten Practices, and the inferior faculties in the Ten Dedications—when it is asked how one who cultivates the "Round Middle" (yuanzhong) within the Ten Dedications can be received into the "Ordinary Middle" (danzhong), what is the answer? Answer: There are many paths regarding the meaning of the distinct ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*).

First, there are those who, according to the teachings of the Path of Doctrine (*jiaodao*), cultivate the Ordinary Middle, yet in reality no such person exists. Second, there are those who cultivate the Provisional and receive the reception [into the Round]. Third, there are those who [cultivate] the Three [Truths].

Regarding those who practice the "Perfect" (yuan) [teaching], it is said that they "connect the Perfect Middle with the Separate Middle. In general discussions of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), all say it is merely the "Separate Middle" (*butian zhong*);

thus, it is said that the Perfect Middle connects with the Separate Middle. In reality, however, this refers to people who practice the contemplation of the conventional (*jiaguān*) while lacking the realization of the person;

because they do not cultivate the "Middle of the Person" (*ren zhong*), even when they connect with the Separate Middle, it is merely a provisional explanation. Question: How does one of inferior capacity receive [this teaching]?

Question: Is the practice of receiving the transformation (*prativedha*) toward the distinct [Vehicle] and the Perfect [Vehicle] the same or different? Answer: This must be distinguished. What is meant by "inferior faculties receiving the transformation"?

Regarding the transformation from the Perfect toward the Distinct, the Perfect cultivation is the primary cultivation within the Perfect; furthermore, the transformation from the Perfect toward the Distinct applies generally to those at the stages of abiding (*sthiti*) and practice (*caryā*).

As for the person who cultivates the Perfect, their distinct [practice] lies specifically in the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*). Moreover, regarding the reception of the transformation, it refers to transforming one's own cultivation of the provisional toward the Perfect.
Cultivating [the stages] from this point onward is the second contemplation; if one enters the Middle Way, it is no different from the Perfect [Teaching].

Thus, while receiving the transmission must necessarily involve Perfect cultivation, Perfect cultivation does not necessarily coincide entirely with the transmission, because there are differences between the universal and the restricted, and between the provisional and the true Middle.

Question: Since both the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings equally constitute the Three Vehicles, equally sever the four abodes of ignorance, equally transcend the triple world, equally realize partial truth, equally travel three hundred yojanas, and equally enter the illusory city—why are they divided into two?
Third, a general selection of the texts of the *Zang* (Treasury) and *Tong* (Common) teachings is divided into two parts. First, the question:

since the severances and realizations of the three vehicles are not different, why are they divided into two distinct teachings? One should know that this objection uses the identity of severance and realization to challenge the difference between the teachings regarding their underlying essence (*ti*).
Answer: It is indeed as you have asked.
The response to these two questions is divided into two parts. First, the acceptance of the question: since both abandonment and realization are identical, why are there two teachings?

However, while they are the same yet not the same, although that which is realized is the same, the Great and Small Vehicles differ eternally in their skillfulness and crudeness. These two teachings are the teachings within the realm [of saṃsāra].

Second, "However, below" is the actual answer regarding the similarities and differences, which is divided into two parts: first, answering how they are the same yet different; second, answering how, although the severance and realization are the same...

What prevents the teachings from being distinct? Although the teachings differ when categorized by their doctrinal systems, what prevents the realization [of the fruit] from being the same? Though they differ, they are the same;

though they are the same, they differ. Since the *bie* (distinct) and *yuan* (perfect) [teachings] speak of "provisional" lands and so forth as being "beyond the realms," while the *zang* (treasury) and *tong* (common) [teachings] speak only of the three realms and six paths as being "within the realms," and although the *zang* and *tong* claim that one leaves the realms by severing delusions, this is actually the case only in terms of the ultimate principle (*li*).

The practice involves both external phenomena and the principles of those phenomena, wherein waves and water are mutually identical; it is not that there is a separate realm or land outside the *dhātu*.
It is only in terms of the distinct and perfect [teachings] that one speaks of "external.

The *Āgama* (Tripitaka) is "internal" because it is small and clumsy, lacking penetration into the Great [Vehicle]; it is "small" because it analyzes form to enter into emptiness, and it is "clumsy" because this teaching [is limited].
Although these three types of persons differ within the teaching as superior, middling, and inferior, when viewed collectively, they are all uniformly of dull faculties;
therefore, [the teaching] must be broken down [into two].

Second, the separate explanation of the distinct meanings of the two Piṭakas is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the Hīnayāna: it is "crude" because it does not penetrate the Mahāyāna.

The "lesser" refers to the *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattvas, who merely suppress their afflictions; the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), however, have extinguished their perceptions and their roots are destroyed so that they do not arise [in further rebirth].
These descriptions are all made in reference to what was taught prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Therefore, the *Tripiṭaka* does not extend to the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, regarding the Two Vehicles, they do not extend to the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas, who are then transformed into those within the Mahāyāna. Moreover, when the Two Vehicles reach the Vaipulya period, they enter *parinirvāṇa*.

If one attains both general and specific benefits, that is not the intended meaning of the present text; rather, it follows the provisional teaching which does not accord with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Because that treatise refutes form (*rūpa*) to enter emptiness (*śūnyatā*), those who are clumsy claim that phenomena truly exist and that the state of seeing emptiness is reached only after they have been completely refuted.
If this is their contemplation, is it not indeed clumsy? Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "It is like a physician who employs needles and medicinal drugs; this is called 'clumsy.'"
For example, crossing over using a raft made of grass is called "crude. As for what is termed "breaking" (*zhé*), "breaking" means to break apart.

This name "breaking" originates from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who contemplate whether a single atom is exhausted or not; thus, the contemplation of impermanence and so forth in the Tripiṭaka Teaching is also called "breaking.
However, this "breaking" is used to refute the non-Buddhist form of breaking, which is not the correct [method]; therefore, it is designated as "breaking."

To perceive the principle of emptiness while remaining within the conventional reality is called "correct refutation. Regarding the sequence of the Three Vehicles as corresponding to the superior, middling, and inferior capacities is like using a level, a bushel, or a measure of wood;
it is called a "standard" (*gai*). To view the Lesser Vehicle in comparison with the Mahāyāna through this single standard is dullness indeed.
In the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), "great" refers to the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) as the initial gateway, and "skillful" refers to the realization that form is empty of intrinsic nature.
Although within this teaching there are three types of practitioners—superior, middling, and inferior—when compared to the Treasury Teaching (zangjiao), they are all uniformly considered sharp.

The second section provides a general explanation of the "Great Skillful Means" (Mahā-upāya) in two parts: first, the formal explanation; and second, the specific application. Regarding the phrase "the Great refers to the initial gate of the Mahāyāna":
the question is whether this initial gate of the Mahāyāna belongs specifically to the present teaching or applies generally to the *Bie* (Separate) and *Yuan* (Perfect) vehicles.

The answer is that within the *Miaoxuan*, this very question is raised, and in the response, it is established that the initial gate pertains to the *Tong* (Common), *Bie* (Separate), and *Yuan* (Perfect) vehicles. This is how the three types of faculties receive [the teaching].

This accords with the meaning; furthermore, it is said that for Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles, "skillful means" refers to the realization that the substance of form enters into emptiness.

This is because it is discussed in terms of the Three Vehicles according to their respective teachings. That is to say, the dharma is illusory existence, and by realizing its substance as being immediately empty, such a correspondence between object and contemplation is clearly skillful.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "For example, there is a physician who employs incantations and spells; this is called..."
Skillfulness is also like a person crossing a river using a large boat; this is called skillfulness because it carries those who look toward the small [vehicle] across.
Question: Since the teaching is already the Mahāyāna, for what reason are there people of the two vehicles?

The second section, "Distinguishing the Categories," is divided into two parts. First, the question: It should be understood that if one simply says "Mahāyāna," it refers generally to this specific teaching as well;

however, if one says "the initial gate of Mahāyāna," one takes the general [Teaching] and the subsequent distinct and perfect [teachings]. Now, since this is Mahāyāna, why are there instead the middle and lower vehicles?

Answer: What prevents commoners from entering and exiting through the Vermilion Bird Gate? Therefore, although the person has received the Lesser Vehicle teachings, they will certainly become a great practitioner of the Mahāyāna who incorporates the Lesser Vehicle as a gradual introduction to the ultimate reality; is this not indeed skillful?

In the second response, it is simply stated that within the Mahāyāna answers, the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is still adopted; thus, it says they are "gradually led into the true teaching.

Although this does not preclude the two types of persons [of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles] from being generally categorized as "Small" (*hīnayāna*), in a hidden sense (*samdhāya*), it is argued that even those of the two vehicles may enter the truth.
Now, following the principle of gradual induction, it is as previously stated: "The Emperor [leads them] southward."
The gate is named the Vermilion Bird Gate (Zhūjué mén), through which the common people pass to and fro without obstruction.
Regarding the *Prajñā* and *Vaipulya* sections, those such as the *Sādhāraṇa-prajñā* (Common Prajñā) constitute this very teaching.

At the end of the section on the four *prajñās*, it concludes by indicating that they accord with the meaning of this teaching; thus, "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) refers to the fact that [these teachings] are shared. Now, when the text says "etc. (*diǎng*), it means...

Because it takes up the meaning of the unique [teachings] following the [explanation of] the penetrations, the brief and extensive explanations as well as the concluding demonstration are complete in their two-fold intent.
This concludes the brief clarification of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Third, the brief clarification below is the general conclusion.
Next, the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) is explained.
First, the threefold classification of the Separate Teaching is presented.

This teaching clarifies the dharma for bodhisattvas alone outside the realm (*dhātu*), and its teachings, wisdom, principle, severance, practice, stages, cause, and fruit are distinct from the preceding two [teachings].
It is called "Distinct" (*bie*) because it is distinct from the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Second, regarding the explanation of this teaching [the following three points are presented]: first, the explanation of the meaning of the names; second, the direct explanation of the lands such as the "Skillful Means" (*fangbian*);

and third, the explanation of the term "boundary. Because it is outside the boundaries, it is not for the Two Vehicles or Buddhas; thus it is called "unique" (*du*) to Bodhisattvas. It is a "distinct" name (*bie ming*) and not a "shared" (*bunong*) name. It is not called "not shared" (*bunong*).
To say merely that it is "distinct" (bie) implies it is not shared with the two vehicles and exists only within the *Avataṃsaka*;

however, because we now wish to include it within the two *Sūtras* (*Śrīmālā* and *Nirvāṇa*), we establish the name of the "Distinct Teaching" (biejiao). This is because while this Dharma is heard by those of the two vehicles, it is distinct in that it belongs specifically to the Bodhisattvas.
Thus, "shared" and "unshared" are distinguished according to the persons, whereas the terms "common" and "distinct" are spoken in reference to the Dharma itself.

Regarding the Dharma, the four foundations of mindfulness are distinguished in their teaching; the Buddha-sun first illuminates the bodhisattvas. They are distinguished in principle, as the three truths are distinct and sequential.
They are distinguished in wisdom, as the three wisdoms arise successively. They are distinguished in abandonment, as the three delusions are severed before and after one another.
They are distinguished in practice, as the five practices differ from one another. They are distinguished in stage, as they do not mutually encompass one another. This is the cause.
"Distinct" (bie) means that one cause stands far apart [from others]; "distinct in fruit" means that one fruit is not integrated [with others].

Therefore, these eight meanings all pertain to that which is outside the realms (dhātu), and thus they are distinct from the preceding [teachings], which are entirely the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, and distinct from the subsequent, which is the Perfect [Teaching].
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the causes and conditions of the Four Noble Truths possess immeasurable characteristics that are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.

Second, regarding the citation of evidence from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* to demonstrate that the Four Noble Truths are immeasurable, as previously analyzed, it is said that the two vehicles do not know them;

this is spoken with reference to their "unshared" [knowledge]. Even if they were to hear the teachings of the two "milk-products" (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saṃdhinirmocana*), they would still not penetrate them; thus, they are not objects of their knowledge, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
At one time, while I was on Vulture Peak with Maitreya, we were discussing conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Śāriputra and others did not understand it;
it was just as in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where Subhūti did not know how to answer.
The various Mahāyāna sūtras extensively clarify the sequence of stages and the progression of practice throughout kalpas for bodhisattvas, yet these do not mutually encompass one another;
this is the characteristic of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).

The *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-avataṃsaka-sūtra* is called "Adornment" (*Avataṃsaka*) because it elucidates the adornment of the Dharma-body through the six wheels, the six patiences, and so forth.

however, in Paramārtha’s translation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-rāja-sūtra*, the "Chapter on the Distinction of the Three Bodies" clarifies that after the ten stages, one further enters the stage of the Tathāgata. Thus, [the two texts differ].
Those who come to the stages (bhūmis) are purified in three ways: first, purification of afflictions (*kleśa*); second, purification of suffering (*duḥkha*);

and third, purification of marks (*nimitta*). Therefore, it is said that the ten stages constitute the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the clarification of the ten stages by the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"At that time, there was among the assembly a deva-king named Pāpila; therefore, he is called 'Victorious Deva' (*Suvikrāntavikramī*)."

The "King" is simply a name. As for the five practices of nirvana—the noble practice, the brahma practice, the celestial practice, the practice of illness, and the practice of an infant—these five successive practices belong to the Separate Teaching.

Regarding the differences in increase and decrease among such various sutras: how could it be possible to provide a definitive explanation for the Bodhisattvas outside the realm who benefit beings according to their individual capacities?

Second, the following section clarifies the intent; regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, it states that in the preliminary portion of the Vaipulya [sūtras], they were taught in a scattered manner in response to specific conditions.
Previously, there were no sequential stages; it merely explained the attainment of the Way in a general manner without discussing the levels of attainment.

It was only in the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (The Jewel Garland) that the stages were summarized, clarifying the fifty-two grounds (*bhūmi*). Similarly, in the earlier sections of the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, the teachings were also given in response to specific conditions in a scattered fashion, lacking sequential stages;
it was only in the *Śrīmaladevīsiṃhanāda-sūtra* (The Lion’s Roar of Queen Śrīmālā) that the ten grounds were clarified, as there were no preceding thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*) prior to them.

Later, in the *Wu deng jue miao xuan* (The Profound Mystery of the Peerless Enlightenment), it says: "The *Renwang Banruo* clarifies fifty-one stages, which serve to conclude all *prajñāpāramitā* teachings.
To infer its intent: it is like a military commander who, having finished clearing out the rebels, then recounts their meritorious achievements and establishes their ranks and emoluments.
The sutra’s elucidation of the stages is likewise so. Thus, the various stages differ from one another because they all follow [the specific circumstances]."

In the *Jishuō* (Discourse on the Capacity), it is asked: "Why does the *Lotus Sūtra* not clarify the stages? The answer is: "The *Yingluo* [Sūtra] establishes the various Vaipulya [teachings], and the *Renwang* [Sūtra] establishes the various Prajñā [teachings];
the *Lotus Sūtra*, however, merely resolves all provisional means so that they may enter into the ultimate reality."

However, as no other text provides such a complete and systematic presentation of the stages as the *Sūtra of the Necklaces* (*Yingluo jing*), I shall now briefly clarify the characteristics of the Bodhisattvas' progression through the stages, their severances, and their realizations based upon it.

Second, "Now, below," specifically relies on the text of the *Yingluo* [Sūtra] and is divided into two parts. First, the statement of intent, which is further divided into two: first, establishing the thesis; second, relying upon...

The *Sūtra on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states: "The various Mahāyāna sūtras within the gateway of the teachings for a single lifetime differ from door to door, and the stages are distinct;
thus, the methods adopted by practitioners also vary. To fully perfect the sequence of stages, one must rely on the *Ābharaṇa-sūtra* (Yíngluò) and the *Wondrous Profundity* (Miàoxuán).

It says: 'One must rely on the two sūtras, the *Ābharaṇa* and the *Benevolent Kings*. If one discusses the relative heights of abandonment and suppression, one must rely on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.'"
Regarding the three contemplations in this chapter, if one were to correlate them with the Dharma-gates, they must rely upon the five practices and ten merits of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
synthesizing the intent of various scriptures to establish the contemplative teachings for the initial stage of the path.
The fifty-two stages are condensed into seven categories— namely, the stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, ground, and so forth— which are further unified within the "wondrous" [stage].

Regarding these two [categories], there are first the ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and second the noble ones (*ārya*). Within the ordinary persons, there are again two: the external ordinary persons, consisting of the stages of faith (*śraddhā*), and the internal ordinary persons, consisting of the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation (*vihāra-pratipatti-mukha*), which are also called the "sages" (*bhadra*).

Regarding the noble ones, there are also twenty stages, from the *bhūmi* up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyogajñāna*), which serves as the cause, and Sublime Enlightenment (*prabhāsvarajñāna*), which serves as the fruit.
The general outline is thus; below, it will be explained in detail.
The second [category] is evident from the text on the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya*).

Regarding the first, the "ten levels of faith" (*daśa śraddhā*): first, faith; second, mindfulness; third, diligence; fourth, wisdom; fifth, concentration; sixth, non-retrogression; seventh, dedication;

eighth, protection of the Dharma; ninth, precepts; and tenth, vows. Because these ten stages subdue the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*) within the three realms, they are so named.

This is called the stage of Subduing Patience (the outer ordinary person), which is equivalent to the seven stages of the Worthies in the Tripitaka Teaching and the Stage of Dry Wisdom in the Shared Teaching.

Second, the section beginning with "First, regarding the following" explains [the text] in two parts. First, the ordinary stage is divided into two. First, the outer ordinary stage consists of the ten faiths.

Since the stages of the Distinct Teaching follow the *Ratnakūṭa-śāstra* (Yingluo jing), we shall now explain the meanings of the names and terms based on that scripture. In the first fascicle of that sutra, [the Buddha addresses] Jingshou...

The Bodhisattva asked what the names of all the worthy sages were, and the Buddha replied by explaining the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the stainless stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), and the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Furthermore, prior to the ten abodes, he clarified the names of the bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten *gaṅgā* rivers;
these are the bodhisattvas who constantly practice the ten minds, which are precisely the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). That sutra also lists the ten faiths [at this point].
After the forty-two stages, the terminology used therein differs somewhat from that listed here; this will be pointed out one by one below when we encounter the text.

In the "Chapter on Explaining the Meaning" (*Vyākhyāna-paṭala*) of the lower fascicle of that sutra, only the stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and the grounds (*bhūmi*) are explained in detail, yet even the names of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are not explained there.
Now, I shall cite the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Śrī-mālā-sūtra*) to explain these stages of abiding and practice.

Regarding the wondrous stages such as the Grounds (*bhūmi*), one may provisionally interpret the names of the Ten Faiths according to the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi Sūtra*. However, within the *Śūraṃgama*, these stages correspond precisely to the Perfect Faith (*pariniṣpanna-śraddhā*).

To abide in the principle of permanence is called the "Mind of Faith" (*śraddhā-citta*); to recollect without forgetting is called the "Mind of Mindfulness" (*smṛti-citta*); to advance with true diligence is called the "Mind of Diligence" (*vīrya-citta*);
the subtle essence of the mind's wisdom is called the "Mind of Wisdom" (*prajñā-citta*); and to be universally pervasive and profoundly tranquil is called... [the Mind of Samādhi].
It is said: the concentrated mind and the light of concentration that does not regress is called the "non-regressing mind"; maintaining it without loss is called the "mind that protects the Dharma";
dedicating toward the stage of Buddhahood is called the "mind of dedication. In the present text, the dedication is placed before the protection of the Dharma;

this follows the *Yingluo Jing* (Sutra of the Garland), which states that abiding securely without loss is called the "mind of precepts," while following one's vows throughout the ten directions is called [the mind of vows].

Because these ten minds are rooted in faith, they are called the "Ten Faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā*). While this is the case for the distinct (separate) faith, one should consider that it is analogous for the perfect (round) faith;
however, they differ in terms of being immediate or not immediate, and being complete or incomplete. The same applies to all subsequent stages.

Thus, there are further distinctions between ordinary and sage levels, as well as differences in advancement and regression. In the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo), among the six types of patience (*kṣānti*), the first is named "Subduing" (*vāsanā*).

Patience (*kṣānti*) is so named because it involves the patient endurance and subduing of the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Although the teaching gates differ, the subduing of these delusions by external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) is the same; therefore, the *Zang* (Āgama) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings and those below are to be understood accordingly.

Next, to clarify the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*): first, the Abode of Resolving the Mind (*cittotpādavihāra*), which exhausts all delusions of views within the Three Realms and is equal to the First Fruit (*srotāpanna*) of the *Zang* Teaching and the Stage of Seeing (*darśanabhūmi*) of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka*) of the *Tong* Teaching. Consecration (the above three stages exhaust the *chen-sha* [dust-like] delusions within the realms and suppress those outside the realms; the first two do not know their names). This is also called the Nature of Cultivation (*xi zhong xing*), which employs the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional to perceive [reality].
The True Dharma-principle opens the eye of wisdom and accomplishes the practice of all-knowledge for three hundred *yojanas*.

Second, regarding the three stages of the inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), first are the ten abodes (*vihāra*). Because one dwells in these ten within the principle of true emptiness, they are called "abodes.
Throughout various eons, one practices the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) without forming false views, extensively seeking wisdom; this is called "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*).
Abiding in the constant mindfulness of emptiness and purifying all dharmas is called the Stage of Purifying the Ground (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*).

Cultivating and nurturing all practices is called the Stage of Practice (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*). Being born into the family of the Buddhas with a pure lineage is called the Stage of Noble Birth (*janma-vaṃśa-viśuddhi-vihāra*).
