Extensively practicing immeasurable roots of goodness is called the Stage of Endowment with Skillful Means (*upāya-saṃbhāra-vihāra*). The present mention of "endowment with skillful means" is explained according to the new translation.

The accomplishment of the sixth Prajñā-dharmaparyāya is named the Stage of Right Mind (Samyak-citta-vihāra); entering the ultimate realm of non-arising emptiness is named the Stage of Non-retrogression (Avinivartana-vihāra);
not giving rise to false inversions and not destroying the Bodhicitta is named the Stage of Youthful Truth (Kumārabhūta-vihāra);

being born from the teaching of the Buddha-King and attaining understanding such that one shall succeed to the Buddha’s position is named the Stage of the Dharma Prince (Dharmarāja-putra-vihāra); contemplating emptiness and signlessness [is the next stage].
Attaining the mind of non-arising is called the Stage of Empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* states:

"Just as a great king of a kingdom delegates all state affairs to his crown prince, so too when the son of a Kṣatriya king has reached maturity, he is consecrated with the rite of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*).
Taking water from the four oceans and placing it within a golden vase, he pours it over the crown of the prince's head; now, the Dharma is likewise."
The "Water Initiation" (abhiṣeka) is so named for this reason. "Dust and sand" is a metaphor for the vast number of Dharma gates.
Because it can transform the six classes of ordinary beings within the segmented [realms] of the triple world, it is said to "sever that which is within the realm.

Because one is able to cultivate and study the dharmas of the four types of noble ones regarding the transformative [rebirths], it is said to "subdue that which is outside the realm. Those of the previous two vehicles—the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha—do not know the name of what lies outside the realm.
Regarding the "nature of the stage of cultivation" (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*): the six types of natures are named after the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ratnavyūha-sūtra*).

"Cultivation" (*śikṣā*) refers to the practice of cultivation; "nature" (*bīja*) refers to the capacity to produce [the fruit]. It is called "unchanging" because it is through the power of cultivation that it can produce [the result] without alteration.

The *Commentary on the Precepts* (*Śīla-śāstra*) states that this capacity to produce the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*) proceeds from the provisional into emptiness; this sequence constitutes the third contemplation as set forth in the *Necklace Sūtra*.

In the first fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, one investigates the falsity of birth and death through the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) and thereby perceives the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
thus, it is called the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*saṃvṛti-śūnyatā-praveśa-bhāvanā*), also known as the contemplation of the two truths (*dvi-satya-bhāvanā*).

That which is without falsehood is called "true" (*satya*); that which is not empty is called "truth" (*satya*). To perceive the principle distinct from phenomena and clearly see true emptiness is termed the "eye of wisdom" (*prajñā-cakṣus*), by which one knows the One.

All phenomena are empty, quiescent, and of one mark; this is called the wisdom of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). The possession of the three wisdoms is as described in the "Chapter on the Three Wisdoms" in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The possession of the three truths is as described in both the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā Sūtra* and the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*. The sūtras state: first, the truth of existence;

second, the truth of non-existence; and third, the supreme truth of the middle way. The truth of existence is also called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and the truth of non-existence is also called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The new translation of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* simply mentions the "two truths," while Ci'en does not establish a "third truth," thereby discarding the old translation—how erroneous, how erroneous!
Next, the ten practices are explained: first, joy; second, benefiting others; third, non-opposition; fourth, lack of dejection; fifth...

10. Non-delusion, 11. Non-confusion, 12. Sixfold Good Manifestation, 13. Sevenfold Non-attachment, 14. Difficult-to-attain, 15. Good Dharma, and 16. Reality (which severs the dust-like afflictions beyond the realm of cessation).

It is also called the "nature-lineage" (*gotra-bhūmi*). By employing the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness, one perceives the conventional truth, opens the Dharma-eye, and achieves the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñatā*).
Second, the explanation of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). These ten all involve the practice of transforming others; thus they are called "practices.

Entering into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) without being moved by evil is named the Practice of Joy (*pramuditā-caryā*). Constantly transforming sentient beings so that they obtain the benefits of the Dharma is named the Practice of Benefiting Others (*sahitā-caryā*).

Attaining the mind of dharma-patience (*dharma-kṣānti*) such that there is no self or what belongs to a self is named the Practice of Freedom from Anger (*arakta-caryā*). In the present text, it says:
The "practice of non-opposition" (*anikṣiptadhura*) refers to relying on the newly translated [scriptures] to constantly cultivate the dharma of patience, humility, and reverence;

the "practice of being ever-abiding" (*nityodyukta*) refers to manifesting transformations for sentient beings. As for what is now called in this text "non-deflection" (*anavalīna*—the character *nu* being pronounced as *jiào*;
it means "crooked"; that which follows the radical for "hand" is incorrect), this also relies on the new translation to mean practicing great vigor so as to cause all [sentient beings]...
Reaching ultimate *nirvāṇa* is called the practice of being without yielding or cowering; not being lost or distracted by ignorance is called the practice of being without delusion or confusion;

being born life after life always within the Buddha-lands is called the practice of excellent manifestation; the fact that both "self" and "what belongs to self" are entirely empty is called the practice of non-attachment;
and constantly practicing reverence and compliance toward the Buddhas of the three periods of time is called the practice of honor.

Regarding the "Difficult-to-Attain Practice" (*dur-labha-caryā*) mentioned in the current text: it refers to the practice based on the newly translated [scriptures] concerning the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of rare roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*).
The "Practice of Good Dharmas" (*saddharma-caryā*) refers to the rules for teaching the Dharma to others and bringing sentient beings to maturity.

The "True Practice" (*bhūta-caryā*) refers to the Two Truths being neither like [the conventional] nor non-characteristic [of the ultimate]. As for the "Dust-Sand" [defilements] beyond the realms, they are already severed.

The expedient means of the Earth stage arise from the nature of prior habituation to form this capacity to give rise to the Buddha-dharma; this is called the "nature-seed-nature" (*prakṛti-bīja-gotra*).
In the Shared Teaching, one emerges into the provisional by means of emptiness; in the Distinct Teaching, one emerges into the provisional by breaking through emptiness.

Because the Distinct Teaching possesses the Middle Way, it accords with the fundamental principle of breaking through emptiness to enter the provisional. This provisional is precisely the provisional of establishment.
Contemplation is also called "contemplation of equality. To examine differentiated phenomena with precision and without error is termed the "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Question: Since the conventional resides in phenomena (*vastu*), why is it called "truth"? Answer: The *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* provides this analysis, citing the *Bodhisattva-bhūmi* which clarifies that there are two natures of phenomena:
the conventional and the ultimate. Since the nature of phenomena is designated as the conventional truth, how could that nature not be the truth?
Furthermore, one should know that the samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges which take conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as their object are called "conventional principles" (*sūn-li*).

Those [samādhis] which take the illnesses of sentient beings, supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and other such deeds for benefiting living beings as their objects are called "conventional matters" (*sūn-shì*).

To clearly perceive all phenomena (*dharma*) one by one without error is called the "Dharma-eye" (*dharmacakṣus*). To know the various distinctions among the ten dharma-realms and to achieve success in the path of transformation is called "attaining fruition."

The Knowledge of the Modes of the Path (*mārgākārajñatā*). Next, the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are explained: first, rescuing and protecting sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings; second, the indestructible; third, equal to all Buddhas;
fourth, reaching all places; fifth, the inexhaustible treasury of merit; sixth, entering into all equanimity.
1. Equalizing roots of goodness; 2. Universally conforming to all sentient beings; 3. The characteristic of true suchness (*tathatā*); 4. Unbound and unattached liberation; 5.
Entering the immeasurable dharma-realm (subduing the latent tendencies of ignorance through the Middle Way). These are also called the practices of the lineage of the path (*mārgajñatā-gotra*).

[This stage] extends for four hundred *yojanas* and resides in the stage of skillful means with remainder (*upāyavaśitā-śeṣa-bhūmi*). (The above thirty stages constitute the Three Worthies; they are also called the Inner Worldlings. From the eighth abode onward, this constitutes the stage of non-retrogression in practice.)
These ten dedications all involve turning causes toward fruits and turning phenomena toward principle; thus they are called "dedications" (*pariṇāmanā*).

With a mind free of conceptualization, one constantly traverses the six realms of existence; yet while entering into karmic retribution, one undergoes it without being subject to it, which is termed "protecting and saving sentient beings.
One remains detached from the mark of a "sentient being," observing that all dharmas have both reception and function, and that they do not abide for even a single moment.
Named "The Unbreakable Practice of the Buddha-dharma of the Three Times at All Times," equal to all Buddhas;
entering all Buddha-lands by the power of great vows to make offerings to all Buddhas; named "Reaching All Places" because of bestowing the eternally abiding Dharma upon others;
named the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit"; practicing untainted goodness; [transcending] both good and evil.
The term "non-duality" (*advaya*) refers to the roots of goodness that accord with equality; in the present text, it is said that one "enters into all," which also relies on the new translation.
The explanation of the meaning in the new translation also states that it is "in accordance. Because of this accordance, one is able to enter into all things.
By contemplating that good and evil are non-dual and possess a single characteristic, it is called the contemplation of accordance. Within the present text... [contemplating] all sentient beings.

Regarding those instances where the character "equal" (等) appears above but the character "contemplate" (觀) does not, these also follow the new translations because they are "equal to the equal" and "conform to the conforming.

Because the mind attains mastery through contemplation, the Buddhas of the three periods of time constantly illuminate existence and non-existence; this is called the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness).
By means of *prajñā*, one illuminates all phenomena of the three periods of time as a single unified whole; this is called the "unfettered, unattached liberation-awakening of oneness."

Among all phenomena, the Middle Way is signless; this is called "entering the Dharma-realm. When the immeasurable mind of emptiness and provisionality is already fulfilled, one correctly cultivates the contemplation of the primary meaning of the Middle Way.

Because ignorance does not arise and is suppressed by patience (*kṣānti*), and because by suppressing ignorance one achieves the nature of the semblance Middle Way (*sādṛśa-madhyamā-prakṛti*), it is established within its own stage according to the path of contemplation.
That which is named "Path" (mārga) is so called because it can produce the fruit of Buddhahood hereafter; that which is named "Seed" (bīja) does not change its nature.
Three hundred *yojanas*, as previously analyzed, refer to the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) when including the land of skillful means (*upāyabhūmi*);

if one adds the dust-like sands of afflictions (*kleśa*), or if one adds the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) regarding observational wisdom, these additions to the previous total constitute four hundred. This is the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
Is this the contemplation of ultimate emptiness, or is it provisional? The term "provisional" refers to skillful means (*upāya*).
Having already severed the four abodes of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), there remains one further abode, that of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsa*); this is called "having a remainder.

One must understand that the passage cited above from the *Siddhārthabuddhi-sūtra* (or *Cintavistara-sūtra*) is as follows: The Buddha Sūryacandraprabha commanded the Brahmā to come to this land, saying: "You should employ..."
The *Daśadharmaka-sūtra* states that one travels to that world, the Sahā world, which is named the "World of Defilement and Purity" (the Land of Common Dwelling for both ordinary beings and sages).
As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "I act as a Buddha in other lands. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Although those of the Two Vehicles are not born within the triple realm, outside the realm there is a Pure Land where they receive the Dharma-nature body; this is the Land of Residual Conditioning."
It is as stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in the fruit-retribution," which refers to the Land of Real Reward.
It is as stated in the *Sūtra of the Visualization of Samantabhadra*: "The dwelling place of that Buddha is named Constant Tranquil Light," which refers to the Land of Constant Tranquil Light.

From the seventh stage downward, one is called "non-retrogression in name and rank," because by severing the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), one realizes the emptiness of True Suchness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) and does not fall away from one's own station.

"Retreat" refers to the eighth stage; reaching this is called "non-retrogression in practice," for by severing the *rajas* (dust-like afflictions) and fulfilling the practice of transforming others, there is no retrogression in the practice of transforming others.
If one reaches the first ground (*bhūmi*), it is called "non-retrogression in mindfulness," for the mindings of the two extremes cannot cause retrogression.
One must know that these apply to the third fruit of the Tripitaka teaching, the sixth ground of the Shared Teaching, and the sixth dwelling of the Distinct Teaching.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), those with residual thoughts who have not yet exhausted their afflictions remain in the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*).

When the thoughts of the four fruits, the seven stages (*bhūmi*), the seven abodes (*vihāra*), and the seven levels of faith are exhausted, one is born into the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*).

From the eighth stage, the eighth abode, and the eighth level of faith upward, although the dust-like afflictions (*pāṃśu-kleśa*) are destroyed and ignorance (*avidyā*) is suppressed, since these dust-like afflictions do not moisten the realm beyond [this world], the birth and karmic retribution are both caused by ignorance.

Because outflows serve as their cause, they also reside within the land of expedient means; it is only those who have attained the first stage of the Distinct or Perfect [Teachings] and obtained wondrous karmic retribution that dwell in the Land of True Retribution.
Those who are born with a physical body, have attained the stages of patience (*kṣānti*), and have not yet entered extinction are merely said to possess "flower-retribution" (the intermediate fruit).

Next, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are explained: first, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). From this point onward, by employing the Middle Way contemplation, one destroys a portion of ignorance and manifests a portion of the three virtues; this continues up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samalaṃbuddhi*), all of which are termed the "Noble Seed-nature" (*ārya-gotra*).

This constitutes the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), as well as the stage of Effortlessness (*anābhoga*). Here, one acts as a Buddha within the hundred realms, accomplishing the eight phases of enlightenment to benefit sentient beings.
Having traversed five hundred *yojana*, one first enters the Land of Real Reward and Non-obstruction, and for the first time reaches the Precious Abode.
2. The Ground of Freedom from Defilement; 3. The Ground of Radiance; 4. The Ground of Blazing Wisdom; 5.
The Ground Difficult to Conquer; 6. The Ground of Presence; 7. The Ground of Far-Going; 8. The Ground of Immovability; 9. The Ground of Excellent Wisdom; 10. The Ground of the Dharma Cloud.
(In these nine grounds, each ground respectively abandons one grade of ignorance and realizes one portion of the Middle Way.)
The second [section], the division of the stages of the sages (*āryabhūmi*), has two parts. First, the causes, which also have two parts. First, the names of the ten stages:

they are called "stages" (*bhūmi*) because they can sustain the realization of the Middle Way and can sustain all manner of virtues. Having abandoned the state of ordinary beings and entered the state of sages, being unmoved by the four māras, and simultaneously illuminating both existence and non-existence in their ultimate equality, it is named the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). The Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation are called the "Three."
"Permanence, bliss, self, and purity" refers to the three virtues (triguṇa) that are both vertical and horizontal.

Because the stage of the Sage can give rise [to these qualities] without change, it is called the "Noble Seed-nature" (āryagotra). Because one perceives the Middle Way, it is called the "Path of Seeing" (darśanamārga).

Because one enters [the flow] spontaneously without applying effort, it is called "Effortless" (anābhoga). Manifesting bodies horizontally to respond to the hundred realms and deliver sentient beings is called the "Hundred."
Regarding the manifestation of Buddhahood within the realms: if one attains the second bhūmi, one manifests Buddhahood in a thousand realms;

from the third bhūmi onwards, these numbers increase tenfold at each stage. These are the eight phases: first, dwelling in Tuṣita; second, entering the womb; third, abiding in the womb; fourth, emerging from the womb; fifth, leaving home;
sixth, attaining enlightenment; seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma; and eighth, entering nirvāṇa. If categorized [by realm]:

To the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the Land of True Reward (*vipākabhūmi*) is added; if one considers afflictions (*kleśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is further added; if one considers contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*), the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is further added.

By augmenting the former with these, it is called the "five hundred. Because one cultivates the cause of the Middle Way and accordingly realizes the true reward, there is no separation between the primary and secondary environments (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*);
because matter and mind are unimpeded, it is named the "Land of True Reward Without Obstruction" (*vipākānāvaraṇa-bhūmi*). This is the division.

Realizing the *śāntaprabhāsvara* (tranquil light) is called "first entering the treasure-store" (*ratnagotra*). Because one enters the realm of sentient beings through correct non-characteristic (*animitta*) in a manner identical to empty space, it is called the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Because the path of the Buddha is cultivated through the patience of faith in radiant wisdom (*prabhāsvareti-prajñā-kṣānti*), and an utterly pure clarity arises, it is called the "Radiant Ground" (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
This is the new translation; the old translation calls the third ground the "Luminous Ground" (*prabhā-bhūmi*), for "radiance" (*prabhā*) is indeed "luminosity."
Furthermore, observing all phenomena in accordance with the patience toward non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

Cultivating the path through this conforming patience, one realizes that the ignorance of the three realms is entirely empty; this is called the Difficult to Conquer Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*). Next, observing all phenomena in accordance with them as being quiescent and non-dual throughout the three periods of time is called the Manifest Stage (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
One observes that all afflictions are neither existent nor non-existent, constantly progressing toward the higher stages.

The state in which every thought-moment is quiescent is called the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*); by means of the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-darśana*), one relinquishes the three realms and this is called the Ground of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Entering the superior illumination and witnessing the manifold transformations of the Buddhas through the path of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is called the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

The *Ratna-alaṃkāra-sūtra* refers to it as the Ground of Wondrous Wisdom; "wondrous" (*miao*) is synonymous with "excellent" (*sadhu*). Having entered the contemplation of the Middle Way, one receives the rank of Buddhahood. Since—
Being identical with True Suchness and equal to the Dharma-realm, the wondrous clouds universally cover all; this is named the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
A single point of the Middle Way is above, representing the vertical; the two points of Prajñā and Vimukti are below, representing the horizontal.
What was previously called the "Three Virtues" is here described as the Middle Way manifesting both vertically and horizontally in mutual interpenetration.

Furthermore, by severing one more grade [of affliction], one enters the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); this is also called the Diamond Mind (*vajracitta*), the Stage of One Birth Remaining (*ekajātipratibaddha*), and the Superior Person (*uttamapuruṣa*).

Second, the stage of Equal Enlightenment is also called the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*); having transcended the ten grounds, one understands and enters hundreds of thousands of samādhis, illuminating [all things].

When the state of one mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*), signlessness (*animitta*), quiescence (*śānti*), and unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*) is compared to wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is still one grade below;

thus it is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhisama*). Although there remains a single grade of the dust and defilement of ignorance (*avidyā-rajas-mala*), it is as if it did not exist, and is therefore called "Stainless" (*vimala*).
The contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) cultivated therein is pure, singular, firm, and sharp, resembling a diamond (*vajra*); hence it is called the "Diamond Mind" (*vajracitta*).

One who has not yet fully exhausted their remaining lifetimes is called a "One-Life [Bodhisattva]" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). After this point, one is said to be in the station of "Filling the Place" (*kṣāntipratilabdha*) at the stage of the Buddha’s Wondrous Enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
Furthermore, because there remains a higher station of Wondrous Enlightenment to be ascended, they are called a "Superior Being" (*uttarapudgala*).

Question: Is it by means of Vajra-wisdom (*vajrajñāna*) that one cuts off ignorance (*avidyā*), or is it by means of Wondrous Enlightenment-wisdom (*abhisambodhijñāna*)? Answer: [It is by means of] Vajra-wisdom.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states that those who have something to be severed are called "those with a superior" (*sopadhiśeṣa*), while those who have nothing to be severed are called "those without a superior" (*anuttara*).

Question: For what reason does the *Śrīmālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* state that the power of the ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is the greatest, and that it can only be severed by the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment (*buddhabodhijñāna*)?
Answer: From the stages of the Separate and Complete Teachings up to the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksaṃbodhi*), there is none that does not employ the wisdom of Buddha-enlightenment.
It is said that wisdom severs the defilement of ignorance; thus it is merely stated as such.

In various texts, it is taught that the Buddha’s supreme wisdom severs the most inferior delusions, and that even the most inferior wisdom can sever the most superior delusions. One may understand this by reflecting upon the principle explained above.
Furthermore, by breaking through one more grade of ignorance, one enters the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue),
sits beneath the seven-jeweled Bodhi tree in the Lotus Treasury World upon the Great Jewel Flower King Throne, and manifests the Perfect Reward Body (Bao-shen).

The second part, concerning the stage of fruition, is divided into two sections. First, regarding the attainment of Buddhahood: through the supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) of wondrous contemplation, one enters the great quiescence of signlessness, which is termed "wondrous enlightenment.

This occurs within the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*), as described in the "Flower Treasury World" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where there is a precious king-of-flowers throne, also as described in the *Avataṃsaka*.
Furthermore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "At the site of the terrace of quiescent extinction, one sits upon a diamond-flower throne."

The *Old She lun* states that the Buddha’s seat is the "Pure World of the Great Lotus King," while the *New She lun* states it is the "Pure Buddha-land of the Great Jewel Flower King. As previously analyzed, the abundance of the seven jewels signifies the infinite;
thus, this differs from the previous representation of the Dharma in the Shared Teaching.
For the assembly of bodhisattvas of dull faculties, he turns the immeasurable wheel of the Four Noble Truths; this is precisely this Buddha.

Second, for those who preach the lower teachings but do not know that the principle is inherently complete—being called "dull faculties" because their delusion within the provisional is profound—he preaches the immeasurable contrast between the partial and the perfect.
That which is called the "dull middle" (the but-middling) is distinguished from the perfect; all [those who understand] the true middle are sharp.

There are sutras and treatises which state that the stages prior to the seventh ground are called the Path of Effort (*sābhoga-mārga*), while those from the eighth ground upward are called the Path of Effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*);

furthermore, the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue-wei*) refers to the mere breaking of a single grade of ignorance—all of these explanations are made in terms of the Path of Teaching (*jiao-dao*).

Regarding the third section, "The Sūtras and Śāstras on the Three Existences," which explains how [the teachings] are indefinite according to the capacities of beings, the text is divided into two parts. First, the main explanation of the three [stages].
Regarding the initial point showing that from the path of instruction up to before the seventh bhūmi, as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

"When a bodhisattva has not yet reached the eighth bhūmi, it is like a person riding a boat wishing to cross the great ocean; as long as they have not reached the great ocean, they must exert much effort."
Upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one approaches the Buddha’s wisdom through great skillful means (*upāya*) with a mind free from effort, no longer applying further exertion.

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that in the fifth stage, one studies worldly dharmas such as secular texts, literature, mathematics, and the divination of auspicious and inauspicious signs;
yet, it is said that even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), these are all merely the meaning of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), which is described as "wondrous."
Regarding the statement that "one who breaks through one grade in the stage of awakening" (*jue-wei*), it is not yet known from which sūtra or śāstra this is drawn;
the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) merely states that breaking through twelve grades is designated as "wonderful awakening" (*miaojue*).

Therefore, since what was previously explained—from the initial stage of the ten faiths (*shixin*) up to wonderful awakening—is entirely the path of teaching (*jiaodao*), why does the present text alone mention the seventh ground (*dì*) and so forth? However, the previous discussion of the first ground mentioned "entering" [the ground].

Regarding the statement that the "land of no obstacles" (*anāvaraṇa-bhūmi*) exists at the place of the jewels, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) already states that this refers to the "True Reward" (*sambhoga-kāya*) as being distinct.

This is based on the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) and the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*). Since there can certainly be no land of no obstacles within the path of teaching, the mention of "no obstacles" here must refer to the path of realization.
If the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is already identical in its realization to the Perfect [Teaching], then who would realize a separation from the second stage onward?

Question: Are all twelve chapters throughout [this treatise] teachings on the path of practice (*pratipatti-mārga*)? Is it a teaching on the path of practice in terms of its application, or is it a teaching on the path of practice in terms of its exposition? Answer: It is a teaching on the path of practice in terms of its application;
this refers to practitioners who are still at the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*). It is a teaching on the path of practice in terms of its exposition;

this refers to what the Tathāgata has taught, which applies to the entire process from beginning to end. As for the path of realization (*adhigama-mārga*) in terms of application, it pertains to the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*); as for the practitioner’s own realization, it pertains to those who have already attained realization.
It is no different from the Perfect [Teaching]. Regarding the explanation of the Path of Realization (sākṣātkriyāmārga):

although it is spoken of in relation to the Tathāgata’s teaching on the Dharma already realized, one should know that the discussion of the Path of Realization in the Separate Teaching (pratyekayāna) is not a discourse concerning the specific stage of the Separate Teaching itself;

rather, it is a pointing out that the practitioner personally realizes a state where distinctions do not exist, as well as the perfect fusion (yuanrong) already realized by the Sages. Therefore, it is explained in terms of realization.
The Way is not something fragmented or sequential. If, in terms of practice, it is already identical to the Perfect [Vehicle], how could it not be so in terms of its exposition?

Therefore, regarding the realization of the Way through practice, the cause that is cultivated is precisely the person who practices the dedication toward the Perfect; regarding the realization of the Way through exposition, it is simply applied to the person who practices the Perfect.
Why is this? Because those who are specifically directed toward the Perfect cultivate the contemplation of non-duality. If...
If a Sage were to preach that he has already realized the fused and wondrous Dharma and yet respond to others' needs, it would follow that there is a stimulus but no response.
If, in terms of practice and realization, the Way were not a distinct orientation toward the cause of perfect cultivation, it would follow that there is a fruit but no cause.

Some may say that while those on the stages (bhūmi) are perfectly integrated, those before the stages are still separated and sequential, and this refers to the initial mind of the distinct-capacity person.
Regarding the claim that the "Perfect Interfusion on the Grounds" (*dìshàng yuánróng*) is taught as a provisional exposition of the Path of Realization for others with a beginner's mind:

such groundless talk is not to be relied upon. Question: Does the "Distinctive Orientation toward Perfect Cultivation" (*biéxiàng yuánxiū*) refer to the first *pariṇāmanā* (dedication) or the tenth? Answer:

According to the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yíngluò jīng*), it is at the tenth *pariṇāmanā* that one first cultivates the Middle Way’s contemplation of the primary truth (*prathama-artha-darśana*). This is stated from the perspective of those with inferior faculties.

If one discusses the Middle and Superior [Vehicles], they actually encompass the preceding nine stages; thus, the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) follow the sequence of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
If one enters the Middle Way, it is no different from the Perfect [Teaching]. This distinction is analyzed in the *Yi Zhang* (Chapter on Meaning).
Where it is stated that the abandonment of views occurs in the first stage, while the abandonment of afflictions through cultivation from the second to the sixth stages is equal to that of an Arhat,
this is merely using the names of the stages of the Separate Teaching to designate the stages of the Shared Teaching.

Second, regarding the instances where a specific name is borrowed to apply to both the texts on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: first, a specific name is borrowed to refer to the common stage of the Three Vehicles;
second, a specific name is borrowed to refer to the stage of the Bodhisattva within the common [vehicle]. This present passage encompasses both of those explanations.

As for the former: the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) constitute the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*), while the three [stages] of the internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*)...

The "Worthy One" (*ārya*) corresponds to the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*). The "Eight Persons" (*aṣṭamaka*) and those in the Path of Seeing correspond to the first stage, the Joyful (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Those in the Path of Training (*śaikṣa*) in the Thin Stage correspond to the Stainless (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Those in the Fruit of the Thin Stage correspond to the Radiant (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*). Those in the Path of Training in the Desireless Stage correspond to the Blazing (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

Those in the Fruit of the Desireless Stage correspond to the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*). Those in the Path of Training in the Stage of Completion (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*) correspond to the Manifest (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*). The fruit of the Stage of Completion corresponds to [the next stage].
That is to say, the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (Far-Reaching Ground) is the eighth stage of the Śrāvaka; the Acalā-bhūmi (Immovable Ground) is the ninth Bodhisattva ground;
the Sādhumatī-bhūmi (Good Wisdom Ground) is the tenth; and the Buddha-ground is the Dharmameghā-bhūmi (Dharma-Cloud Ground). By employing these specific names, one distinguishes the common stages:

thus, the first ground is called the "severing of views," the second ground is the "severing of the first or second category of desire-realm *vitarka*," and so on, up to the seventh ground where [the remaining afflictions] are severed.
Regarding the phrase "the residual thoughts are exhausted," the second passage cites an elder of the past who says that the exhaustion of thoughts in the sixth stage is equal to that of an Arhat;

others say it is equal to an Arhat in the seventh stage. The intention of our own school is that, according to the principle of the ten perfections, the sixth stage—the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā*)—is equal to an Arhat because delusions are exhausted through the wisdom of emptiness. However, if one correlates the various stages with their respective fruits, it is the seventh stage.
Since it is identical to the fourth fruit-stage, the stage of "having accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), one knows that this passage encompasses both of those explanations.
In general, these are all cases where specific names are borrowed to designate the universal. While the names may be borrowed from the specific, their meaning must necessarily rely on the universal;

as explained previously in the *Miaoxuan*, this is already clear. As for the mention of the "ten perfections" (*daśapāramitā*), they are combined as merely the six perfections, but when expanded, they become ten.

What are the ten? Within dhyāna, there is the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) which gives rise to the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhānapāramitā*); there is the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) which gives rise to the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*).

Regarding the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*), they maintain the fundamental dhyāna-perfection. Within the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), there is the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) which gives rise to the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*);

there is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) which gives rise to the perfection of knowledge (*jñānapāramitā*). All-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) maintains the fundamental perfection of wisdom. This is it.
Borrowing from other meanings, as is fully detailed in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it is said that "there are places where this is taught.

Some say: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in retributive fruit; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land. This borrows the terminology of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) to clarify the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Third, there is a tradition which states that the following is borrowed from the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Renwang Banruo Jing), specifically the verses spoken by King Prasenajit:
"The three sages and ten saints" refers to the distinct stages (*bie-wei*), while "abiding in the fruition of retribution" (*zhu guobao*) refers to the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-yi*).

This is because those in the distinct teaching of the three sages have not yet destroyed ignorance and do not abide in the fruition of retribution, whereas in the Perfect Teaching, one abides in the fruition of retribution.

Judging from this, the designation of the "Three Sages" (san-xian) borrows the positions of the three sages and ten saints to clarify the meaning of the perfect fruition and retribution; it is not established in vain.

There are many such categories, and one must understand in detail the stages of severance and realization within this specific teaching—reaching which stage one severs what [afflictions], and so forth.
Having investigated what principles are deluded or realized, he judges all teachings and stages without failing to penetrate them.
Second, from "In this way" onwards, he concludes with an exhortation.
This concludes the brief explanation of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).
The third section clarifies the conclusion for the lower teachings.
Next, to clarify the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the text of the fourth [section] on the Perfect Teaching is divided into three parts; first is the heading.
The term "Complete" (Yuan) refers to being perfectly wondrous, perfectly complete, perfectly sufficient, and perfectly sudden; for these reasons, it is called the Complete Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Second, the explanation of the name "Complete" is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the meaning of the name; second, the formal explanation of the name. Regarding the first:

the perfect fusion of the three truths, which is inconceivable, is called "perfectly wondrous"; the fact that the three aspects are mutually identical and without deficiency is called [perfectly complete].
The perfection of the threefold one (trikāya-ekayāna) in which all masteries are mutually possessed is called "perfectly complete" (*yuanzu*).
That which is without discrepancy and does not proceed by gradual stages is called "perfectly sudden" (*yuandun*).
This refers to what is known as perfect subduing, perfect faith, perfect severance, perfect practice, perfect stages, perfect mastery and adornment, and perfect establishment.
Sentient beings.
Second, [the text] shows the essence of the Dharma below and explains the name above, asking: "What is meant by 'wondrous fulfillment' and 'sudden'? Therefore, it is now shown:
"The three contemplations are cultivated in a perfect manner (*yuanxiu*); all five stages of dwelling are suppressed; this is called 'perfect suppression' (*yuansu*). One believes in everything."
The Dharma is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; this is called perfect faith (*yuanxin*). The simultaneous severance of the three delusions is called perfect severance (*yuanduan*).
The fulfillment of a single practice with all practices is called perfect practice (*yuanyanxing*). The fulfillment of a single stage with all stages is called perfect stage (*yuanyuwei*).
Principle is that which is adorned, and contemplation is that which adorns; when the internal adornment of subject and object is complete, external function is sovereign.
The six sense organs and six sense objects—each and every one of them—enters into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and each and every one of them emerges from it to preach the Dharma.

Manifesting both entry and emergence, they demonstrate the mutual identity of the primary and secondary realms; the sense organs and sense objects are mutually pervasive. This is called the practice of "Perfect Sovereign Adornment.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; speaking or remaining silent; acting or non-acting—each and every instance causes all sentient beings to attain emptiness and the provisional.

The benefits of the fourfold *siddhi* (the four means of conversion) within this [teaching] are called the "perfect establishment of sentient beings. These matters are explained in detail as they appear in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras state that the Buddha’s realm and the unique (*asādhāraṇa*) stages not shared with the three vehicles all belong to this teaching.
Second, the explanation of the stages and positions in the section on the various Mahāyāna schools is divided into two parts. First, a general clarification of our own school’s judgment:

among all the Mahāyāna traditions that discourse upon the Buddha-dharma, they are all exclusively the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), differing from other sects which limit themselves to the partial calculations of a single sutra or treatise.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the four characters "open, reveal, awaken, and enter" correspond to the forty stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)—namely, the stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and realization.

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one immediately attains perfect awakening; the entire body of wisdom does not depend on others for realization;
this pure and wondrous Dharma-body is profound and still, responding to all things. This clarifies the forty-two stages of the Perfect Teaching. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
In a grove of *campaka* trees, one does not smell any other fragrance; likewise, those who enter this chamber perceive only the fragrance of the merits of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, it is said that entering the gate of non-duality clarifies the *prajñā* of the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*), while entering *nirvāṇa* clarifies the single mind of the five practices (*pañca-karma*).
Moreover, a sutra states: suppose there is a person who enters the great ocean to bathe, and having done so, uses the waters of all rivers, including the Sāgara.
When the dragon Rāvaṇa causes rain to fall like the axle of a chariot, only the great ocean can receive it; other lands cannot endure it.
Furthermore, if ten thousand kinds of incense are ground into pellets, a single grain of it, when burned, possesses the full fragrance of them all.

Second, the *Lotus Sūtra* section provides a specific exposition, which is divided into two parts: first, the formal clarification of the stages and positions; second, a general listing of various sūtras.

Within the first part, there is a formal listing of the four characters—“opening,” “showing,” “awakening,” and “entering”—which correspond respectively to the stages of abiding (*vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), direction (*pratiṣṭhāna*), and ground (*bhūmi*).

This can be seen in the text. The citation from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding “the initial arousal [of the mind],” etc., intends to take the development of the three bodies at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) as an analogy for the second [stage].

From the stages of abiding and departing up to the wondrous enlightenment, it is thus in every case; therefore, it is said that this clarifies the forty-two stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
In the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the goddess rebukes Śāriputra, saying, "The campaka grove...
The "campaka grove" is a metaphor for the Perfect Teaching. "Not smelling other fragrances" is a comparison to the three [other] teachings. Pure.
It is called the "Empty Chamber" because it manifests the Constantly Quiescent Light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*), wherein the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all dwell.

Therefore, one who enters this chamber is said to enter the Quiescent Light, becoming one body with no difference from the Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas of the Tathāgatas. Its wondrous fragrance of merit universally perfumes all things;
therein lies the essence of the Middle Way, where sense organs, objects, and the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are non-dual. This is the *Campaka* [Flower].
This refers to the *pāṭalī* tree; the character "zhàn" (dǐng gǎn qiè) is an error and should be written as "zhān.
In the "Chapter on the Dharma-gate of Non-duality," the thirty-first chapter of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the bodhisattvas each proclaim the dharma-gate of non-duality.
To use words to speak of the wordless is termed the "Distinct Teaching" (*biejiao*). If each individual gate can encompass all other gates, [it is the Perfect Teaching].
This is called the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Mañjuśrī speaks of the ineffable through non-speech, while Vimalakīrti likewise employs non-speech within non-speech;
this is termed "non-duality" within the Perfect Teaching. This vehicle is subtle and wondrous, with nothing superior to it, and is thus named the Supreme Vehicle (Anuttarayāna).
Furthermore, there is a single practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata—namely, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The principle of the Buddha-nature is called Nirvana; the "one mind and five practices" mentioned in the sutras is also Nirvana.
The principle inherently contains all dharmas, like the water of the great ocean; practicing contemplation based on this principle is like bathing in the sea.
These practices universally encompass all other practices, just as the waters of all rivers have already been utilized within it, such as those of the Sāgara and other oceans.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Sāgara" is translated here as the "Salt Sea"; it is named after its location.
The dragon is likened to the Tathāgata, the rain to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), and the ocean to those with perfect faculties. The remaining lands represent the persons of the three teachings.

The "rain upon the axle of the chariot" refers to the magnitude of the rain; "pouring down timely rain" likewise refers to its timing. Furthermore, ten thousand kinds of incense were ground together...

The passage concerning "the pill" and so forth appears in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra*. The principle encompasses all phenomena, just as ten thousand kinds of incense [are contained within a single substance].

Phenomena are themselves the principle, just as when [incense] is pounded and formed into a pill. According to the nature of the principle as it is observed, a single phenomenon is present; this is like burning a single particle of incense.
That a single phenomenon inherent in the principle universally subsumes all phenomena is like the complete presence of all fragrances within [that single particle].
All such categories as these belong to the Complete Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

As will be concluded below, we shall now briefly clarify the stages and positions according to the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, which consist of eight: first, the stage of the five grades of disciples (the outer ordinary beings).

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* sets forth twenty stages of faith (the stage of ordinary persons), thirty stages of abiding (the first stage of the noble ones), forty stages of practice, fifty stages of dedication, sixty stages of the grounds,
the seventh stage of equal enlightenment (the end of the causal stage), and the eighth stage of wondrous enlightenment (the resultant stage).

Second, "Now, below," the section specifically based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Ratnakūṭa-vaipulya-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) is divided into two parts. First, the titles of the five chapters are listed:

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is clearly shown that from the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) through the eight stages (*bhūmi*), one reaches the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in a single lifetime, attaining opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
This corresponds precisely to the stages of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) and so forth. In the *Ratnakūṭa-vaipulya-sūtra*, the sequence of stages is clearly and fully enumerated.
The *Śrī-mālā-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Shì fǎhuá) explains that while the *Yíngluò jīng* encompasses both the Separate (bié) and the Perfect (yuán) teachings, one must now take the Perfect.

Regarding the first stage, the five grades of the position (*wǔpǐn wèi*), there are two parts: first, the five grades at the beginning; second, the explanation of the text, which is divided into two sections. First, the ordinary person (*fánfū*), which is further divided into three parts. First, the external ordinary person (*wàifán*), which begins with the heading.
First, the Chapter on Rejoicing.
Second, [the following] is explained as five parts; first, the Chapter on Rejoicing is divided into two. First, the heading.
The Sūtra says: "If one hears this sūtra and does not disparage it, but gives rise to a mind of rejoicing..."
Regarding the second part of the sutra’s explanation, there are two sections. First, citing the sutra:

following nineteen lines of verse from the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," it first clarifies the four kinds of faith in the present, and subsequently explains the five grades after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa. One should understand that the subsequent citations of the sutra follow this same principle.
Question: What dharma does one rejoice in?
Part Two: Distinguishing the Categories, divided into two; first, the question;
second, the answer: the Sublime Dharma.

The second response is divided into two parts. First, it provides a general demonstration that the three truths are perfectly interfused; this is called the "Marvelous Dharma. The *Wenju* states: "Sui" means to accord with;
to accord with the non-duality and non-distinction of phenomena and principle. "Xi" means to rejoice; to rejoice for oneself and others.
Rejoicing for oneself signifies possessing wisdom, while rejoicing for others signifies possessing compassion. Thus, the equality of phenomena and principle is precisely the Marvelous Dharma.
The wondrous Dharma is precisely the mind.

Regarding the two aspects of the wondrous Dharma, the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation divided into three parts. First, the Dharma of the initial mind; this further divides into three: first, showing that the Dharma is the mind;

third, the meaning of the wondrousness of these three dharmas—this is the dharma of the mind. As for the dharma of the mind, it exists in the causal stage; the dharma of sentient beings generally encompasses both the cause and the fruit.
The two results are restricted to the past, while the Buddha-dharma is fixed in the result. As the Sūtra says: "Gathering the mind in a secluded place" refers to the wondrousness of the mind-dharma;

"causing sentient beings [to realize this]" refers to the wondrousness of the sentient-being-dharma; and "the ultimate reality-mark (dharmatā) realized only by Buddhas and Buddhas" refers to the wondrousness of the Buddha-dharma.
These three—the mind, sentient beings, and the Buddha—are mutually exclusive yet interdependent; these are what the title of the *Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*) signifies.
The wondrous mind is inherently endowed [with all virtues].
Second, the manifestation of the attributes of this essence—that is, the phrase "the wondrous mind is inherently endowed"—should be understood as follows:

within a single thought-moment of the causal stage, there is not a single mark of either unity or difference. To realize this marklessness is to be endowed with all minds; the three thousand realms are fully present.

This is what is called the wondrous mind whose essence is inherently complete; it is because this essence is complete that the wondrous mind is manifested. The wondrous mind exists precisely because its essence is complete. Why is this?
A single thought-moment possesses no characteristics of unity or difference. Being without characteristics is emptiness, yet within this emptiness there is a substantial reality.

This substantial reality spontaneously and naturally possesses the three thousand realms. Thus we know that it is only through the inherent completeness of the essence that there is the wondrous mind.
If the essence were not complete, how would it differ from the partial principle of emptiness in the Hīnayāna?

If the complete were not empty, how would it differ from the obstructive substances of the mundane world? Therefore, one should know that completeness is itself the provisional, and the provisional is itself the middle.

Those at or below the level of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha) do not yet recognize completeness, much less recognize emptiness and the middle. Completeness is the essential attribute (*de*), while emptiness is the essential dimension (*liang*). It is not [the case that they are identical].
Virtue that is beyond measure is called the essence of nature; this essence is the Middle Way. Measure is the True (paramārtha), and its fullness is the Conventional (saṃvṛti).
They are blended yet not intermingled; they are distinct yet not divided. Although each one is all-pervasive, it has no fixed location.
The mirror’s substance, its light, and its images can be understood by comparison: the vessel and the rice serve as analogous examples. Since the wondrous mind is thus, so too is the wondrous form.

The same applies to form and mind as a single entity, both fully possessing the three thousand [dharmas]. How could one selectively calculate that while the mind possesses the three thousand, form does not?
Since form is identical to mind, it possesses the three thousand; and since mind is identical to form, how could it not possess them?

Because they are possessed by nature (*xingju*), form and mind thus possess [them]. The possession of form and mind is distinguished according to phenomena (*shi*), whereas the possession of nature is the possession of the essence (*ti*).

To discuss this fully according to principle: there is the nature-inclusive (xingju) and the cultivation-inclusive (xiuju), the mind-inclusive (xinju) and the nature-inclusive-mind (xingjuxin), the pervasiveness of nature (xingbian) and the pervasiveness of mind (xianbian), and the transformation of nature (xingbian).
If one reflects upon these in accordance with their standards, they cannot be explained in exhaustive detail;

however, it must be understood that the reason for "immediate inclusion" (*ji*) is precisely to manifest non-duality (*buer*). "Inclusion" (*ju*) reveals the essence and its attributes; because the essence is inclusive, "immediacy" (*ji*) is therefore non-dual.

All of these belong to the Perfect Vehicle and are not the partial teachings of the Lesser Vehicle; other schools also discourse on the principle of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as being like empty space.
However, while this [Perfect Teaching] shares with them the essence and magnitude of the body [of reality], others fail to establish that the body possesses the three thousand realms.

Thus, they lose the essential virtue of the Perfect Principle, rendering their application of it in vain. For this reason, Jingxi [Zhiyi] frequently employed the meaning of "possessing" (*ju*) to refute the doctrines of other schools. Unfinished.

Those who excel in discussing the nature [of reality] today do not understand this because they cling exclusively to the doctrine of inherent inclusion (*xingju*) and do not allow for cessation or extinction.

This is why they lose sight of the essence and the magnitude of the nature. Thus, if they hear that the three thousand realms are extinguished within emptiness, they claim it is identical to the principle of the great void of the Lesser Vehicle;
yet if they hear that the ten realms are inherently complete and perfectly manifest, they then claim—

The Mahāyāna is ultimately perfected and reaches its ultimate limit; yet, if one does not engage in contemplation, how can the three thousand virtues be manifested when the substance of nature (*prakṛti*) and the measure of essence have both been extinguished?
Therefore, throughout the various texts, there is no "nature-endowment" (*xingju*) or "principle-endowment" (*lijù*) that transcends the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

All phenomena endowed within emptiness are entirely provisional (*prajñapti*), for the substance of emptiness is fundamentally extinguished and non-existent; thus, it is able to fully possess the three [thousand realms].

A thousand similes illustrate that because emptiness is as clear and pure as a mirror, it manifests forms both large and small. Since the nature and principle are already complete therein, how can one claim they are non-existent?

That which is "complete" is itself provisional; what, then, is meant by "emptiness within emptiness"? If emptiness were to exist [as a thing], how could the various marks be described as conventional and provisional?
Furthermore, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the "True Reality of All Dharmas" (dharmatā) is designated as the chapter on the provisional and the real; "all dharmas" is the designation.
Conventional reality is provisional; the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the signifier, while emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the reality. The passage beginning with "That which is called...

is the explanation of the chapter on the provisional and the real. Thus, this explains emptiness; the phrase "the nature and characteristics of all phenomena" explains the reason why all phenomena are such.
It is for this reason that our school employs the threefold reading of the text; therefore, all phenomena are themselves the reality.
The three thousand [realms] vanish and cease, yet the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the ten realms of all phenomena (*dharmas*), which remain perfectly distinct. Thus, Jingxi said:
"Such marks as these are themselves the turning explanation of the true mark of all phenomena. Because there are all phenomena, there are marks;
because there is the true mark, all marks are the true mark. Being without marks, marks and non-marks are both suchness; being suchness, they are all suchness."

Is this not the case where "emptiness within emptiness" takes principles such as "conventional designation" (*prajñapti*) as its phenomena? How much more so for the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which must necessarily encompass all phenomena;

since all phenomena are by their very nature empty and middle, how much more so for true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*), which possesses no diversity, whereas expedient wisdom (*upāyajñāna*) does possess differentiated dharmas.
Just as the earth possesses both peach and plum trees, there is indeed the existence of expedients. Therefore, regarding the four eyes:
The two wisdoms manifest the myriad phenomena in their distinct clarity; the Buddha-eye and the seed-wisdom are the profound stillness of true emptiness.
Moreover, in the Constantly Quiescent Light, both beauty and ugliness are extinguished. Within this Quiescent Light, all that is confronted exists as either pure or defiled;

the intent of what is discussed in various texts is entirely thus. May the wise and discerning ones deign to observe this. Lately, students have held to various fragmented attachments, some speaking only of—
Whether discussing emptiness and quiescence as mere essence, or mutually refuting one another through pen and tongue, are these not all instances of extreme views?
Read the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) on the three meanings of clarifying the nature, and you will understand the wondrous teaching of our school’s perfect and sudden approach.
To focus exclusively on existence is what Nāgārjuna called "hearing that all phenomena are empty and having one's heart wounded by it," wherein one only delights in [the former].
In the *Śūnyatā-śānti-vāda*, that which is said to be "not delivered by the Buddha"—if one prefers this "double negation"—is called the foolish proliferation of conceptual play (*prapañca*).
If there is neither speech nor demonstration, would those who are mute be considered people who have attained the Way? From what means can one emerge from the dense forest of false views?

Therefore, the sages, through their *siddhāntas* (established tenets), respond to beings according to their needs; they employ both existence and non-existence until reaching the state of the "double."
It is not as if one were to personally practice and illuminate [the truth], for when the roots of both emptiness and existence are found to be "neither," how could anything be attained?
Therefore, one should know that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), even a single dharma cannot be found; how much less so the three thousand [worlds]?

Within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are already immeasurable things—how could it be limited to just the three thousand? Failing to comprehend this principle is to waste one's spirit and energy in vain. Long! (A cry of lamentation.)
The meaning of the parable of the ox-hide with its hair can be understood by those who still do not know that even the "Three Thousandfold World" is termed illusory existence;
how much less could they understand that this very emptiness is itself empty? They would surely be bewildered at heart even upon hearing this.

If they are thus deluded and ignorant regarding this, how much more so when it comes to the Great Body of the Sage’s teachings—the causes and conditions for self-cultivation, realization, and benefiting others? Alas!
Having studied for many years, one remains as lost in darkness; how much more so when relying on worldly discourse—whom could truly embody this?
It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
The three metaphors mentioned here are precisely what is meant by the phrase "like a wish-fulfilling jewel. Regarding the wish-fulfilling jewel, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
At the time when the Dharma perishes within the *śarīra*, all *śarīra* become wish-fulfilling jewels (*cintāmaṇi*). As the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"The supreme treasures of the heavens are shaped like mustard seeds; though they are the seven precious gems and *linglang* stones, they are neither stored within nor enter from without.
Abundant or frugal according to one's wishes, they rain down in profusion. If even material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are thus, how much more so the spirit and mind, which are numinous and wondrous!"
The essence of the cintāmaṇi jewel represents the principle within the void; the seven treasures and so forth represent the inherent presence of that principle;

and the falling of rain and so forth represent its phenomenal function. Since phenomenal function exists only because the principle is inherently present, these metaphors are employed to illustrate that the essence of the wondrous mind is replete with all things.
Furthermore, even when the three poisons arise within the deluded mind, they already possess the eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*). Moreover—
If even in sleep or dreams one may see hundreds of thousands of things, how much more so for the wondrous mind!

These three metaphors are like those used in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* [Treatise] to illustrate the three inconceivable objects. Having grasped the purport of the preceding text, these three metaphors can be understood;
yet there are many who have misunderstood them.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.

Second, regarding the passage "mind, Buddha," and so forth: since the wondrous nature of the mind, Buddha, and the dharmas of sentient beings is thus, it follows that for all sentient beings and Buddhas, this is invariably the case;
the wondrousness of these three dharmas truly resides herein. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The mind is like a craftsman..."
The painter creates all manner of five aggregates; there is no phenomenon in any world that he does not create.
As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
When it is said that the mind creates, two meanings are intended: first, from the perspective of principle (*li*), "creating" means "possessing"; second, from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*).
That which is not produced does not exist within the three periods of time; yet these three periods are also one. First, that which was produced in the past produces the present;

second, that which is produced in the present produces the future; third, that which is produced through the transformations of the sages is produced from the present. All of these arise because they are fundamentally endowed with principle, and only then do they manifest as phenomena.
Since this is so for the mind and its dharmas, it is likewise so for birth and Buddhahood. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. However...
One must clearly understand that the principle is the principle of emptiness; in reality, it is fully endowed with the three thousand [realms]. Conventionally, they are provisional;

yet in terms of the principle, they are fundamentally complete, and in terms of phenomena, they give rise to function. Thus, the three dharmas—nature-endowment (*xingju*), cultivation-endowment (*xiuju*), and the non-differentiation between them—are without distinction. Since the nature-principle is already complete, this completeness is itself the principle;

therefore, one realizes that the completeness of the principle is identical to emptiness and the middle way. If one were to speak of the three as non-differentiated merely on the basis of their completeness, [it would not suffice].
This, then, would be to lose the principle within emptiness. To claim that only the names "three" within emptiness are without difference would be to lose the reality, qualities, and phenomena.
If one can clarify both principle and phenomena together, then there will be no error.

Thus, while the three—sentient beings, Buddhas, and the Middle Way—are called different in name, each is identical to the principle and fully possesses all phenomena; this is what is meant by "the three being without difference. (From the *Fuxing*).

Because they are explained as being created by the mind, the three dharmas—principle (li), inclusion (ju), and phenomena (shi)—each possess these three aspects and are thus called "undifferentiated" (wucha).

Since that which possesses phenomena is called undifferentiated, and what possesses them is necessarily identical to principle, one realizes that principle, inclusion, and phenomena are simultaneously empty (kong) and middle (zhong).

In the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), because the relative superiority and inferiority of the three dharmas and the differences between their phenomena and functions were distinguished, the essence of principle was shown to be designated as "non-existence" (wu).

It is indeed so; yet the essence of principle is not devoid of phenomena. Thus, the *Golden Scalpel* states: "Sentient beings possess both phenomena and principle within their delusion, while the Buddhas possess both phenomena and principle within their awakening.
Although delusion and awakening differ, the essence of phenomena and principle is one. Since this is the case for both sentient beings and Buddhas, how could it not be so for the mind?
Therefore, these three dharmas all possess the name "inherent" (*li-jù*) as well as "emptiness" (*kōng*). As for "non-existence" (*wú*), it refers to the absence of deluded grasping.
This is mistaken; moreover, while conventional designations are differentiated, true emptiness is without differentiation.

In the Middle Way, which is the double negation of both difference and non-difference, one simultaneously illuminates both difference and non-difference. Therefore, the functions of difference and non-difference are not the same;
if one adheres to them in a biased manner, it will truly be difficult to achieve harmonious understanding.
This mind is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle; the constant object is signless, and the constant wisdom is without conditions.

Third, below this, the text clarifying the contemplation of the truths is divided into two parts. First, the direct clarification, which is further divided into two. First, the simultaneous illumination and negation:
"this mind" refers to the illumination of emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle; "signless" and "without conditions" refer to the negation. "This mind" refers to...

This refers to the "wondrous mind" (*miaoxin*). Because one generates understanding based on principle, it is called the wondrous mind; to contemplate based on that understanding is precisely the realm of the aggregates (*skandhas*).

Viewed from the perspective of contemplation, these belong to the category of phenomena (*dharma*); this is what is meant by that. Thus, when one contemplates a single thought-moment of the causal mind through the three contemplations, one immediately perceives that this single thought-moment is without marks—this is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
That no phenomenon is not fully contained within it is called the provisional (*prajñapti*). That it is neither identical nor different... [is called the middle].

"Different" refers to the middle [truth]. Since that which is capable of contemplation consists of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), and that which is contemplated is named the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāḥ*), and because the realm of the truths (*satya-viṣaya*) is eternal, the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is also eternal.

Although the names "truth" and "contemplation" differ, their essence is fundamentally identical. Taking the mind as the object, the mind is also able to illumine; thus, subject and object are both mind.
The mutual illumination of mind and mind is analyzed according to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) as found in the *Yìlì* (Exemplification of Meaning). This is so.

This is because the wondrous mind, being fully endowed with the essence of nature, takes that which arises from nature as its cultivation; thus, realizing nature constitutes practice, and the entirety of reality is the contemplation of non-duality.

Therefore, in the lower fascicle of the *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* (Yingluo jing), it is said that when the Bodhisattva Jingshou asked the Buddha about the three contemplations, the pure path of the dharma-realm, the Buddha commanded the great assembly to all cultivate and study such a Dharma-gate. For this reason, [it is] by means of this mind...

"Phenomena born of causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle"—this is the heart-seal of Nāgārjuna, for it is precisely because of this that the object illuminated is negated;
thus it is said that the "constant object is signless. This means that the three truths of one mind are all unattainable.
Because the observing contemplation is also negated, it is said that "constant wisdom is without conditions. This refers to the three [truths] of one mind.

When even [the objects of] contemplation are found to be unattainable, how much more so are the signless (*animitta*) and the objectless (*anālambana*)? Since these themselves cannot be apprehended, how could they possibly persist when one contemplates them with clear insight?
To take the objectless as the object is none other than the three contemplations; to be signless yet manifest signs is the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāni*) in their full clarity.

The second, "non-conditioning while conditioning" (*wúyuán ér yuán*), refers to the simultaneous negation and illumination of that which is below; although neither is attained, they ultimately shine forth by themselves.

Because the wisdom that can contemplate is simultaneously negating and illuminating, it is said to be "conditioning while non-conditioning. This means there is nothing that is not the three contemplations (*sānguān*).

Because the object being contemplated is simultaneously negating and illuminating, it is said to be "characteristic while non-characteristic" (*wúxiàng ér xiàng*); thus the three truths (*sāndì*) are perfectly distinct. Day and night, these two [aspects] are practiced in tandem.
To cease [conceptual proliferation] while illuminating both [truths] throughout the day is the provisional establishment of the *siddhānta*;
that it is thus is because when one seeks for oneself through investigation, all is clearly tranquil and still—this is precisely what occurs when the mind is gathered in a secluded place.
The beginner knows this and rejoices for themselves and others; therefore, it is called "Rejoicing" (Anumodanā).

Second, the initial section concludes by indicating the textual divisions, which is divided into two parts. First, the conclusion of the title: this is the conclusion that establishes the title of the "Chapter on Rejoicing.
"The beginner" refers to the first of the five stages. "Knows this" points toward the directed contemplation of the truths.

The beginner knows that this constitutes the fulfillment of *anurāga* (joyful attachment). To accord with phenomena and principle as non-dual and undifferentiated is precisely the contemplation of the truth of emptiness;
conventional, provisional phenomena are the mundane aspect. Rejoicing in oneself and rejoicing in others constitutes the fulfillment of *muditā* (sympathetic joy).
Because one accords with the wondrous Dharma through both its phenomenal and principled aspects, one rejoices in oneself for possessing wisdom, and furthermore, one rejoices in others.
Because the practice of compassion is itself the principle, it is called "rejoicing in oneself"; because the principle is itself the practice, it is called "rejoicing in others.
Therefore, although the beginner primarily establishes their own practice, they also rejoice in others through the power of their vow.
That one’s own practice transforms others is made possible precisely by this; such a person is said to possess "sympathetic joy" (*anumodana*). Otherwise, they are said to be "defiled."

[The author] comments: Internally, one uses the three contemplations to contemplate the three truths; externally, one diligently applies the five repentances with vigorous精进 (vīrya) to assist in the realization of understanding. Second, from "internally" onwards, the text clarifies that the internal requires external assistance. This section is divided into three parts:

first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent [section], beginning with "internally... *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on a Buddhist treatise concerning the practice of the three contemplations (sān guān), the three truths (sān dì jìng), and the five repentances (wǔ huì). The term "zī yān" (訾焉) indicates a critical or explanatory remark by the commentator.*

The phrase "the three contemplations contemplate the objects of the three truths" concludes the preceding section. The phrase "externally using the five repentances to assist in the completion of understanding" introduces what follows.

This means that although one has previously used the three contemplations to contemplate the objects of the three truths, the three delusions have not yet been subdued, the first stage of clarity has not yet been attained, and external obstacles remain manifold;
therefore, one must add ritual practice and cultivate the five repentances so that external obstacles do not arise and internal [realization] may flourish.
This is because contemplating that which can give rise to understanding is itself the contemplation directed toward the principle (*li*).
Regarding the "five repentances" (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*), there are two types:

first, the principle (*li*), and second, the phenomenon (*shi*). The section following the phrase "the second" explains these in two parts; first, the principle and phenomenon are presented together. Here, "principle" refers to the meaning of the internal contemplation discussed previously.
What is indicated here, however, is presented in contrast [to the former].

As for the "principle repentance" (lǐchàn), if one wishes to repent, one should sit upright and contemplate the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); all transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can eliminate—this is precisely that meaning.
Second, the ritual repentance based on principle (*li-xian*). This section consists of two parts: first, the general explanation of principle and phenomena; second, the specific explanation of each.

Regarding the first, it cites texts to re-demonstrate the contemplation of principle within the fivefold repentance (*wu-hui*). This is because the headings are presented in pairs, and thus their explanations follow suit.

This passage originates from the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-samadhi-sutra* (Puxian guan jing).
