As for the phrase "sitting upright," this refers to the physical posture (*shen-yi*); while such postures encompass four types, it is here simply referred to as "sitting. This pertains to one's own practice (*zi-xing*).

In the midst of emptiness, that which is called "mindfulness of the true aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) involves the wondrous provisional transformation of others; the three thousand realms of all phenomena, when summarized, are neither self nor other.

When the three contemplations are perfected and principle and phenomena are fused and obliterated, such that one realizes that deluded thoughts possess not even a single mark of identity or difference, this is called "mindfulness of the true aspect.
If one penetrates the signless, then within that very signlessness, the three thousand realms appear vividly, without a single mark of identity or difference.
Therefore, various offenses do not arise; this can be understood through the metaphors of frost and dew versus the sun of wisdom and the Dharma.
Since it was previously stated that there are two types of repentance, we know that the repentance of principle (*li-xian*) must be complete in five aspects.

This is because everything from the act of repentance up to the making of vows requires mindfulness of the empty, true reality (*śūnyatā-bhūta-lakṣaṇa*)—the signless (*animitta*) within which the three thousand [realms] are perfectly manifest. Thus, one attains the repentance of principle.
Since one should repent and eliminate all transgressions through each of the five types of fivefold penetrations (*pañcābhijñā*), it is simply called "repentance by principle" (*li-xian*).

If one does not provide this explanation, how could repentance by principle differ from the aforementioned contemplation of truth? The Sanskrit term is *kṣamā*, which here means "to repent of one's faults.
Because both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together, it is called "repentance" (*chanhui*). This explains the name of repentance to demonstrate its meaning.

The methods for repentance are distinguished within the section on repentance; the stages of repentance, the practice of not grasping at signs, and so forth— these three, as well as the meanings concerning *tathatā*,
*vijñaptimātra*, the four kinds of *samādhi*, the ten objects, and the ten vehicles, including their reliance on phenomena and attachment to dharmas according to practice—
are explained extensively in various sections [of the scriptures], and it is difficult to present them all here in detail.
Regarding the confession of transgressions: during the six periods of day and night, with the three karmas purified,
one stands before a sacred image and discloses all faults and offenses committed from beginningless time until the present life— namely, killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an Arhat,
causing a schism in the Sangha, shedding the blood of a Buddha, sexual misconduct, stealing, false speech, frivolous speech, double-tongued speech, and harsh speech.

Regarding the confession of greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth—including these five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*), and all other transgressions—one should openly reveal them according to one's will without further concealment;
thus, having exhausted the old, one does not create the new.

Second, as for the "confession through ritual action," the following section clarifies the external assistance of ritual practice, consisting of the five repentances (*pañca-pratikramaṇa*). This text is divided into two parts; first:

The explicit clarification of the two types of bonds is divided into five parts. The first part, the section on confession (*pratideśanā*), is further divided into two. The first of these, the "explicit explanation," is divided into two. First, regarding the method:
"prostrating at the six periods of day and night" and so forth refers to the method; "disclosing one's transgressions" and so forth refers to the act of prostration (*deśanā*).

This includes the method for the three-week period as found in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as well as the various ritual procedures for walking meditation found in other sūtras. [Note: The phrase "one category of lateral embroidery" appears to be a scribal error or a misplaced annotation.]

Speech that deviates from reason is called frivolous chatter (*sambhinna-pralāpa*). Speech that incites strife and causes others to suffer gain or loss through division is called slander (*paiśunya*).
Harsh speech directed at others to cause them distress is called abusive language (*pāruṣya*).
The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* adds "meaningless speech" to these to constitute the five evils. The *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* states:
This refers to the five kinds of unwholesome karma of harsh speech arising from the faculty of the tongue.
People who do not understand this claim that the translator erred by stating there are "five kinds," yet here the text on the ten non-virtues is abbreviated, mentioning only the first, killing;
the rest are as explained previously. One must know that the purpose of repentance is precisely to eliminate the offenses of violating the precepts.
If it is thus, then external obstacles will gradually be eliminated and internal contemplation will increase in clarity.
Second, if it is as follows, it forms three parts: first, internally aided by the external; if it is thus, this points toward the method;
"external obstacles gradually eliminated" refers to adverse conditions and the like; "internal contemplation increases in clarity" refers to the aforementioned contemplation of reality.
When practice possesses power, external obstacles do not arise and internal contemplation attains clarity; this is the power of external assistance.
It is like a boat going with the current that is further propelled by oars and poles—would it not reach its destination with great speed?
Second, regarding the illustration of practicing contemplation based on principle, it is like the case of a boat going with the current;
its initial subduing is like adding oars and rudders, and its perfect subduing and perfect severance begin from the fifth stage and culminate in wondrous enlightenment.
Because this differs from the partial and gradual sequential cultivation and realization, it is said that one "swiftly arrives at the place of rest."

The practitioner who cultivates the perfect practice is also like this: by correctly contemplating how the perfect principle and phenomena assist one another in their practice, will they not swiftly reach the other shore of wondrous enlightenment?
The text of these three harmonies is perfectly clear.
Do not, upon seeing this teaching, claim that there is only gradual practice and no such thing as sudden, perfect practice; such a misconception is extremely grave.
Second, the section refuting errors based on the following text is divided into two parts: first, citing the error to provide a general refutation;

second, explaining that the principle-contemplation and ritual repentance elucidated above are all based upon the various Mahāyāna sūtras, yet the ignorant and foolish, having heard this teaching, do not understand it.
Consequently, one might claim that the intent of the gradual *Hīnayāna* is such while the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) teaching is not at all like this;
hence it is said: "If one has not yet attained sudden transcendence, one should for the time being apply the mind to the teachings.

This is truly because worldly people are deluded regarding the Mahāyāna methods of practice, mistakenly fixating on the principle-nature (*li-xing*) as being without speech or demonstration, and thereby neglecting the cultivation of attainment.
Those who, under the two gates of understanding and practice, sit with folded hands in non-action, neither paying homage to the sacred countenance nor reading the scriptures and teachings, yet claim,

"I am of the Mahāyāna sudden-capacity type and enter directly"— such individuals are precisely the "darkly realized" followers whom our school rejects as being merely suited for the middle and lower capacities of gradual progression found in various sutras and śāstras.
Where is there a natural Maitreya or a spontaneous Śākyamuni?
Second, the section on the specific refutation of the lower [views] is divided into two parts. First, the refutation that results can exist without a cause:
since Maitreya and Śākyamuni are persons who are results, results must necessarily arise from causes; yet now they do not cultivate the causes of principle and phenomena.
There is no cause; "no cause" is called the Heavenly-Natured (tiānrán) and the Spontaneous (zìrán). How could a fruit be elicited without a cause?
Therefore, it is refuted by saying that Maitreya is the Heavenly-Natured and Śākyamuni is the Spontaneous.

If this were so, the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas and Mahāsattvas, as well as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, would be rendered useless. How then could Yongjia say that one must cultivate for many kalpas? Yet, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*...
It is said that just as a poor person may enumerate the treasures of others without ever practicing the Dharma themselves, so it is with those who merely study texts.
Therefore, the Buddha bestowed his teachings so that people might rely upon them for practice and realization. Is this not like pointing at the moon with one's finger?
Thus, how could the sūtras and śāstras harm anyone? Why fear liberation through words? Whatever one does will be nothing other than right action.

What is meant by "gradual practice"? Outside of this teaching, what else could there be to transmit separately? If you have failed to understand it by examining the commentaries and seeking the sutras to distinguish their names and characteristics, that is simply your own lack of comprehension;
it is not the fault of the sutras or the treatises. Furthermore, I do not know whose commentary you are referring to when you say "examining.

If it refers to the commentaries of Ci'en (Xuanzang) and others, then that may well be so. However, if it refers to the commentaries of Tiantai, they all possess systematic methods for subsuming phenomena into the [Dharma].

When mental contemplation accords with the sutras, it is not merely the "counting of others' treasures" (i.e., mere intellectual analysis); how could it be limited to the differentiation of names and characteristics?
It has misled immeasurable people; the harm caused by rejecting and disparaging the sutras and śāstras is truly great, and one must therefore be extremely cautious.

Master Quanling (Zhiyan) said: "I have extracted the profound essence of the three contemplations of Tiantai and Huiwei, so that the teachings accord with the intent of the ineffable and the mind becomes one with all Buddhas."
The Buddha’s mind does not depend on looking at another's face, nor does it suggest that there exists some separate gate of "extinguishing the faculty" (wang-ji).
Those of old who did not associate with virtuous friends, but merely prized the pursuit of texts, would—once their years had somewhat declined—wish to abandon the teachings to seek only dhyāna.
This not only suppresses the Buddha’s mind, but also leads subsequent learners into error; for this reason, they are unable to practice according to the teachings.
The Tathāgata severely rebuked those who merely listen to the words of others; what fault, then, do the sūtras and śāstras possess?

Therefore, my ancestors criticized those who do not understand the cultivation of the mind, saying: "Having pursued this for many years and observed the mind for some time, they eventually cease to investigate and interrogate the mind.
Consequently, they do not defile themselves with internal dharmas, yet they become attached to external words and characters, memorizing notes and rushing about."
Those who carry the sutras and śāstras about while wandering aimlessly are all merely rejected by those who lack understanding; they are no different from one who counts another's jewels.
When the vulgar and base among the learned hear but a single verse or phrase, they immediately claim it is a separate transmission outside the teachings (*jiaowai biezhuan*);
this is because they do not know that the treasury of our Buddha-dharma and the ocean of the Tathāgata’s teaching are all-inclusive and harmonious.
Because it encompasses all phenomena, Chan ultimately surpasses the teachings. What, then, is meant by "teachings" and what is meant by "Chan"?
How lamentable, how lamentable! The rest is as analyzed in the supplementary notes to the Great Treatise.
If, upon merely hearing that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa, afflictions are themselves bodhi, and the mind is itself the Buddha,
one reaches [enlightenment] without movement and achieves perfect awakening without the addition of cultivation.
2. Regarding the second [section], the refutation of those who, upon merely hearing [the teachings below], erroneously cling to specific doctrinal gates, this text is divided into two parts.
First, the presentation of their attachments, which is further divided into two. First, the presentation of the objects of their attachment: "Merely" (*cái*) means just or a little.

To call this the "separate transmission outside the teachings"—is this not to deceive Heaven?

To hear these teachings and give rise to conceptual attachment, one should know that all such instances are the foremost of the great delusions of those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) within the Mahāyāna.

One must understand that the term "identity" (*tādātmya*) is used to manifest "separation," for just as ice is not separate from water, the principle requires that the ice be melted; only when the meaning is identical to separation can it truly be so.
This reveals that you, who are currently fully possessed of birth-and-death and afflictions, have never yet awakened to or entered into Bodhi and Nirvana.
If you had already awakened to and entered them, you would be equal to the supreme sages; why then do you not emit light and ascend into the void?
What you conceive is like something empty; though I grant your feelings, your contemplation of the Way remains merely a semblance.
The worlds of the ten directions are entirely pure lands; wherever one turns or faces, there is nothing that is not the Awakened One.

"Although it is so now, this is the 'identity with principle' (li-ji) Buddha; it is also the unadorned Dharmakāya, so how does it concern cultivation and realization?
