This is merely a name; because there is no cultivation or realization, it is in no way different from the state of "principle-as-such" (*riji*). That "the mind itself is Buddha"—who would not agree with this?

However, if one does not cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) to adorn the Dharma-body, and if one's physical body remains base or inferior, how could one be equal to the Greatly Awakened One, whose fruit-body is adorned by the purity of the ten thousand practices? Therefore, those who are mired in the darkness of meditation...

Many Dharma masters who rely on mere words are full of overweening pride and constantly seek high positions; this is entirely due to their failure to study the Tiantai Dharma-gate of "Six While Yet Being Identical.
We foolish folk, upon merely hearing of "immediate emptiness," immediately abandon practice, failing to understand the reason for this "immediacy"—we are like mice squeaking in a corner.
Seek and contemplate the "Birds in the Void" (Niao-k'ung) section of the sutras and treatises.

Regarding the second point, "We and others," etc., this reiterates the previous position to further censure it. As for the "mole-crickets and birds-in-the-vacuum," this censures those who rely on obscure testimony and fail to penetrate the principles of the Truth, yet erroneously claim that what they say is no different from the chirping of a mole;
such a comparison is truly strange, for the mole makes a "chirp-chirp" sound, which is merely a noise devoid of meaning—a case of false analogy.
The proposition that birth-and-death is itself nirvana is like the cry of a strange bird that utters the sound of "emptiness" (kūṇa-kūṇa);

yet since this sound of emptiness lacks any essential meaning, how could it be indiscriminately equated with the samādhi of emptiness? Therefore, according to Tiantai, from the perspective of principle (li), not even a single dharma can be established;
yet from the perspective of practice (xiu), the myriad practices are perfectly fulfilled. Practice is entirely within nature, and nature gives rise to practice entirely; yet nature remains unchanged.
Cultivation remains ever-vivid; if one attains this meaning, then upon hearing various strange accounts, the mind remains serene and unperturbed.

The wondrous vehicle of the Perfect and Sudden finds a place to settle in the heart precisely because one understands that the fundamental nature is empty and quiescent; thus, in cultivating all practices, there is no obstruction.
Second, regarding the exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*): it is the exhortation to all Tathāgatas of the ten directions to remain in this world for a long time to deliver all sentient beings.
This second exhortation is specifically intended to destroy the sin of slandering the Dharma;

because we ourselves have, since beginningless time, acted as false followers who requested the Buddhas to enter *parinirvāṇa* and thereby severed the wheel of the True Dharma, one must perform this [exhortation] in order to eliminate such sins.
Exhorting the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to remain long in the world for the benefit of sentient beings;
third, rejoicing, which means to rejoice in and praise all roots of goodness.
This third practice of rejoicing is specifically for the purpose of eliminating the fault of envy, arising from having envied the virtues of others in the past.
Because it is the root, one now reverses and refutes [wrong views] and gives rise to sympathetic joy.
Regarding the four types of dedication: all praised virtues are fully dedicated toward Bodhi.
As for the four dedications: one dedicates one's own merit to other sentient beings so that they may together realize unsurpassed Buddha-Bodhi.
Just as an echo entering a horn will surely be heard at a great distance, this is precisely the refutation of the fault of outflows (*āsrava*).

Because one’s past good roots were not dedicated toward the wondrous wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one has consequently wandered in saṃsāra; this is also called the fault of breaking through attachment to existence.
Fifth, regarding the making of vows: if one lacks the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), nothing will be accomplished; therefore, one must arouse the mind to guide the preceding four practices.

Fifth, although one may perform the preceding four, if there is no vow, there is much regression—like an ox without a driver that cannot reach its destination, like a painting without glue, or like unbaked clay. Therefore, one must make vows to strictly restrain the mind; this is for the sake of correctness.
This breaks the transgression of retrogression;
these constitute the five repentances.

The phrase "these two" serves as a concluding summary for the five repentances. Although the five dharmas differ, they are all none other than the repentance of transgressions; therefore, it is so stated.
One performs the five repentances.

For all subsequent stages down to the level of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), these five repentances are applied universally; they need not be mentioned again, as this pattern can be understood by analogy.

Third, regarding the various stages below: to illustrate one example, since it is thus for the first stage, it should be known that the same applies to the four stages of the ten levels of faith (śraddhā).

This remains true for all stages up to Equal Enlightenment; thus, the *Sūtra on the Fifty Calculations* states that from the level of ordinary beings up to Equal Enlightenment, one practices the five repentances.

If even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment still cultivate them, how can you suddenly abandon them? As for the school that relies on realization through darkness (*andhakāra-pratyakṣa*), why do you disregard it?
Second, the Chapter on Recitation.
This chapter is divided into two parts; first, the heading.
The Sūtra says: "How much more so for those who read, recite, receive, and uphold it."

The second explanation is divided into two parts. First, citing the scriptural passage: "How much more so for reading and reciting? This means that if even rejoicing [in merit] is thus, how much more so for reading and reciting?
That is to say, internally through perfect contemplation, one further adds the practice of reading and reciting.

The second refers to the internal [practice], which is explained as twofold. First, the direct explanation of the internal: as previously clarified, one employs the circular contemplation (*yuánguān*);
furthermore, one adds recitation and chanting, such as the method for reciting sutras shown by the Great Master, which is not recorded here.
It is like grease assisting fire.
Second, regarding the metaphor: "grease" refers to animal fat; "grease" is a metaphor for external recitation, and "fire" is a metaphor for internal contemplation.
Third, as for the section on the teaching of the dharma:
The third section, "Explaining the Dharma," is divided into two parts. First, the heading:
the Sūtra says, "If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others.
Second, the explanation, which is further divided into two parts. First, citing the Sūtra: "explaining it for others" is precisely "expounding the Dharma."

First, internal understanding becomes increasingly superior, guiding and benefiting others while dedicating the merit of such transformation to oneself; thus, the mind surpasses the previous two stages.
Second, "internal understanding" and below explain how the merit of transforming others is attributed to oneself, and that this clarity of mind surpasses the first two sections.
In the text, the character "pei" (陪) is an error and should be "bei" (倍); therefore, the *Zhi guan* says, "it doubly assists the contemplative mind."
"Twofold" means increasing and excelling by equal multiples.
Regarding the fourth [stage], "Practicing the Six Perfections Simultaneously," the section on practicing them simultaneously is divided into two parts; first, the heading.
The Sūtra says: "How much more so for one who can uphold this sūtra while also practicing giving and other virtues.

There are two interpretations, each with two parts. First, citing the Sūtra: "兼" (jiān) means mutual inclusion; it refers to being able to employ them together, though not yet having fully mastered their correct practice.

The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-vyākhyā* states: "Previously, in contemplating the mind, there was no leisure to engage with external phenomena; now that the correct contemplation is somewhat clear," and so forth.

"Accompanying and benefiting others" means that while one can take the contemplation of the principle—that even a small gift is equal to empty space—as the primary practice, one takes actual conduct as the secondary practice;
"secondary" (bàng) carries the sense of being "concomitant" (jiān), hence it is called "concomitant. This refers to the five perfections beginning with giving.
By the power of merit, one augments the contemplation of the mind.

Second, regarding "inferior merit," this explains the practice of giving and so forth, which constitutes merit; that merit serves as a support for wisdom, making it superior to what preceded—it should be understood thus.
The character "pei" (陪) in the text is also an error.
Regarding the five correct practices of the six perfections:
the Chapter on the Five Correct Practices also has two parts, the first of which is the heading.
The Sūtra says: "If a person reads and recites [this] for others, and furthermore is able to maintain the precepts, and so forth."
The second [section], the explanation, is divided into two parts. First, citing the scripture:

it states that because one’s own practice and the activity of transforming others are complete in both principle and fact, the contemplation of the mind proceeds unhindered and excels the former beyond comparison.

The second refers to the fact that, while for oneself one constantly contemplates the principle of emptiness as explained below, for others one always employs the phenomena of the three thousand worlds;

thus, self and other are non-dual, and principle and phenomenon are harmoniously integrated. Since one correctly practices the six pāramitās without being obstructed by emptiness, this is already superior to the previous four [stages] and cannot be compared to them.
These five grades of practice constitute the stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) who have fully suppressed the afflictions of the five abodes.

Third, this section on the conclusion of the lower grades is divided into two parts: first, the formal conclusion; it should be understood that one enters the five grades only after the contemplation has been perfected;
do not assume that the five grades begin with the initial cultivation of contemplative practice.
The first [point] is the same as the separate ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The second is the same as the subsequent examples; one must understand that there are differences in the various texts concerning the five grades and the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*).
If the five grades are placed before the ten stages of faith, it is as stated in the present text; if the five grades are placed within the ten stages of faith, [it is as in other texts].
This is as clarified in the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* (Puxian guan jing), with full details provided in the supplementary notes (*buzhu*) of the *Fenbie* (Analysis).
Next, advancing to the stage of the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) constitutes the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

This section on the two types of inner ordinary beings (*adhyātma-prthagjana*) is divided into two parts: first, the general presentation of the purity of the six sense faculties, as described in the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the merit of the Dharma-preacher (*dharma-bhāṇaka*).

This is elucidated within the "Chapter on Virtues" (*Guṇavarṇa-parivarta*); it refers precisely to the six sense organs becoming pure in a manner that is "similar" [to the ultimate], which constitutes the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching.

Other masters, however, take the "Ten Good Deeds Bodhisattva" from the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (or *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*), who has "permanently parted from the sea of suffering," as representing the gradual-perfect teaching, while they designate the "six sense organs" from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* as the sudden-sudden teaching. Jingxi uses the analogy: "The various schools of our Mountain Gate..."
Both take the *Renwang jing* as evidence for the *Fahua jing*, differing only slightly in that one emphasizes cause and the other effect;
why, then, would you divide these into two sudden teachings? In the true stage, the six sense faculties are as described in the *Avataṃsaka*.

At the initial stage of faith, one severs the delusions of views and manifests the true principle; this is equivalent to the first fruit of the Tripitaka Teaching, the stage of the eighth person and the stage of seeing in the Shared Teaching, and the first dwelling in the Distinct Teaching—attaining the rank of non-retrogression.

The second [section] begins with a detailed explanation, which is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the first stage of faith through to the seventh stage of faith, which is further divided into three sections. First, the formal explanation; within this, first is the explanation of the first stage of faith.

Next, from the second stage of faith through to the seventh stage of faith, the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) are exhausted; this distinguishes it from the Buddhas of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Shared* vehicles, as well as from the seventh stage of abiding (*vihāra*) in the Distinct Teaching.
One completely eradicates the suffering and its accumulation within the three realms, leaving nothing remaining.
This is evident in the texts from the second stage of liberation and the second stage of faith up to the seventh stage of faith.

Thus, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "The Bodhisattva of the Ten Wholesome Paths, having resolved upon the Great Mind, forever parts from the ocean of the wheel of suffering in the three realms."
Second, citing the *Ratnarājasūtra* (Renwang jing) in two parts: first, the citation from the sūtra, specifically from the verses spoken by King Prasenajit.
The commentary states:
"The ten wholesome [actions] means that each possesses the ten wholesome [paths of action]."

Second, the section on explanation has two parts. First, the actual explanation, which also has two parts. First, the explanation of the ten wholesome actions: that sutra also does not list or explain them, but they are:
non-killing, non-stealing, non-sexual misconduct, non-lying, non-slander, non-harsh speech, non-frivolous speech, non-covetousness, non-anger, and non-wrong view.
Each of these eleven [factors] has both the aspect of cessation and the aspect of practice, and all are able to accord with [the path].
The principle is termed the "ten wholesome actions"; thus, each of the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā) possesses the ten wholesome actions.
This does not mean that the ten stages of faith are specifically correlated with the human and celestial realms through a sequential correspondence of non-killing, non-stealing, and so forth.
If one were to interpret the "Ten Faiths" as distinct [stages], they would merely suppress afflictions without severing them; therefore, they must certainly belong to the Perfect (yuan) faith.

Regarding the second interpretation, since the scriptural passage on the distinct suffering states that one is "permanently separated from the sea of suffering," we know this refers to the stage of the Ten Faiths of the Perfect teaching, wherein one has already severed the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāva-āsrava*) before being separated from the sea of distinct suffering. Were it not for our school’s reliance on the text of the *Lotus Sūtra*, how could this be determined?
If the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) sever the suffering of the three realms, what is the intent of the *Renyō-kyō* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra) that allows it to be dispelled?

And how can one judge that the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* constitutes the stage of a sage (*ārya*)? Nevertheless, the original aspiration of the person of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) is not to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) or the afflictions of dust and sand (*rajas-aṇu-kleśa*), but rather intends to sever ignorance (*avidyā*) upon entering and abiding in the [first] dwelling, thereby beholding the Buddha.

Nature. Second, "then below" clarifies that this is not the original intent; this section is divided into three parts: first, the correct clarification that the intent of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings in entering emptiness is primarily to sever the two delusions of views and thought;

second, the separate teaching (*biejiao*) of emerging into the provisional (*chujia*) to specifically sever the delusion of *chen-sha* (dust-like afflictions); and third, the perfect teaching (*yuanjiao*) of entering the middle way to correctly sever [all delusions].

Ignorance is now severed along with the afflictions of views and thoughts, as well as the *rajas* (dust-like) afflictions; yet this was not the original intention. Although it was not the original intention, these [afflictions] naturally fall away first.

It is like smelting iron: the coarse impurities are removed first, though this was not the primary aim, for the purpose was to forge a vessel. Before the vessel is complete, [the impurities] must first be cleared away.
At that time, [the metal] naturally falls first; although it is seen to depart first, the person does not have a single thought of joy.
Why is this? Because they have not yet accomplished what they expected.

Second, the phrase "then below" uses the metaphor of smelting (*yè*, pronounced *yáng*); "furnace" refers to the smelting hearth. Smelting iron to form vessels is a metaphor for the severing of non-existence.

The eighth stage of the clear realization (abhisamaya) is illustrated by the metaphor of coarse impurities falling first; this signifies the removal of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), as well as the "sands of dust" (*rajas*).

It represents the realization of both ultimate and conventional truth. However, this still merely follows the sequential order; in reality, the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) must be cultivated in a perfect, simultaneous manner (*yuganaddha*).
How could the three delusions possibly be eliminated one after another? Therefore, even now, we follow the sequential order of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*).
The practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is also like this: although it was not originally what they hoped for, they naturally fall [into the lower stages] first.
The text regarding the "three rounds" and "downward convergence" is easy to see.
Master Yongjia said: "When the four abidings (si-zhu) are removed together, this stage is equal; if one subdues ignorance (wu-ming), the Tripitaka [teaching] is..."
"Inferior" refers precisely to this stage.
Third, citing Master Yongjia to corroborate [the teaching], which is divided into two parts. First, the citation of the text:
this passage originally derives from the *Tiantai Miaoxuan* (The Profound Mystery of the Stages). Master Yongjia merely cited the *Tiantai* tradition; how could the Master [Zhi]guan possibly...
If you do not understand this, the reason I specifically mention Yongjia here is that I wish to demonstrate that Yongjia originally studied the Tiantai school.
Consequently, the *Yongjia Collection* frequently employs Tiantai methods;

since Yongjia utilized the Tiantai dharma-gates, how can contemporary Chan practitioners claim that what he discussed belongs to the Exegetical School (*Jiao-jia*) rather than the School of the Patriarchs (*Zong-men*)? Nevertheless...
The *Yongjia Collection* frequently relies on the Tiantai school yet does not explicitly mention "Tiantai. Why is this? Furthermore, it simply says, "One who recognizes Caoxi.
The explanation is as follows:

the "four abidings" (catvāraḥ-vāsabhūmayaḥ) are merely the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *vitarka-āsrava*). That is to say, "view" is designated as one name for the stage where [delusions] abide in all places.

The afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) are divided into three categories: first, the ground of attachment to desire (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*), consisting of the nine grades of thought-afflictions of the desire realm;

second, the ground of attachment to form (*rūparāga-vāsabhūmi*), consisting of the nine grades of thought-afflictions for each of the four stages of the form realm; and third, the ground of attachment to the formless (*ārūpyarāga-vāsabhūmi*), consisting of the nine grades of thought-afflictions for each of the four stages of the formless realm.
Because the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka and those who have attained the purity of the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddha*) sever these four grounds equally, it is said that they are the same.
This excludes the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*).

Second, the section on interpretation is divided into two parts. First, explaining why the identical views are consolidated into one: because the waves of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are vast and pervasive, touching the mind and giving rise to attachment;

when these are severed, they are all severed together, and thus they are combined into one. Regarding "all places," the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the root, for it calculates [the self] as existing everywhere.

Regarding the third section, "The Contemplation of All Places with Immeasurable Names," it is divided according to the sequential abandonment of afflictions: first desire, then form, and finally the formless.
As for the fact that the three abodes of the afflictions of thought (*cetanā-kleśa*) are all termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), this refers specifically to greedy craving.

While the afflictions of thought actually encompass greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, the present text merely indicates the category of greed. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Desire-greed."
This refers to the ground of abiding in desire-attachment (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*); the greed for the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-arūpya-rāga*) is likewise so designated.

Some scholars refer to that of the desire realm as "greed" (*rāga*) and that of the upper realms as "attachment" (*tṛṣṇā*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* (Cheng lun) challenges this as a partial judgment, stating that all who say "abiding" mean it in the sense of "dwelling with attachment.
Because one possesses these delusions, one dwells in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Non-abiding is... [text fragment].

Because this is the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), one knows that "non-abiding" is itself the fifth stage; although it is called non-abiding, it nonetheless constitutes the sense of "abiding.
Whether there is abiding or non-abiding is left to that text for detailed treatment.

Regarding the statement that "the Threefold Canon (Tripiṭaka) is inferior because it suppresses ignorance": ignorance refers to the specific delusions that obstruct the Middle Way beyond the [three] realms.
The teachings of the Tripiṭaka only discuss the pervasive delusions within the realms; they cannot even know the names of this ignorance, let alone suppress or sever it.
Therefore, it is said that the Tripiṭaka is inferior.
Regarding the second explanation concerning the subduing of inferior statements on "distinct delusions": let us set aside the *saṃsāra* like grains of sand and speak only of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Next, from the eighth stage of faith up to the tenth stage of faith, one exhaustively severs the *dhūli-saṃsāra* (delusions like grains of sand) both within and outside the realms; the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) manifests before one, and one perceives the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

One opens the Dharma-eye and achieves the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), traveling four hundred *yojanas*, which corresponds to the eighth and ninth stages of the Separate Teaching (*bhinna-śāsana*).
The ten abodes (*bhūmi*) and the stages of practice leading toward them (*pratipannaka*) constitute the simultaneous practice of non-retrogression.
The second interpretation covers the eight levels of faith up to the tenth level of faith.

Next, one enters the first abode (*prathama-bhūmi*), where one severs the first grade of ignorance and realizes a portion of the three virtues (*tri-dharma*), namely liberation (*vimukti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the Dharma (*dharma*).
These three virtues of the body are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the three dots of the world-sign *i* or the three eyes of the Lord of Heaven (*Indra*).

Regarding the two stages of the sages, there are two parts; first, the stage of the cause, which has three initial sections. First, the detailed explanation of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), which has two initial sections. First, the detailed explanation of the first abode, which is divided into three parts.
First, the actual explanation, which further has two parts. First, clarifying that internal realization is free from ignorance, and how the three virtues are also one.

The distinction between the divisions of the *pin* (chapters/sections) is designated as "shallow or deep wisdom" based on the person’s realization and verification; thus, they are called "divisions of the *pin*.

As for the designation "not vertical or horizontal," it refers to the refutation of the "vertical" and "horizontal" models. In the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the three dharmas of the nature-merit (*xingde*) are explained without mutual fusion, which is termed "horizontal.
The three dharmas of the cultivation-merit (*xiude*) are termed "vertical" because they occur sequentially. This is a classification based on cultivation and nature.

Regarding the dialectical discourse on "vertical" (*zhōng*) and "horizontal" (*héng*): there is the sequence of the preceding dharma, the subsequent retribution, and the final response, which is termed "vertical.
This is discussed in terms of a single nature and two types of cultivation. "Vertical" refers to the verticality of dripping water, while "horizontal" refers to the horizontality of spreading fire.

Since these involve both verticality and horizontality, they are not perfectly sublime (*yuánmiào*). Now, as for the three virtues realized within the stage of the first *bhūmi* in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching:

Because it is not like this, it is neither horizontal nor vertical. This is the nature-three of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjia); it is not a horizontally cultivated three, nor a vertically cultivated one.
The unity of nature and duality of cultivation are likewise neither vertical. This statement is made in relation to their opposites;

in reality, the subtle and wondrous Three Virtues of the Perfect Teaching are entirely neither vertical nor horizontal. Why? Although the single point of the Dharma-body is situated above, [it is not separate from the other two].
Because two are one, they are not vertical; because although the two—prajñā and liberation—are situated below, they are one and yet two, they are not horizontal.
Therefore, the three virtues (triguṇa) are called "neither vertical nor horizontal. Whether in terms of nature (prakṛti) or cultivation (bhāvanā), all are thus.
Within nature, the three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal; for now, the state of being non-horizontal is used to refute the "nature" (prakṛti) of the Separate School (Bie-jia).

Regarding the three horizontal cultivations, the middle three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal; they first counteract the vertical cultivation of the three [stages] by other schools through the principle of non-verticality.

This refers to the cultivation of each of the three natures as distinct entities. However, if these are combined into two cultivations with a single nature, this too is neither vertical nor horizontal;
it further counters the sequence of "first dharma, then retribution, and finally response" maintained by other schools through the principle of non-verticality.

Because they are not sequential, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The three tracks of the nature-virtue are neither sequential nor horizontal; the three tracks of the cultivation-virtue are neither sequential nor horizontal.
It further states: "The three dots are positioned one above the other, yet are not sequential; they face each other, yet are not horizontal. The *Shiqian* explains:
"Although one dot is at the top, it is not like the sequence of dots in writing water; the three virtues are also thus. Although the Dharma-body..."

Originally there was a difference: the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is obscured by delusions; thus, although the two dots are situated below, they do not differ from the three virtues arranged horizontally like fire.

The three virtues are likewise so: although they are accomplished through cultivation in the Separate Teaching, in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the principle and substance are fully possessed and do not mutually exclude one another.
Thus, in the present text, with respect to the upper dot, it is called "not vertical" (feizong); with respect to the lower two...
To designate them as neither horizontal nor vertical means that the two must be entirely one, and that the non-horizontal must be entirely two.

One should know that this is discussed in terms of the single nature and the dual cultivation: the single nature is not without the conditions of the three natures (the perfect, the dependent, and the imagined), and the dual cultivation is not without the single nature.
Thus, the three [natures] are manifest within the single nature, and the single nature and dual cultivation are neither [separate].

If the three natures and the three cultivations are both vertical and horizontal, how could they not be so? Therefore, whether the three virtues are separated or combined, they are neither vertical nor horizontal.
Furthermore, the *Wenju* states: "The three dharmas of other schools, whether in the causal stage or the resultant stage, are all vertical and horizontal.

Thus we know that the Perfect Dharma, whether in the causal or resultant stage, is termed "neither vertical nor horizontal. Regarding terms such as "world" (*se*) and "I" (*yi*), these are cited as metaphors.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Lamentation," says: "What is called the secret treasury? It is like the three dots of the letter *i*.
If they are placed side by side, they do not form an *i*; if they are placed vertically, they likewise do not form one.
Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara do they constitute an *i*. If the three dots are separate, they also do not form an *i*. I am also like this."
This Dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa; the body of the Tathāgata is also not nirvāṇa;
and Mahāprajñāpāramitā is likewise not nirvāṇa. That these three dharmas are distinct from one another is also not nirvāṇa.
I now abide in these three dharmas, yet for the sake of sentient beings, I enter nirvāṇa. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "In the West, there is a new [tradition]..."
The "Old Yi" and "Two Yi" are like fire spreading across a horizontal stream or sparks scattering upon water; these may be used as metaphors for other sutras.
The "New Yi" is like the characters in Chinese cursive script (*caoshu*), where the strokes below are connected by fine lines that are neither vertical nor horizontal.

Therefore, it is used as a metaphor for the perfect fusion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*): the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is simultaneously illumination and simultaneously sovereignty; thus, one is named as such.
The three threes have no separate substance; therefore, they are neither horizontal nor sequential. Thus, they are not vertical. One is precisely three, like a large dot;
three are precisely one, like fine strokes. It is merely a single letter *i* that possesses three dots. Speaking from the perspective of the three, it is called "one yet three";
though there are three dots, they are but a single *i*. They are not horizontal. Although there are three dots, they constitute only one *i*.

Speaking from the perspective of the One, it is called "the Three being identical to the One" because they are not vertical; thus, the One does not become vertical and the Three do not become horizontal.
This is no different in meaning from the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*), differing only in that it mentions "Two and Three" as slightly distinct.
Since "Three" is a general enumeration while "Two" is a specific statement, one may also say "the One being identical to the Two," wherein the Two are not horizontal.

Although they are two, they are one; yet this oneness is not a vertical alignment. Although they are not three, they are called three; thus they are called "not one. Although they are not one, they are called one; thus they are called "not different.

Therefore, regarding the relationship between cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the masters of the Mahayana and Hinayana employ six meanings arranged both vertically and horizontally.

Our own school provides three interpretations: first, concerning principle (*li*); second, concerning practice (*xing*); and third, concerning the application of characters (*zi*). In all these cases, there is no vertical or horizontal arrangement.
The six minor meanings pertain to the partial and limited; therefore, the three interpretations of our school pertain to the perfect and interfused.
Maheśvara is translated as "Great Sovereign," the lord of the Form Realm heavens, possessing three eyes and eight arms, constantly riding a white ox.
One face with three eyes and three eyes with one face cannot be spoken of in isolation; to speak of them in isolation would result in a confusion of vertical and horizontal dimensions. Thus it is.
In various texts, the three dots (*bindu*) are used as a metaphor for the three gates of liberation because the dot is a written character;
the three eyes are used as a metaphor for the three types of *prajñā* because the eye is capable of illuminating.
These are metaphors based on following the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Furthermore, within the *Zhi guan*, the metaphor of the mirror is also employed—namely, the mirror.
The substance (*tǐ*) is used as a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*; the clarity of the mirror is used as a metaphor for *prajñā*;

and the images reflected in the mirror are used as a metaphor for *vimukti*. The *Fuxingji* (Record of Auxiliary Practice) states: "In using worldly phenomena as metaphors for the Dharma, all are partial metaphors (*fen-yù*). Among them, the mirror is the most intimate metaphor for its intended meaning. Why?
Because the entire mirror is clarity, and the entire clarity consists of images; they are neither unified nor separate, neither vertical nor horizontal, yet distinct."
Regarding the letter "I" and the Heavenly Eye, reflect upon this analogy and the meaning of the three thousand realms and the three truths will become crystal clear.
He manifests his body throughout the hundred worlds, attaining enlightenment through the eight phases to extensively save all sentient beings.

Second, the manifestation of the external transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) in the present is clarified below. As previously explained regarding the eight phases of attaining enlightenment (*aṣṭākārābhisambodhi*), the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Some see the Buddha preaching the Dharma; some see him entering the womb; some see him being born;
some see him attaining parinirvāṇa; or they see him leaving home. Within each of these phases, the text repeatedly uses the term "some," indicating that each one fully possesses all eight phases.

Question: For what reason do you ask about the internal realization and external manifestation? Answer: Internal realization consists of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) in which self and other are non-dual;

one’s own practice exists solely within the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā*. External transformation for others involves the three thousand realms responding to things according to their capacity through liberation.
The nature within emptiness inherently possesses the three thousand; because this nature is inherently complete, there is subsequently external function. It is like... [as in the original].
When a mirror manifests clarity, it can reflect images; the clarity-nature of the mirror gives rise to the images of the ten realms, and thus one cultivates these ten realms.

Therefore, external function is entirely dependent upon internal realization. This is why the three virtues (triguṇa) are fully perfected for both self and others, as explained in the "Gate of the Non-duality of Self and Others.
Those who do not understand this harbor attachments and engage in contentious disputes.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening;
the body of wisdom is not realized through another, for the pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all things."
Second, citing evidence from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. First, the citation of the scripture.

The commentary states: "The first arousal of the mind" refers to the name of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). "Attaining perfect enlightenment" means becoming a Buddha through the eight phases (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*).
This is the partial realization of the fruit, which is the true cause within this teaching.
Second, the section on explanation has two parts. First, the initial explanation, which further divides into two. First, the direct explanation:
"To claim that the attainment of wondrous enlightenment is an error is most extreme.
Second, the refutation of errors below, which divides into three parts. First, the refutation using the true cause as the ultimate fruit. Others say this refers to the *Avataṃsaka*.

To claim that one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta is to treat the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment as such; therefore, this view is now refuted as erroneously taking the true cause to be the ultimate fruit.
If it were so, then all the subsequent stages from the second abode onward would be rendered superfluous.
Second, the section on pointing out errors and posing challenges, which is divided into two parts. First, pointing out the error and posing the formal challenge:
If, as you claim, the eight phases of the first stage constitute wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), then from the second stage onward, they would become redundant.

Regarding the statement that this is a redundant repetition, there are two parts. Second, regarding the citation of a defense against the repeated interrogation, there are also two parts. First, restating their defensive argument:
others defend [the position] by saying that from the point of "dwelling in the two" onwards, this is the Buddha’s redundant explanation.
The Buddha would incur the fault of redundancy.
Second, if the Buddha were to interrogate [the interlocutor] with excessive severity, then the Buddha would commit the transgression of being prolix.

In various texts, the masters of antiquity have stated that from initial sudden enlightenment up to the tenth abode (*bhūmi*) is precisely the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), yet they further speak of [an additional stage].
Regarding the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), these are restatements.

Furthermore, some say that within the samādhi of the equal dharma (*samatā-dharma-samādhi*), there are definitively no sequential positions. Others say that sudden awakening at the initial mind is itself the ultimate consummation;

thus, the further teaching of forty stages and so forth is a skillful means (*upāya*) for those of dull faculties. Still others say that sudden awakening is itself Buddhahood, and there is nothing beyond it.

Furthermore, the present school now critiques the sequence of stages [proposed by others], asserting that their partial exposition takes the direct pointing to the initial mind as the state of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi*).

Because they prioritize only the sudden gate and achieve Buddhahood with such rapidity, they incur the fault of redundancy in establishing the final stage of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) and the simultaneous attainment of Buddhahood.
The profound judgment of the *Yītā* (The Meaning of the Ten Stages) is therefore deemed unacceptable; students of the present school must not conflate these views.
Others offer groundless discourse, such as claiming this is a redundant repetition; yet,
although there are statements that each stage encompasses all stages, one must also understand the reason for such inclusion— namely,
that the initial resolve and the ultimate consummation are non-dual— and thus clearly recognize the principle of their non-duality.
Third, although there are citations from lower [texts] that encourage study, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "From the first bhūmi, one is fully endowed with the merits of all bhūmis.
Thus, it is said that each stage subsumes all other stages. Even though they are mutually inclusive, the sequence of cause and effect remains distinct;

how then could the first dwelling (prathama-vihāra) be identified as the state of wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi)? The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate [attainment] are two..."

These two minds are not distinct. The former mind is difficult to describe; "arousing the mind" refers to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), while "ultimate" refers to wondrous enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*).
Although the beginning and end differ, their merits are no different; therefore, it is said they are not distinct.

How should one understand the meaning of this non-duality of mutual inclusion? One should know that because the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) realized therein are identical, one attains them at every stage.
The principle of non-duality lies herein: it is the reason why mutual inclusion does not involve dualistic grasping.

That the Dragon Girl immediately attained perfect enlightenment, and that the Śrāvakas received the prediction of future Buddhahood—all these are manifestations of attaining Buddhahood within this very stage.

Regarding the two dragon girls who descend [to be reborn], this is cited as being in accord with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which describes how an eight-year-old dragon girl transforms into a male and becomes a Buddha in the southern region.
The text further cites the *Garbha-sūtra*, stating that daughters of Māra, Brahmā, and Śakra do not discard their current bodies nor receive new ones;
rather, they all attain the Buddha-dharma in their very present bodies. The nature of the Dharma is like a great ocean, in which one does not speak of right or wrong.
Ordinary beings and sages are equal, with no distinction of high or low; it depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements.
To attain realization is as easy as turning over one's hand. Jingxi asked: "Does this mean that one becomes a Buddha without abandoning the stage of *parīttābha* (segmented existence)?

If one does not become a Buddha in this very body, how can this be reconciled with the account of the Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood and the verses in the *Garbhavakrānti-sūtra*? He replied: "As for the passage concerning the Dragon Girl..."

Speaking from the perspective of provisional means to certify the Perfect Sūtra, attaining Buddhahood is swift; if one practices according to reality, it is not swift, whereas provisional practice merely leads [to the goal indirectly].
Thus, the meanings of the provisional and the real are equal, and this principle is not in vain. Therefore, the verse of the *Garbha-sūtra* speaks from the standpoint of "attaining through reality.

If one attains through reality, then from the purification of the six sense faculties up to the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one may manifest [various forms] according to what sentient beings prefer.
If one manifests the attainment of Buddhahood through spiritual transformations and realizes the Perfect Sūtra, one immediately realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Since one already knows that there is fundamentally no [distinction between] renunciation and sensation, what hindrance is there to abandoning this state and proceeding to that?

As for those Śrāvakas who have received the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) for the future but have not yet manifested the body of a Buddha, why is it that Śrāvakas must form karmic connections [before being predicted]? The prediction should be understood as distinct [from the immediate realization].

The wisdom-body is the development of the nature of the revealing cause of the virtue of *prajñā*; the marvelous Dharma-body is the development of the nature of the true cause of the virtue of the Dharma-body;
and that which responds to all things is the development of the nature of the conditional cause of the virtue of liberation.
Since these three bodies are attained as inherently existent, it is said that they are not realized through another.

Regarding the second point, "The Two Wisdoms," the *Vajra Needle* (Jingangbei) provides the following explanation of the Three Bodies (*trikāya*): Generally, when names such as "nature" (*prakṛti*) are used, they mostly pertain to the principle of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

This is because terms such as "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*) and "true nature" (*tathatā*) are so designated. The three factors—provisional cause (*upaniṣad*), contributing cause (*hetu*), and direct cause (*pratyaya*)—are termed "nature" (*prakṛti*).

When these three dharmas reach the initial stage of progression [toward Buddhahood], they are all fully developed and thus called the "Three Bodies. Names that do not refer to a specific nature generally apply to ordinary beings.
The principles of the phenomena of the noble causes and effects—such as the *dharmadhātu* and *tathatā* (suchness)—if they exist only in the fruit, are as follows:
the profound penetration of universal illumination, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, is the *saṃbhogakāya*;
the subtle and wondrous pure dharma is the *dharmakāya*; and the possession of the thirty-two and eighty marks is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Furthermore, "profoundly penetrating equality" refers to the signs of upholding the sutra and attaining understanding; the "subtle, wondrous, and pure Dharma" refers to the True Body (dharmakāya);
and "possessing the thirty-two marks" refers to the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya). Although cause and effect differ, the three bodies are not distinct.
Many students are confused regarding the cause, so this has been pointed out and shown. The rest is clarified as explained in the supplementary notes to the main body of the text.
The Middle Way manifests before one, opening the Buddha-eye and accomplishing the practice of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Having traveled five hundred *yojanas* to reach the precious destination, one first dwells in the Land of True Reward Free from Obstruction, the stage of non-retrogression through mindfulness.
The three [stages] conclude with the lower [level] of the Middle Path.
Subsequently, from the second dwelling up to the middle dwelling, one severes one grade of ignorance at each stage and increases one portion of the Middle Path,
becoming equal to the tenth bhūmi of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
Second, a general explanation of what is visible in the nine stages of abiding (*navasthāna*).

Next, upon entering the first practice (*prathama-caryā*), one severs one grade of ignorance and becomes equal to the "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-sambodhi*) of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra-śāsana*). Next, upon entering the second practice, one becomes equal to the "Sublime Enlightenment" (*miao-jue*) of the Separate Teaching.

Second, a general explanation of the stages of practice toward the grounds, which has two parts. First, explaining the two practices, which is divided into three sections. First, the formal explanation of the two practices being identical to those of the distinct [teachings]:

If one follows the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra), which opens the ten grounds into thirty stages, these are likewise merely the thirty stages of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching.
If one speaks in terms of correspondence, the Perfect Teaching does not open the ten abidings into three [separate categories].
The ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching correspond to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), and ten transferences (*pratisaṃyukta*) of the Perfect Teaching;
the "Sublime Enlightenment" (*miao-jue*) of the Separate Teaching corresponds to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching.

To speak more strictly, the thirty stages of the Separate Teaching are merely the ten *bhūmis*; thus, the ten *bhūmis* of the Separate Teaching are equivalent to the ten abodes of the Perfect Teaching.
The Separate Teaching (biejiao) equates the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (miaojue) with the initial stage of practice in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao).
Since the *Renyang jing* does not establish the stage of Equal Enlightenment (dengjue), it holds that immediately after the tenth ground is the Buddha-ground.

If this is so, then the "breaking of the eleventh grade" is designated as Wondrous Enlightenment; is this not what was previously stated in the passage concerning the Path of Cultivation (wenda)? How could it be otherwise?

One must consider that [the stage of] "certainly falling away" is the tenth; according to the fifty-two stages of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) breaks through twelve grades of delusion and is thus named "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue), which is therefore equal to the two stages of practice in the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao).
Beyond the three practices, those of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha) do not even know the names [of these afflictions], let alone subdue or sever them;
for the Separate Teaching merely destroys twelve grades of ignorance.

Second, from the third [section] downward, the subsequent stages are presented alongside their distinctions from the worldly calculations regarding the existence or non-existence of the realms of the aggregates (*skandha*).

If one understands this text, obstructions will naturally be dispelled. Why is this? To distinguish between the partial and the perfect: the ten realms, such as the aggregates, appear in the first two teachings;
however, the inconceivable realm belongs to the Perfect Teaching. What the person of the Perfect Teaching contemplates is the realm of the three teachings.

All these are the wondrous realm of the *Vairocana* Buddha-nature; from the perspective of the ultimate perfect teaching (*yuan*), the principle is simply delusion, while at the ultimate limit it is awakening.
As for the intermediate four *yi*, they are divided alternately between delusion and awakening; once delusion and awakening are distinguished, the realms of the five aggregates can be known.

How much more so for the ten realms, which are what is contemplated within the Perfect Teaching—since the object of contemplation is subsumed within the perfect principle, this includes both the first principle (*paramārtha*) and...
Setting aside the ultimate perspective to observe the progression through the stages of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one reaches the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

From the first stage upward, one naturally flows into the delineated realms of the aggregates (*skandha*), which are described as belonging to the three teachings. Others may raise the objection: "The Perfect [Teaching] is characterized by perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*);

how can there be such realms of the aggregates? Now, I shall answer this: it is precisely because of this perfect interfusion that distinctions of wisdom regarding intimacy and distance vanish, yet delusion gives rise to them.

The thickness and thinness of the three delusions are distinguished, opening up the meaning of the six stages of identity (*liujie*). Because they are light within the midst of delusion, they derive their names from principle;

thus, there are eight distinct meanings: teaching, principle, wisdom, severance, practice, stage, cause, and fruit. Regarding the objective realm of the aggregates (*skandha*) in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it is explained according to the path of teaching;
however, from the second or third stage onwards, these are themselves the delusions severed within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), and are therefore equal to the Perfect.

Because this single chapter "Awakening from Delusion" establishes the existence of self and other based on the aggregates (*skandha*) and objects of the environment, the person [who critiques] instead reverses it by claiming that the subtle principle of the teaching lacks such aggregates and environmental objects; this is utterly inconsistent with what was previously analyzed.
Therefore, I take the true cause of my own house as the ultimate fruit of your house.
Thirdly, I shall explain the preceding two lines through three sections, using parallel passages from other teachings for comparison. First, I contrast the real cause with the provisional fruit;
now, because this clarifies the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is called "my house," while by comparison with the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it is called [the other].

The true cause of your family is precisely the second practice of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), while its ultimate fruit is the Wondrous Enlightenment (*miaojue*) of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*).
This is because the more provisional the teaching, the higher the rank; the more real the teaching, the lower the rank.

Second, as for the reason why [the text] below provides this indication, the passage is divided into two parts. First, it is presented as a provisional teaching (*upāya*) because it is explained according to the path of the doctrinal teachings;
thus, while the teaching is extremely provisional, the breaking of the twelve stages is called "wondrous enlightenment" (*miao-jue*), and thus the stage is extremely high.

Second, it is explained according to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) teaching; thus, while the teaching is extremely real, it abides in the second practice, and thus the stage is extremely low. "Mi" (extremely) means "increasingly" or "profoundly."
For example, when a frontier region has not yet been pacified, one may borrow a high office; yet while the conferred rank is high, the actual position based on merit is low. Second, the analogy:
"the frontier region not yet pacified" represents possessing provisional means (*upāya*); "borrowing a high office" represents possessing provisional fruits;

"discussing merit based on a fixed rank" represents returning to the ultimate reality (*pariniṣpanna*); and "its actual position being low" represents abiding in the two [provisional] practices. "Merit" refers to one's achievement.
The term "rank" (*jue*) refers to measurement; it measures one's office and exhausts one's talent. It is also a matter of enfeoffment.
There are three grades of rank—duke, marquis, and baron—or five grades when the son and viscount are added.

Thus, in determining the distinctions of the Buddha’s ranks, when discussing the twelve grades of merit that he has destroyed, these refer only to the two practices of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Therefore, although the provisional teaching refers to "wondrous enlightenment," it is merely the second stage of practice within the true teaching.

Thirdly, the concluding passage at the end of the section on the provisional teaching clearly demonstrates that the causes and fruits of the provisional and the true are identical; the text is very explicit.
Next, from the third stage (*bhūmi*) onward through the tenth stage, one eliminates one grade of ignorance at each level;
thus, in the middle way, forty grades of delusion are severed.
Second, an explanation of the three stages through the tenth stage.

Furthermore, by breaking one more grade of ignorance, one enters the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); this is the state of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

As an Equally Enlightened One endowed with the three knowledges (*traividyā*), one proceeds to break one final grade of subtle ignorance, entering the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*) and attaining ultimate liberation, forever parting from the parents that are ignorance.
Ascending to the summit of the Mountain of Nirvāṇa, all phenomena are non-arising and Prajñā is non-arising; this "non-arising of non-arising" is called Great Nirvāṇa.

The section on the two levels of fruition is divided into two parts. Regarding the first level, the accomplishment of wisdom and the severance [of afflictions], the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Kill the father, ignorance, and sever..."
Craving is the mother and ignorance and karma are the moisture that nourish one within birth and death;

thus, like parents who can produce the physical body of the aggregates (*skandha*), they cause it to be forever exhausted without remainder at the stage of wondrous enlightenment, abiding in Great Nirvana. "The mountain peak of all dharmas" and "the mountain peak of parents" are both metaphorical expressions.
All dharmas are like a disease and Prajñā is like medicine; because there is a disease, there is medicine, and when the disease is gone, [the medicine is no longer needed].
Because the medicine has perished, all dharmas arise; if prajñā does not arise, or if prajñā arises, then all dharmas do not arise.
Since all dharmas do not arise, prajñā also does not arise; the mutual extinction of both is Great Nirvāṇa.
Taking empty space as one’s seat, one accomplishes the pure Dharma-body and dwells in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light; this is the mark of a Buddha according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Second, taking empty space as one’s seat, the bodies and lands perfectly encompass the names of the four lands, as previously demonstrated regarding the three bodies.
Regarding this title, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* state: "The Buddha’s three bodies arise from the Vaipulya [sūtras]. The *Miaoxuan* says:
"Some say that the space of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) serves as the seat; once it is established, all are established.
The three Buddhas—Vairocana, Śākyamuni, and Lokeśvararāja—are fully present and pervade all places. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) indicates: "It is also like a flower."
The present text clarifies that the Dharma-body dwells in the land of quiescence; thus, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* explains that Śākyamuni is named Vairocana.
The Buddha’s dwelling place is called the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānti-prabhāsa*). This quiescent light of empty space is all-pervasive.
How could the pure Dharma-body have a specific location? Thus, the seat, the body, and the land are a perfect unity, neither identical nor different.
That which undergoes transformation yet remains unchanging is called "constant" (*nitya*); thus, the Sūtra says it is "constant, self, bliss, and pure.
That which is serene and free from all burdens is called "quiescent" (*śānta*); thus, the Sūtra says it is "like quiescence and liberation. That which is brilliantly luminous is called "prajñā";

the Sūtra says, "This form is the eternally abiding dharma. Therefore, regarding the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*), how can it be both with marks (*sa-nimitta*) and without marks (*a-nimitta*)?

If one analyzes these according to phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), there are three lands: the land of phenomena possesses characteristics; the land of radiance is the principle, which is signless;

and the land of empty space is the principle, while the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) constitutes the phenomena. Furthermore, regarding the Middle and the Extremes (*madhyānta*), there is both separation and integration.

"Separation" refers to the three [aspects] each for cultivation and nature; "integration" refers to two [aspects] for cultivation and one for nature. Cultivation resides in the three lands, while nature resides in radiance.

The nature of the *prabhāsvara-locana* (Light-Quiescence) is neither existent nor non-existent; the cultivation of the two lands consists of both the phenomenal (*sanimitta*) and the non-phenomenal (*animitta*).

In the land of True Reward, there is the non-phenomenal, while in the land of Expedient Means and the Land of Common Residence, there is the phenomenal. This is explained in terms of the duality of cultivation and the unity of nature.
The nature of the *prabhāsvara-locana* is not devoid of the merit of cultivation, and the cultivation of the three lands is not devoid of the merit of nature.
One should reflect upon the characterized and the uncharacterized according to the above; nature is the Middle Way, while practice constitutes the two extremes.

If one distinguishes them, there are three aspects each for practice and nature, all of which reside together within the stage of expedient means. Since these are characterized, the characterized is not non-existent; the uncharacterized is not non-existent either.

The simultaneous negation of both refers to the True Reward [Land], where the uncharacterized is not non-existent and the characterized, as well as their simultaneous negation, are present. The simultaneous negation of both refers to the Peaceful Light [Land], where the simultaneous negation is not non-existent.
The signless and the sign-possessing are eternally the Dharmakāya; the Dharmakāya is the negation of both extremes, and its quiescence is liberation.
Liberation possessing signs is radiance, which is Prajñā; Prajñā is signless. These two modes of cultivation are identical to the nature, being neither existent nor non-existent.

This nature is identical to the two modes of cultivation, yet it is both existent and non-existent. Because phenomena are identical to principle, not even a single characteristic can be apprehended; this principle is—

Although the myriad phenomena are manifest within the events, the principles, the middle, and the extremes are neither separate nor united; furthermore, the Nameless Dharma-body (Jikō) is termed the "Substance" (Tai).
This Substance is the True Aspect (Shisō), which is devoid of discrimination. The three lands constitute the "Function" (Yū); as for this Function, the established dharmas differ in their gradations.
Since it is thus with the four lands, so it is with the three bodies (Sanshin). If one considers them according to the two bodies, the True Body (Shinshin) is non-existent.

Regarding the presence of marks in the corresponding body (*sambhogakāya*): if one considers it in relation to the three bodies, the *dharmakāya* is neither of the two [having marks nor being markless], while the *saṃbhogakāya* possesses the corresponding body with marks.
Whether they are separated or combined, one should reflect upon this according to the [four] lands (*kṣetra*). Therefore, the three bodies and four lands are maintained.

The *dharmakāya* of the Land of Peaceful Light (*śāntaprabhā*) is certainly markless; as for the *saṃbhogakāya* of True Reward, it encompasses both meanings: the reward for oneself and the reward for others.

Because existence and non-existence differ, they coexist as the provisional response-body (*upāya-sambhoga-kāya*) which possesses marks. If those marks were identical [to reality], then both would simultaneously possess marks and both would simultaneously lack marks.
If it proceeds solely from principle, it is neither mark nor non-mark. When phenomenon and principle are contrasted, non-mark is precisely mark, and mark is precisely non-mark;
when the sentiments are harmonized through wondrous realization, all contentious calculations are lost. This is what the people of recent times describe as the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*).
Regarding the three bodies (trikāya), there have been disputes over whether they possess marks or are markless, with various commentaries and sub-commentaries conflicting in their arguments.
Alas! The writings of the Patriarchs have not yet perished; why do scholars so recklessly conform to worldly sentiments?
How lamentable! What can be done about it? Since the past cannot be altered, one may still pursue the future; thus, I have written this out of indignation to clarify the matter.

However, regarding the stages and positions of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), if one does not employ the "six levels of identity" (*liujie*) to distinguish them, there will be much confusion with those of superior sages; therefore, it is necessary to use the six levels to determine the positions.

Second, below this, the text uses the six levels to analyze the passage, which is divided into four parts. First, it clarifies the reason for determining the positions, stating that there is much confusion.

Furthermore, this is explained from the perspective of ignorance regarding the six positions; yet, if it were explained from the perspective of ignorance regarding the principle itself, one should further state that it leads to much despondency.
Thus, the general meaning is that while the principle is identical, the phenomena are different.
In various sutras, it is said that "birth-and-death is itself nirvana," all of which uses these six positions to distinguish them so that the principle remains identical from beginning to end.

Furthermore, because the initial and final stages do not overlap and their respective matters differ, there are six [levels]: the principle-as-such (*li-ji*), the name-as-such (*ming-zi-ji*), the practice-as-such (*guan-xing-ji*), the semblance-as-such (*xiang-si-ji*), the partial realization-as-such (*fen-zheng-ji*), and the ultimate-as-such (*jui-jing-ji*). These six positions differ in terms of delusion and awakening;

yet, because the principle is identical, they are "as-such" (*ji*)—for the principle of the three truths is present throughout all six positions. Thus, one speaks of the principle-as-such, the name-as-such, and so on, up to the ultimate-as-such. Since...
It is said that birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa; it is further said that afflictions are themselves bodhi, and karmic fetters are themselves liberation.

This means that the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) serve as the subject (*viṣayin*), while the three virtues (*triguṇa*) serve as the object (*viṣaya*). These three virtues are also the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāḥ*), differing only in name.

Yet people fail to perceive this and instead claim that the "three thousand" [realms] are merely provisional (*prajñapti*) because they are distinct phenomena; thus, they speak of the six [thousand realms] within the emptiness of the three thousand.

If one argues that because the principle is the same, the "wondrous provisional" (miao-ja) is the subject of identity (*neng-ji*) and "emptiness-and-middle" (*kong-zhong*) is the object of identity (*suo-ji*), then since the subject of identity is already erroneous, the object of identity is likewise incomplete.
Furthermore, the claim that wisdom is the subject of identity is also incorrect. Regarding the six stages of identity as being like a dung beetle (*qie-qiang*):
this too would imply that the dung beetle exists within the three thousand realms, the provisional, and emptiness-and-middle. But how could there be a dung beetle therein?
If one understands the three bodies and four lands as they have been explained above, then this meaning will naturally be mastered.
However, because students have long been accustomed to delusion, I shall speak further. Why is this? The nature of the mind is unmoving; it is provisionally designated by the name "Middle.

When the three thousand [realms] vanish, it is provisionally designated by the term "Emptiness. Although they vanish, they persist; thus, it is provisionally named "Provisional. Yet, within this emptiness, there is the Middle.

Quiescent cessation is signless, yet this signlessness differs from that of the Lesser Vehicle; it is not a mere void, for it is fully endowed with the three thousandfold wondrous provisional phenomena within emptiness.

Here, the principle is the wondrous provisional, and the phenomenon is emptiness; yet, when these phenomena and principles are viewed in relation to the three obstructions, all obstructions are phenomena and all three truths are principle.
Within the three truths themselves, the truth of emptiness is termed "principle" and the conventional truth is termed "phenomenon."

In these three truths and six stages, there are all conventional truths (sāṃvṛti-satya). Since the three thousand [realms] pervade all six stages, how could the dung beetle (kīṭa-kīṭaka) ever be absent?

The six stages are themselves the dung beetle; what is there that is improper about this? However, when one speaks of the three thousand as being identical to emptiness (śūnyatā), identical to the Middle Way (madhyamā-pratipad), and as the quiescent extinction of emptiness and the Middle, how could the dung beetle exist?
Therefore, by realizing that the three thousand are identical to emptiness, the provisional (prajñapti), and the Middle, the dung beetle [is seen as such].

Existence and non-existence are vividly visible; if one grasps this meaning and principle, the application of defiled poisons will be subdued, and the deluded attachments to existence and non-existence will suddenly cease.
What room is there for doubt regarding the great purport of our school?
This means that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, the characteristics of this nature remain eternally present.
Furthermore, such statements as "a single form or a single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way" constitute the stage of *li-ji* (identity with principle).

Next, hearing and seeing these words from a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*) or from the scriptures constitutes the stage of *ming-zi-ji* (identity in name). Practicing according to the teachings constitutes the stage of *guan-xing-ji* (identity in contemplative practice), which corresponds to the five ranks (*wu-pin-wei*).

The development of a corresponding understanding is "corresponding identity" (the stage of the ten faiths); the partial breaking and partial seeing is "partial realization" (from the first bhūmi up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment);
and the perfection of wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions is "ultimate identity" (the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment).

The second [point] refers to the formal determination of the stages and positions: although all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, this is called a "cause" and not yet a "Buddha," nor is it called "fruition-nirvana.
In many places within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the term "Buddha-nature" is used because "Buddha" refers to one who has attained fruition;
thus, it is said that all sentient beings possess the nature of such a person who has attained fruition. As for why the cause is named "Buddha-nature," it is because sentient beings...

In truth, one has not yet attained Buddhahood; rather, by realizing the principle and verifying the Truth—that the afflictions and the cycle of birth and death are the very nature of the Buddha—one is shown to practice this, and it is thus called "Buddha-nature.
There are three aspects of Buddha-nature, namely the Three Thousand [Realms], which are emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

These are termed the "correct" (正因), the "enabling" (緣因), and the "actualizing" (了因). Therefore, know that the Three Thousand do not transcend the ten realms, the three types of worlds, and the provisional designations of the five aggregates.
That which is called "insentient" within the world of sentient beings and lands is not called "sentient" if one speaks of the insentient, nor is it called "insentient" if one speaks of having nature.

Now, wishing to demonstrate that the source of delusion transforms from nature, and further to reveal that nature so as to cause them to reform their delusions—pointing out the provisional as the real—it is said: "Sentient and insentient have nature."
Therefore, the ten realms and the three types of worlds are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—these are the three Buddha-natures. People have not reflected upon this;
instead, they often claim that insentient things possess Buddha-nature simply because they can be seen to move and change. This is truly laughable.
Thus, one should know that both sentient and insentient beings are, without exception, phenomena produced by causes and conditions, arising through dependent origination.

The dharmas of this [teaching] are entirely devoid of reality; they possess only names. Names are themselves emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and emptiness is itself the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the middle (*madhyama*).
Therefore, it is said that both sentient and insentient beings possess the nature of reality, which is emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—the three causes of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
This wondrous principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) remains eternally constant and unchanging, whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, for it is due to this very nature.

Because the principle does not change, that which was discussed by Master Xianshou (Zhanran) regarding the Buddha-nature and dharma-nature of sentient and insentient beings—as fully analyzed in the *Supplementary Notes* (*Buzhu*) to the *Great Section*—holds that not a single form or scent is not the Middle Way. While the six sense objects are mentioned, only form and scent are cited;
the Three Truths are simply termed the "Middle Way. Form and scent are the Middle Way of phenomena (*shi*), whereas the Middle Way itself is the principle (*li*).

Because one perceives the principle through phenomena, it is said that form and fragrance are none other than the Middle Way. That form and fragrance are the Middle Way is something everyone agrees upon;

however, the notion of "insentient Buddha-nature" merely startles the ears and agitates the mind. All such things are ultimately the "principle-as-such" (li-ji) within sentient beings who remain in the realm of birth and death;
because they know the names and recognize the characters, it is called the "name-and-word" [stage].
This consciousness that cognizes form and mind is the fundamental basis for the three thousand realms and the three truths; its names depend upon these three thousand realms and three truths.
Based on the understanding of these three thousand realms and three truths, one gives rise to the practice of the three thousand contemplations, which is called "contemplative practice" (*kango*).
It is like comparing brass to gold, or a gourd to a melon; it is like the fire being first warm or the sea being initially level. Because these two things are similar, it is so named.
To realize [the truth] partially and to a limited degree is called "partial realization" (*fenzheng*); if categorized by what is realized, it is called "partial true" (*fenzhen*).

To exhaustively and ultimately reach the end is called "ultimate" (*jiujing*). These six stages (*liu jiwei*) originate from this school; within the *Awakening of Faith*, there are already three stages, namely:
semblance awakening (*xiangsi jue*), partial awakening (*suifen jue*), and ultimate awakening (*jiujing jue*). The remaining three stages are found in the sutras.

The treatise necessarily states this; thus, the meaning of the "six identities" (*liù jí*) also applies to the Three Teachings. If one discusses the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuán wèi*), the six identities are sufficient—why must the forty-two stages be further enumerated?
This is because the stages of partial realization (*fēn zhēn*) are extensive; therefore, it is necessary to borrow the provisional (Distinct) teaching to differentiate their ranks.
Furthermore, while the six identities encompass both principle and phenomena (*shì lǐ*), the fifty-two stages pertain specifically to phenomena.
The fifty-two stages are numerous and limited, being restricted to the levels from the "Ten Faiths" onward;
the six stages of "realization" (liu-ji) are few and universal, encompassing everything from the "Five Ranks" downward.

They are called "six" because they refer to the sequence of practice from shallow to deep, and they are called "stages" (*wei*) because they refer to the positions within the essence of the revealed principle (*li-ti*).
Because they are non-dual, they are called "identical" (*ji*). Third,
regarding the explanation of the names based on practice (*xiu*), although the principle-identity (*li-ji*) has not yet entered into practice and is entirely the nature giving rise to practice—
just as the meaning of practice already possesses the ninefold aspects— it is said that "based on practice, they are named the six."

Therefore, those with deep understanding of these six characters will not give rise to arrogance; they will clearly comprehend that the very characters themselves do not arise, and thus, without self-defeat, they may take refuge and rely [upon them].
Reflect upon this and choose accordingly.
